fleet

fleet

fleet is one multicall binary for the fleet’s tools. A multicall binary is a single executable that behaves as many different programs depending on the name it is invoked under and the first argument it is given. The fleet binary is version 0.1.0. Invoked as fleet, it dispatches to one of nineteen domains — a domain is a named tool area, such as the work queue or the secrets resolver — and invoked under one of its alias names (repo-queue, queue-broker, secrets-broker, laptop-agent-broker, atlas-search, laptop-agent) it routes straight into the corresponding domain. There is one binary to build, one binary to install, and one binary to keep current on every machine the fleet runs on.

Source: https://github.com/developing-today/code/blob/main/pkgs/fleet/Cargo.toml

Why fleet exists

Before fleet, each fleet tool was its own script or program, installed its own way, and each one re-solved the same four problems. Fleet solves them once, inside one binary:

  1. A shared work queue. Agents on different machines need one place where work is filed, claimed by exactly one worker at a time under a lease (a time-limited claim that expires if the holder stops reporting in), and completed with evidence. The queue domain and its resident queue broker provide that queue, backed by a dedicated Turso database. See The queue: tasks, lanes and leases.
  2. Secrets without vault sprawl. Resolving a secret by shelling out to the Bitwarden Secrets Manager command-line tool (bws) on every call cost 10–40 seconds per invocation. Fleet instead runs a secrets broker: a resident cache of the vault that answers by name in milliseconds, refreshes itself on a timer, and falls back to bws only when it must. Callers name a secret; they never hold a vault credential of their own. See Secrets and the secrets broker.
  3. Remote build placement. A limited sandbox is the wrong place to compile. Fleet decides, from live capacity data, which GitHub Actions copy of the fleet repositories should run a build — a personal copy, an organisation copy, a forks copy, a Blacksmith runner, or a codespace — and dispatches the job there. See Placement and remote dispatch.
  4. Agent coordination. Agents need a mailbox, a way to prove what their seat can reach, and one rule for what work to take next. The bridge domain provides the mailbox, the agent domain provides enrolment, a four-leg health check called doctor, and the intake ladder that decides what an agent works on next. See The bridge: fleet messaging and Agents: enrolment, doctor and the intake ladder.

Who it serves

  • Agents on seats. A seat is one running agent instance in one place: a Muse session in a sandbox, an OpenCode session on the laptop, a chat assistant connected over HTTPS. An agent uses fleet to enrol, check its seat, take work, resolve secrets, message other agents, and run builds where builds belong.
  • Operators. A human (or a supervising agent) running the fleet uses fleet to inspect queue health, read the message log, check which token sources still have GitHub rate-limit headroom, and run the daemon roles in the foreground under a supervisor.
  • Developers. A developer changing fleet itself uses the same binary’s registry and capability output to see exactly what a given build contains, and uses the Nix build variants described in Installation and bootstrap.

The domain map

Every build of fleet knows every domain. Whether a given invocation can use a domain depends on the capabilities compiled into that build, on the name it was invoked under, and on the host’s configuration; a domain it cannot use answers with a stub message and exit code 69. The full mechanics are in The shape of the binary.

DomainPurpose
queueThe repo work queue: enqueue, claim, and complete tasks through the queue broker. Alias: repo-queue.
serveRun a fleet daemon role (queue-broker, secrets-broker, search, proxy) in the foreground. Aliases: queue-broker, secrets-broker.
proxyThe session proxy: serve the broker socket, connect or init through it, run recovery SSH, splice raw TCP streams, or transfer files (get/put). Alias: laptop-agent-broker.
dispatchThin client over pm-stack dispatch: status, launch, and enqueue verbs.
dispatch-testExplicit-dispatch CI test: scan fleet repos for free Actions capacity, submit a job, track its stored status.
secretsResolve secrets by name: the secrets broker first, Bitwarden as fallback.
ghThe real gh CLI, passed through under a rotating fleet token (the fleet’s GitHub Apps, then personal last); rate-limit and permission failures fail over to the next token.
bridgeFleet messaging through the message bridge: central sends messages or commands to an agent, a group, or all; agents read their mailbox, answer, and ack.
orgsTurso-backed GitHub org, App and installation registry.
agentThe agent’s front door: enrol an agent of any kind, check what this seat reaches, and take the next piece of work down the intake ladder.
shellRun a command, or open a shell, where builds belong: the laptop, a codespace, or here.
searchAtlas corpus search over the session history (hybrid full-text plus vector search). Alias: atlas-search.
certPKI/X.509: root and issuer CAs, leaf certificates, chains and bundles. Alias: pki.
laptop-agentClient for the laptop-agent daemon: run and manage jobs on the laptop. Alias: laptop-agent.
commanderTier T1 (commander/fleet) of the laptop route forms: run commands on the laptop through the Desktop Commander MCP endpoint.
httpTier T2 (http/fleet) of the laptop route forms: the laptop-agent daemon HTTP API as a fleet subcommand (HTTP legs only; never ssh).
sshTier T3 (ssh/fleet) of the laptop route forms: real SSH to the laptop under a binary-owned client contract.
laptopTier T0 (tiered/fleet) of the laptop route forms: the generic tiered command — walks T1 → T2 → T3 and reports the serving tier.
actionsLive short-lived exec sessions inside GitHub Actions runners: start a session in a runner, run commands in it, stream its IO, renew or extend its lease, close it.

Alongside the domains there are five built-in commands that are not domains: init (autostart this host’s roles per the host manifest), session bind (validate and persist a session identity), version, capabilities, and help.

How to read this book

  • New seat, first hour: Installation and bootstrap, then Quickstart. You will have a working binary and will have run the five commands that prove the seat works.
  • Agent or operator who wants to understand the system: The shape of the binary, then Architecture, then the concept chapter for the domain you are working in.
  • Someone debugging a specific behaviour: go straight to that domain’s concept chapter. Every concept chapter is self-contained: it defines its terms, states its defaults and exit codes, and does not require reading the others first.
  • Someone changing fleet: the concept chapters state the behaviour your change must preserve; the development part of this book covers how changes are built, tested, and shipped.

Conventions used in this book

  • Commands are shown as they are typed, for example fleet agent doctor. Inside the queue domain, the binary’s own usage strings spell the program repo-queue (the argv0 alias), so queue examples may show either fleet queue claim or repo-queue claim; they are the same code path.
  • Flags and defaults. When a flag has a default, the default is stated as a number or a literal value, for example “lease default 2700 s (45 minutes)”. Where the help text and the source disagree, this book states the source behaviour and says so.
  • Exit codes. Fleet uses a small shared vocabulary: 0 success, 2 usage error, 3 transport down / unresolved / a needed leg down, 69 capability unavailable (the stub). Individual domains add codes — 1, 4, 5, 6 appear in the queue, bridge, agent, and dispatch chapters — and each chapter lists its own codes in full.
  • Secrets are named, never valued. This book gives secret names (for example fleet.secrets-broker-token) and token file paths. It never prints a secret value, and neither does the binary: values go to the one place each command defines (standard output for fleet secrets get, a single header for an authenticated request) and nowhere else.
  • Source references are provenance only. Each chapter names the source files it was written from, as absolute URLs under https://github.com/developing-today/code/blob/main/pkgs/fleet/. The chapter text itself is complete without following them.

Installation and bootstrap

There are two ways to get fleet onto a machine:

  1. The static release — a single statically linked musl binary published as a GitHub release asset. This is what a fresh sandbox seat installs, through scripts/muse/bootstrap.sh. It needs no Nix and no shared libraries, which is the point: a glibc-dynamic build names Nix store paths that a non-Nix host does not have.
  2. A Nix build — one of the variant packages from the repo flake, for machines that are part of the Nix fleet (the laptop, NixOS hosts).

The static musl release

The release is produced by scripts/muse/publish-fleet.sh:

  • It builds the fleet-static package (the full capability profile on the musl pkgsStatic Rust platform) in a throwaway detached git worktree at the requested revision (default origin/main).
  • It refuses to publish an artifact that is not statically linked, and it probes the artifact’s capabilities output: a build whose bridge domain is not available is fatal, because a Muse seat’s bootstrap requires the bridge-capable full profile.
  • The release tag is fleet-static-<short>, where <short> is the first 7 characters of the commit SHA. The asset name is fleet-x86_64-linux-musl, published alongside fleet-x86_64-linux-musl.sha256 containing the asset’s SHA-256 sum.
  • The script prints exactly two lines for the operator to pin in the bootstrap script: tag=fleet-static-<short> and sha256=<sum>. Re-publishing an existing tag only re-uploads when the sum differs.

Source: https://github.com/developing-today/code/blob/main/scripts/muse/publish-fleet.sh

Bootstrap: scripts/muse/bootstrap.sh

A Muse sandbox seat is rebuilt from scratch whenever the sandbox is recycled: no fleet binary, no laptop link. bootstrap.sh rebuilds the seat. Every phase is idempotent and skips work already done. Exit codes: 0 success, 1 a phase failed (the message names it), 2 usage. Phases are selectable with --only <list> / --skip <list>; --all additionally restores ~/git and ~/agents.

The pin. Read the matched asset URL and SHA-256 from the same checkout of scripts/muse/bootstrap.sh that you intend to run:

grep -E '^FLEET_(URL|SHA256)=' scripts/muse/bootstrap.sh

Bootstrap uses those defaults and verifies the downloaded binary. When overriding the release, supply both FLEET_URL and FLEET_SHA256 for the same published asset. After installation, check fleet version and fleet capabilities on the seat.

FLEET_AGENT (default muse) and FLEET_AGENT_GROUPS select the seat identity; groups are never hardcoded for another agent kind.

The phases, in the order PHASES="tools token restore tailnet fleet persist init check":

  1. tools — downloads the pinned fleet binary, verifying its SHA-256, into $HOME/.local/share/muse-bootstrap/fleet/fleet. It is kept under the name fleet in its own off-PATH directory because fleet picks its verb set from argv0 (the name it is invoked under). The download is skipped when the existing copy is present and passes the bridge-capability probe. The phase also installs bws, restic, and tailscale into the seat’s bin directory; a tailscale failure only skips the tailnet phase.
  2. token — obtains the Bitwarden Secrets Manager access token for the seat.
  3. restore — restores the seat’s files with restic, and provisions the three shared broker token files from Bitwarden Secrets Manager, each with owner-only (0600) permissions: fleet.secrets-broker-token → ~/tools/secrets-broker-token, fleet.queue-broker-token → ~/tools/queue-broker-token, and fleet.laptop-agent-token → ~/tools/laptop-agent-token. Bitwarden is the source of truth for these three names. A missing name is not fatal: the enrolment continues and the check phase names the gap. See Secrets and the secrets broker for why these files matter.
  4. tailnet — joins the tailnet and points fleet’s laptop link at it. In kernel mode the seat dials the laptop directly; in userspace mode traffic goes through tailscaled’s CONNECT proxy, which fleet expects on port 3130, and the phase writes fleet-proxy.env with HTTPS_PROXY=http://127.0.0.1:3130. The phase also writes the [host] config into ~/.config/fleet/fleet.toml.
  5. fleet — installs the binary at ~/tools/fleet. If the existing file is not writable it is moved aside to ~/tools/fleet.old (with sudo when available). The install is atomic — install -m 755 to ~/tools/fleet.tmp, then mv -f over ~/tools/fleet — and happens only when the bytes differ. The phase then creates two symlinks: ~/tools/bin/fleet → ~/tools/fleet and ~/tools/bin/repo-queue → ~/tools/fleet. The repo-queue link is the argv0 alias doing the work; there is no second binary.
  6. persist — writes ~/tools/muse-bootstrap.sh plus a boot hook that, after a sandbox recycle, re-runs --only tailnet,fleet under flock -n $HOME/tools/.muse-boot.lock with a 300 s timeout. Only /home/hatch survives a recycle, so persistence lives there.
  7. init — brings up the seat’s init stack (brokers, the gh shim, the laptop channel) from the restored tools. This is the same work fleet init does; see Proxy, sessions and recovery.
  8. check — verifies the seat: fleet version and fleet capabilities run and the bridge capability is present; the laptop link is reachable the way fleet dials it; fleet secrets get tailscale.auth-key (a secret name) resolves; fleet secrets list answers (the session broker answering is the expected path; the bws fallback is noted as acceptable); and a bridge hello/inbox probe succeeds as the seat’s agent.

Source: https://github.com/developing-today/code/blob/main/scripts/muse/bootstrap.sh

Nix build variants

From the repo root, the flake exposes the fleet packages:

nix build .#fleet .#fleet-serve .#fleet-connect .#fleet-connect-static

pkgs/fleet/default.nix returns six attributes:

AttributeCargo featuresPlatformInstalled alias linkSize gate
fleetdefault (= full)glibc—no
fleet-serveserveglibcfleet-serveno
fleet-connectnone (--no-default-features)glibcfleet-connectyes
fleet-brokersfleet-queue with client,queue-broker,secrets-broker, --binsglibc—no
fleet-staticdefault (= full)musl (pkgsStatic)—no
fleet-connect-staticnonemusl (pkgsStatic)fleet-connectyes

Facts that matter when choosing one:

  • The installed binary is always named fleet. A hyphenated name (fleet-serve, fleet-connect) is installed as a symlink to the same binary; the name narrows the capability surface at invocation time. See The shape of the binary.
  • The size gate is the connect variant’s budget: the stripped binary must be at most 2 MiB (2,097,152 bytes) or the build fails.
  • fleet-brokers builds the three standalone broker artifacts repo-queue, queue-broker, and secrets-broker from the fleet-queue crate. They are the migration’s rollback inventory and retire only at the close of the multicall epic.
  • The static builds carry no ONNX Runtime library path: the search-serve role in a static binary needs ATLAS_ORT_LIB supplied at runtime. The glibc non-connect builds bake the path in.

Source: https://github.com/developing-today/code/blob/main/pkgs/fleet/default.nix

Verifying an install

Two built-in commands verify any install. Both take no arguments — a trailing argument, including --help, is a usage error (exit 2).

fleet version
fleet capabilities

fleet version prints five lines: the version (fleet 0.1.0), the build name (fleet, fleet-serve, or fleet-connect, derived by matching the compiled capability set against the variant sets — with an annotation when the invocation name narrowed the surface), the derived version (of the form 0.1.0-dev+g<rev>), the source revision (the full commit SHA the build was cut from), and the enabled capabilities — the usable set for this invocation, in registry order, or none.

fleet capabilities prints the same facts as JSON, plus the full domain registry with, for each domain, its summary, aliases, required capabilities, and a state of available, not-in-build, narrowed-by-name, or disabled-by-config. It prints two distinct lists: capabilities (what this invocation can use) and compiled_capabilities (what the binary was built with). Their difference is exactly the narrowing applied by the invocation name and the host config. On a full build both lists are the same 15 capabilities and every domain is available. The Quickstart chapter, Quickstart, walks through what to do with this output.

Quickstart

The five-minute path. It assumes fleet is installed (see Installation and bootstrap) and runs five commands, in an order that checks each layer before the next one depends on it: the binary, the seat, a secret, the queue, and finally taking work. Every command here is read-only except the last, which claims a task only when work is available.

1. fleet version and fleet capabilities — the binary

fleet version
fleet capabilities

fleet version prints five lines: version, build name, derived version, source revision, and enabled capabilities. What you are checking: the build name is fleet (the full build) and the enabled-capabilities line is not none. The short form fleet --version prints only the first two lines.

fleet capabilities prints the registry as JSON. What you are checking: the capabilities and compiled_capabilities lists match (both are the full 15 on an unnarrowed full build), and every entry in domains has "available": true. If a domain shows "state": "narrowed-by-name", you invoked the binary under a variant name such as fleet-connect; invoke it as fleet. If it shows "disabled-by-config", the host’s fleet.toml disables that domain under [domains]. If it shows "not-in-build", the binary is a narrowed build. Invoking an unavailable domain prints a stub and exits 69; see The shape of the binary.

2. fleet agent doctor — the seat

fleet agent doctor

Doctor probes the seat’s four legs — a leg is one route the seat needs — in parallel, each by running a real fleet verb as this seat, and prints one JSON object:

LegProbeWhat “up” needs
bridgebridge inbox --agent <name> --limit 1 (with a known agent name)HTTPS to the message bridge, and the fleet token resolved by name through fleet secrets
queuequeue healthThe queue broker: its socket on the laptop, or the laptop transport from elsewhere
githubgh api rate_limit through fleet gh (falling back to a plain signed-in gh)A working gh token, by fleet rotation or by sign-in
shelllaptop-agent healthA route to the laptop: its broker, the Cloudflare tunnel, the tailnet, or SSH

The bridge probe is deliberately a read made as an agent: service health alone proves nothing about whether this seat holds the fleet token, so with no agent name known the bridge leg is reported not ok even when the service answers.

From the legs, doctor derives the rungs map — which rungs of the intake ladder (see step 5) this seat still has: push follows the bridge leg, queue follows the queue leg, shortlist is always true (it is a local file), and priority follows the github leg. It also reports builds: whether fleet shell reaches the laptop from here.

Exit codes: 0 when any intake rung is live (bridge, queue, or github), 3 when none is, 2 for a usage error. A seat with only HTTPS still has rungs 1 and 4 of the ladder; doctor tells you exactly which world you are in. The full treatment is in Agents: enrolment, doctor and the intake ladder.

3. fleet secrets get <name> — a secret, by name

fleet secrets get tailscale.auth-key

(Any secret name your seat is entitled to works; tailscale.auth-key is the name the bootstrap check phase uses.)

This resolves the secret by name: the secrets broker first, Bitwarden (bws) as fallback. The value goes to stdout and nowhere else — not to a log, not to an error message. Resolution order and cache semantics are in Secrets and the secrets broker; the short version is that a broker cache hit answers immediately and carries the value’s age, and a miss on a loaded cache reads through to Bitwarden so a freshly minted secret is visible at once.

Exit codes: 0 ok, 2 usage (for example, no name, or more than one name), 3 unresolved / broker unavailable and the fallback also failed. The companion verb fleet secrets list prints the names in the broker’s cache, one per line, never values; unlike get, list has no bws fallback — a broker failure is exit 3, because a vault listing is not the same thing as a cache listing.

4. fleet queue health — the queue

fleet queue health

This asks the queue broker for its health table. The first output line is project: <netloc> (resolved via <source>); the table that follows carries per-queue counts by task status, or (no queues have tasks) when empty. Exit 0 means the broker answered. Exit 3 means the transport path to the broker failed. Exit 6 is special: it is the fallback switch — the primary queue store failed and this work has been switched to the GitHub fallback queue; the output is one JSON object saying so, with a hint naming the fleet queue fallback … verbs to continue with. See The queue: tasks, lanes and leases.

Note that queue health (this verb, an authenticated broker call) is a different thing from the broker’s unauthenticated GET /healthz probe.

5. fleet agent next — take work

fleet agent next

next walks the intake ladder — four rungs, in order — and returns the first piece of work it finds, as one JSON object {agent, rung, task, then, tried}:

  1. Push — a command addressed to this agent on the bridge. Work a person or central already chose outranks everything.
  2. Queue — a claim on the fleet queue, taken with a 4-hour lease (14,400 s — the queue’s own default lease is 45 minutes, which lapses mid-task). The then lines in the answer name the lease deadline and the queue checkpoint / queue complete commands for the claimed task.
  3. Shortlist — the top of this host’s local shortlist, re-checked against GitHub before hand-out. If the list is at or below its low-water mark (default 3 entries) with nobody refilling it, next returns a refill task instead of handing out a stale remnant.
  4. Priority — the highest-priority open issue straight from GitHub, reserved into the shortlist file as it is handed out so two seats on one host do not take the same issue.

tried is the per-rung log: each rung is recorded as skipped, empty, down, or rejected, with a reason. A rung that is down is skipped, not fatal — that is what doctor’s rung map predicted. Exit codes: 0 when work was handed out, 5 when no rung had work, 3 when a needed leg is down in a way that leaves nothing to try, 2 for a usage error.

That is the whole loop. An agent’s working cycle is: next, do the task, run the then lines (checkpoint as you go, complete at the end), and call next again while the run has budget.

The shape of the binary

Fleet is a multicall binary: one executable whose behaviour is selected first by the name it is invoked under (argv0, the zeroth argument — the name the operating system was asked to run), and then by its first real argument. This chapter describes that shape: the personalities, the domain registry, the capability system, the build variants, and what happens when an invocation asks for something it cannot do.

argv0 personalities and aliases

There are three classes of invocation name:

  1. fleet — the full root dispatch: domains, plus the built-in commands.
  2. Variant names — fleet-serve and fleet-connect. These select an invocation profile: a capability ceiling. A profile can only narrow the surface, never widen it. Invoking a serve build as fleet does not give it client capabilities it was not compiled with; invoking a full build as fleet-connect restricts it to the connect profile for that invocation.
  3. Alias names — each routes straight into one domain, some with an implied argument prepended:
argv0Routes toImplied argument
repo-queuedomain queue—
queue-brokerdomain servequeue-broker
secrets-brokerdomain servesecrets-broker
laptop-agent-brokerdomain proxyserve
atlas-searchdomain search—
laptop-agentdomain laptop-agent—

An argv0 that is none of {fleet, a variant name, an alias} is a usage error: the binary prints the expected names and exits 2. Aliases are how the install works in practice — ~/tools/bin/repo-queue is a symlink to the fleet binary, not a second program (see Installation and bootstrap).

Dispatch order, exactly: argv0 alias → domain route; argv0 variant name → root dispatch with that profile as the ceiling; argv0 fleet → root dispatch; then, for a domain, the capability checks below decide between the domain handler and the stub; an unknown name is a usage error, exit 2. The dispatch is hand-rolled — deliberately not a command-line parsing library — so that it behaves identically in every variant, including the tiny connect build where the registry and the stub machinery are the product.

The domain registry

The registry is compiled into every build, including fleet-connect: every build knows every domain’s name, summary, aliases, and required capabilities, whether or not it can run it. That is why fleet --help prints “the full registry — every build knows every domain” on every variant, and why domain help never stubs — help is registry data and renders identically everywhere, with unavailable domains marked inline.

The nineteen domains, in registry (help) order, are queue, serve, proxy, dispatch, dispatch-test, secrets, gh, bridge, orgs, agent, shell, search, cert, laptop-agent, commander, http, ssh, laptop, actions. Their purposes are tabulated in the introduction.

Each domain declares a primary capability — the capability its headline availability keys on. One consequence worth knowing: on the serve build the search domain is marked absent, because its primary capability is the search client, even though the search-serve capability exists in that build under the serve domain.

Capabilities: the 22

A capability is an atom of function that a build can include or omit. There are 22, in registry order:

proxy-connect, proxy-serve, proxy-raw-splice, queue, queue-broker,
secrets-broker, search, search-serve, dispatch, dispatch-test,
laptop-agent, secrets, gh, bridge, agent, commander, laptop-http,
laptop-ssh, laptop, cert, actions, orgs

Notes:

  • proxy-connect is unconditional: it is compiled into every variant, and is not even a Cargo feature. proxy-raw-splice joins it in the runtime’s always-present set.
  • There is no shell capability atom: the shell domain rides on the agent capability.
  • A domain can require several capabilities. serve requires four (queue-broker, secrets-broker, search-serve, proxy-serve) — one per role — and the capability checked for a serve invocation is the one for the role named. proxy requires three (proxy-serve, proxy-connect, proxy-raw-splice), checked per verb.

Three sets decide whether a domain runs for a given invocation: the compiled set (from the build’s Cargo features), the profile set (from a variant invocation name, if any), and the host config’s [domains] table, which can disable a domain on one host. The effective set is the compiled set intersected with the profile; the usable set further removes every capability of every config-disabled domain. fleet version reports the usable set; fleet capabilities reports both the usable set (capabilities) and the compiled set (compiled_capabilities).

Build variants

The variant is a property of the artifact. The same names double as the invocation profiles above.

VariantInstalled nameCompiled capabilities
Fullfleetall 22
Servefleet-serveproxy-connect, proxy-serve, proxy-raw-splice, queue-broker, secrets-broker, search-serve, secrets (7) — daemon roles plus proxy, no working-seat clients
Connectfleet-connectproxy-connect, proxy-raw-splice (2)

The profiles nest: connect ⊂ serve ⊂ full. The binary reports its variant by matching its compiled capability set against the variant sets; an unrecognised compiled set is reported as a custom build.

Alongside the three variants, the Nix package set builds fleet-brokers — the three standalone artifacts repo-queue, queue-broker, and secrets-broker — and the two musl statics, fleet-static (full profile) and fleet-connect-static (connect profile, size-gated at 2 MiB). See Installation and bootstrap.

The stub and exit 69

A domain this invocation cannot use answers with a stub: a block on stderr, always exit code 69 (EX_UNAVAILABLE). There are four wordings, one per reason:

  1. Not in build — “this build does not include ‘<domain>’”, followed by the enabled capabilities and the build name, plus “The full build is ‘fleet’” when the build is not the full one.
  2. Narrowed by name — invoked as fleet-serve or fleet-connect, the name scoped the surface away: the stub says the invocation is name-scoped to that profile, and that invoked as fleet it carries the full surface.
  3. Disabled by config — the [domains] table in this host’s fleet config set the domain to false; the stub names the config file to re-enable it in. This is the per-host shaping / incident lever: one host’s fleet can have a domain switched off without a rebuild.
  4. Available but not implemented — “included in this build but not implemented yet”, with the stub’s third line naming the build and the not-implemented state.

Every stub’s second line is Enabled capabilities: <comma list> (none when empty), so a stub always tells you what the invocation can do.

Built-in commands overview

Five root built-ins are handled before domain dispatch. They take no arguments: a trailing argument is a usage error naming it, exit 2 — and that includes --help, so fleet version --help is an error, not help.

Built-inBehaviour
initAutostart this host’s roles per the [host] manifest; a no-op when they are already running. Byte-identical to fleet proxy init — one implementation, two spellings. With an unknown location it reports state, starts nothing, and exits 69: it never guess-starts a role.
session bindValidate and persist an explicit or inherited session identity (an OpenCode session id, ses_ followed by ASCII letters/digits). The identity is stored in a .fleet-session-id marker at the git worktree root, and is used only when the session is verified live.
versionFive lines: version, build, derived version, source rev, enabled capabilities. fleet --version / -V print only the first two lines.
capabilitiesThe registry and this build’s capabilities as JSON (see the Quickstart for how to read it).
help [domain]fleet help ≡ fleet --help: the full registry, exit 0. fleet help <domain> prints one domain’s help and rejects any second argument. An unknown name is a usage error, exit 2.

Bare fleet with no arguments is a missing-subcommand error: the message and the full help go to stderr, exit 2.

Two more root-level facts: every domain invocation first runs session initialisation (the session bind machinery with no explicit id), and every invocation — whatever its outcome — appends a payload-free record (invoked as, arguments, exit code, elapsed milliseconds) to an invocation ledger; failing to write the ledger never alters the result.

Source: https://github.com/developing-today/code/blob/main/pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet/src/main.rs and https://github.com/developing-today/code/blob/main/pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-registry/src/lib.rs

Architecture

Fleet is a self-contained Cargo workspace at pkgs/fleet/ in developing-today/code: its own Cargo.toml, Cargo.lock, and rust-toolchain.toml (channel 1.99.1), with no workspace relationship to the repo root. The workspace package is version 0.1.0, edition 2024, Rust 1.85 minimum, licensed MIT OR Apache-2.0. The release profile is a size contract, not a speed profile (opt-level = "z", LTO on, one codegen unit, stripped): the connect variant’s budget is a target of at most 1.5 MiB and a hard limit of 2 MiB, stripped.

Source: https://github.com/developing-today/code/blob/main/pkgs/fleet/Cargo.toml

The crates map: 16 crates

CrateOwns
fleet (the bin)The multicall entrypoint (src/main.rs), root built-ins, dispatch and the stub machinery, plus the domains that live in the bin crate itself: secrets verbs (over fleet-secrets), and gh with its cache, closure, guard, and metadata modules.
fleet-registryThe domain registry: the 22 capability atoms, the three variants and their capability sets, the 19 domain entries (name, summary, capabilities, primary capability, aliases, subcommand inventory), and the argv0 alias map. Dependency-free; compiled into every variant so help is always complete.
fleet-configThe one place config resolves: fleet.toml (default ${XDG_CONFIG_HOME:-~/.config}/fleet/fleet.toml, overridable with FLEET_CONFIG), the [domains] switches, [proxy], [secrets], [queue-broker], [secrets-broker], [dispatch], [host] sections, and the fleet’s path/port/socket constants. Resolution order is environment → config file → compiled-in defaults. A missing file is not an error; a malformed file — including unknown sections or keys — is a loud error on every path, never a silent fallback.
fleet-secretsThe secret resolver library: the broker-first, Bitwarden-fallback chain, by name only. Every domain that needs a secret resolves it through this crate; no domain shells out to bws or reads a token file on its own.
fleet-proxy-protoThe session-broker wire protocol: 8-byte big-endian length-prefixed JSON frames, the hello/capability handshake, and the protocol version window (current and previous major, plus legacy proto 0).
fleet-proxyThe session proxy: the broker (serve), the client (connect, init, ssh, get/put), raw splice, tunnels, and shims. The client half is in every variant; only the broker half is feature-gated.
fleet-queueThe queue domain end to end: the client (32 verbs), the queue broker, the secrets broker, the Turso queue store, packet validation, the GitHub fallback queue, placement, the creation outbox, and merge-intent stacks. Its features split the surfaces: client, queue-broker, secrets-broker.
fleet-dispatchThe dispatch domain: a single-file thin client over the pm-dispatch HTTP service.
fleet-dispatch-testThe dispatch-test domain: scan/submit/status over GitHub and its Turso jobs store.
fleet-laptop-agentThe laptop-agent client: verbs, transport legs, and the connection ladder for the laptop-agent daemon.
fleet-searchThe search domain: the Atlas client surface, and — behind its serve feature — the Atlas search service itself, consuming the atlas-core/atlas-embed/atlas-proto crates from pkgs/atlas-search by relative path.
fleet-bridgeThe bridge domain: the mailbox client for the message bridge (send/agents/log for central; hello/inbox/post/ack/health for agents).
fleet-agentThe agent and shell domains: kinds, enrolment, doctor, the intake ladder (next), the shortlist, and the shell target planner. It links only fleet-config: it runs the other domains’ verbs through this same binary rather than linking them.

| fleet-kv | Identity-scoped local SQLite storage: the local store other fleet surfaces build on. | | fleet-cert | The cert domain: PKI/X.509 roots, issuers, leaves, chains and bundles over a library-first Rust API, plus the OCSP verb group. | | fleet-orgs | The orgs domain: the Turso-backed org/App registry, synced from each GitHub App’s own JWT. |

Domain ownership, one line each: queue → fleet-queue; serve → bin-crate glue over fleet-queue / fleet-search / fleet-proxy; proxy → fleet-proxy (+ fleet-proxy-proto); dispatch → fleet-dispatch; dispatch-test → fleet-dispatch-test; secrets → the bin crate over fleet-secrets; gh → the bin crate; bridge → fleet-bridge; agent and shell → fleet-agent; search → fleet-search; orgs → fleet-orgs; cert → fleet-cert; laptop-agent → fleet-laptop-agent.

The brokers and their ports and sockets

A broker in fleet is a resident process that other processes ask for a service, as distinct from a library they link. There are three fleet brokers, plus the laptop-agent daemon and two auxiliary services:

ServicePortUnix socket (default)Notes
laptop-agent daemon4799—The Python daemon on the laptop that runs jobs. Not a fleet binary, but the proxy’s routing table names it.
secrets-broker4800~/.config/secrets-broker/broker.sockThe Bitwarden cache. Dual-binds TCP and the Unix socket with identical routes and auth. On the sandbox its TCP bind is forced to 127.0.0.1:4800.
queue-broker4801~/.config/queue-broker/broker.sockThe work queue service. Dual-binds TCP (100.99.113.103:4801, the laptop tailnet address) and the Unix socket.
gh cache daemon4802—Loopback token/secret cache for the gh passthrough. See The gh passthrough.
pm-dispatch4879—The TypeScript/Bun dispatch service the dispatch domain is a client of.
session broker (proxy)— (socket only)~/.cache/laptop-agent/broker.sockThe sandbox-side broker every local client talks to; it tunnels framed requests to the laptop’s services. Socket overridable with FLEET_BROKER_SOCKET.
RustDesk direct access21118—Also the loopback listen port of fleet proxy splice.
tailnet egress proxy3130—The host session’s CONNECT proxy. Not a fleet listener; fleet is its client.

The session broker’s routing table maps port → service name — 4799 laptop-agent, 4800 secrets-broker, 4801 queue-broker, 21118 rustdesk — and that map is what its hello frame advertises to clients.

Daemon-side token files live in each broker’s own config directory (~/.config/queue-broker/token, ~/.config/secrets-broker/token). They are different files from the client-side token files under ~/tools/; see Secrets and the secrets broker.

The brokers are run by fleet serve: one role in the foreground, or a list of roles in one process, one thread each, fail-fast — the first role thread to return or panic takes the whole process down and the external supervisor (systemd) restarts the unit. A role that exits cleanly is converted to exit 1, because a daemon role returning at all is abnormal. See Proxy, sessions and recovery for the proxy’s own serve behaviour.

The Turso store

The queue’s only backend is a dedicated Turso (libSQL) database named fleet-queue. The queue broker is the only process that talks to it; clients never touch the database. Because libSQL is single-writer, a claim is one conditional UPDATE whose WHERE clause re-checks claimability against the picked row — the equivalent of FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED; a competing claim that loses matches no row and is answered as “no claim”. The schema (tasks, leases, lanes, workers, checkpoints, the lane ledger, events, the creation outbox, merge intents) is detailed in The queue: tasks, lanes and leases.

dispatch-test keeps a second, separate Turso database for its job rows; see Dispatch and dispatch-test.

The session proxy

Sandbox seats cannot dial the laptop’s services directly. The session proxy is the bridge: a broker process on the sandbox side, owning the session broker Unix socket, which tunnels framed requests (8-byte big-endian length-prefixed JSON) to the laptop. Token files are read per request and never stored or logged; the broker persists nothing — its routing table comes from config and its tunnels live in memory. The full mechanics — warm tunnel pools, the Cloudflare leg versus the tailnet fallback, recovery — are in Proxy, sessions and recovery.

Data flows

The claim path (an agent takes queue work)

  1. The agent runs fleet agent next; the queue rung runs fleet queue claim through this same binary, with a 4-hour lease.
  2. The queue client chooses a route to the queue broker: a configured direct URL (TCP or the broker’s Unix socket) on the laptop, or — the sandbox default — a framed exchange through the session broker socket to port 4801, naming the client token file ~/tools/queue-broker-token. The session broker reads that file on the laptop side and forwards the token as the X-Agent-Token header.
  3. The broker authenticates from headers alone (a wrong or missing token is 401, an oversized body 413, before any body byte is read), then runs the claim against the Turso store: expire lapsed leases, pick the highest-priority due row, stamp worker/lane/session/model, set the lease, write the claimed event — in one conditional update.
  4. The client checks the claimed task’s issue against the GitHub fallback queue; if the fallback currently holds that issue under a different worker, the client blocks the task back with reason class fallback_held and reports no claim (exit 5). If the GitHub check itself fails, the claim is served with a warning — the guard fails open.
  5. The client prints the task row as JSON, plus a mode_line describing the route the claim took. No matching row is {"task": null}, exit 5.

The secret path (a caller resolves a name)

  1. A caller — a domain inside fleet, or fleet secrets get <name> — asks fleet-secrets to resolve a name. Nothing else in the system resolves secrets.
  2. The chain tries the broker leg first: directly over the secrets broker’s Unix socket where that socket answers (the laptop), else by a framed exchange through the session broker to port 4800, naming the token file ~/tools/secrets-broker-token. The session broker reads the file per request; the value never transits fleet’s own memory on this leg.
  3. A broker answer of 404 is definitive about the name and is not retried. A broker that cannot answer is retried with a bounded backoff budget sized to real restart windows, then the chain moves on.
  4. The fallback leg runs bws secret list + bws secret get, with the machine-account credential from the BWS_ACCESS_TOKEN environment variable or the on-disk token file.
  5. The value is returned in a type whose debug output is redacted. For fleet secrets get, it goes to stdout and nowhere else. Broker-side cache semantics — ages, read-through, refresh — are in Secrets and the secrets broker.

The dispatch path (a build runs remotely)

  1. A caller runs fleet queue dispatch --repo <owner/name> --command '<cmd>' --dispatch (or fleet shell --target actions, which drives the same verb).
  2. Placement loads the surface registry — data, not code: --registry or FLEET_PLACE_REGISTRY, else a home copy, else the source-tree path, else the copy embedded in the binary — and measures live load: for each owner, the in-progress plus queued run counts on that owner’s fleet runner-host repos, read from the GitHub API.
  3. The tier cascade picks a surface: a hard --surface pin first, then follow-up affinity, then free GitHub-hosted Actions (least-loaded owner, least-recently-used rotation), then Blacksmith within its minute budget, then codespaces as the last resort. Every step appends a reasoning line.
  4. The adapter mints the token the surface dispatches as (a GitHub App installation token, or the signed-in user’s token), snapshots the host repo’s existing workflow runs, and POSTs the fleet-command.yml workflow dispatch. Anything but HTTP 204 is fatal.
  5. It polls the run list (up to 12 polls, 3 s apart) for the new run — matched by a fresh dispatch id in the run title when the surface declares one — and writes a session record under a handle fp_ plus 32 hex characters in ~/.local/state/fleet-place/sessions.json.
  6. The caller follows the run with fleet queue session status|result <handle>; the portable form OWNER/REPO#RUN_ID resolves the same run without the local store. Full detail: Placement and remote dispatch.

The queue: tasks, lanes and leases

The queue is the fleet’s shared work queue: one queue of tasks (units of repo work), served by the queue broker over a dedicated Turso store, with a GitHub-issue-comment fallback queue behind it. The client surface is fleet queue (argv0 alias repo-queue) with 32 verbs. Inside the binary, every per-verb usage string spells the program repo-queue; the two spellings are the same code path.

Source: https://github.com/developing-today/code/blob/main/pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-queue/src/client.rs

The task model

A task is created from a packet: a JSON document validated against repo-task-v1.schema.json plus the fleet queue validator. The envelope fields live outside the payload: title, body, dedupe_key, priority, not_before, max_attempts. The payload (schema const "repo-task/v1") carries:

FieldShapeNotes
kindenumThe validator accepts six: pr_shepherd, triage, small_fix, ci_investigation, plus second_pass and feature_slice. (The schema file lists only the first four; the validator is the wider, operative list — source behaviour wins.)
repoenumThe validator’s allowlist has nine repos, including the legacy dezren39/nix name kept valid for in-flight dedupe keys. (The schema lists eight.)
implementation_repoowner/name, optionalThe repo receiving the implementation when it differs from the issue repo. Required when risk.flags contains cross-repo-change.
problemstring, non-empty
evidencestring array, at least 1
acceptancestring array, at least 1
scope{include, exclude}, both required, exclude non-empty
testsstring array, at least 1
risk{level: low|medium|high, flags: string[]}
priority_reasonstring, non-empty
timebox_minutesinteger 1..=240Design values are 20 (triage) and 45 (standard); other values warn.
max_attemptsinteger 1..=1000Design default 1000 for every kind.
context_refsstring array
dedupe{checked_at, basis}, both non-emptyThe producer’s dedupe attestation.
required_budget_minutesinteger ≥ 1, optionalThe minimum uninterrupted budget a claimer must declare; absent means no requirement.
identityone of issue, prs, set, sourceAt least one is required: an issue {number ≥ 1, url?, title?, state_checked_at?}, a non-empty PR list, a PR-set, or a pre-filing triage source {pr, finding}.

Envelope rules: priority must be on the design scale [10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 70, 90] (lower is sooner); payload size has a hard ceiling of 16,384 bytes (a warning above 4,096); not_before must be a non-empty RFC 3339 timestamp no more than 366 days in the future. Durations and limits throughout the queue are rejected, never clamped, identically at client and broker.

Two stored-priority exceptions: at enqueue, a payload whose labels array contains expedite stores priority 15, else next-up stores 25. These stored values are deliberately not on the packet scale.

Dedupe. Enqueue dedupes on (queue, dedupe_key) among live rows, and separately on work identity (repo, issue, kind family): a live task already holding the work identity means nothing is filed, unless the packet sets payload.dedupe_override. A key held only by terminal rows accepts a new row. A cancelled row is revived in place by a re-enqueue; a failed row deliberately is not — re-enqueueing a failed identity files a new row.

Enqueue has no default queue. The queue resolves from --queue, else the packet’s own queue field, else the REPO_QUEUE_DEFAULT_QUEUE environment variable; with none of the three, enqueue exits 2. (The old shadow default silently misrouted work.) Enqueueing into a queue whose name ends in -shadow additionally requires --shadow-intent. Most other verbs default --queue to repo-health-code-shadow via the same environment variable, but claim and list are unscoped when neither flag nor env is present: the broker works across the one fleet queue.

States and transitions

Live states: queued, claimed, parked, blocked, needs_review. Terminal states: done, failed, cancelled.

  • enqueue → queued (attempts = 0).
  • claim: queued → claimed; a due parked row is also claimable and resumes without consuming an attempt.
  • release: claimed → queued, immediately claimable.
  • park / wake: claimed → parked → (condition met, due, or woken) queued.
  • block / unblock: claimed → blocked → queued.
  • complete: claimed → done. fail: claimed → failed. cancel: queued or parked → cancelled, for a task that will never be worked.
  • revive: a terminal row, or a queued row dead at the attempt cap, is resurrected in place with attempts = 0.
  • Lease expiry: claimed → queued with a lease_expired event, or — when the row is out of attempts — it sits dead at cap with a lease_expired_at_cap event until revive.

Every transition writes an event row; fleet queue timeline <task-id> (aliased history) renders the 14 event kinds the timeline reads.

Lanes and workers

A worker is the claiming identity stamped on a row (default repo-worker-code; cancel defaults its worker to fleet-monitor). A lane is a finer identity used when many scheduled lanes share one worker id: the lane tells the broker whose claim a holder verb acts on. Holder verbs (heartbeat, checkpoint, park, release, block, fail, complete) resolve --lane from the flag, else the REPO_QUEUE_LANE environment variable, else null — in which case the broker checks the worker alone. A lane is validated broker-side against the lane registry at claim time: an unknown lane, a worker mismatch, a disabled lane, or a queue mismatch each refuse and claim nothing. The canonical lane universe is 6 families (code, any, not-code, opencode, openchamber, nix) × a..=z = 156 lanes, all enabled, seeded into the store’s lanes table.

The claim pick is atomic: highest priority first (priority ASC, created_at ASC) among due queued rows and due parked rows. A claim with no task, no filter, no queue scope, no count, no handoff/bind, and no identity marks is refused before any broker contact, exit 2 — a bare claim has repeatedly stolen the queue’s top task during CLI probing. Batch claims take 1..=5 rows (--count). Claim flags also carry marks, not filters: the claimer’s platform, pool, session id, and model stamp (--model-provider/--model-id/--model-variant, derived from the session’s own record when not given) are recorded on the row. A --remaining-budget-minutes declaration gates requirement-bearing tasks: the broker only matches tasks whose required_budget_minutes fits, and omitting it leaves such tasks unclaimed. No claimable task is {"task": null}, exit 5, with counts (queued, at_cap_queued, queued_not_yet_due, parked_due) explaining why.

Leases and heartbeat

A lease is the claim’s expiry. Claim’s default lease is 2700 s (45 minutes), range 1..=86400, rejected outside it; a zero or negative lease is born expired. fleet agent next claims with a 14,400 s (4-hour) lease instead, because 45 minutes lapses mid-task.

heartbeat keeps the later of the current deadline and the time of the heartbeat plus extend_seconds. The default renewal window is 900 s (15 minutes), range 1..=86400. A heartbeat five minutes into a four-hour claim preserves the original four-hour deadline. A default heartbeat five minutes before expiry moves the deadline ten minutes later. It may also merge a progress value (--progress / --progress-file, mutually exclusive). checkpoint records progress plus a required --stage (the help line brackets it optional; the source requires it — missing --stage exits 2) without touching the lease. Lease expiry is opportunistic — every claim first sweeps expired leases — plus a broker sweep, because a scheduler firing irregularly must not strand work.

Holder verbs are holder-checked: the row must be claimed by this worker (and lane, when supplied) and non-terminal, else exit 5 with “no matching claimed row”. release requires --reason (the help line brackets it optional; the source exits 2 without a non-empty reason). cancel likewise requires --reason. fail requires --error, and its --reason-class is a closed enum — transient (the default), deterministic, blocked — whereas block’s --reason-class is free-form.

Park, wake, and ready-conditions

park moves a claimed task out of the way until a ready-condition says the wait is over. --reason is required; --delay-seconds (range 1..=604800, 7 days; 0 is rejected — a zero-second park is a requeue, and release exists) and --not-before are mutually exclusive; with neither, the broker’s historical default delay is 1200 s.

The ready-condition is a JSON object. Kinds a database sweeper can verify from store state: task_terminal {task_id}, task_status {task_id, status}, event_seen {task_id?, event_kind}, time {until}. External kinds (ci, pr_merged, issue_closed, person_answer, review, …) are recorded faithfully but cannot be verified by the sweeper. With no explicit condition the broker derives one from progress.ready_condition, else {"kind":"time","until":<not_before>}. The condition kind determines the wait kind (time→timer; ci/ci_green/pr_merged/issue_closed/ upstream_pr→ci; review/codex_review/pr_review/person_answer→ review; capacity/quota_reset→capacity; triage→triage; anything else→external), and the broker enforces wait floors whatever delay was asked: a triage wait is held at least 6 h (21,600 s), a ci or capacity wait at least 1 h (3,600 s). The park revalidation sweeper later records check_outcome as confirmed (condition unmet), released (condition met → back to queued), or stale (cannot verify). wake releases a parked wait now that its condition is satisfied.

A park (or block) that waits on a person — a person_answer condition, a person-wait reason class, or blocker text naming the owner as the release — is refused client-side, exit 2, unless it is a valid hands item: --hands physical|interactive-login|payment|signature plus --action with one sentence a person can do in five minutes (a single line, at most 200 characters, not itself asking for a decision). The rule’s point: a choice that is the worker’s to make is never parked onto a person.

Block and dependencies (dep_blocked)

block sets status blocked. --reason-class and --blocker are both required. A classic block waits for a manual unblock. A typed dependency block names machine-watchable dependencies instead of prose: --blocked-by-pr, --blocked-by-issue, --blocked-by-ci take comma-separated owner/repo#N refs (for CI, N is an Actions run id), and --blocked-by-task takes bare task ids. Bad refs die client-side, exit 2.

The parsed deps are stored on the task row in the blocked_deps column (JSON); a task with a non-empty blocked_deps is in the dep_blocked state. Alongside sit dep_recheck_seconds (clamped broker-side to 300..=3600, default 900), dep_next_recheck_at, and dep_blocked_until from --dep-max-ttl-seconds (default 3 days (259,200 s), floor 60 s, ceiling 7 days). The broker’s sweep rechecks deps every minute and releases the task itself when they clear or the TTL expires; dep-recheck is the manual trigger. unblock is the manual override: without --drop-dep it clears the blocked state entirely; with --drop-dep <list> (comma-separated kind:ref — issue:owner/repo#N, pr:owner/repo#N, ci:owner/repo#RUN, task:ID) it drops only the named entries — the task stays blocked on the remaining deps, and dropping the last one releases it. The broker audits who overrode and what was discarded. A separate sweep, quarantine-recheck, re-validates blocked dep-free rows whose recorded error is a claim-path quarantine and requeues the ones whose error no longer reproduces.

The evidence gate and verify-disposition verdicts

Shape validation alone once let a fix-class task complete done on any non-empty evidence string while its issue was still open and a draft PR still carried the work. Now a completion that requires a disposition must carry result.disposition: a verified readback record produced by fleet queue verify-disposition <issue> --repo <owner/name>.

verify-disposition reads the issue and its linked PRs back from GitHub, live — never from a remembered claim. A PR counts as linked when named by queue provenance or --pr, or when its body carries an explicit marker (Refs #n, Fixes #n, Related program: #n); a bare prose #n is not a link. --repo is required (exit 2 without it). The record is {checked_at, source, issue: {number, state, state_reason, closed_at, closed_by}, pulls: [{number, state, is_draft, merged_at}], verdict, follow_up}.

The gate is pure (no network). It checks freshness (at most 1800 s old by default; more than 300 s in the future is unreadable clock skew), that the record describes the task’s issue, that the verdict matches the readback, that every PR the completion result links appears in the readback, and any follow-up. Every rejection leaves the task claimed and names the defect. verify-disposition itself exits 0 when its record would pass the gate, 1 when the gate would reject it or the readback cannot be read.

The five verdicts:

VerdictDerived whenGate requires
merged_verifiedsome pull in the readback is mergedat least 1 merged pull in the readback
closed_verifiedissue closed and no unfinished pullsthe issue state actually closed
open_draft_with_followupunfinished pulls exist, nothing merged, issue not cleanly closeda recorded follow_up
open_draft_supersededoperator-asserted, same familya recorded follow_up
invalid_no_worknone of the aboverejected if any linked pull still carries work

A pull is unfinished when it is not merged and not closed. A follow-up is exactly one of --follow-up-task <id> (checked by the broker at completion — only the queue knows if it is live), --follow-up-issue <n|url> (same-repo, open, must link the completed issue and every unfinished PR), or --follow-up-pr <n> (must be in the readback and merged); any follow-up target requires --reason. One exception: a closed issue may leave related work open when the close was a deliberate act by a person (the readback’s closed_by is checked against automation) and a verified follow-up owns the remainder.

complete’s other rules: --result/--result-file must be a JSON object (the file wins when both are given); --telemetry accepts only the keys pool, model, effort, cost_usd; --queue is parsed but never used — a dead flag, stated here because the source says so.

The fallback queue and the permanent fallback switch

The fallback queue is a queue with no database: all state lives in GitHub issue comments. Work items are open issues carrying the labels queue/queued (waiting), queue/claimed (held), or queue/blocked (blocked) — the same labels the broker-backed system maintains. The sweep covers five repos in pilot order: developing-today/code, developing-today-forks/opencode, developing-today-forks/openchamber, dezren39/darwin-nix, dezren39/fleet (shortcuts code, opencode, openchamber, nix, fleet).

A claim is the first line of a comment, exactly <!-- fleet-claim v1 kind=claim worker=<id> ts=<rfc3339-utc> --> (kinds: claim, heartbeat, release, unblock), with a human-readable line under it. Because every fleet worker posts to GitHub as the same account, the marker’s worker id is the only identity the lease can be keyed on, so --worker is required, never defaulted (or the FLEET_FALLBACK_WORKER environment variable). The lease window is 30 minutes by default (--lease-min per verb, or FLEET_QUEUE_FALLBACK_LEASE_MIN). Folding an issue’s markers in comment order gives its claim state: free, released, live, stale (older than the lease — any worker may claim, superseding), or contested (a claim posted during another’s live claim; hands-off for everyone while the contest is younger than the lease). Claimable = free, released, or stale. Fallback complete runs the same offline disposition gate as the broker path before posting anything; a rejection posts nothing and exits 1.

The fallback switch is permanently armed. For the work verbs — claim, heartbeat, checkpoint, complete, health — any primary-store failure (broker unreachable, or an {ok:false} envelope) switches the caller to the GitHub fallback for that work instead of dying: a message on stderr, one JSON object on stdout with "fallback": true, "switch_to": "github-fallback" and a hint naming the fallback verbs, and exit code 6, so a worker loop can branch on it without parsing prose. The escape hatch REPO_QUEUE_NO_FALLBACK_SWITCH=1 restores plain die-on-error. The primary claim path also guards the other direction: it refuses to double-serve an issue the fallback currently holds (see the claim path in Architecture).

Queue client exit codes, in full: 0 success; 1 gate failure / task not found; 2 usage; 3 transport or broker-path failure; 4 a broker {ok:false} envelope carrying no exit of its own (and broker-side store failures); 5 no matching claimed row / no claimable task; 6 the fallback switch.

The creation outbox

Creating GitHub objects (issues, PRs, comments) must survive crashes and rate limits, so creation goes through the creation outbox: producers enqueue, a single serial drainer creates through gh, verifies by read-back, and resolves. There is no dual-write and no automatic fallback to direct creation — a broker failure stops the drain visibly.

Entry kinds: issue, pull_request, issue_comment, pr_comment. States: pending, leased, uncertain, done, blocked. Constants: claim lease 120 s, minimum gap between creates 2 s, hourly create budget 300, retry backoff base 30 s capped at 3600 s, a circuit breaker that opens after 3 consecutive rate limits for 300 s, default max attempts 8. Entries carry a fleet-outbox:<id> marker in the created object’s body so the drainer can reconcile by search and read-back. The verbs are outbox enqueue|list|metrics|claim|resolve|drain; drain defaults to at most 20 items (--max, floored at 1), and an uncertain entry is reconciled by marker first — a lookup that could not check keeps the entry uncertain and never re-creates.

Merge-intent stacks

A stack is a recorded, ordered set of merge intents — finished branches with their authoring lane, worker, and session — stored in the broker’s merge_intents table, unique on (stack_id, position) and (repo, branch). Intent states: intended → replaying → landed, plus conflicted and abandoned; the legality of every move is decided by a pure transition table, never in SQL, and a conflicted intent returns only through its recorded authoring lane.

The verbs are stack record|list|transition|restack|replay. record requires --stack, --repo, --branch, and --lane. A transition to conflicted requires --conflict-detail naming what the authoring lane must resolve. replay is the executor: it walks the stack’s recorded merge order bottom-up — rebase onto new main, push (force-with-lease pinned to the verified pre-rebase tip), open PR, merge, mark landed, post the outcome note — one intent at a time. Replay never resolves a conflict itself. Its exit codes: 0 landed or idle, 4 a conflict was recorded conflicted and routed to its authoring lane, 3 any other step failure (the intent is left replaying and a later replay resumes it).

The Turso store

The broker creates its schema at backend start. The tasks table carries: id, queue, title, body, payload (default '{}'), dedupe_key, priority, status (default 'queued'), not_before, worker_id, claimed_at, lease_until, lane_id, platform, attempts (default 0), max_attempts (default 1000), the claim stamps (claim_provider, claim_model, claim_variant, claim_session_id), progress and result (default '{}'), last_error, the park columns (park_kind, wait_kind, ready_condition, required_budget_minutes, last_checked_at, check_outcome), the dep-block columns (blocked_deps, dep_next_recheck_at, dep_blocked_until, dep_recheck_seconds), timestamps, and completed_at. Its (queue, dedupe_key) index is deliberately not unique — enqueue dedupe is a read-then-insert check. Alongside: leases (one row per task), lanes (seeded with the 156 canonical lanes when empty), workers, checkpoints, repo_task_lane_ledger, events, creation_outbox (+ its circuit singleton), and merge_intents.

Broker protocol facts: every verb is one POST /<command> with a JSON args object; the response envelope is {ok:true, ...} or {ok:false, exit, error}. The only unauthenticated route is GET /healthz. The broker binds first and brings the Turso backend up on a startup thread, so /healthz and /validate answer immediately while other verbs answer exit 3 with a turso_pending reason until the backend is ready. A transient store error carrying PostgREST code 57014 or PGRST002 is retried client-side with exponential backoff and jitter: base 500 ms, doubling, cap 20 s, at most 6 attempts.

Placement and remote dispatch

Placement is the decision of where a build job runs. The live engine is Rust, inside the queue crate, exposed as fleet queue dispatch, fleet queue session …, and fleet queue surfaces. (A Go directory at pkgs/fleet/placement/ is an unwired proof of concept for a different placement-record design; it is not this engine, and its own README says so.)

Source: https://github.com/developing-today/code/blob/main/pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-queue/src/placement.rs

Surfaces as data: the registry

No surface is hardcoded. A surface is one entry in the registry file fleet-surfaces.json (version 2), and adding a location is adding an entry. Resolution order: --registry <path> or the FLEET_PLACE_REGISTRY environment variable (strict — a bad path is fatal, never a silent fallback); else $HOME/git/code/pkgs/fleet/fleet-surfaces.json when it exists; else the cwd-relative pkgs/fleet/fleet-surfaces.json; else the copy embedded in the binary. fleet queue surfaces prints the resolved registry verbatim as pretty JSON.

The top level is {comment, version, laptop: {busy, busy_source, note}, owners: {…}, surfaces: […]}. Each surface entry carries:

FieldMeaning
idSurface identity; the --surface pin, session records, and tie-breaks key on it.
kindAdapter selector: github-actions, blacksmith, codespace, or laptop. Any other value has no adapter and is invisible to the cascade (and cannot be pinned).
statusbase_eligible requires exactly active for Actions/Blacksmith surfaces. Shipped values: active, standby, pending-scope, handoff-only.
ownerThe account whose cap, load, and budget the surface draws on. Load is aggregated per owner, not per surface.
repoThe runner-host repo the workflow is dispatched in (not the target repo); null for codespace and laptop.
workflowThe workflow file dispatched; fleet-command.yml for all Actions/Blacksmith surfaces.
targetsTarget-repo patterns: exact owner/repo, owner/*, or *.
dispatch_asuser = the signed-in user’s token; absent/app = a GitHub App installation token. Any other value fails eligibility.
dispatch_id_inputThe workflow declares a dispatch_id input (used for exact run correlation).
platform_inputThe workflow declares a platform input; gates macOS eligibility and sending the input.
previous_run_id_inputThe workflow accepts the follow-up output-download inputs.
container_inputThe workflow accepts container_image; --container is only sent when this is true.
sticky_queue_thresholdFollow-up stickiness threshold; code default 2, minimum 1. All shipped surfaces: 2.
selection_priorityTier-1 sort key; code default 50. Shipped: 10 everywhere except org-run at 20. Lower sorts first.
public_targets_onlyOnly fleet-forks (true): eligibility does a live repo read and requires "private": false.
budgetBlacksmith: {free_minutes_monthly, paid_cap_minutes, rate_note}. Codespace: {core_hours_monthly, note}.
max_liveOnly codespace-overflow: 3. Printed in the capacity summary; never enforced (source behaviour).

The seven shipped surfaces: fleet-personal (github-actions, dezren39/fleet, App dispatch, active), fleet-org (github-actions, developing-today/fleet, user dispatch, active; also the Blacksmith host), fleet-forks (github-actions, developing-today-forks/fleet, user dispatch, active, public targets only), org-run (standby — because eligibility requires active, it can never be selected or pinned; retained for manual use), fleet-org-blacksmith (blacksmith, Linux-only fallback on the fleet-org host), codespace-overflow (codespace, pending-scope), and laptop (handoff-only — a placement record only; its adapter never runs shell commands on the laptop). Actions/Blacksmith surfaces target dezren39/*, developing-today/*, and developing-today-forks/*, except org-run, which targets only developing-today/*.

Target matching: a repo must be a valid owner/name (one slash, both parts non-empty, characters [A-Za-z0-9._-]); * matches any valid repo, owner/* matches that owner exactly with a single-segment name, anything else is exact equality. A --repo failing validation is a fatal usage error, exit 2 — and every error in the dispatch/session family prints repo-queue: <msg> and exits 2.

Owners and caps

From the registry’s owners table:

Ownerconcurrent_jobs_capconcurrent_macos_capplanprivate_minutes_monthly
dezren39405pro3000
developing-today205free-org2000
developing-today-forks205free-org (assumed - confirm)2000

So the working summary is caps of 40/20/20, and a macOS cap of 5 for every owner. An owner missing from the table, or a missing cap field, yields cap 0 — zero free slots, unusable in Tier 1. plan and private_minutes_monthly are registry documentation only; the placement code never reads them, and GitHub private-repo minute billing is not modelled in the cascade.

For a macOS job the effective cap is min(concurrent_jobs_cap, concurrent_macos_cap) — 5 for every owner — and the adapter counts all of the owner’s active host runs (Linux included) against that minimum, so dispatch never oversubscribes the small macOS pool. There is no macOS-specific load measurement anywhere.

The tier cascade

decide evaluates, in order:

  1. Hard pin. --surface ID looks the id up in the adapter map (unknown id is fatal) and runs that adapter’s eligibility; ineligible is fatal — no fall-through. A pin is a placement choice, not a paid-usage authorisation: a pinned Blacksmith surface is still subject to its budget check.
  2. Follow-up affinity — a soft preference (below); falls through on failure.
  3. Tier 1 — free GitHub-hosted Actions. Every github-actions surface that is eligible with free_slots > 0, sorted ascending by (load, owner_last_dispatch, selection_priority, surface_last_dispatch, surface_id): least-loaded owner first; among equals, the least-recently-used owner (an owner never used sorts before all used owners); then registry priority; then per-surface last dispatch; then the surface id alphabetically. The rotation is owner-first. Surfaces whose owner load is not fully observed carry no numeric estimate; if no eligible surface has measured headroom, one unknown-capacity surface may still be picked — deterministically, by the same rotation order minus load — under the unknown-capacity rule, which the pick’s reasoning line names. A surface whose known subtotal already reaches its cap is proven saturated and is never picked this way.
  4. Tier 2 — Blacksmith. blacksmith surfaces in registry order; the first eligible one with remaining_total_minutes > 0 wins.
  5. Tier 3 — Codespaces. codespace surfaces in registry order; the first eligible wins. Eligibility itself enforces the last-resort condition.
  6. Exhaustion. The decision is queued: with --dispatch, a session record with state: "queued" and no surface or run is still written and its handle printed — the job stays queued, recorded, never dropped; the repo queue remains its system of record.

Runner pinning interacts before sorting: --runner blacksmith makes every github-actions adapter ineligible, --runner github makes the Blacksmith adapter ineligible, and --runner auto (the default) leaves both open.

Load measurement

There is no account-wide Actions endpoint, so load is a proxy counted only over each owner’s fleet runner-host repos (the distinct repo values of that owner’s github-actions/blacksmith surfaces). For each host repo, with that surface’s token, placement reads only total_count from GET /repos/{host}/actions/runs?status=in_progress&per_page=1 and the same with status=queued — the run lists themselves are never enumerated. Tier-1 load per owner is running + queued, summed across its host repos. Failures are soft but never silent: no token, a non-200, a transport error, or a 200 whose body lacks a valid total_count makes that repo/status read missing rather than zero, adds a load_read_errors entry (surfaced in the dispatch output when non-empty), and is recorded in the owner’s load coverage. Coverage is one of measured (every required read returned a count), partial (some did), unknown (none did), or simulated (an --assume-owner-load override supplied the figure). The decision output carries owner_load_coverage per owner — status, known running/queued subtotal, configured cap, read time, source, and the missing reads — and session records store the same fragment. The known subtotal is exact for measured/simulated coverage and a lower bound for partial coverage; only measured or simulated coverage (or proven saturation) yields a numeric free-slot estimate — any other owner reports unknown capacity instead of a dressed-up zero. Owner and surface last-dispatch times come from the local session store, not the API. Two testing overrides exist (--assume-owner-load owner=N,… and --assume-blacksmith-used MINUTES); they are simulation, are labelled as such in the output, and do not appear in the printed usage string.

LRU rotation

The Tier-1 sort’s second and fourth keys are the rotation: owner_last_dispatch and surface_last_dispatch are the epoch of the most recent stored session for that owner/surface, or 0 if never. Because load dominates, rotation only decides among equally loaded owners — which is the common case at zero load, where it spreads work across owners instead of always picking the first.

Follow-up affinity

--followup HANDLE|OWNER/REPO#RUN_ID chains a dispatch after a previous run: it sets the preferred surface to the previous session’s surface and carries the previous run id and runner-host repo for the output-download inputs. Before Tier 1, the preferred surface is kept if and only if its adapter exists and is eligible, it has capacity, and the owner’s queued count is strictly below the surface’s sticky_queue_threshold — shipped value 2 on every surface. With 2 or more runs already queued on that owner, stickiness is released and the cascade proceeds; the reasoning line records exactly why. Two pre-dispatch guards apply to real dispatches: a previous run that is not yet terminal is fatal (“wait for a terminal result before downloading its output”), and one still in dispatched state (no run correlated yet) is fatal. In dry-run mode neither guard fires.

Staying on the same host matters beyond queueing: GitHub Actions caches are scoped to the repository the workflow runs in, so the same cache key string in two host repos is two different caches.

Blacksmith budget rules

Blacksmith is orgs-only: 3,000 free minutes per month, then paid per-minute (it charges for public-repo minutes past the free tier). The registry budget on fleet-org-blacksmith is free_minutes_monthly: 3000, paid_cap_minutes: 0 — paid overage is disabled unless a dispatch explicitly supplies --allow-paid-blacksmith. Code defaults if the budget object is absent: free 3000, paid cap 0.

Eligibility, in order: the owner must not be dezren39 (“Blacksmith is orgs-only; never the personal copy” — a hardcoded owner check, not a registry flag); Linux only; base eligibility (active, targets, dispatch_as); not runner-pinned to github; a surface token must be obtainable; and the budget must have minutes left: remaining = free_minutes_monthly + paid_cap_minutes + job.allow_paid_blacksmith − blacksmith_used_minutes.

--allow-paid-blacksmith MINUTES semantics, precisely: it is parsed as a floating-point number (fractional minutes are accepted, default 0) and added to the paid cap for this one decision only. It is an eligibility allowance — not a per-run spending cap, not a workflow input, and not persisted as an allowance anywhere. Once eligible, the run runs to completion however long it takes; the actual minutes are reconciled into the ledger afterwards and count against future decisions. --runner blacksmith alone does not authorise paid minutes.

Usage accounting is local: blacksmith_used_minutes is the sum of minutes over the session store’s blacksmith_dispatches entries for the current UTC month. A new dispatch appends an entry with minutes: 0.0, reconciled: false; when the run reaches a terminal state, reconciliation replaces the minutes with the run’s real duration, rounded to 2 decimal places. Before any real dispatch decision, outstanding Blacksmith handles are reconciled first (unless the used-minutes override was given). The runner name on the wire is blacksmith-4vcpu-ubuntu-2404; the workflow’s normalize job also errors if runner=blacksmith arrives with platform=macos or from any host repo other than developing-today/fleet.

The Actions cache and the Nix cache push

--actions-cache KEY:PATH (a single value; both sides must be non-empty) becomes the workflow inputs actions_cache_key / actions_cache_path; --actions-cache-restore-key PREFIX is repeatable, requires --actions-cache, and travels newline-joined. Without --actions-cache, placement sends no cache inputs and the workflow’s own defaults apply: key prefix fleet-deps-v1, empty path, empty restore keys.

On the workflow side, the cache root is $GITHUB_WORKSPACE/.fleet/cache with cargo, cargo-target, rustup, and Go subdirectories exported as the matching environment variables. A dependency hash (the first 20 hex characters of a SHA-256) is computed over every lockfile-shaped file in the target checkout plus the rustc/go/nix version strings. The full cache key is {PREFIX}-{RUNNER_OS}-{dependency_hash}-{target_ref}, per host repo in effect. Restore keys, in order: the caller’s prefixes, then {PREFIX}-{RUNNER_OS}-{dependency_hash}-, then {PREFIX}-{RUNNER_OS}-. Prior-output reuse is a separate channel: when a follow-up supplies a previous run, the action downloads that run’s fleet-output artifact (14-day retention) into .fleet/previous-output.

--push-nix-cache sends push_nix_cache: true. The push step runs only on success with the flag set; if either of the repo secrets named NIX_CACHE_SIGNING_KEY / NIX_CACHE_UPLOAD_URL is unset, or ./result does not exist in the target checkout, it notices and skips. Otherwise it signs the result’s recursive path closure with the key (written to a 0600 temp file) and copies it to the upload URL — the shared Fleet R2 cache. The endpoint is secret-configured, never hardcoded in the workflow.

Two workflow-contract facts placement users hit: placement never sends the workflow’s timeout_minutes input, so all dispatches run under the 60-minute default (the workflow validates 5–120); and the dispatch_id input is a fresh correlation id minted per dispatch, not the session handle, despite the workflow describing it as one.

Sessions: fp_ handles and portable references

A dispatched job gets a session handle: fp_ plus 16 random bytes from /dev/urandom, hex-encoded — fp_ plus 32 lowercase hex characters, 128 bits. The local store at $FLEET_PLACE_STATE/sessions.json defaults to ~/.local/state/fleet-place/sessions.json. Dispatch commits locally and then mirrors the record to the queue broker’s placement_sessions table. The placement decision uses the local session history. The store is guarded by a lock directory (waiters poll every 50 ms up to 15 s; a lock older than 120 s is stale and is broken) and written by rename of a temp file, with keys recursively sorted.

A record carries the job, the surface (null in the queued case), the runner repo, the decision reasoning, the run id and URL, the state (queued|dispatched|running|succeeded|failed|cancelled), submitted_by, timestamps, and — when the run is known — the portable id OWNER/REPO#RUN_ID (for example developing-today/fleet#45146933211). One recorded-field caveat, stated as the source behaves: actor is hardcoded to developing-today[bot] (GitHub App dispatch) even for surfaces that dispatch as the user.

An fp_ lookup for status, result or follow-up selects the newer copy by updated_at across the local store and the broker mirror. Status and result can seed the local store from that record.
