The session verbs then work as follows: status refreshes the record from GitHub and prints its state, surface, and run URL; result adds terminal (true exactly for succeeded|failed|cancelled) and, when not terminal, the note “not terminal yet — reconnect with the same handle”; list combines local records with up to 200 from the mirror, then prints them newest first without refreshing GitHub (--mine filters to the current USER@hostname). Anywhere a handle is accepted, the portable OWNER/REPO#RUN_ID is accepted too and is resolved directly against GitHub without the local store — the repo must be a registered Actions/Blacksmith surface’s host repo. Session state mapping from GitHub: queued|waiting|pending|requested → queued; in_progress → running; completed with conclusion success|skipped|neutral → succeeded, cancelled → cancelled, anything else → failed. Note that a help flag after the subcommand prints the session usage — session status --help is a help request, never a handle lookup.

Secrets and the secrets broker

Fleet resolves secrets by name, through one crate (fleet-secrets). No domain shells out to bws (the Bitwarden Secrets Manager command-line tool) or reads a token file on its own. A caller names a secret; the chain finds the value; the value goes only where the caller’s contract says it goes.

Source: https://github.com/developing-today/code/blob/main/pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-queue/src/secrets_broker.rs and https://github.com/developing-today/code/blob/main/pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-secrets/src/lib.rs

The broker: a resident cache of the vault

The secrets broker is a resident cache of the Bitwarden Secrets Manager vault. It exists because the per-call alternative — bws secret list plus bws secret get on every invocation — made every queue call pay 10–40 seconds. The broker binds the laptop tailnet address 100.99.113.103:4800 plus a Unix-socket dual-bind at ~/.config/secrets-broker/broker.sock, with identical routes and auth on both transports; a socket bind failure degrades to TCP-only with a log line. Sandbox consumers reach it through the session proxy — except on the sandbox itself, where fleet init runs a local loopback copy: when FLEET_LOCATION=sandbox, the bind is forced to 127.0.0.1:4800 at the bind itself, whatever the environment says, so a stale or widened bind can never expose the vault off-host. (The domain summary’s phrase “the laptop secrets-broker” is therefore location-relative.)

Endpoints (the X-Agent-Token header is required on everything except /health; an empty expected token never authenticates, not even against an empty header):

RouteAnswer
GET /health{ok, serving, secrets, last_refresh_unix, refreshing, oldest_secret_age_seconds}; 503 while serving is false
GET /secrets{names: [...]} — names only, sorted
GET /secret/<name>{key, value, fetched_at_unix, age_seconds, source}, or 404 / 502 / 503 (below)
POST /refresh202 {ok: true, refresh: "started"} — kicks a refresh on a new thread

Auth failures are 401. Startup exit codes: 2 for a bad home or a refused TTL, 3 for a token-file or bind failure. The broker’s own token file is ~/.config/secrets-broker/token (SECRETS_BROKER_TOKEN_FILE).

The serving gate: 503 until loaded

serving is true only once at least one refresh has succeeded. Before that, public /health answers 503 with ok:false, serving:false. An authenticated GET /secret/<name> answers 503 with error: "secrets not loaded yet" and includes refresh_error when a refresh has failed. A live process whose bws cannot run is not serving, and health says so: not-loaded is a distinct, diagnosable state, not a 404. Clients key on this gate.

Cache semantics: age and source

A cache hit answers 200 immediately with source: "cache", the value’s fetched_at_unix, and its computed age_seconds. Every cached value carries the time the broker last fetched it from Bitwarden, precisely so a rotation runbook can tell “the broker is serving a value N seconds old” from “Bitwarden itself holds this value”.

Read-through on miss. A miss on a loaded cache is not final: the broker reads through to Bitwarden for that one name and serves what it finds with source: "bitwarden-read-through", age_seconds: 0 — a secret minted moments ago is visible immediately instead of at the next TTL tick. Read-through is single-flighted per name: concurrent misses for the same name wait on one gate instead of stampeding bws, and the cache is re-checked after acquiring the gate in case a refresh landed the value meanwhile. Outcomes: found → 200; definitely absent → 404 {error: "no such secret"}; source failure → a loud 502 {error: "bitwarden read-through failed"} — never a silent 404-as-if-absent.

Refresh: startup, TTL, and per-secret install

A background thread runs a full refresh immediately at startup, then sleeps the TTL and repeats — stale-while-revalidate: the cache keeps serving during a refresh, and a failed refresh keeps the old values. One refresh is bws secret list (parsed strictly — a malformed entry fails the parse loudly rather than silently dropping a secret), then one bws secret get per secret, fetched 8-way parallel (an 8-worker pool over the name list). Each bws child has a deadline, so a hung child fails its fetch instead of wedging the refresh — and the refreshing flag — forever. The authenticated POST /refresh acknowledges the request with 202. If a sweep is already running, the worker skips the overlapping sweep. Use last_refresh_unix and refreshing on /health to follow progress.

A refresh installs per secret, not all-or-nothing: fetches that succeed land immediately with the batch’s install time; a secret whose fetch fails keeps its previous value and age; deletions follow the authoritative list. Only a refresh in which every fetch fails keeps the whole previous cache untouched. Net effect: a rotation lands within one TTL of the edit, bounded and observable via the exposed age, and one broken fetch cannot block every rotation in the vault.

TTL. SECRETS_BROKER_TTL_S: default 900 s (15 minutes), minimum 30 s. Unset → 900, no warning. Unparseable → 900 with a warning naming the offending value. Parsed but below 30 (including 0) → startup refuses to run, exit 2, with an error naming the variable, the value, and the minimum — because one interval costs a full vault refresh, and 0 would spin that loop with no sleep at all (measured at roughly 110 full refreshes per second).

The client chain: broker-first resolution

fleet secrets get <name> takes exactly one name. The value goes to stdout and nowhere else; errors are value-free shapes on stderr; a broken pipe on stdout is a quiet success (the Unix-filter rule). fleet secrets list prints the names in the broker’s cache, one per line, never values. Exit codes for both: 0 ok, 2 usage, 3 unresolved / broker unavailable.

The resolution chain (Resolver::default_chain):

  1. Broker leg(s) first. Where the secrets broker’s own socket answers (the laptop), a direct source speaks GET /secret/<name> over that Unix socket. Elsewhere (the sandbox), the broker leg is a framed exchange through the session broker to port 4800: the request names the token file ([secrets] token_file, default ~/tools/secrets-broker-token); the session broker reads the file per request and sends its contents as X-Agent-Token — fleet only ever names the file, and the value never transits fleet’s own memory on this leg. Exactly one broker leg owns the retry budget; when a direct leg exists, the session-broker leg behind it gets no retries.
  2. bws fallback. bws secret list + get, the same shape the broker itself uses. The fallback carries its own credential: the BWS_ACCESS_TOKEN environment variable when non-empty, else the on-disk machine-account token file, handed to the bws child via its environment.
  3. At library level, a 1Password source exists for seats that keep secrets there; the same names resolve without a broker or a Bitwarden token. It is not part of the fleet secrets command’s headline chain.

Retry semantics: a broker leg that cannot answer is retried before the chain moves on — the budget is sized to real restart windows (a full switch restarts broker and tunnel together; the broker is back in about 16 s) without making a genuinely dead broker a hang: the first pause doubles per attempt up to a cap, with a per-attempt ceiling on a single exchange. A broker 404 is definitive about the name and is not retried. If the session-broker socket file does not exist at all, the leg does not burn the retry budget — no broker on this box is not a broker mid-restart.

list has no bws fallback. A broker failure is loud (stderr, exit 3), because a bws listing enumerates the vault, not the broker’s cache, and is never silently substituted. For list, the source selection mirrors get’s first leg only.

The three token files and bootstrap provisioning

Names and paths only — never values.

In Bitwarden Secrets Manager, the three broker service tokens are published under the names fleet.secrets-broker-token, fleet.queue-broker-token, and fleet.laptop-agent-token. On a seat they live as mode-0600 files: ~/tools/secrets-broker-token, ~/tools/queue-broker-token, and ~/tools/laptop-agent-token. Two of the paths are compiled defaults in fleet-config: the secrets token file is the one the session broker reads per request for secrets-broker calls (overridable via [secrets] token_file), and the laptop-agent token file is the one the session broker reads when a request names none. Do not conflate these client-side ~/tools/*-token files with the daemon-side files in each broker’s own config directory (~/.config/secrets-broker/token, ~/.config/queue-broker/token).

A newly enrolled seat does not arrive with these files. The bootstrap token phase (in scripts/muse/bootstrap.sh’s restore phase — the seat-bootstrap layer, not the fleet crates; no code under pkgs/fleet/crates/ reads those three Bitwarden names to create the files) fetches the three names into the ~/tools/*-token paths with 0600 permissions, so a seat can speak to all three brokers from its first command. The known failure shape this prevents: a seat kind whose bootstrap skips the token phase can enrol — its bridge leg answers, because that leg is HTTPS plus a by-name secret — yet fail its queue, secrets, and shell legs with synthesised transport errors, because the three shared files were never provisioned for it. Note that the older Bitwarden name secrets-broker.token is a different value and is never used as the client token.

What the binary itself provisions at runtime is narrower: fleet init spawns the sandbox secrets broker (which then reads its own daemon token file), and the brokers read their token files per startup or per request. Token files stay files — read per request, never stored in memory long-term, never logged.

The bridge: fleet messaging

The bridge is the fleet’s message bus. The bridge service itself lives at https://bridge.security.cab (a separate worker, pkgs/message-bridge); the fleet bridge domain is its mailbox client. The model: every fleet agent has a mailbox on the bridge named after it, and registers with optional groups (for example muse, codex, code-lanes). Central sends a message or a command to one agent, a group, or all; the agent reads its mailbox, does the work, and posts its answer back, which marks the command handled.

Source: https://github.com/developing-today/code/blob/main/pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-bridge/src/lib.rs

One documentation fact first: every verb has its own help — fleet bridge <command> --help prints that verb’s usage section plus the shared defaults-and-exit-codes footer, and a bare fleet bridge --help prints the whole-domain usage text. This chapter is the per-verb reference in prose form.

The two verb families

The verbs split by which token they use and which routes they call.

Central verbs (the owner token — full control):

VerbRouteBehaviour
send --to <targets> [--command] [--sender NAME] <text | ->POST /api/<owner-token>/fleet/sendTargets: agent:<name> (or a bare name), group:<name>, all; repeat --to or comma-separate. --command marks the item a command (default: a plain message). - reads the text from stdin.
agentsGET /api/<owner-token>/fleet/agentsRegistered agents, their groups, and unread counts.
log [--agent A] [--direction inbound|outbound] [--kind message|command] [--since-id N] [--before-id N] [--limit N] [--order asc|desc]GET /api/<owner-token>/fleet/messages?…The central message log, filtered.

Agent verbs (the fleet token — mailbox access only; it cannot send commands):

VerbRouteBehaviour
hello [--agent A] [--groups g1,g2]POST /fleet/<fleet-token>/hello with {agent, groups}Register or refresh this agent and its groups. This is the registry write: the bridge’s agent registry is exactly the set of agents that have said hello (name, groups, last-seen, unread counts).
inbox [--agent A] [--groups g1,g2] [--commands | --messages] [--all] [--since-id N] [--limit N] [--take] [--wait SECS] [--interval SECS]GET /fleet/<fleet-token>/inbox?…Unread items by default; --all includes read ones; --take marks what it returns as read; --wait polls (default interval 15 s; wait capped at 24 h in source) until something arrives or the seconds pass.
post [--agent A] [--reply-to ID] [--to ADDR] [--instruction | --kind K] <text | ->POST /fleet/<fleet-token>/sendA message to central by default. With --reply-to it answers that row (and marks it read). --to sends to any address instead: drew, claude, chatgpt, connectors, agent:<name> (or a bare name), group:<name>, agents, all; repeat or comma-separate. --instruction (or --kind instruction) makes it an instruction, which requires --to.
ack [--agent A] (--up-to ID | ID...)POST /fleet/<fleet-token>/ackMark messages read: either a list of ids, or everything up to an id.
work [--agent A] --state acted|queued|done [--task ID] ID...POST /fleet/<fleet-token>/workRecord the work-item lifecycle of your own instructions: acted (handled in-session), queued (became queue task --task), done. Forward only, from received; only the receiving agent can mark its own copy.
healthGET /healthzThe bridge’s health probe. No token.

Defaults and config: the agent name defaults to $FLEET_AGENT, then [bridge] agent; groups to $FLEET_AGENT_GROUPS, then [bridge] groups; the bridge URL to $FLEET_BRIDGE_URL, then [bridge] url, then https://bridge.security.cab — environment beats file throughout. Output is the bridge’s JSON, passed through.

Exit codes: 0 ok, 2 usage, 3 transport or credentials, 4 the bridge refused the request (its JSON error goes to stderr).

Mailbox and ack semantics

A mailbox item is a message or a command (the kind is set by the sender: send --command, and the intake ladder’s push rung reads commands only). Items are read or unread. Reading is non-destructive by default: inbox without --take shows unread items and leaves them unread. Three operations change read state:

  • inbox --take marks exactly what it returns as read — the “I have this now” claim. fleet agent next’s push rung uses --commands --take, so a pushed command is consumed by exactly the hand-out that returns it.
  • post --reply-to ID answers a row and marks that row read.
  • ack marks explicit ids, or everything up to an id with --up-to.

Read state is not the whole story for instructions. An instruction is a work item with a lifecycle the receiving agent records with work: received → acted (handled in-session) or queued (it became a named fleet queue task) → done, forward only, each recipient’s copy independent on a group send. The owner’s pipeline shows the state and the queue task id, so an instruction that is neither acted on nor queued stays visible at received — the defect the task-it-or-queue-it rule (in the reference chapter, and in the text the intake ladder hands a woken agent) exists to prevent. Notes instructions carry the same fields on the notes surface; connector-channel instructions store none — their read state stands in for acted.

The registry side is equally simple: there is no separate enrolment store on the bridge. Saying hello is registering — name, groups, and last-seen are refreshed on every hello — and agents reports the registry as the set of agents that have said hello, with their unread counts. fleet agent enroll builds on this: its bridge-leg probe is a hello in register mode (see Agents: enrolment, doctor and the intake ladder).

Tokens and the HMAC derivation

Auth is by secret name through fleet-secrets; values are never printed, logged, or put in argv. Central verbs use the owner token, secret name message-bridge.access-token ([bridge] owner_token_name can rename it). Agent verbs use the fleet token, secret name message-bridge.fleet-token, which opens only the agent routes.

Tokens travel in the URL path (see the routes above), so every error string is scrubbed of token values (replaced with <token>) before it is printed, and a 404 is reported as “a wrong token, an old bridge without fleet mailboxes, or a wrong URL”. Plain http URLs are accepted only to this machine; anything else must be https, because tokens ride the path.

Derivation fallback. When the fleet token’s secret is missing but the owner token resolves (the laptop seat’s shape), the fleet token is derived from the owner token exactly as the bridge derives it: base64url(HMAC-SHA256(key = owner token bytes, message = "message-bridge/fleet-token/v1")) — the fixed label constant is the string message-bridge/fleet-token/v1. The derived value is used in-process only; it is never written anywhere. (Construction and label named, no values — that is the whole public shape of the derivation.)

Notes and the public wake signal — the next bridge surface (in flight)

Everything above this section is the bridge as built and shipped: the mailbox system the fleet bridge verbs drive today. A second, smaller surface is being built on the same service — recorded as the design of record in developing-today/code#13895 (filed 2026-11-23) and in flight, not landed, as of 2026-11-23: no part of it is in pkgs/message-bridge on main yet. This section documents the design as recorded, so the book is ready for it; it will be revised against the code when the build lands.

Addressing: class/name identities. A note’s recipient is an identity written class/name (for example muse/archer). An authenticated sender can address one identity, or use a wildcard in either segment — muse/* (every identity in a class), */archer (that name in every class), or */* (every identity). Notes are stored server-side in the bridge’s Durable Object and delivered to every registered identity matching the address. This is a different grammar from the mailbox system’s agent: / group: / all targets above: classes are part of the identity itself, not a separate group registry an agent joins by saying hello.

The public signal. GET /<class>/<name> is a public, content-free wake signal. It returns the same bare UUID shape for registered and unregistered paths. A registered path’s signal changes when a note is delivered to it — and every path, registered or not, also rotates on a deterministic, per-path jittered schedule. The privacy properties are the point of the design:

  • the signal carries no note content;
  • its shape is identical for registered and unregistered paths, so it is not an identity-existence proof;
  • because every path rotates on its own jittered schedule, a change does not prove a delivery happened — decoy rotation is built in, and an unregistered path still rotates its synthetic UUID across windows.

Inbox and acknowledgement. The signal only says “look”; the notes themselves sit behind the identity’s own token. Authenticated inbox and acknowledgement endpoints belong to that identity token: token values are kept in the vault by name and are represented server-side only by hashes — never committed, printed or logged. The recorded flow is: poll the public signal, and when it changes, fetch the inbox with the identity token, act on the notes, then acknowledge them (the acceptance proof ends with the inbox empty after acknowledgement).

The client side, as designed. A small standalone bridge helper provides send, inbox and ack against these endpoints without hand-written HTTP calls, and the first consumer is a Muse hook for Archer: it polls only the public muse/archer signal, compares one UUID to its last-seen value, and wakes only when it changes; on waking, Archer fetches and acknowledges the inbox and surfaces or acts on the notes in the main chat. The recorded end state for the client surface is a fleet subcommand family — the follow-up issue linked from #13895’s record and from the fleet book programme (#13900) — at which point this section’s verbs move into the reference chapter alongside the mailbox verbs above.

Agents: enrolment, doctor and the intake ladder

The fleet already had the legs — bridge mailboxes, the queue, the laptop transport, GitHub, secrets by name. What a new kind of agent lacked was one place to enrol, check its seat, and take work. fleet agent is that place. Its verbs are kinds, enroll, doctor, next, and shortlist; every verb prints one JSON object. fleet shell is its sibling domain, riding on the same agent capability.

Source: https://github.com/developing-today/code/blob/main/pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-agent/src/lib.rs

As with the bridge, every verb has its own --help: the verb’s synopsis and description over the shared output/exit-code footer. This chapter is the per-verb reference.

Kinds and seat shapes: 16 × 3

A kind says three things: which bridge groups the agent joins, how it reaches the fleet from where it runs, and what to tell it at enrolment. fleet agent kinds prints the table as JSON — for each kind its name, summary, bridge groups, seat, and enrolment note, plus the three seat definitions. Adding a kind is adding a row; no verb changes.

A seat shape is how the agent runs:

  • binary — has a shell and runs the fleet binary itself: enroll, then next.
  • http — no shell of its own; speaks the bridge’s fleet routes over HTTPS (the reference client is scripts/fleet/bridge-mailbox.py) and gets work from its mailbox.
  • connector — a chat assistant with the Message Bridge connector attached; it has a channel address, not a mailbox.

The 16 kinds:

KindGroupsSeatNote
musemusebinaryA fresh Muse gets a bridge-capable static build from scripts/muse/bootstrap.sh; older installs run the same commands on the laptop install via ~/tools/laptop-ssh.sh.
opencodeopencodebinaryRuns on the laptop seat, so every leg is local.
openchamberopencode, openchamberbinaryJoins opencode too, so group:opencode reaches both pipelines.
openclawopenclawbinary
claude-codeclaude-codebinaryA cloud session has no tailnet: messaging and the priority rung work over HTTPS; builds go through fleet shell.
codexcodexbinary
geminigeminibinary
antigravityantigravitybinary
grokgrokbinaryA bot with no shell enrols as kind http under the same name and groups.
dotdothttpIts Slack and ChatGPT transports are carried elsewhere; the mailbox is the same store.
duetduethttp
claude(none)connectorFixed bridge address claude; set a wake hook for channel:claude so a send starts a session.
chatgpt(none)connectorFixed address chatgpt; woken by its MCP Events subscription.
laptoplaptopbinaryA job or service on the fleet laptop.
http(none)httpAnything that can make an HTTPS request and nothing else.
generic(none)binaryAny other agent with a shell — the fallback the enrolment error names.

Enrolment and the profile

fleet agent enroll --kind K --name N [--groups a,b] [--dry-run] [--profile PATH]

The kind is validated (an unknown kind is a usage error listing all kinds — “use generic for anything with a shell”). --groups adds to the kind’s built-in groups. For a binary or http seat, the bridge leg is probed in register mode — a bridge hello with the name and groups, which is what actually registers the mailbox. Connector kinds instead get the “attach the connector” instruction and a fixed channel address. The four legs are probed (below) and the saved profile — at the default path, or --profile — records the agent, kind, groups, and leg state. --dry-run probes nothing and registers nothing.

The JSON answer carries the profile, registered (true only when it is not a dry run and the bridge leg answered), the legs, the rungs map (below), and seat-specific next-step lines: for a binary seat, the run loop (fleet agent next --agent <name>, do the task, run its then lines, repeat while the run has budget) and the fleet shell line (“runs where builds belong; never build in a limited sandbox”); for an http seat, the token-by-name note and the reference-client commands; for central, the fleet bridge send lines. Exit 0 for a dry run, or when any intake rung is live; otherwise 3.

Doctor: the four legs

fleet agent doctor [--agent N]

The four legs are bridge, queue, github, and shell. There is no secrets leg: secrets is folded into the bridge leg’s stated need (“HTTPS to the message bridge, and the fleet token by name through fleet secrets”). Any text describing the legs as bridge/queue/secrets/shell is wrong — the source is explicit, and this book follows the source.

The four probes are independent, issued together (one parallel call), and each is a real fleet verb run as this seat:

LegProbeNeeds
bridgebridge hello (enrol) / bridge inbox --agent A --limit 1 (doctor with a name) / bridge health (no name known)HTTPS to the bridge + the fleet token by name through fleet secrets
queuequeue healthThe queue broker: its socket on the laptop, or the laptop transport from elsewhere
githubgh api rate_limit via fleet gh; if that fails, plain signed-in gh api rate_limit (the answer records route: "fleet" or "plain")gh with a token: fleet gh’s rotation, or a signed-in gh
shelllaptop-agent healthA route to the laptop: its broker, the Cloudflare tunnel, the tailnet, or SSH

Doctor’s bridge probe with a known agent is a read that takes nothing (inbox --limit 1): service health alone proves nothing about whether this seat holds the fleet token, so only a call made as an agent counts. With no agent name, the bridge leg is reported not ok even when the service answers (“the service answers, but no agent name is known to read a mailbox with: enrol, or pass –agent”).

From the legs, doctor derives the rungs map — which intake rungs this seat still has: push = the bridge leg, queue = the queue leg, shortlist = always true (it is a local file), priority = the github leg. It also reports builds: “fleet shell reaches the laptop” when the shell leg answers, else “fleet shell has no laptop route from here; it will try a codespace, then run here”. Exit 0 when any intake rung is live (bridge, queue, or github), else 3.

next: the intake ladder

fleet agent next [--agent N] [--lane L] [--repo OWNER/NAME] [--low-water N]
     [--shortlist PATH] [--platform P] [--pool P]
     [--remaining-budget-minutes N] [--filter EXPR] [--queue Q]
     [--no-push] [--no-queue] [--no-shortlist] [--no-priority]

next tries four rungs in order and returns the first that yields work. A rung that is down (bridge unreachable, broker not answering) is not the same as a rung that is empty: down rungs are recorded and skipped, so a seat with only HTTPS still gets work from rungs 1 and 4. Every answer is {agent, rung, task, then, tried} — tried is the per-rung log (skipped/empty/down/rejected, with a reason), and then is the list of follow-up commands the runner should execute for the handed-out task. The default repo is developing-today/code. The --no-* flags skip individual rungs (recorded as skipped); --low-water N overrides the shortlist low-water mark for this call; --lane, --queue, --platform, --pool, --remaining-budget-minutes, and --filter are carried into the queue claim.

  1. Push — a command addressed to this agent on the bridge (bridge inbox --commands --take). This rung outranks everything: a command a person (or central) pushed is work already chosen.
  2. Queue — a claim on the one fleet queue (queue claim with the agent’s lane; the lane defaults from the agent name, known lane families are validated by the queue, and a lane registered to a shared queue worker is honoured). next claims with a 4-hour lease (14,400 s, overriding the queue’s 45-minute default, which lapses mid-task), and the task’s then lines name the lease deadline plus the queue checkpoint / queue complete commands with the claimed worker/lane. A broker refusal that is really a lane verdict (lane bound to another queue, registration did not land) is reported as rung rejected, distinct from down.
  3. Shortlist — the top of this host’s local shortlist. Entries are re-checked against GitHub before hand-out (an issue closed, assigned, or owner-parked since listing is dropped with a named reason), then handed out in rank order. Refill switch: if the list is at or below low-water with nobody refilling, next does not hand out a stale remnant — it returns rung refill instead, a purpose-switch task (purpose: "refill-shortlist", target the shortlist default target) whose instructions and then lines are the shortlist fill / shortlist add commands. One run refills; the marker it leaves keeps the rest working.
  4. Priority — the highest-priority open issue straight from GitHub. Label queries run soonest-first over the priority label family (priority/critical, then priority/high, … — the same ordering as the shortlist ranks below); candidates are filtered (owner-parked labels — the user/owned, user/review, user/escalated class — are kept out), and the winner is reserved into the shortlist file as it is handed out, so two seats on one host do not take the same issue.

The shortlist: ranks, low-water, refill

The shortlist is a local JSON file on this host (default path from the profile/state directory; --shortlist PATH overrides), guarded by a lock file (stale after 30 s; 100 tries at 50 ms). Entries are {repo, issue, title, rank, why, added_at}, plus handed-out records and an optional refill marker. The queue verbs neither read nor write it — the shortlist is the agent domain’s concern, and any interplay is at the caller level.

Rank (lower is sooner): expedite → 0, priority/critical → 1, now → 2, priority/high → 3, next → 4, priority/normal → 5, anything else unranked = 6. Hand-out order is lowest rank, then oldest added_at, then lowest issue number.

Defaults: low-water 3, target 8. A list is low when entries ≤ low_water — so a list of exactly 3 is already low. shortlist status [--low-water N] reports the list, its count, low, and the refill state. shortlist add --issue N --title T [--repo R] [--rank N] [--why TEXT] adds one entry (rank defaults to unranked 6; duplicates — same repo and issue already listed — are refused). shortlist take hands out the soonest entry; shortlist clear empties the list and clears the refill marker. shortlist fill [--repo R] [--target N] tops the list up to the target (default 8, clamped 1–50) from the priority candidates: it fetches 2× target candidates from GitHub, adds them in rank order until the target is met, records the fill, and clears the refill marker.

Refill bookkeeping. A refill marker (by, at) lasts 1800 s (30 minutes); a list needs refill when it is low, no marker is live, and no fill finished within the window. A handed-out issue is kept from being handed out again on this host for 7200 s (2 hours); pruning drops expired handed records and expired markers.

Exit codes

The agent domain’s vocabulary: 0 ok; 2 usage; 3 a needed leg is down (doctor/enrol with no intake rung live); 5 — next only — no work on any rung.

Proxy, sessions and recovery

The session proxy is how a sandbox seat reaches the laptop’s services. The proxy domain’s verbs are serve, connect, init, ssh, splice, get, and put, gated per verb on the capabilities proxy-serve (serve), proxy-connect (connect/init/get/put/ssh), and proxy-raw-splice (splice). The proxy succeeds an earlier Python trio of broker/connect scripts, behaviour for behaviour. The wire is the fleet-proxy-proto protocol alone: 8-byte big-endian length-prefixed JSON frames.

Source: https://github.com/developing-today/code/blob/main/pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-proxy/src/serve.rs

The session broker socket

fleet proxy serve runs the broker. It takes no arguments (a trailing argument is a usage error naming it, exit 2; --help prints the usage, exit 0). It binds the session broker Unix socket from fleet config — FLEET_BROKER_SOCKET or [proxy] broker_socket, default ~/.cache/laptop-agent/broker.sock. If a live broker already owns the socket, it exits quietly; if the socket file is stale, it unlinks and binds.

The broker persists nothing: its routing table comes from config, its tunnels live in memory, and token files are read per request and never stored or logged. The routing table — the services map — is port → service name: 4799 laptop-agent, 4800 secrets-broker, 4801 queue-broker, 21118 rustdesk. The hello response carries that map and the broker’s capability list.

Hello negotiation. Sessions speak the legacy dialect (proto 0: request frames from the first frame — the old Python clients) or negotiate a hello first (proto 1, fleet clients), decided per connection by peeking at the first frame, never by configuration. A too-old peer gets the proto-too-old frame and exit 69 on the client side.

Keepalive and idle exit. A keepalive thread pings the laptop-agent’s /health every 180 s. The broker exits once client requests have been idle for idle_exit_secs ([proxy] idle_exit_secs, default 3600 s; 0 is rejected at config load) — keepalive traffic does not count as use. A warmth cache that exits when cold is a feature on a shared sandbox. Inside a multi-role fleet serve list, the idle exit is disabled, so an idle proxy cannot exit the shared process and kill its sibling roles.

Colocated brokers. For the queue/secrets broker ports, the broker first tries the role’s own Unix socket with a bounded dial — the dial is the probe; a socket that answers within the deadline is used, any other outcome selects TCP within the same attempt — before tunnelling to the laptop.

Warm pools

The broker keeps per-port pools of warm CONNECT tunnels to the laptop’s services. Pool size comes from LAPTOP_AGENT_POOL, compiled default 50 (sized from a concurrency benchmark: the old default of 12 cliffed at roughly 12 concurrent consumers; 32 already restored direct-class latency). A request takes a pooled connection and on any failure retries once on a fresh one. Overflow policy: idle → grow (below the live ceiling) → wait briefly for a returned tunnel → grow anyway. A request never fails because of the pool. Pools key on (port, transport), so the two laptop reaches (below) never share warmth or failure state.

Two reaches to the laptop: the CF leg and the tailnet fallback

Sandbox↔laptop transport lives in this binary. There are two legs:

  1. The Cloudflare leg is primary for the laptop-agent daemon port when its Access file exists: ~/tools/laptop-agent-cf-access.json — a JSON {client_id, client_secret} file, mode 600, read per request, sent only as CF-Access-* headers, never stored or logged. No file, no leg. The leg is TLS through the platform egress proxy to the tunnel hostname sandbox-link.security.cab, whose ingress lands on the daemon’s own listener laptop-side; the daemon’s token auth is preserved end to end.
  2. The tailnet leg is the automatic fallback: a CONNECT through the host egress proxy to the tailnet target host 100.99.113.103. It is selected on connection failure and on a Cloudflare edge error status (502/503/530) alike.

Port 3130 is the host egress proxy port — the CONNECT proxy named by the session’s HTTPS_PROXY environment. It is not a fleet listener. The tailnet leg’s shape is: fleet → HTTP CONNECT to the egress proxy at <egress host>:3130 → tailnet target 100.99.113.103:<service port>. (The URL’s own port in HTTPS_PROXY is not used; 3130 is fixed by the tunnel setup.) Fleet contains no 3130 listener to restart — 3130 belongs to the session/host layer, and the recovery story below is layered accordingly.

connect and init

fleet proxy connect ensures a broker answers — spawning fleet serve proxy detached when the socket does not answer, then waiting for the hello (a legacy proto-0 answer still counts as running; its services map is the built-in table) — syncs the PATH shims from the broker’s services map, and optionally issues one request over the negotiated stream:

fleet proxy connect [--print-path] [--stdio [--host H] [--port N]]
      [--request METHOD PATH [--service-port N] [--token-file F] [--body JSON]]

--print-path prints the shim directory and exits (the shell-integration spelling). --request prints {"status": …, "body": …} as JSON; --service-port N selects the laptop service port (default: the request’s implied route, 4799), --token-file F names the token file the broker should read for this request, and --body JSON must be valid JSON. --stdio is the raw relay spelling (SSH’s ProxyCommand shape): --host H (default: the config target host) and --port N (default 22) relay stdin/stdout over one tunnel. Flag discipline: each flag at most once; --stdio and --print-path are mutually exclusive with --request; --host/--port require --stdio; --service-port/--token-file/ --body must follow --request. Exit codes: 2 usage, 3 transport, 69 protocol/capability unavailable.

fleet init (byte-identical to fleet proxy init — one implementation) autostarts this host’s roles per the [host] manifest. Manifest resolution: FLEET_HOST_CONFIG (a complete inline manifest; wins outright) → FLEET_LOCATION (roles from the config file’s [host] only if its location matches, else the built-in map) → the config file’s [host] section. Only two built-in locations exist: sandbox (init mode spawn; roles proxy, secrets-broker) and laptop (init mode systemd; roles laptop-agent, queue-broker, search, secrets-broker). The full role vocabulary is five names — those four plus proxy.

  • Unknown location: init reports state (every source consulted, plus detected hostname/OS/systemd for the report only — detection never selects roles), starts nothing, and exits 69. It never guess-starts a role.
  • Spawn mode (sandbox): for the proxy, init probes the broker socket and says hello; a live broker means status plus PATH-shim sync and out — a strict no-op, never a spawn, never a restart; init never fights an incumbent broker. Only an unanswered socket spawns fleet serve proxy detached. For the secrets broker, a live socket answer means status and out; otherwise init spawns fleet serve secrets-broker detached with SECRETS_BROKER_BIND=127.0.0.1:4800 set explicitly, then waits (50 × 100 ms probes) for the socket to answer. Any other role in a spawn manifest is reported and skipped, never spawned.
  • Systemd mode (laptop): init never detached-spawns a daemon systemd owns. For each role it reports fleet-<role>.service state via systemctl --user is-active; an active unit is a no-op; an inactive but existing unit is started; a missing unit is reported and skipped, not an error.
  • Roles the manifest itself disables are reported as skipped with their reason, and the [domains] config gate is applied after the manifest and wins over it.

Recovery: connect and ssh pinning

The recovery story is layered: the broker’s Cloudflare leg is independent of the tailnet CONNECT path, so it carries the laptop-agent port when the tailnet leg is what is broken; proxy connect re-ensures a dead broker; stale sockets are unlinked and rebound. The operator’s recovery shell is fleet proxy ssh:

fleet proxy ssh -- [ssh args...]

It runs system OpenSSH through the fleet proxy, as the route you use when the normal laptop channel is what is broken. Everything that decides where the connection lands is pinned by fleet; the caller supplies only extra SSH options and an optional remote command. A literal -- is required first; a second -- inside the SSH arguments is an error (“the SSH destination is fixed; do not pass a second ‘–’”).

The pinned argv: destination user@<target host> with HostName=<target host> (default 100.99.113.103), User=user, identity ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 with IdentitiesOnly=yes, UserKnownHostsFile=~/.ssh/known_hosts_laptop, StrictHostKeyChecking=yes, ConnectTimeout=60, ConnectionAttempts=3, ServerAliveInterval=15, ServerAliveCountMax=8, ControlMaster=auto with ControlPath=~/.ssh/cm-%r@%h:%p and ControlPersist=3600, and ProxyCommand=<this fleet binary> proxy connect --stdio --host <target host> --port %p. The fleet proxy credential stays in the environment and is sent only by the CONNECT relay — never in the SSH argv. The command execs the system ssh (Unix only; elsewhere exit 69).

get/put: verified transfers

Both verbs talk to the laptop-agent daemon’s file routes (port 4799) through the broker, in JSON envelopes carrying 2 MiB raw chunks, base64-encoded (about 2.67 MiB on the wire, far under the 64 MiB frame ceiling). The whole file’s SHA-256 is verified at commit (put) and after the last chunk (get). Transfer temps are deterministic — .<name>.fleet-part-<sha256[..12]> beside the destination — so an interrupted transfer resumes by re-issuing begin and continuing from the temp’s size.

  • fleet proxy put [--mode OCTAL] [--no-resume] <local-path | -> <laptop-path> hashes the file, uploads it in chunks to the deterministic temp on the laptop, and atomically renames it over the destination only after the daemon verifies the hash. The recursive form is put -r … <local-dir> <laptop-dir>. - reads stdin (spooled locally first; mode defaults to 0644). Progress and the final sha256 go to stderr.
  • fleet proxy get [--mode OCTAL] [--no-resume] <laptop-path> <local-path | -> lands chunks in a deterministic local temp; the SHA-256 from the daemon’s stat must match before the temp is renamed over the destination. - streams to stdout — the hash is still verified at the end, and a mismatch fails the command after the bytes were emitted, so check stderr. Recursive get is deferred in v1: the daemon protocol has no directory-listing route.

Exit codes for both: 2 usage, 3 transport, 69 capability-unavailable.

Splice: raw TCP for RustDesk

fleet proxy splice takes no arguments. It listens on 127.0.0.1:21118 (loopback only — a pinned constant with a test asserting both properties) and relays each accepted TCP stream through the fleet broker to the laptop’s RustDesk direct-access service (port 21118 laptop-side). It requires the broker to advertise raw-splice support in its hello (the proxy-raw-splice capability plus the service flag); a legacy or non-advertising broker is a transport error, not a silent fallback. This is the RustDesk direct-access path that avoids the relayed session.

The Commander door: Desktop Commander over MCP

The Commander door is the fleet’s public path to the Desktop Commander MCP server running on the laptop. Desktop Commander gives an AI client terminal and filesystem access to the machine it runs on; the vendor sells that reach as a metered hosted relay. The fleet instead runs its own unmetered path, end to end on its own Cloudflare account and its own hardware: a Cloudflare Worker holds the public door, a second, service-token-only door guards the bridge into the laptop, a Cloudflare Tunnel carries the traffic, and a small gateway on the laptop turns the HTTP stream back into the packaged server’s stdio.

Tracking issue: developing-today/code#13404. The Worker source is pkgs/desktop-commander/worker/; the packaged server is pkgs/desktop-commander; the laptop unit is defined in home/common/default.nix.

Source: https://github.com/developing-today/code/blob/main/pkgs/desktop-commander/worker/src/index.ts

The chain, hop by hop

AI client
  -> POST https://commander.security.cab/mcp          (the public door)
     the desktop-commander Worker: OAuth 2.1 / machine-bearer gate
  -> POST https://commander-link.security.cab/mcp     (the bridge door)
     Cloudflare Access app: service-token-only policy
  -> sandbox-link Cloudflare Tunnel
  -> http://127.0.0.1:8931/mcp on the laptop
     supergateway (desktop-commander-bridge user unit), streamable HTTP
  -> the packaged Desktop Commander (stdio), version 0.2.52
  1. The client speaks streamable-HTTP MCP to https://commander.security.cab/mcp. Hosted clients (Claude, ChatGPT) connect from their own servers; header-capable clients (Claude Code, Cursor, mcpx, and the fleet’s own fleet commander) connect directly with a bearer token.
  2. The public-door Worker (desktop-commander, pkgs/desktop-commander/worker/src/index.ts) checks the bearer, then proxies the request transparently: method, path, query, headers and body pass through, and the response — including the Mcp-Session-Id header and any SSE stream — passes back untouched. Before proxying it deletes the caller’s own credentials (authorization, cf-access-jwt-assertion, cf-access-client-id, cf-access-client-secret) and substitutes its own bridge-door service token. workers_dev is off: the custom domain is the only public door.
  3. The bridge door at commander-link.security.cab is a Cloudflare Access application with a service-token-only policy (the atlas-search pattern). Only the Worker holds that token; nothing else can present it, so the bridge door accepts the Worker’s egress and nothing else.
  4. The tunnel is the existing sandbox-link Cloudflare Tunnel: it terminates the bridge door on the laptop at http://localhost:8931.
  5. supergateway (the desktop-commander-bridge systemd user unit in home/common/default.nix, wrapping pkgs/supergateway) serves the packaged Desktop Commander in streamable-HTTP mode on 127.0.0.1:8931, path /mcp, stateful sessions, with /healthz for gateway health.
  6. The packaged Desktop Commander (pkgs/desktop-commander, @wonderwhy-er/desktop-commander version 0.2.52, built from the npm registry tarball) runs as a stdio MCP server under the gateway. It is the same package the vendor device agent runs; only the transport and the door in front of it are the fleet’s.

The fleet binary’s own client for this door — fleet commander health and fleet commander exec, tier T1 of the laptop route forms — is covered in fleet laptop route forms. This chapter is about the door itself, not that client.

Auth at each hop

HopWho is checkedHow
Client → public door, /mcpThe calling clientA Bearer token the Worker accepts: an OAuth 2.1 access token it issued, or the machine bearer (see below). Anything else gets a 401 (see Failure shapes).
Client → public door, /authorizeThe ownerThe one path still behind Cloudflare Access: the desktop-commander Access app is scoped to commander.security.cab/authorize with an owner-Google-identity policy only. The Worker also verifies the Access JWT itself — RS256 against the team JWKS, the app audience, the owner email — before rendering the approval page.
Worker → bridge doorThe WorkerThe Access service token for commander-link.security.cab, presented as CF-Access-Client-Id / CF-Access-Client-Secret headers, swapped in by the Worker in place of the caller’s credentials.
Tunnel → laptopNobody newThe tunnel and the gateway add no auth of their own; the gateway binds 127.0.0.1 only, so the tunnel is the only way in. Every earlier hop has already authenticated the request.

The OAuth 2.1 front door

The Worker runs its own OAuth 2.1 authorization server (src/oauth.ts), because hosted clients cannot pass a Cloudflare Access login at /mcp — they arrive from their vendors’ servers, not from a browser the owner is signed into. It landed in PR #13488, superseding the original #13404 design in which the whole hostname sat behind Access and machine clients used a public-door service token; that public-door token is retired at this door (the token still exists; nothing accepts it here any more). The bridge door did not change.

  • Discovery (public): GET /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource (also under /mcp) and GET /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server. Issuer https://commander.security.cab, resource https://commander.security.cab/mcp, scope commander.
  • Registration (public): POST /register (RFC 7591). Public clients only (token_endpoint_auth_method: "none"); redirect URIs must be https or loopback http. Clients are stored in the OAUTH_KV namespace under client:<id>.
  • Authorize: GET /authorize renders the approval page (behind Access, above); approving is a form POST back to /authorize that issues a single-use authorization code, valid 10 minutes and bound to the client’s PKCE S256 challenge.
  • Token: POST /token exchanges the code (PKCE verified; a code is consumed on any attempt, successful or not) for an opaque access token valid 1 hour and a rotating refresh token valid 30 days.
  • State: codes, access tokens and refresh tokens are stored in OAUTH_KV under the SHA-256 of the presented value (code:<hash>, at:<hash>, rt:<hash>), never in the clear. Revoke a client by deleting its at: / rt: entries and its client: record from the namespace.

The machine bearer

The owner’s own tooling skips the OAuth flow with a single static bearer token, compared in constant time. Its canonical value lives in fleet secrets under the name desktop-commander.machine-bearer; the Worker receives it as the per-version secret MACHINE_BEARER, staged by the publish workflow from the GitHub environment secret of the same name. fleet commander resolves it by that fleet-secret name at call time and never stores it.

Configuration and secrets reference

Every name below was verified by grepping the repository — the Worker config, its source, and the home configuration that runs the laptop half.

Laptop configuration (home/common/default.nix)

  • desktop-commander-bridge.service (systemd user unit): supergateway wrapping the packaged Desktop Commander — --outputTransport streamableHttp --streamableHttpPath /mcp --port 8931 --host 127.0.0.1 --stateful --healthEndpoint /healthz, restart on failure. Its start script exports the real user PATH first, because the wrapped server exists to run the user’s commands.
  • desktop-commander-remote.service (systemd user unit): the vendor device agent (desktop-commander remote). It stays running until the self-hosted endpoint is stood down as a separate recorded step; the two paths coexist deliberately.

Failure shapes

SymptomWhere it stopsWhat it means
401 {"error":"unauthorized"} from /mcp, with a WWW-Authenticate: Bearer resource_metadata="https://commander.security.cab/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource" headerPublic doorNo bearer, an expired OAuth access token (1 hour), a revoked token, or a wrong machine bearer. The header is the signal that sends hosted clients into the OAuth flow; header-capable clients should check the machine bearer’s fleet-secret name resolves.
A redirect to a Cloudflare Access login at /authorizePublic door, approval path onlyExpected for anyone who is not the owner: only the owner’s Google identity passes, and the Worker re-verifies the Access JWT (signature, audience, owner email) before rendering the page. A login wall at /mcp itself is not this shape — /mcp is not behind Access any more; if a client reports one, it is holding a pre-OAuth configuration.
500 {"error":"bridge credentials are not configured"} from /mcpPublic doorThe live Worker version was uploaded without its ACCESS_CLIENT_ID / ACCESS_CLIENT_SECRET version secrets. Re-run the publish/promote pipeline so the version carries them.
404 {"error":"not found"}Public doorA path other than /mcp, /healthz and the OAuth surface. A wrong hostname (for example the workers.dev address) lands here or nowhere — workers_dev is off.
405 {"error":"method not allowed"}Public doorA non-POST to /register or /token, or a method other than GET/POST to /authorize.
An Access refusal or 403 between the Worker and the bridge doorBridge doorThe bridge-door service token is wrong, rotated without re-publishing the Worker version, or the Access app’s service-token policy changed. The token’s fleet-secret names are the desktop-commander-link pair above.
The Worker answers, the bridge door passes, but calls time out or 502Tunnel or laptopThe sandbox-link tunnel is down, or the laptop half is stopped: check systemctl --user status desktop-commander-bridge and the gateway’s own http://127.0.0.1:8931/healthz on the laptop.
MCP session errors mid-stream (lost Mcp-Session-Id, cut SSE)Laptop gatewayThe gateway runs stateful sessions; a unit restart drops every live session. Clients reconnect and re-initialize.
Markdown-to-PDF tool calls fail on the laptopPackaged serverA packaging limit, not a door failure: the package is built with --ignore-scripts, so the Chromium its PDF path downloads never arrives. Recorded in pkgs/desktop-commander/default.nix.

Operations

  • Health: GET https://commander.security.cab/healthz answers {"ok":true,"service":"desktop-commander"} with no token — it proves the Worker answers, nothing about the hops behind it. End-to-end health is an MCP initialize + tools/list against /mcp with a valid bearer (fleet commander health does exactly this through the whole chain), and the laptop-local check is the gateway’s http://127.0.0.1:8931/healthz.
  • Deploys are Cloudflare version deployments from GitHub Actions, modeled on the id-mail publisher/promoter pair:
    1. Publish (desktop-commander-worker-publish.yml, manual dispatch on main, confirm_upload): runs the Worker’s tests (pkgs/desktop-commander/worker/test/ — proxy, OAuth and promote suites), a credential-free dry run, then uploads a new version with its secrets file. Uploading changes no traffic. The run emits a provenance artifact naming the exact version, tag and baseline.
    2. Promote (desktop-commander-worker-promote.yml, manual dispatch with the publish run id and attempt, confirm_promotion): verifies the run was a successful manual publish on main, checks the live deployment still matches the manifest baseline, then creates a deployment with exactly that version at 100%. Tests (desktop-commander-worker-tests.yml) also run on pushes and PRs touching the Worker directory.
  • Token rotation: rotate the bridge-door service token or the machine bearer in fleet secrets / the desktop-commander-production environment, then publish and promote a new Worker version — version secrets are per-version, so a rotation only takes effect on a version uploaded with the new values. Rotating the machine bearer also means every machine client picks the new value up by name on its next call; nothing caches it.
  • Revoking a hosted client: delete its at:<hash> / rt:<hash> entries (and its client: record) from the OAUTH_KV namespace. There is no admin UI; the namespace is the record.
  • The vendor agent stand-down is a separate recorded step on #13404, deliberately not part of any deploy: desktop-commander-remote keeps running alongside the self-hosted door until it is taken.
