Search: the Atlas corpus

The search domain (argv0 alias atlas-search) is the client surface for Atlas: hybrid search over the fleet’s session-history corpus. The domain has two client verbs — search and get-chunk — and, under fleet serve search, the search service itself. init and fetch-model deliberately stay on the standalone atlas-search artifact; invoking them through fleet is a usage error naming that artifact.

Source: https://github.com/developing-today/code/blob/main/pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-search/src/cli.rs

Hybrid FTS + vector

A search is hybrid: a full-text (FTS) branch and a vector branch each produce candidates, and the results are fused. The default mode is hybrid; --mode fts|vector runs one branch. The embedding model is Snowflake arctic-embed-m-v2.0 — the source constant is Snowflake/snowflake-arctic-embed-m-v2.0 (the help text’s spelling drops the org slash; the source spelling is the operative one).

Client flags with their defaults:

FlagDefaultMeaning
--k N10Final result count.
--pool N100Per-branch candidates; validated 1..=400.
--mode MODEhybridhybrid | fts | vector.
--kind CSV / --topic CSV / --project CSV / --client CSV—Classification filters.
--since YYYY-MM-DD / --until YYYY-MM-DD—Sessions created on/after / on/before (inclusive).
--max-sensitivity LVpersonalshareable | personal | local-only | secret-bearing. A request; the server clamps it (below).
--group-by-sessionoffRoll chunk hits up to sessions.
--expand N0Include N neighbouring chunks around each hit.
--with-messageoffInclude the parent message text.
--no-cacheoffBypass service cache reads; the fresh result still lands in the cache.
--no-waitoffDo not block: print the service job handle and return. (The one-shot default waits for the job.)
--hydrate N0Hydrate the top N results to full content.
--raw-rows[=branches]—Ungrouped rows: bare = flat fused rows; =branches = pre-fusion branch rows.
--textoffHuman-readable output instead of JSON (JSON is the default).
--model NAMESnowflake arctic-embed-m-v2.0Embedding model.
--embedder NAMEautoauto | fastembed | st.
--trunc N0Truncate vectors to N dims (0 = full).
--vector-backend Bscanscan | index-fill | index-fixed.
--service-url URLhttp://127.0.0.1:18760Service base URL; env ATLAS_SEARCH_URL, then fleet.toml [search] url, override it.

Standalone-only engine knobs (--backend, --db) are deliberately not part of this surface.

get-chunk <chunk-id> [--neighbors N] [--text] fetches one chunk with its provenance (session, client, sensitivity); --neighbors N includes N chunks either side in the same message.

Invocation shapes: fleet search <query> [options], and fleet search search <query> [options] (atlas-search’s own shape — the leading search token is stripped). Exit codes mirror atlas-search: 0 ok, 2 usage/validation, 1 service-job/backend failure surfaced without a fallback, 3 routing unavailable (no service and no standalone artifact).

Via-service vs standalone, by seat

There are two routes, and the seat decides the default:

  • Via-service: an in-process client speaking the Atlas service’s loopback HTTP job protocol to the service at --service-url (default http://127.0.0.1:18760): submit a search job, wait for it (unless --no-wait), and render the result through writers ported for byte-for-byte shape compatibility with atlas-search. The backend behind the service is a read-only Turso corpus store with one shared Snowflake embedder.
  • Standalone: there is no second embedder or backend in the fleet workspace — the client delegates to the kept standalone atlas-search binary on PATH, passing the caller’s arguments in atlas-search’s own shape (with --via-service/--standalone stripped, and ATLAS_SEARCH_VIA removed from the child’s environment so an ambient value cannot silently re-route it), inheriting its stdout byte-for-byte. A missing artifact is exit 3, naming it as “the search domain’s kept standalone”.

Routing precedence: explicit --via-service / --standalone first (the two together are a usage error); then env ATLAS_SEARCH_VIA=service|standalone; then fleet.toml [search] via; then the seat default:

  • Sandbox seat → via-service, with a loud standalone fallback (a warning on stderr naming the failure). The via-service client is proxy-blind; the sandbox reaches the laptop’s loopback service through the loopback forward on the shared laptop-ssh control connection — the deployed atlas-search wrapper’s pattern, not a second mechanism.
  • Laptop seat → standalone. The seat signal is the service’s own config file, ~/.local/state/atlas-search/service.json: only the serving host has one.

get-chunk always runs standalone — it is job-scoped in the protocol, so it cannot ride the service route. When via-service was requested (by flag, env, or config — the seat default does not count) it prints the loud fallback note first.

Sensitivity clamping

Terminology: the ladder’s canonical names are public < internal < private < sensitive. The flag values and identity caps in this chapter are spelled as the service spells them today (shareable / personal / local-only / secret-bearing) until the identifier rename (#13506) lands.

The via-service client presents a per-seat bearer token — env ATLAS_SEARCH_TOKEN, else the JSON file at ~/.config/atlas-search/client.json (a JSON object with one token string field, file mode 0600). Identities are named in the service config, and the server clamps --max-sensitivity to the identity’s ceiling: identity drew-cli → secret-bearing; identity sandbox-scripts → personal. The fleet verb adds no ceiling logic of its own — a client can ask for more than its ceiling, and the service silently serves at the ceiling. A seat with no client.json cannot use the service route and falls back to standalone.

The serve search service shape

fleet serve search (also spelled fleet search serve, and reachable via the atlas-search serve argv0 route) is the atlas-search service rehomed into fleet — same config, same wire. Both spellings require the search-serve capability, not the search client capability.

usage: fleet serve search [options]
  --config PATH     service config (default ~/.local/state/atlas-search/service.json;
                    env ATLAS_SEARCH_SERVICE_CONFIG)
  --listen ADDR     listen address override (loopback only)
  --job-ttl-ms N    completed-job TTL override, ms (default 600000)
  --hard-ttl-ms N   submit hard-cap override, ms (default 3600000)

Its guarantees:

  • One shared embedder per process: a single lazily loaded embedder (one ONNX session, mutex-held), loaded on the first vector query only — FTS-only jobs and a cold service work without it. Its load state is what /health reports. The model is the Snowflake snowflake-arctic-embed-m-v2.0 model at a pinned snapshot revision; the model directory resolves from ATLAS_MODEL_DIR or the Nix closure.
  • A mechanically read-only backend: the Turso backend’s token comes only from the service config chain, never the environment; the resolution chain is env, the Bitwarden item named atlas-ro, or the turso CLI’s --read-only mint; the query layer issues nothing but SELECTs. There is no write path to opt into.
  • The job protocol is a bounded async queue with in-memory temp state, per-client recovery listing, and dedupe keyed by the effective request (never across effective sensitivity ceilings).
  • The engine is a verbatim copy of atlas-search’s, held byte-for-byte by a parity check script and the code repo’s fleet-search-parity-guard workflow. Rollback is pointing the unit’s ExecStart back at atlas-search serve.

Exit codes for the service: 2 usage/config, 1 runtime failure; a running service never exits 0.

The gh passthrough

fleet gh runs the real gh CLI (GitHub’s command-line tool) under a rotating fleet token. Every argument passes to the real gh binary unchanged (FLEET_GH_BIN selects the binary, default gh) — except the four shadow subcommands (tiers, cache-serve, cache-status, closures), which fleet implements itself. The domain help’s status line still claims the implementation “lands in a later step” of the multicall epic; that wording is stale — the source is a complete implementation, and this chapter documents the source.

Source: https://github.com/developing-today/code/blob/main/pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet/src/gh.rs

The passthrough contract

Before each attempt, one token is resolved by name through the fleet secrets chain and exported as GH_TOKEN for that attempt only. Attempts are captured (piped), not streamed, because the failure text is what classifies a failover; the caller sees the final attempt’s stdout, stderr, and exit code byte-exact as gh produced them. Attempts are silent by default; FLEET_GH_TRACE=1 names each attempt’s token source (never a value) on stderr. Tokens are never printed, logged, or written to a file; provider errors name source and stage only. The audit log redacts secret-carrying arguments (gh secret set bodies, Authorization headers) in its copy only.

Raw mode — fleet gh --raw <args…> or FLEET_GH_RAW=1 — is the first-class bypass: the real gh execs directly with the caller’s ambient credentials; no token is resolved or injected, and there is no rotation or failover. It exists so callers that must pin one identity — and the gh → fleet gh PATH shim, whose escape hatch this is — never have to choose between the rotation and bypassing fleet entirely.

Token rotation: three Apps, then personal

The rotation order in source (the top-level help understates it as one App):

  1. Fleet App installations — the “developing.today fleet” App, App ID 5612056 (FLEET_GH_APP_ID may override). Private key by secret name github-app.developing-today-fleet.private-key. Default owners, in order: developing-today, developing-today-forks, dezren39.
  2. developing.today App installations — App ID and key both by name (kaneo.github-app-id, kaneo.github-app-private-key). Default owners: developing-today, dezren39.
  3. developing-today-backup App installations — by name (github-app.backup-app-id, github-app.backup-private-key). Default owner: developing-today.
  4. Personal — the user’s gh OAuth token, parsed out of the broker secret named github-cli.hosts-yml (the hosts.yml file itself, stored by name; the parser extracts its oauth_token). Tried last (the user, 2026-11-23): the personal credential is the final fallback, not the first identity used.

Per App leg: the private key is resolved by name; an RS256 JSON Web Token is signed with the system openssl, the key passed over an inherited file descriptor — never written to disk, never in argv; the owner’s installation is resolved live from GET /app/installations, paginated at 100 per page (the App has 100+ installations).

Hint-first. When the call names a repo or org, that owner’s installation moves to the front of each App leg, because an installation token only sees its own installation’s scope.

Controls: FLEET_GH_ORDER (a comma list fixing the rotation exactly: personal, app:<owner>, devtoday:<owner>, backup:<owner>); FLEET_GH_APP_OWNERS / FLEET_GH_DEVTODAY_OWNERS / FLEET_GH_BACKUP_OWNERS (comma lists replacing an App’s default owners).

Failover triggers: the retry-safety rule

A failed attempt’s combined stdout+stderr is classified:

ClassTrigger strings (case-insensitive)Retry?
RateLimitrate limit, rate_limit, too many requests, http 429Yes — any call
Permissionmissing required scopes, insufficient_scopes, resource not accessible, not accessible by integration, not accessible by personal access token, this endpoint requires you to be authenticated, bad credentials, http 401Yes — any call
NodeResolutioncould not resolve to a nodeRead-only calls only
Otheranything elseRead-only calls only

The rule: a write is only repeated under a fresh token when the failure proves GitHub refused the request before processing it. Rate-limit rejections (the limiter answers before the mutation runs) and permission/scope rejections are both pre-execution refusals. Node-resolution is explicitly not one: GraphQL executes mutation fields serially, so a batched mutation may already have run an earlier field before a later field’s node fails to resolve; replaying would duplicate the part that landed. Any other write failure is returned as-is — the request may have landed, and repeating it could double-post. Reads repeat on any failure class.

A token provider failure (a source that cannot resolve or mint) skips that source silently (named under trace) and the rotation continues; if no attempt produced output, the caller gets the provider errors and exit 3. If the last failover has no successor, the caller is shown the real gh failure, not a summary.

Two wrappers sit in front of the rotation:

  • Close guard. issue close and issue edit --add-label status:done are refused (exit 2, never reaching the rotation) when the queue broker has a claimed or parked task bound to that repo#issue, unless the bound task’s completion record (a fleet-closure/v1 record carrying its task id) is presented with the wrapper-only flag --completion-record <path>, stripped before gh runs. The queue query fails open — a broker outage must not block every close.
  • Metadata create path. issue create / pr create bodies are stamped with the fleet metadata block before the rotation runs, and the full record is inserted into the metadata store after a successful create; a malformed caller block refuses the create before any write; a failed insert never loses the item (reported on stderr; ingestion heals it).

The 4802 cache

fleet gh cache-serve [--bind <addr>] runs the credential/token cache daemon in the foreground. It caches four things, memory-only, with single-flight minting (concurrent requests for one key block on the in-flight mint):

Entry kindTTL
Secret resolutions60 s
App JWTswithin their expiry, minus a 60 s skew
Installation tokensuntil shortly before expires_at, minus the same 60 s skew, floored at 1 s
Per-App installation lists300 s

Nothing is written to disk; a restart is a cold cache, never a stale one. The wire is newline-delimited JSON over TCP, protocol version 1 — a daemon that does not know a request’s version answers {ok:false, …} rather than guessing. Bind: --bind beats FLEET_GH_CACHE_BIND beats the default 127.0.0.1:4802; a bind without a port gets 4802. Every normal fleet gh call resolves through the localhost daemon first, then the laptop daemon (the proxy’s reach target at the same port); with no daemon answering it resolves in-process over the same cache implementation and says so on stderr (“resolving in-process”).

fleet gh cache-status probes the configured cache daemons and prints each one’s snapshot — entry counts by kind, hit/miss counters, soonest expiry. Key names and values never leave the daemon; counts only. It exits 3 when no daemon answered.

The shadow verbs: tiers and closures

fleet gh tiers probes every rotation source and prints its core and GraphQL rate-limit headroom — labels and numbers only; token values never leave the provider. Exit 0 when every source answers, 3 when any source is down. Source behaviour: fleet gh tiers --help prints the verb’s own usage and exits 0; any other argument errors.

fleet gh closures [<item>] reads back the closure log. The policy layer behind it: issue|pr close|reopen through the rotation must carry a --reason from the taxonomy — implemented, superseded, cancelled, started-incorrectly — enforced with the policy error “Please give a reason. This is required by policy.” The reason is written into the close comment, and every successful close or reopen appends one fleet-closure/v1 JSON-line record to closure-records.jsonl in the fleet state directory (backed up with it); closures prints the log, optionally filtered to one item. Source behaviour: the verb produces no help output at all — its behaviour is documented only in source, and here.

Dispatch and dispatch-test

Two different domains share the word “dispatch”, and a third verb besides. This chapter keeps them apart:

  • fleet dispatch — a thin client over pm-dispatch, an existing TypeScript/Bun service that is not rewritten in fleet. Its verbs are status, launch, and enqueue.
  • fleet dispatch-test — an explicit-dispatch CI test: scan fleet repos for free Actions capacity, submit a job, track its stored status. Nothing here is trigger-driven; every verb runs only when a caller invokes it.
  • Not this chapter: fleet queue dispatch, which is placement — see Placement and remote dispatch.

Source: https://github.com/developing-today/code/blob/main/pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-dispatch/src/lib.rs and https://github.com/developing-today/code/blob/main/pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-dispatch-test/src/lib.rs

fleet dispatch: the pm-dispatch client

Per-task status is deliberately not here: a task’s state is the repo queue itself, so per-task status reads ride the queue domain (fleet queue list). The client’s routes are exactly three:

VerbRouteAuth
fleet dispatch statusGET /healthunauthenticated
fleet dispatch launch …POST /v1/sessionsBearer
fleet dispatch enqueue …POST /v1/tasksBearer

The connection ladder (transport selection, in order):

  1. Direct URL: env FLEET_DISPATCH_URL or fleet.toml [dispatch] url (must be http://host[:port] with no path — a path is a usage error; a missing port gets the configured port appended).
  2. Laptop zero-config: probe 127.0.0.1:{port} with a 750 ms connect timeout; if it answers, direct to loopback. The port is [dispatch] port, default 4879.
  3. If config proxy_direct() is set: direct to {target_host}:{port}.
  4. Tunnel: a CONNECT through the fleet proxy egress to the target host’s dispatch port (the sandbox route). The client opens its own tunnel on the egress because the framed session-broker shape forwards only an X-Agent-Token header, which pm-dispatch does not accept.

Auth is Authorization: Bearer <token>, the token resolved by name through fleet-secrets: default name pm-dispatch.api-token, overridable with [dispatch] token_name. The value enters exactly one header per request and is never printed, logged, or stored. An HTTP 401 is reported as a transport-class error naming the mismatch with the service’s own token env (name only).

Exit codes: 0 ok, 2 usage, 3 transport down / credentials unresolved or rejected, 4 the service answered with an HTTP error status. Success bodies print to stdout as pretty JSON exactly as the service sent them; errors go to stderr prefixed fleet dispatch: . The shared argument parser accepts --flag value and --flag=value; duplicate value flags, unknown options, values on boolean flags, and stray positionals are all usage errors.

status

No arguments (any argument is a usage error; --help/-h prints usage and succeeds without contacting the service). It prints the service’s /health body as a JSON object plus an added "transport" field describing the route taken, for example direct http://127.0.0.1:4879 or tunnel via proxy egress to {host}:4879. A non-object health body is wrapped as {"health": <body>, "transport": …}.

launch

fleet dispatch launch --repo <owner/name> --prompt <text> [options]
  --prompt-file <path>    read the prompt from a file
  --title <text>          default: the prompt's first line
  --model <provider/id>   model hint for the session
  --directory <path>      must be the repo's laptop primary or inside it
  --priority <p>          integer 10-90, or critical|high|normal|low
  --issue / --no-issue    create the tracking issue (default: issue)
  --wait / --no-wait      wait for the launch to complete (default: wait)

--repo must be an allowlisted fleet repo (the allowlist check is service-side). The POST to /v1/sessions creates the tracking issue and queue task, starts the session, and assigns the task to it — all service-side. The client sends only the fields the caller set: repo and prompt always; title, model, directory, priority when given; issue only when --issue/--no-issue was given; wait only when --wait/--no-wait was given. The defaults named in the help (title = first prompt line, issue on, wait on) are the service’s defaults, applied because the client omits the fields. --prompt + --prompt-file together is a usage error (never a silent preference), as are --issue --no-issue and --wait --no-wait in either order. --priority crosses the wire as a JSON number when it parses as an integer, otherwise as the raw string — validating the 10–90 range and the named scale is the service’s job, not the thin client’s.

enqueue

fleet dispatch enqueue --repo <owner/name> --title <text> --prompt <text> [options]
  --prompt-file <path>    read the prompt from a file
  --kind <kind>           triage|small_fix|pr_shepherd|ci_investigation (default: triage)
  --priority <p>          integer 10-90, or critical|high|normal|low
  --model <provider/id>   stored as the payload's model hint only
  --issue                 create a tracking issue first (default: no issue)
  --issue-number <n>      attach to this existing issue instead
  --dedupe-key <key>      default: canonical key from the issue, else unique

Enqueue only, no session (POST /v1/tasks). Differences from launch: --title is required; --kind is validated client-side against the four kinds — an unknown kind is a usage error listing the four — but is only sent when given (the triage default is service-side); --issue is a one-way boolean with no --no-issue, and the service default is no issue — the opposite default from launch; --issue-number must parse as an integer (sent as issue_number); --dedupe-key is sent as dedupe_key; --model goes in the task payload as a hint only.

fleet dispatch-test: scan, submit, status

Verbs: scan, submit, status. Exit codes: 0 ok, 2 usage, 3 transport down / credentials unresolved / no eligible scope, 4 an HTTP error status from GitHub or Turso (including an unknown job id on status).

Execution homes. One repo — the fleet repo, config [dispatch-test] fleet_repo, default dezren39/fleet — holds the other fleet repos as git submodules and carries the generic workflow fleet-dispatch-test.yml. Eligible homes are its copies: the source repo plus its fork network, discovered per invocation by breadth-first traversal of GET /repos/{r}/forks, depth-capped at 8 levels, deduplicated, source first, then copies in API order — unless [dispatch-test] scopes pins an explicit list (the pin wins; scan output reports scopes_source: "config" vs "fork-network").

Capacity counting. For each scope, ACTIVE = (jobs with status in_progress or queued across all in_progress runs — fetched paginated, page size 100, max 100 pages) + (the number of queued runs, from total_count, counted as 1 active unit each — a queued run has not started and exposes no jobs, so it counts once regardless of its eventual fan-out). Workflow presence: the repo’s workflows list contains a workflow whose path ends with fleet-dispatch-test.yml and whose state is active (a missing state counts as active). Eligible = workflow present and active < threshold. The threshold is --threshold N, else [dispatch-test] threshold, else 40; --threshold 0 is a usage error (“can never be satisfied”) — a rule the help text does not mention.

Auth, by name through fleet-secrets only: the GitHub token name is [dispatch-test] token_name, default github.ghcr-classic-pat; the Turso token name is [dispatch-test] turso_token_name, default turso.fleet-dispatch-jobs-token. Each value enters exactly one Authorization header per request.

scan

fleet dispatch-test scan [--threshold N] [--json]

Scans every scope in order. Human output: a first line scopes source: {config|fork-network} (fleet repo {repo}), then one line per scope <repo> active=<n> workflow=<yes|no> eligible=<yes|no>, then chosen: <repo|none> (the first eligible scope). --json prints {threshold, fleet_repo, scopes_source, scopes: [{repo, active, workflow, eligible}], chosen}.

submit

fleet dispatch-test submit --submodule NAME [--threshold N]
                           [--repo owner/name] [--ref REF]
                           [--name TEXT]
                           [--commands TEXT | --commands-file PATH]

--submodule is required: a single path segment (alphanumerics, -, _, .; never empty, . or .., never a slash). Examples: code, opencode, openchamber, nix, hatch. --ref is a ref inside the submodule repo; default empty = the submodule stays at the umbrella’s recorded SHA. --commands / --commands-file are mutually exclusive; the default commands are set -eux; echo dispatch-test smoke; git rev-parse HEAD; uname -a. The job id is generated client-side (a time-based base36 string plus a random hex suffix).

Forcing --repo bypasses the eligibility rule: the forced repo is scanned only to report active_at_scan; active < threshold and workflow presence are not checked for it.

The sequence is load-bearing, in this order:

  1. Connect to GitHub and to the Turso jobs store; run the idempotent schema migration.
  2. INSERT the job row with status='queued', target_repo=NULL, target_ref, script and commands (both carry the commands, so MVP-era readers still see the payload), submodule, and run_id/run_url/exit_code/output_tail=NULL.
  3. Pick the home: the forced --repo, else the scan rule. No eligible scope is a transport-class error (exit 3): “no eligible scope … (job {id} remains queued in the store)”.
  4. Dispatch: UPDATE the row’s target_repo; POST the fleet-dispatch-test.yml workflow dispatch with {"ref": <that repo's default_branch>, "inputs": {"job_id": id}} — the job id is the workflow’s only input; only then UPDATE the row to status='dispatched'. Any failure stops the sequence: a failed dispatch leaves the row queued, with its target repo recorded.
  5. Print {job_id, repo, submodule, ref (null when empty), active_at_scan, threshold, status: "dispatched"} as JSON.

The Turso jobs store

The endpoint is [dispatch-test] turso_url, default https://fleet-dispatch-jobs-dezren39.aws-us-east-1.turso.io; requests are POST {url}/v2/pipeline in the hrana-over-HTTP v2 shape. A non-2xx is exit 4 with the first 300 characters of the body; a non-JSON body or a pipeline-level error object is a failure, never an empty result.

The jobs table’s full row is: id, created_at, name, target_repo, target_ref, script, status, run_id, run_url, exit_code, output_tail, updated_at, submodule, commands. The phase-2 migration (adding submodule and commands) is applied idempotently by submit and status; a “duplicate column” error means already-migrated and is ignored.

Row lifecycle: queued (the client’s insert) → dispatched (the client, after the workflow POST) → running (the workflow itself writes this, with run_id/run_url, when it fetches the job) → a terminal status with exit_code/output_tail, written back by the workflow always, even on failure — with one exception: a cancelled run is best-effort, and its row may stay running, which status reports honestly.

The workflow itself (fleet-dispatch-test.yml in the fleet repos) is workflow_dispatch only, with the single required input job_id. Its one job runs on ubuntu-24.04 with a 120-minute timeout in the container ghcr.io/developing-today/fleet-build:full: it reads the job from the Turso store, marks it running with the run id and URL, checks out the fleet repo, checks out the named submodule at the named ref, runs the commands inside it, and writes status and output back. Its baked-in Nix substituters are https://nix-cache.developing-today.workers.dev and https://developing-today.cachix.org.

status

fleet dispatch-test status <job-id>

Exactly one positional (else a usage error). It prints the stored row as pretty JSON with all columns, values typed from the Turso cells. An unknown id is an HTTP-class error 404, exit 4: “job {id} not found in the jobs store”. This reads the store only — it never queries GitHub for live run state.

The hosted edition: fleet-hosted

fleet-hosted is a Cloudflare Worker (pkgs/fleet/hosted-worker/, TypeScript, package name fleet-hosted, version 0.1.0) that is the hosted peer of the native fleet binary. It is component C of the hosted-editions epic #9078, designed in #9081 (design record doc/2026-11-22T14-28-45Z_design_fleet-tool-workers-edition, §3.1). One Worker puts five front doors — stamping, query, queue, ingestion, sync — plus a session registry over one shared auth/tenancy plumbing layer. Work enqueued at the hosted queue door is claimed at the native door and vice versa, because both editions speak the same broker protocol over (backends intended to be) the same stores.

The edition-parity rule runs through the whole package: the same checks, the same envelopes and the same id formats in both editions. Where the hosted edition deliberately diverges, the divergence is named in the code and in this chapter — the queue door’s refusal of anonymous claims is the one deliberate case.

Status, stated plainly (2026-11-23): implemented and tested, never deployed — local-only. The package’s own wrangler.toml header says the config is for wrangler dev and tests and authorises no account-level deployment; the platform registry (pm-stack/platform/workers.json) records state: "not deployed", deploy: "none", address: null. The package documentation’s phrase “every door is live” is true of the code — /capabilities reports all five doors state: "live" and an in-process smoke run answers the acceptance checks end to end — and false of the service, which has never run in production. This chapter follows the code and the config, not the shorter phrase (disagreement D35 in the survey record for programme #13900).

The plumbing layer

Every non-public route runs the same pipeline, in this order: route match (an unmatched path is a 404 that advertises nothing) → authenticate (401/403/503) → caller-tenancy assertion (a cross-tenant assertion is a 403) → service-token route scope (403) → handler.

Three caller kinds share one Bearer credential form:

Caller kindCredentialWhat caps it
rpA #9077 relying-party token: a JWS validated against the provider JWKS (WebCrypto, RS256/ES256), then issuer, audience and lifetimeThe tenancy mapping for its subject
agentAn RP token carrying the #1253 agent roleIts lane and session claims are required, and cap what the caller may assert
serviceAn opaque per-caller service token recorded in the tenancy plane, looked up by SHA-256The named doors its scope lists

A validated subject maps to a tenancy account keyed by its minted binding_id — 32 lowercase hex characters, the component E / #2258 contract — never by an email address or a provider subject. An unmapped or inactive subject fails closed. An x-binding-id or x-tenancy-binding header that disagrees with the credential is refused as a cross-tenant attempt. A per-user Turso database credential (the libsql access-claim shape) presented as service auth is refused with its own code, data_plane_credential_refused — design §3.3 rule 3: a data-plane credential is never a service credential.

Configuration is by name only. The environment names are verified in src/config.ts (HostedEnv): RP_ISSUER, RP_AUDIENCE (the one [vars] entry in wrangler.toml, value fleet-hosted), RP_JWKS_URI, TENANCY_FIXTURE_JSON, STAMP_SIGNING_KEY_PKCS8, STAMP_SIGNING_KEY_ID, STAMP_VERIFY_KEYS_JSON, GITHUB_APP_ID, GITHUB_APP_PRIVATE_KEY_PKCS8, GITHUB_APP_INSTALLATION_IDS, GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET, INGESTION_REPOS, METADATA_DB_ID, QUEUE_DB_ID, DIRECT_READ_SIGNING_KEY_PKCS8, DIRECT_READ_SIGNING_KEY_ID, DIRECT_READ_VERIFY_KEYS_JSON and DIRECT_READ_MAX_TTL_SECONDS (default 3600). Malformed key material parses to null and the dependent path fails closed; it never falls open.

The five doors

Stamping — the hosted world’s only stamping authority

POST /v1/stamps (#12585) parses the caller’s pm-metadata block — a malformed block refuses the create — stamps every fleet-owned provenance field from service sources only, signs the provenance (#12586, Ed25519), creates the GitHub item through the App installation-token rotation point, and inserts the full record in the same request. Signing is refused before any GitHub write when the signing material is unconfigured (503). A create whose database insert failed is not failed back to the caller: the response reports metadata_inserted: false, and the ingestion check below heals it.

GitHub writes go through the fleet App installation-token rotation (AppRotationGitHubWriter, #12585) when App material is configured: a rate-limit or permission refusal fails over to the next installation, the native #8887 rule. Without App material, writes go through a fixture writer — one of the seams listed below.

Query

The query door (#12587) answers GET|POST /v1/query: it lists and filters issues and pull requests by Metadata fields from the metadata store, tenancy-scoped. GitHub is the fallback for fields an item has not been ingested with yet; the fallback scan is bounded at 10 pages of 100 per repo. Where the stored record and the item body diverge, the divergence is reported and the body wins.

Queue

The queue door (#12589) answers 25 verb routes under POST /v1/queue/<verb> — validate, enqueue, claim, lane, bind, heartbeat, checkpoint, park, release, wake, block, unblock, dep-recheck, cancel, fail, complete, list, show, timeline, health, revive, events-append, events-seen, events-count, events-prune — plus four fallback-claim routes under POST /v1/queue/fallback/ (status, claim, heartbeat, release). It answers the broker envelope at HTTP 200 exactly as the native broker does, and stamps the caller’s credential-resolved binding_id into every event detail as claim provenance. The one deliberate divergence from the native broker: the hosted door requires authentication and refuses anonymous claims.

Ingestion — one check, two triggers

The ingestion door (#12590; design §7.3, #9060 §16) is the hosted half of ingestion; native ingestion (#9076) is the peer, and both run the same check. The check reads the item fresh through the GitHub item source — never the delivery payload’s copy — parses its pm-metadata block, and inserts or refreshes the database record keyed on the item under the block’s own stamped tenancy. A block-less item gets an ascertained block (its parent taken from its primary-parent/<slug> label, its provenance signed when the service holds stamp material), stored and written back where the fleet has write access. Metadata that stays insufficient is forwarded as one deduped repo-task/v1 triage packet per item.

Two triggers run that one check:

  1. The webhook route. POST /v1/ingestion/github is public at the router — GitHub deliveries carry no fleet credential — and the handler authenticates each delivery itself, by the X-Hub-Signature-256 HMAC-SHA256 over the raw body, before any parsing. An unconfigured webhook secret is a 503 and an unverified signature a 401, both before parsing; out-of-scope events are acknowledged 200 as ignored.
  2. The sweeper. POST /v1/ingestion/sweep behind the normal plumbing, and the Worker’s scheduled handler on its one cron trigger (*/15 * * * *), re-scan the configured repo scope (INGESTION_REPOS) to catch listener misses.

The check is idempotent by construction: duplicate deliveries converge on one database row and at most one triage task, and a create that reported metadata_inserted: false at the stamping door is healed by the first check that sees the item.

Two operator surfaces complete the #9074 remainder (#14312). A backfill (POST /v1/ingestion/backfill) is the sweeper’s whole- scope pass with a recorded run: the run record — scope, the check’s counts in/out, and every per-item failure named — is stored as the sweep completes and read back via GET /v1/ingestion/backfill/runs, so a re-run over an unchanged store is a recorded no-op (0 inserted / 0 refreshed), not a claim. A divergence report (POST /v1/ingestion/divergence) is the aggregate counterpart of the query door’s per-result divergence finding: over the scope it compares every item’s body block against the database and names three classes with counts — missing_row (an item with no row), stale_field (a row whose body block differs, naming the top-level fields, or pm_meta_block when the block was removed or no longer parses), and orphan_row (a row whose item is gone from GitHub, visible only through the store’s cross-tenancy repo seam). The report heals nothing; the backfill is the heal. The CLI reaches both as fleet-hosted backfill [--repo <owner/name>]..., backfill runs, and divergence [--repo <owner/name>]....

Sync

The sync door (#12591) answers POST /v1/sync/project and POST /v1/sync/queue-github: it hosts project-reconcile’s write set and the named queue/GitHub flows, as marker-checked posts and serial operations. The package README’s skeleton-era table still describes these routes as stubs answering 501 not_implemented; the code disagrees — src/capabilities.ts marks the door live and src/routes/sync.ts implements it — and this chapter follows the code (disagreement D31).

Sessions and the CLI

The session registry (#12584) answers POST /v1/sessions{,/resume,/resolve,/close}. Session ids are server-minted in the native #9075 format: ses_ plus 128 bits in hex. The CLI’s session resolution order is explicit argument > FLEET_SESSION_ID > OPENCODE_SESSION_ID > per-workspace stored state, with a parity test transcribed from the native resolver’s own tests. Another tenancy’s session answers identically to an unknown one (404 session_unknown) — there is no existence oracle — and a closed session is a 409 session_closed.

The package also carries a thin TypeScript CLI (cli.ts / src/cli.ts, #12588) whose verb set is a fixed, caller-owned allowlist, and the two public routes GET /health and GET /capabilities; /capabilities mirrors the native fleet capabilities JSON shape.

The direct-read path

The direct-read mint (#12592) issues scoped, expiring, read-only libsql tokens bound to the metadata database only. The token claims are a: "read-only", id, binding_id and exp, and the package ships a scope inspector beside the mint. The queue database is refused: the mint is for the metadata store, not the broker’s store. The wiring today is library only — no HTTP route and no CLI verb expose the mint (grep-verified in the survey).

Seams: why implemented is not deployed

src/worker.ts wires fixture, in-memory, module-scope implementations of every store interface:

Seam in the WorkerProduction home
FixtureSessionRegistryThe session registry’s production store
FixtureMetadataStoreThe #9074 metadata database
FixtureQueueStoreThe existing fleet-queue Turso database (#6741), behind a libSQL QueueStore
The fixture tenancy directory (TENANCY_FIXTURE_JSON)Component E’s tenancy database, which does not exist yet

wrangler.toml declares no bindings at all — no D1, KV, R2, Durable Objects or queues — and INGESTION_REPOS is commented out, so the scheduled sweep currently has nothing to scan. A later component-C issue owns the production deployment; neither wrangler.toml nor the README names its number, and this chapter does not invent one.

Verification is in-package: there is no GitHub Actions workflow for fleet-hosted. npm test runs node –test over 18 test files with no network and no wrangler, npm run smoke runs the acceptance checks end to end in-process, and npm run typecheck covers the types.

Failure shapes

Every refusal is a FailClosed rendered as { "error": <code>, "message": ... }:

ShapeMeaning
404 not_foundUnmatched path; the Worker advertises nothing
401 missing_tokenNo credential on a route that requires one
403Cross-tenant assertion, or a service token outside its door scope
503One row per unconfigured dependency: auth, stamp signing (refused before any GitHub write), session registry, metadata store, queue store, webhook secret
500 {error: "internal"}An unhandled error

Door-specific shapes sit on top of the plumbing ones: sessions add 404 session_unknown, 409 session_closed and 400 invalid_session_id, and an agent lane beyond the caller’s credential is refused; stamping reports metadata_inserted: false instead of failing the create; queue verbs answer {ok:false, exit, error} envelopes at HTTP 200 while plumbing refusals stay 400/503, and fallback-claim answers 200/409/400/502 by failure class. The rule that runs through every door: unconfigured means fail closed, never fall open.

Sources

Package pkgs/fleet/hosted-worker/ (wrangler.toml, src/config.ts, src/router.ts, src/routes/, src/auth.ts, src/jwt.ts, src/tenancy.ts, src/capabilities.ts, src/worker.ts); design #9081; issues #9078, #12583–#12593; platform registry pm-stack/platform/workers.json. Survey: programme #13900, lane FLEET-GAPS-SURVEY, 2026-11-23 (disagreements D31 and D35).

The queue watchdog: queue-transport-alert

queue-transport-alert is a Cloudflare Worker (pkgs/queue-transport-alert/worker/, plain JavaScript, #6369) that watches the repo-queue broker from off the broker’s own host. It exists because of a blind spot: when the queue broker’s transport is down, every worker lane exits silently at its Step 0 health gate, so a total queue outage produced no signal. Issue #5708 (2026-11-04) was filed by hand; the 2026-11-18 outage — tailscaled stopped during a rebuild — was noticed only from lane reports. The Worker closes that hole: every 10 minutes it probes the broker’s public route through Cloudflare Access, and on a confirmed outage it files or comments a GitHub incident, pushes to the phone, and — once the broker is back — enqueues one triage task into the queue it watches.

Status (2026-11-23): live and in service. The platform registry (pm-stack/platform/workers.json) records state: "in service" with the address https://queue-transport-alert.developing-today.workers.dev, and the Worker has filed a real incident (#12414, 2026-11-22, closed).

The probe

The probe is GET {BROKER_URL}/healthz, where BROKER_URL is https://queue-broker.security.cab, sent with the Cloudflare Access service-token headers CF-Access-Client-Id and CF-Access-Client-Secret, redirect: "manual" and a 10-second timeout (PROBE_TIMEOUT_MS=10000). That route is the tunnel to the broker’s Tailscale listener, so the probe fails when the laptop is off, when tailscaled is stopped, or when the broker itself is down. A probe is healthy only on HTTP 200 with a JSON body of {"ok": true} (classifyHealthz).

The failure class is the diagnosis, and the probe carries it in its detail string:

Probe resultWhat it means
301/302/303/307/401/403“Cloudflare Access refused the probe’s service token, or it is unset”
502/503/504/530“The tunnel could not reach the broker”
200 with a non-ok:true or non-JSON bodyThe body itself, clipped to 200 characters
TimeoutThe URL and the timeout, named

When the Access secrets are missing, the probe returns skipped and the pass only logs. A watchdog that cannot authenticate its own probe does not alert — that posture is deliberate.

The state machine

All state lives in one Durable Object: the binding TRANSPORT_STATE (class TransportState, SQLite storage, migration tag v1 with new_sqlite_classes). A single instance (idFromName("broker")) holds everything, so passes never race. Its keys are state, push_subs, last_push and vapid — the VAPID P-256 key pair is generated once inside the Durable Object and never leaves it.

The machine (src/logic.js and src/run.js, a direct port of the local script below) is small:

  • THRESHOLD (2) consecutive failed probes open an alert window. Below the threshold, a failing window stays quiet.
  • One alert per outage window: the Worker finds an open issue titled with the prefix Queue transport incident: and comments on it, or files one titled Queue transport incident: repo-queue broker unreachable since <window_start> with labels kind/bug, priority/high, area/infra and source/fleet-monitor.
  • The first healthy probe after an alerted window posts exactly one recovery comment carrying the outage span.
  • The Worker never closes the incident. There is deliberately no close() in src/github.js — rule #10136.

The three side-effect channels

Alert and recovery each fan out to the same channels, under one retry discipline: notifications and the recovery enqueue ride a pending list in Durable Object state (capped at 20) and retry on later ticks. A failed GitHub write leaves the window un-alerted, so the next tick retries it rather than losing the incident.

  1. GitHub. Find-or-file by the title prefix, with the labels above. This is the durable record of the outage.
  2. Web Push. Payload-free: the push carries no incident text; the service worker reads the current state from /status.json’s last_push field. Push endpoints the push service reports gone (404/410) are dropped, and at most 20 devices may subscribe.
  3. Telegram. One message per alert and per recovery, through the existing OpenClaw bot; the chat id is the TELEGRAM_CHAT_ID variable in the Worker config.

The master switch is APPLY: the deployed value is true, which files, comments, pushes and enqueues. Any other value — or a missing GITHUB_TOKEN, TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN or BROKER_AGENT_TOKEN — degrades that one side effect to log-only, independently of the others.

The recovery triage task

On recovery the Worker also enqueues one triage task into the queue it watches (src/queue.js): a POST {BROKER_URL}/enqueue with the broker’s X-Agent-Token header plus the Access headers, carrying a repo-task/v1 triage packet anchored to the incident issue, on queue QUEUE (repo-health-code-pilot) at priority 20, with dedupe key repo-health:v1:triage:<repo>:issue:<N>. A dedupe error from the broker counts as success — the task already exists, which is the point. The enqueue is only attempted while the broker answers, which is precisely why it is filed on recovery and not during the outage: the queue that would carry the triage is the thing that was down.

The status surface

RouteWhat it serves
GET /The status page: PWA-installable, auto-refreshing every 60 seconds
GET /status, GET /status.jsonThe same view as JSON, CORS-open
GET /sw.js, /manifest.webmanifest, /icon.svg, /vapid.jsonThe PWA and push plumbing
POST /subscribe, POST /unsubscribeDevice push registration
POST /test-pushA push to that device only, at most once per 30 seconds
POST /admin/test-pushA push to all devices; X-Admin-Token must equal the Access client secret, compared in constant time

The status values are up, degraded, down, stale (no probe in 25 minutes) and unknown, with last_check, last_ok, failing_since, consecutive_failures, last_failure, incident, last_outage (start, end, duration, incident), pending_deliveries, last_errors, last_push and issue_title_prefix. The status surface carries no secrets.

HTTP edges: a subscribe body over 2048 bytes is a 413; an invalid push endpoint a 400; the 21st device a 409; a test-push from an unsubscribed device a 404 and a repeat within 30 seconds a 429; a bad or missing admin token a 403; other POSTs and methods a 405; an unknown GET a 404.

Two implementations, one contract

The Worker is a port of the local script scripts/fleet/queue-transport-alert/check_transport.py, which still exists with its systemd units. The two share one contract and one incident title, and dedupe onto the same GitHub issue when both run — the find-by-title-prefix step is what makes the overlap safe.

Configuration, deploy and rollback

The deploy source of truth is cloudflare.config.ts (the cf versions flow); wrangler.jsonc mirrors it for wrangler dev, and test/config.test.mjs keeps the two in step. Name queue-transport-alert, main src/index.js, compatibility_date = "2026-10-25", observability on, cron */10 * * * *. The plain variables are BROKER_URL, REPO (developing-today/code), THRESHOLD, PROBE_TIMEOUT_MS, QUEUE, TELEGRAM_CHAT_ID, PUBLIC_URL and APPLY. The secrets are named here and never written in any config file; deploy.mjs uploads them per version from Bitwarden: ACCESS_CLIENT_ID and ACCESS_CLIENT_SECRET (the Access service token for the broker route), GITHUB_TOKEN, TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN and BROKER_AGENT_TOKEN (the broker’s X-Agent-Token).

The primary operator path is nix run .#queue-transport-alert-deploy: upload a version tagged git-<sha12> with its secrets piped in, deploy it at 100%, apply the triggers, and verify the serving version and /status.json. Passing --deploy-version <id> rolls back to an older version as it was. An optional, manual-only GitHub Actions release also exists (.github/workflows/queue-transport-alert-deploy.yml): main-only, behind the cloudflare-queue-transport-alert environment with an independent required reviewer, no self-review and an admin-bypass attestation checked by a verify-environment job, with upload and promote as separate dispatches and no automatic rollback. Tests are node --test test/*.test.mjs, also run in the flake package’s checkPhase. The Worker is registered in the deploy registry as queue-transport-alert.

One record lags the code: the platform registry still describes this Worker’s deployment as “by hand” with Actions deployment as future work. The workflow exists and #12550 (deploy through trusted GitHub Actions) is closed; this chapter follows the repo (disagreement D32).

The dispatch-test jobs store: fleet-dispatch-jobs

fleet-dispatch-jobs is a Turso (libSQL) database whose single table, jobs, is the stored record of the explicit-dispatch CI test jobs submitted by fleet dispatch-test. The operational story — how submit, scan and status behave — lives in Dispatch and dispatch-test and the fleet dispatch-test reference. This chapter treats the database itself as the subject: its connection by name, its schema and provenance, its two writers, and its place in the estate.

Three different things share the word “dispatch”, and only one of them touches this database:

NameWhat it isTouches fleet-dispatch-jobs?
The dispatch domainA thin client over the pm-dispatch serviceNo
pm-dispatchThe laptop service (pkgs/pm-dispatch, pm-stack/dispatch)No
dispatch-testThe fleet dispatch-test domain (design #6580)Yes — its sole owner in this repo

Status (2026-11-23): live, small and current. The #13844 Turso audit read the store on 2026-11-23 and counted jobs, 6 rows. The owner crate is in the fleet binary’s workspace, and its phase-2 migration runs idempotently on every submit and status, so the schema below is the schema the code maintains today.

Connection by name

The connection names are verified in pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-config/src/lib.rs:

  • The default URL constant DEFAULT_DISPATCH_TEST_TURSO_URL is https://fleet-dispatch-jobs-dezren39.aws-us-east-1.turso.io — config key [dispatch-test] turso_url. The database’s name is the URL’s subdomain.
  • The Turso token is resolved by name only through fleet-secrets: the default name is turso.fleet-dispatch-jobs-token — config key [dispatch-test] turso_token_name. The GitHub token for the same domain defaults to the name github.ghcr-classic-pat.
  • Token values enter exactly one Authorization header per request and are never printed, logged or stored. Requests are POST {url}/v2/pipeline — hrana over HTTP v2, one execute and one close per call.

The jobs table

The table has 14 columns: id, created_at, name, target_repo, target_ref, script, status, run_id, run_url, exit_code, output_tail, updated_at, submodule and commands.

Phase 2 (#6595) gave two of those columns their current meaning: target_ref carries the submodule ref (empty means the umbrella’s recorded SHA), and script mirrors commands so MVP-era readers still see the payload. Job ids are generated client-side in the form dt-<unix_millis base36>-<4 hex chars>.

Schema provenance: the migration that is not a creation

No CREATE TABLE for jobs exists anywhere in the searched repo — not in pkgs/fleet, pkgs/pm-dispatch, pm-stack/dispatch, home/ or pkgs/fleet/migrations/ (those migrations belong to the fleet-queue database, not this one). The table predates the crate: it is an MVP-era artifact created outside the repo’s recorded history. The only DDL the code runs is the idempotent phase-2 migration in ensure_schema() — ALTER TABLE jobs ADD COLUMN submodule TEXT and ALTER TABLE jobs ADD COLUMN commands TEXT — applied by submit and status, where a “duplicate column” error means already-migrated and is ignored. The schema above is the schema the code maintains; no repo migration creates the table, and this chapter does not imply one (disagreement D34).

The write path

The store has exactly two writers.

The client crate (pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-dispatch-test/src/lib.rs, verbs scan / submit / status) writes in the load-bearing #6598 order:

  1. INSERT the row with status='queued', target_repo=NULL and run_id/run_url/exit_code/output_tail all NULL.
  2. UPDATE the row’s target_repo to the execution-home copy of the fleet repo (dezren39/fleet or a fork) picked for its free GitHub Actions capacity.
  3. Dispatch the generic workflow fleet-dispatch-test.yml in that copy, with the job id as its only input.
  4. Only then, UPDATE the row to status='dispatched'.

The order is the failure semantics: a failed dispatch leaves the row queued with its target repo recorded, and “no eligible scope” is a transport error (exit 3) with the row left queued — never a dispatched row pointing at nothing.

The generic workflow — fleet-dispatch-test.yml in the fleet repos (dezren39/fleet and its copies, not in this repo) — is the second writer. Per the dispatch chapters’ description, it writes status='running' with run_id and run_url when it fetches the job, and the terminal status with exit_code and output_tail at the end — always, even on failure. A cancelled run is best-effort and may leave the row running. No code for that write-back exists in developing-today/code to verify it against, and this chapter says so rather than presenting the workflow’s behaviour as surveyed here.

Reads

fleet dispatch-test status <id> is the only in-repo reader: a SELECT of all 14 columns WHERE id = ?. An unknown id is HTTP 404, exit 4. Status reads the store only, never GitHub — it reports the stored row, not live workflow state, which is why a cancelled run’s row can honestly read running.

scan never opens the store at all. Capacity counting is GitHub-only: active means jobs in_progress or queued across in_progress runs, paginated at 100 per page to a 100-page bound, plus queued runs counted as one active unit each from total_count; a scope is eligible when the workflow is present and its active count is under the threshold (default 40).

Failure shapes

The domain’s exit codes are 0 ok, 2 usage, 3 transport (credentials unresolved, store unreachable, no eligible scope) and 4 for an HTTP status from GitHub or Turso, including the unknown-job-id 404. The Turso-specific shapes: a non-2xx response is exit 4 with the first 300 body characters; a top-level {"error": …} or a per-request results[i].type != "ok" is a transport error, never an empty result; a non-JSON body is a transport error. --threshold 0 is a usage error, and [dispatch-test] threshold = 0 is a config validation error (#6603).

Estate position

The #13844 Turso-to-D1 audit grouped this database under §G8 as MOVE-CLEAN, alongside small product stores. The facts behind that grouping — one table, 6 rows, tiny, join-free — are not in dispute; the classification is. The database’s sole owner is fleet-plane CI infrastructure, configured from the fleet binary’s own [dispatch-test] section, not a product surface, and this chapter does not inherit the product-store framing (disagreement D33). MOVE-CLEAN is a recommendation only: nothing in the code moves the store, and it stays Turso-shaped — hrana pipeline, typed cells, the pipeline failure shapes above — until a programme decides otherwise.

Earlier coverage note: the dispatch chapters already named this store’s endpoint, token name, table and row lifecycle before this chapter existed; what was missing was the database treated as a subject in its own right (disagreement D30).

Sources

Owner crate pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-dispatch-test/src/lib.rs; config pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-config/src/lib.rs (DispatchTestConfig); design #6580; issues #6589, #6595, #6598, #6603, #6605, #6622, #6623, #13844. Survey: programme #13900, lane FLEET-GAPS-SURVEY, 2026-11-23 (disagreements D30, D33, D34).

Temporary builds and custom connections

A temporary build is a machine the fleet does not own, borrowed for minutes: a GitHub Actions runner, started for one session, reached through a connection built for that session alone, and gone when the lease ends. The machinery is fleet actions exec (#13774): live, short-lived exec sessions inside Actions runners, in the #13717 route-family shape — a timeout required by construction, and the serving form named in the output. The verb-by-verb reference is fleet actions; this chapter is the design: the handoff, the two clocks, the tiered extension policy, and the door the runner dials in through.

Drew’s order (2026-11-23 15:17 CST) was for an alternate exec mode that may become the primary: agents connect into Actions runners and exec commands themselves, temporary and short-lived like the commander and route subcommand family, with the central coordinator (#13765) establishing the connection handoff and the fleet command background-watching the run after handoff.

Why the runner dials out

The design was chosen under one hard filter: most off-the-shelf runner-access methods print SSH or connection information into the run log, and in a public repo the log is world-readable. Any method whose connection material can appear in logs is disqualified, however convenient. The survey in #13774 records the verdicts: tmate and upterm rejected on exactly that leak; the Tailscale GitHub Action viable but not picked (it couples runner access to tailnet enrolment for every caller, and the transport design #13752 is moving away from Tailscale-only reach); cloudflared with Access kept as door technology, not as the session protocol; an iroh endpoint on the runner the right long-term transport, but not the v1 session protocol.

The chosen shape inverts the connection: the runner-side agent dials out to the coordinator. The workflow starts a small agent — a mode of the fleet binary, fleet actions agent, invoked by the fleet-exec-session composite action in dezren39/fleet. The agent proves it is inside the run with the job’s GitHub OIDC token, fetched from the Actions runtime and never logged; it registers with the queue broker and holds an outbound long-poll. Commands flow requester → broker → agent; IO flows back the same way. No inbound path is needed, nothing connection-shaped ever exists outside the two endpoints, and the session handle is a public identifier — safe in logs, safe on the run page. Workflow inputs carry only the handle and non-secret parameters, never a token: inputs are visible on the run page.

Three pieces make one flow:

  1. The action — dezren39/fleet .github/actions/fleet-exec-session (composite): sets up the pinned fleet binary, runs fleet actions agent for the session, and ships the egress helper fleet-exec-put on the session PATH.
  2. The workflow — dezren39/fleet .github/workflows/fleet-exec.yml (workflow_dispatch; inputs are the handle, an optional target repo/ref checkout, the runner, the lease and max seconds, and the hide-logs flag; permissions: id-token: write; the job timeout is the max lifespan plus grace).
  3. The subcommand — the actions domain in the fleet binary: fleet actions exec start / run / attach / watch / renew / extend / decide / close, plus fleet actions put <file> for egress.

The handoff: workflow id, run attempt, handle

The handoff is the triple a requester keeps: the session handle, the portable OWNER/REPO#RUN_ID form, and the run attempt. fleet actions exec start asks the coordinator to claim a slot for the session’s host surface and create the session row — composing with #13765’s design, never forking it: when the coordinator’s /placement-claim answers granted, the session proceeds on the coordinator path; when it does not answer, the session proceeds on the singular per-seat path and the output names which happened via placement_path. The subcommand then dispatches fleet-exec.yml with the handle, and binds the resulting run id and attempt to the session row (/actions-exec-bind). Sessions are recorded in the local store under the state dir, so the portable form resolves later, from any seat.

On the runner side, registration is the mirror image of the bind: the broker verifies the agent’s OIDC JWT against GitHub’s JWKS and checks its repository, job_workflow_ref, run_id and run_attempt claims against the session row created at dispatch. Requester-side auth is the existing broker seat auth. The broker surface is twelve verbs in crates/fleet-queue/src/turso_queue/actions_exec.rs, routed beside placement’s: seat-side /actions-exec-open, -bind, -command, -stream, -renew, -extend-request, -extend-decide and -close under the broker token; agent-side /actions-exec-register, -poll, -io and -result under OIDC. Session state lives in the actions_exec_sessions, actions_exec_commands and actions_exec_io tables, and every transition is a conditional UPDATE, so two actors racing a session resolve to exactly one winner.

Disconnect tolerance follows from the broker being the transport: a requester disconnect is a non-event (the broker holds the commands, the IO and the lease), agent network blips retry with backoff against the long-poll, and reconnecting is re-attaching with the same handle. Files leave through fleet actions put: into the session outbox, uploaded as the run’s fleet-exec-out artifact, and — when the workflow populated the FLEET_EXEC_R2_* environment from masked repo secrets — PUT to R2 under fleet-exec/<handle>/ with a SigV4 signature, skipping quietly when the credentials are absent.

Log visibility is a choice, not a leak: by default the agent echoes command IO to its own stdout, so it lands in the public Actions run log; start --hide-logs turns the echo off. Either way the broker’s IO chunk store is the cache of record. The OIDC token and the R2 credentials are never written to any log, and reading the produced public logs end to end for connection material is part of the mode’s acceptance bar.

The door: exec.security.cab is a tunnel ingress, not a Worker

The agent’s verbs need a public route to the broker, which lives on the laptop. That route is exec.security.cab — and it is not a Cloudflare Worker. The WORKER-EVIDENCE survey for programme #13900 settled this first-hand: of the security.cab doors, only commander.security.cab and mcpx.security.cab are Workers, each with a wrangler config in the repo. The exec door has no wrangler config, no OAuth front door and no Access app, because there is no Worker to configure: the sandbox-link tunnel is remotely managed, so its ingress lives in Cloudflare, not in the repo.

What the door is, as deployed (recorded on #13774, Slice 5, 2026-11-23T22:10:06Z): the sandbox-link tunnel (id beginning 722f72ba-), at config version 6, gained one ingress rule — exec.security.cab with path ^/actions-exec-(register|poll|io|result|close)$ forwarded straight to the laptop queue broker at 100.99.113.103:4801 — inserted before the catch-all with every existing rule preserved, plus a proxied DNS CNAME for exec.security.cab in the security.cab zone. There is no Access app in front by design: the runner job’s GitHub OIDC token is the authentication, verified at the broker. The path scoping is enforced at the tunnel and was verified from outside: a tokenless POST /actions-exec-poll returned the broker’s own 401 {"error":"unauthorized"}, while POST /claim and GET / on the same host returned 404. In code, the door is a broker URL and nothing more: pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet/src/actions.rs carries const DEFAULT_BROKER_URL: &str = "https://exec.security.cab";.

Two clocks: the lease and the max lifespan

Every session carries two clocks, both enforced by the broker and by the runner-side agent, which exits at expiry even if partitioned from the broker, after a final IO and egress flush:

  • The lease — set by start --timeout, required, with no default. Renewable through the coordinator (exec renew), clamped at the max.
  • The max lifespan — --max-lifespan, default 30 minutes, ceiling 2 hours, the fleet leg cap. Renewals move lease_until up to the max and no further; past it, only an extension helps.

The tiered extension policy

Extensions past the max are governed by the tiered policy Drew set on 2026-11-23 (~17:06 CST), recorded on #13774 before implementation and landed by PR #13854 (merged f56dc7f713ef, published as fleet-static-f56dc7f, ACTIONS-EXEC-3 complete 2026-11-24T00:39:36Z). Evaluation happens in /actions-exec-extend-request from the session’s extension count, its cumulative approved extension seconds, and the raw ask. The tunables are named constants in turso_queue::actions_exec:

TunableDefaultMeaning
EXT_AUTO_SIZE_CAP_S1800 (30 min)The largest single ask the auto tiers may grant; a raw ask above it is tier 3 even as a first extension
EXT_TIER1_MAX_COUNT1Extension #1 of a session is tier 1
EXT_TIER2_MAX_COUNT2Extension #2 is tier 2, subject to the caps; #3 and beyond are tier 3
EXT_AUTO_TOTAL_CAP_S3600 (60 min)Cumulative approved extension seconds the auto tiers may grant over a session’s life
EXT_DENY_WINDOW_S600 (10 min)Tier 2’s deny window: silence at window end approves
EXTENSION_GRACE_S300The decision grace past the lease while an extension pends
  • Tier 1 — auto + notify. The first extension, within the caps, is applied inside the request itself and recorded ext_state = 'auto-approved'. One notification-only push goes out: a plain PM alert with no needs-drew choice block.
  • Tier 2 — notify + deny window. The second extension pends for the 10-minute deny window. The session’s hard deadline covers the window — max(lease, decide_after) + EXTENSION_GRACE_S — so the agent is not killed mid-window. A deny through /actions-exec-extend-decide ends the extension at once; an approve applies it immediately; silence approves at window end, settled lazily by the next verb that touches the session (in practice the agent’s poll), recorded ext_state = 'silence-approved'. Exactly one push per request: the deny-window warning is the push.
  • Tier 3 — manual only. The original flow: the request pends with a 300-second grace past the lease, the broker raises a needs-drew alert (source fleet-actions-exec), and Drew’s approve or deny returns through exec decide, adding up to +30 minutes to the max and the lease on approval.

The count and total increment on every approval — auto, silence or manual — and never on a deny, so the ladder measures what was actually granted. Every tier’s push carries the detail Drew required: the session handle and its recorded context link, the requesting seat, the host repo, the workflow, run id and run attempt with a click-through run URL, the agent’s stated reason, the lease state, the ask, the cumulative extensions before and after, the tier, and what deny or timeout does at that tier. Alert keys carry the extension ordinal (actions-exec-ext:<handle>:<n>) so successive extensions never dedupe-suppress each other’s pushes. The named gap, unchanged from v1 and stated plainly in the design: the phone tap does not write back to the broker yet — tier-2 denies and tier-3 answers land via a seat running exec decide on Drew’s recorded answer, and the 10-minute window is sized with that relay in mind.

State of the build, 2026-11-23

Landed and deployed: the action and workflow in dezren39/fleet (Slice 2, PR #112 there); the broker verbs, the typed client and the subcommand (PR #13800, merged 5e4107076821); the public door and the R2 provisioning (Slice 5); publication as fleet-static-5e41070 with its bootstrap pin (PR #13817); and the tiered extension policy (PR #13854). The lane’s in-vivo proof battery halted at the Action’s agent-install step when reading the failed run’s log tripped a platform execution-risk check; that stop is recorded on #13774 (2026-11-23T22:57:46Z) with the exact slice state, and the end-to-end live proof — exec on the runner, file out to both the artifact and R2, disconnect/reconnect, renewal, and a short-lease session dying at its cap — remains the open item this chapter does not claim.

Sources

The central compile coordinator

Placement today is a per-seat decision: fleet queue dispatch runs decide() in crates/fleet-queue/src/placement.rs, reads the load its own seat can see, picks the least-loaded surface, and dispatches. The central compile coordinator (#13765) is the designed replacement for the decision’s admission half: a coordinator living in the queue broker that claims slots atomically, holds one true load view, enforces budgets globally, and queues jobs fairly across seats — with the existing singular per-seat dispatch kept, by contract, as the fallback whenever the coordinator does not answer.

This chapter is written from the fleet side: what the coordinator coordinates, where its state lives, and how the fallback works. Placement and remote dispatch covers the engine the coordinator sits under; it stays accurate for the singular path, which is still the only path that runs.

Designed versus built, as of 2026-11-23 — stated once, plainly: the design is complete and of record on #13765 (Drew’s order, 2026-11-23 15:09 CST); the build has not landed. There is no placement_coord module and no coordinator tables in the code on main (grep-verified for this chapter, 2026-11-23). The build was routed as queue task 21517 to a laptop OpenCode session after the first build attempt stopped on a platform execution-risk flag, and task 21517 was then parked — its record states the four-slice build was too large for one unattended run, that no code changed, and that the next step is a dedicated slice-1 task (backend verbs, DDL, tests 1–3). The one piece of the design already in the shipped code is the client-side claim attempt inside Actions exec (below). Every statement in this chapter about coordinator behaviour is a statement about the design, dated here, not about running software.

The four reasons

The design answers four defects of per-seat placement, each with a named proof in the issue’s proof bar:

  1. Atomic slots. Read-then-dispatch is racy: two seats see the same least-loaded pool and both pile in. The observed case in the design record: 62 active org jobs against a cap of 20 — caps steer, they do not gate. The coordinator claims slots atomically. Proof: two simultaneous claims for the last slot — exactly one wins.
  2. One true load view. Load is read per runner-host repo with the seat’s own tokens; a repo the seat has no token for counts as 0 running. (#13611 made the decision logic treat unread load as unknown, but the seat’s view is still only its own.) The coordinator holds the true cross-owner load view, and admission uses it. Proof: a seat with zero coverage for an owner is refused or queued when the coordinator’s view shows the owner full, admitted when it shows room, and /placement-load returns the true counts to any seat.
  3. Global budgets. The Blacksmith budget in the surface registry (fleet-org-blacksmith: budget.free_minutes_monthly = 3000, paid_cap_minutes = 0) is settled today from each seat’s local store — a per-seat honour system. The coordinator enforces it fleet-wide and atomically: reserve at claim, settle at completion. Proof: reservations past the fleet-wide free-minute budget are refused; settle converts a reservation to actual use.
  4. Cross-seat visibility and queueing. Sessions become visible to every seat natively, and when all pools saturate, jobs wait in a real queue with fairness — FIFO per owner — instead of every seat dispatching into the pile. Proof: jobs queue, drain in fair order as slots free, and a claim or session made on one seat resolves from another.

Plus the fallback proof: coordinator down — dispatch still succeeds via singular handling, and the output reports the fallback.

What it coordinates: the three tables

The coordinator’s home is the queue broker’s store — the fleet-queue Turso database, already the fleet’s coordination point, where placement_sessions (#13146) already lives as a best-effort visibility mirror. The design adds three tables there, named in the #13844 Turso audit as “designed to be added to” that store:

TableWhat it holds
placement_owner_stateThe coordinator’s per-owner state: the true load view rows and the active-claim counters admission checks against the owner’s cap (caps from the surface registry: developing-today 20 concurrent jobs, developing-today-forks 20, dezren39 40, macOS 5 each)
placement_claimsOne row per claim: the atomic admission record for a session’s slot on a surface, from grant through confirm to release, including waitlisted claims waiting for capacity
placement_budgetsThe global budget ledger: reservations taken at claim time and settled to actual use at completion, per budget-bearing surface

Admission is the house atomicity pattern — the single conditional UPDATE whose affected-row count decides the winner, the same pattern as task claim in turso_queue/claim.rs — applied to the owner counter in placement_owner_state, with the Blacksmith budget reservation taken in the same flow.

The verbs and the sweep

The backend verbs are designed as a new module, turso_queue/placement_coord.rs, routed in turso_queue::dispatch beside the Actions exec verbs:

VerbJob
/placement-claimAtomic admission: conditional owner-counter UPDATE against the cap, using the coordinator’s load rows plus active claims; budget reservation in the same flow
/placement-confirmConfirm a granted claim with its dispatched run id
/placement-releaseRelease a claim, with budget settle
/placement-claim-statusRead a claim’s state — including from a different seat than the one that made it
/placement-loadThe true load view, readable by any seat

Behind the verbs, a coordinator sweep — a background thread in the queue broker, on the #12247 startup-thread pattern — refreshes the true load view from GitHub on an interval (broker-side reads, the same host-repo counts build_ctx makes, from the seat with full token coverage), expires stale claims and grants, settles confirmed claims whose runs finished, recomputes the active-claim counters from the claims table (self-healing), and grants the waitlist fairly as capacity appears.

The client contract leaves the command surface unchanged. fleet queue dispatch asks the coordinator for a claim on the decided surface before dispatching, in a bounded roundtrip with the same discipline as the #13146 mirror. Granted: dispatch as today, then confirm with the run id. Saturated: the session is committed in state queued with its claim id and full job record — the shape the all-tiers-exhausted path already writes — and fleet queue session status completes the dispatch when the claim is granted.

The fallback: singular per-seat dispatch

The fallback is a contract, not an accident. When the coordinator is unreachable or times out, the command proceeds with today’s singular per-seat dispatch and says so in its output: placement_path names coordinator or singular-fallback, per the estate’s route-visibility doctrine. A down coordinator never hard-fails a build. Scope is the compile/dispatch path only; the agent task queue is untouched, and the two coordinate through the shared broker store.

One consumer already runs this contract. Actions exec (Temporary builds and custom connections) attempts the coordinator claim first, in pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-queue/src/client/actions_exec.rs: ae_placement_claim posts to /placement-claim and returns granted only when a coordinator actually answers; every other outcome — the verbs not live, an error, an ok:false — proceeds on the singular path, named via placement_path. Until the coordinator lands, that is the path every Actions exec session takes.

Dependency map and working order

Prioritised, in the order the build itself must go:

  1. Slice 1 — backend verbs, DDL, proofs 1–3. The placement_coord module, the three tables, and the concurrency, load-view and budget tests. This is the dedicated task the parked task 21517 names as its next step.
  2. Slice 2 — the coordinator sweep. Load refresh, claim expiry, settle, counter recompute, fair waitlist grants.
  3. Slice 3 — client integration. The claim attempt inside fleet queue dispatch, the queued-session completion through fleet queue session status, and placement_path in the output.
  4. Slice 4 — the saturation and fallback proofs. Queueing drains FIFO per owner; coordinator down dispatches singular and reports it.

Dependencies: the broker store and its conditional-UPDATE pattern (landed, #13146); the surface registry’s caps and budgets (landed); broker-side GitHub reads (landed, #8276’s dep probe is the precedent). Nothing in the coordinator blocks Actions exec, which composes with the verbs when they answer and proceeds singular when they do not. A design-review note stands on #13765 (AUDIT-7, #13876, 2026-11-24T00:11:05Z): the design is strong, and one record gap is named — the design of record lives only in the issue body, where comparable programmes keep a dated record under doc/.
