Cross-links: automation, Cloudflare pipes and DNS

Three topics sit on the fleet’s border, with their primary coverage owned by the Lab Book — the book of the Code Book + Lab Book programme (#13905), covering the physical lab, the cluster programme and the network around both, published at developing-today.github.io/code/lab/. This chapter does not duplicate that coverage. It states, for each topic, what the fleet side is and where the primary coverage lives, linking only targets that exist — checked against the repo on 2026-11-23.

A note on timing, because it changed mid-lane: the Lab Book’s part 1 landed while this chapter was being written (PR #13968, merged 2026-11-23 19:25 CST), with sources at pkgs/lab/book/. Part 1 covers the site, the hardware, the cluster programme, the network switches, the ESP32 line and the roadmap. The three topics below map onto it unevenly, and this chapter says which is which: automation has real chapters to link; the pipes are covered inside other chapters, with no dedicated chapter yet; DNS has no Lab Book chapter yet, and its owning programme is named instead of a link invented. The Code Book’s summary chapter, The Lab, remains the one-page overview of the whole lab programme.

Automation and automated scale-up / scale-down

Primary coverage: the Lab Book — landed in part 1. The lab’s automation story is the cluster programme: Talos Linux bootstrapped declaratively with TALM, running Cozystack with FluxCD, on the basement machines of the cluster epic #1817 and the bootstrap epic #1086. Its scale behaviours are the Lab Book’s own chapters:

  • Boot and auto-join — merged priority item 5: all servers online, auto-connecting and presenting to the cluster on boot; no hand-built machine that just exists forever.
  • Talos and Cozystack and The cluster programme — the platform the machines join, and the programme state around it, including “containerised build/compile in the cluster” from #13905’s seed list.

The state those chapters record is the honest one: as of the Lab Book’s latest status record (2026-10-27) nothing in the current cluster programme has been built yet, by design — the machines have no operating system installed, and the build target is the 3–5 best machines first, gated on basement power (#1104, #1105).

The fleet side of scale is a different mechanism, and it is covered here, not there: the fleet scales work, not machines. Placement decides where a build runs (Placement and remote dispatch); the central compile coordinator is designed to admit, queue and drain that work against global caps and budgets (The central compile coordinator); and temporary capacity is borrowed as short-lived Actions runners that scale to zero when their lease ends (Temporary builds and custom connections).

The pipes into Cloudflare and externally

Primary coverage: split, and stated as such. The fleet’s own doors and tunnels are covered in this book and the PM book, because they are fleet machinery: the Commander door (The Commander door: Desktop Commander over MCP), the bridge, the hosted edition’s doors (The hosted edition: fleet-hosted), the exec door’s tunnel ingress (Temporary builds and custom connections) and the queue watchdog that probes one of those pipes from outside (The queue watchdog: queue-transport-alert).

The lab-side half sits inside the Lab Book’s part 1 rather than in a chapter of its own: The cluster programme carries the first lab Cloudflare Tunnel (live 2026-11-06 on the laptop, seed ingress lab.security.cab, #6455) as the programme’s one live artefact, lists the Cloudflare tunnel among the day-one platform services (epic #1088), and holds the egress section — the strategy for the 2 Gbps home fiber, designed in #5030 (open): tunnel or shunt bulk traffic to cheap-or-free-egress services, compress aggressively. Switches covers the physical network the pipes land on. No dedicated pipes chapter exists in either book yet. The estate-wide half — Turso and Cloudflare across databases, edge, gateway and DNS — is epic #8987 (open), with its design record in #8870 and the follow-on record #13912 (both open); until that programme lands its coverage, those trackers are the record and this section is the map to them.

Primary coverage: the Lab Book programme (#13905) for the estate view — no chapter yet; the working machinery is in this repo today. The Lab Book’s part 1 SUMMARY (checked 2026-11-23) has no DNS chapter, and this section names the topic and its owner rather than linking a page that does not exist. Built-in commands

The fleet binary has five root built-in commands that belong to no domain: init, session bind, version, capabilities, and help. They are available in every build variant (fleet, fleet-serve, fleet-connect) because they describe the binary and its registry rather than any domain’s work.

Two rules govern all five, without exception:

  • Built-ins take no arguments. A trailing argument is a usage error naming it, exit 2 — never silently discarded. The one exception is a lone help flag: fleet version --help, fleet capabilities --help, and fleet help --help each print that built-in’s own short usage and exit 0 (#13175) — the same leaf-verb convention as elsewhere in the binary. A help flag followed by anything else is still a usage error.
  • Bare fleet is an error. With no subcommand at all, the binary prints a missing-subcommand message and the full help to stderr and exits 2. fleet --help, fleet -h, and fleet help (exactly one word) print the registry help and exit 0. fleet --version and fleet -V print the short version form (see version below).

A domain an invocation cannot use answers with a stub on stderr and exit 69 (EX_UNAVAILABLE). There are four stub wordings, one per reason class: the domain is not in this build, the invocation name (fleet-serve / fleet-connect) narrowed the surface away, the [domains] table in fleet config disabled the domain on this host, or the domain is included but not yet implemented. Every stub’s second line is Enabled capabilities: <comma list> (none when empty). Help marks unavailable domains inline — [not in this build], [narrowed out by this name], [disabled by config] — but prints the full registry on every variant: every build knows every domain.

Config resolution lives in one place (fleet-config): environment overrides (FLEET_CONFIG, FLEET_BROKER_SOCKET) beat the config file ($FLEET_CONFIG, else ${XDG_CONFIG_HOME:-~/.config}/fleet/fleet.toml), which beats compiled-in defaults. A missing file is not an error; a malformed file — including unknown sections or keys — is a loud error on every path, never a silent fallback.

Sources: fleet main.rs, fleet-registry, fleet-config, fleet-proxy client, session state.

fleet init

Usage: fleet init
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
(none)——init takes no arguments and no flags. Any trailing argument is a usage error, exit 2. The identical command is also spelled fleet proxy init; both spellings resolve to one implementation.

Behaviour. fleet init autostarts this host’s fleet roles if they are not running, per the [host] manifest. It first runs session initialisation (see session bind below); a session error is exit 2 before any role work. The capability ladder applies before anything else: a build whose usable surface lacks proxy-serve can only stub init, exit 69.

The manifest resolution order is:

  1. FLEET_HOST_CONFIG — a complete inline [host] manifest; wins outright. A manifest with no location is a loud error.
  2. FLEET_LOCATION — names the location; roles come from the config file’s [host] section only if the file’s location matches, else from the built-in map.
  3. The config file’s [host] section — location, init_mode, and [host.roles]; the role set is exactly the key set of the roles table, and an unknown role name is a loud parse error, never silently ignored.

Only two built-in locations exist today; a future lab node provisions its own [host] section instead of growing the table:

Locationinit_modeRoles
sandboxspawnproxy, secrets-broker
laptopsystemdlaptop-agent, queue-broker, search, secrets-broker

The full [host] role vocabulary is five names — proxy, queue-broker, secrets-broker, search, laptop-agent — a superset of the serve roles (it includes laptop-agent, which is not a serve role).

  • Unknown location (no manifest from any source, or a location with no roles): init reports state — every source consulted, plus detected hostname/OS/systemd for the report only (detection never selects roles) — starts nothing, and exits 69. It never guess-starts a role.
  • Manifest skips and the kill switch: roles the manifest itself disables (enabled = false) are reported as skipped with their reason; then the [domains] gate is applied and wins over the manifest (the proxy role keys on the proxy domain, the daemon roles on serve).
  • spawn mode (sandbox): spawn semantics exist for exactly two roles; any other role in a spawn manifest is reported and skipped, never spawned.
    • proxy: probe the broker socket and say hello. A live broker (either protocol dialect) means status plus PATH-shim sync and out — a strict no-op: never a spawn, never a restart; init never fights an incumbent broker. Only an unanswered socket spawns fleet serve proxy detached, then reports what it started and syncs shims from the new broker’s services map.
    • secrets-broker: probe its Unix socket; a live answer means status and out. Otherwise spawn fleet serve secrets-broker detached (output appended to secrets-broker.log beside the socket) with SECRETS_BROKER_BIND=127.0.0.1:4800 set explicitly — and the broker forces loopback itself when FLEET_LOCATION=sandbox, so the sandbox broker is loopback-only twice over. Init then waits (50 × 100 ms probes) for the socket to answer before reporting success.
  • systemd mode (laptop): init never detached-spawns a daemon systemd owns. For each role it reports fleet-<role>.service state via systemctl --user is-active; an active unit is a no-op; an inactive but existing unit is started via systemctl --user start; a missing unit is reported and skipped, not an error; unavailable systemctl is a report, not a spawn.

Exit codes: 0 ok (including the all-roles-already-running no-op) · 2 usage error or session-initialisation error · 69 capability stub, or unknown location (starts nothing).

$ fleet init
proxy: running (broker socket answers; shims synced)
secrets-broker: running (socket answers)
$ echo $?
0

fleet session bind

Usage: fleet session bind [--session-id ID]
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
--session-idsession idresolved (see Behaviour)The explicit session identity to validate and persist. Both --session-id ID and --session-id=ID spellings are accepted; at most one value — a second value is the usage error shown in the help dump.

Behaviour. fleet session bind validates and persists this worktree’s session identity. The identity is an OpenCode session id of the form ses_ followed by ASCII letters and digits — anything else fails closed.

Resolution precedence: the explicit --session-id → $FLEET_SESSION_ID → the OpenCode environment → the worktree’s marker file. The marker is a plain one-line file .fleet-session-id at the git worktree root, so each worktree retains its own active session association. A marker is used only when the session is live — checked against the OpenCode server’s session endpoint; a stale marker (ended or unverifiable session) is an explicit error naming the file and the id, never a silent fall-through, and an unavailable server is not proof a recorded session is live.

A successful bind sets FLEET_SESSION_ID for fleet’s child processes and persists the identity to the marker, so a later bare invocation in the same worktree resolves the same session. Every domain invocation runs this initialisation (with no explicit id) before dispatch; fleet init runs it explicitly.

Exit codes: 0 ok · 2 usage error, malformed session id, or stale/unverifiable marker.

$ fleet session bind --session-id ses_01J9EXAMPLE0000000000000
session bound: ses_01J9EXAMPLE0000000000000 (worktree marker .fleet-session-id)
$ fleet session bind --session-id not-a-session
fleet session: invalid session id 'not-a-session' (expected ses_ followed by letters/digits)

fleet version

Usage: fleet version
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
(none)——version takes no arguments. fleet version --help is a usage error, exit 2. The short form is spelled fleet --version or fleet -V.

Behaviour. fleet version prints five lines; the short --version / -V form prints only the first two:

fleet 0.1.0
Build: fleet [(invoked as <name>; surface narrowed to the <variant> profile)]
Derived version: 0.1.0-dev+gb8bbcc0
Source rev: b8bbcc0c49564ab31db8d58b026b67532db9491e
Enabled capabilities: proxy-connect, proxy-serve, … (usable set, registry order)

The fields are: the workspace version; the build name — fleet, fleet-serve, or fleet-connect, derived by matching the compiled capability set against the variant sets (an unrecognised compiled set falls back to the plain build name) — with the profile annotation when the invocation name narrowed the surface; the derived version (the 0.1.0-dev+g<rev> form); the source rev (the full commit SHA the build was cut from); and the enabled capabilities — the usable set (compiled ∩ profile ∩ [domains] enables), comma-joined in registry order, or none. The values above are the reference build’s, as captured in the capabilities dump.

There are 22 capability atoms, in registry order: proxy-connect, proxy-serve, proxy-raw-splice, queue, queue-broker, secrets-broker, search, search-serve, dispatch, dispatch-test, laptop-agent, secrets, gh, bridge, agent, commander, laptop-http, laptop-ssh, laptop, cert, actions, orgs. proxy-connect is unconditional — present in every variant. The three build variants are: Full (fleet, all 22), Serve (fleet-serve: proxy-connect, proxy-serve, proxy-raw-splice, queue-broker, secrets-broker, search-serve, secrets — daemon roles plus proxy, no working-seat clients), and Connect (fleet-connect: proxy-connect, proxy-raw-splice only). Invoking the binary under a hyphenated name selects that profile as a ceiling; profiles can only narrow, never widen. An unknown invocation name is a usage error, exit 2, naming the expected names.

Exit codes: 0 ok · 2 usage error (any argument, including --help).

$ fleet version
fleet 0.1.0
Build: fleet
Derived version: 0.1.0-dev+gb8bbcc0
Source rev: b8bbcc0c49564ab31db8d58b026b67532db9491e
Enabled capabilities: proxy-connect, proxy-serve, proxy-raw-splice, queue, queue-broker, secrets-broker, search, search-serve, dispatch, dispatch-test, laptop-agent, secrets, gh, bridge, agent

Per-domain state is one of available, not-in-build, narrowed-by-name, disabled-by-config (the four reason classes behind the exit-69 stub), and available is exactly state == "available". Note the two distinct capability lists: capabilities is what this invocation can use; compiled_capabilities is what the binary was built with — their difference is the profile/config narrowing. In the reference build both are the full 22 and every domain is available. One registry quirk: the shell domain’s capability list is ["agent"] — there is no shell capability atom; shell rides on the agent capability.

fleet help

Usage: fleet help [domain]
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
<domain> (positional)domain namefull registryWith no argument, prints the full registry help (identical to fleet --help). With one domain name, prints that domain’s help. A second argument is rejected. fleet help --help is an error: there is no domain named --help.

Behaviour. fleet help with no argument prints the full registry: fleet 0.1.0 — one multicall binary for the fleet's tools, the usage lines, all 19 domains with summaries and argv0 aliases, the five built-in commands, and the note that a domain this invocation cannot use answers with a stub and exit code 69. fleet help <domain> prints the domain’s registry help: summary line, Usage: fleet <domain> <command> [args...], argv0 aliases, the command list, and a status line whose wording is per-domain and capability-aware. An unknown name is a usage error: error: no domain named '<name>' — run 'fleet --help' for the registry, exit 2. Domain help is registry data and renders identically on every build, with unavailable domains marked — help never stubs.

Exit codes: 0 ok · 2 unknown domain name or extra argument.

Next: the queue domain itself, starting with fleet queue: core verbs.

fleet queue: core verbs

fleet queue is the repo work queue: enqueue, claim, and complete tasks through the queue broker. Inside the binary the same surface is the standalone repo-queue program, and every per-verb usage string says repo-queue, not fleet queue; the two spellings are identical. The full command list is: validate, enqueue, list, claim, release, lane, bind, heartbeat, checkpoint, park, wake, block, unblock, dep-recheck, quarantine-recheck, cancel, revive, fail, complete, verify-disposition, timeline, history, show, models, health, signal, fallback, dispatch, session, surfaces, outbox, stack.

Task states are queued, claimed, parked, blocked, needs_review (live) and done, failed, cancelled (terminal).

This chapter covers the core verbs — validate, enqueue, list, claim, release, show, health. The lifecycle verbs are in fleet queue: lifecycle verbs, the GitHub fallback in fleet queue: the fallback queue, dispatch and sessions in fleet queue: dispatch and sessions, and inspection/admin in fleet queue: inspection and admin.

How the client reaches the broker

The client never touches the database and never fetches from Bitwarden; it POSTs JSON to the queue-broker, which is the only process that talks to the Turso store (database fleet-queue). There are two routes, in selection order:

  1. Direct route (on-laptop), chosen when a broker URL is configured: environment REPO_QUEUE_BROKER_URL, else the file ~/.config/repo-queue/broker-url. A unix://<path> value selects the broker’s Unix socket; anything else is read as http://host:port TCP (the broker dual-binds TCP + UDS; default TCP bind is the laptop tailnet address, port 4801). The direct-route token comes from env REPO_QUEUE_TOKEN_FILE, else ~/.config/queue-broker/token, sent as header X-Agent-Token. Wire: raw HTTP/1.1, read timeout 300 s, write timeout 60 s. With no configured URL, fleet-config’s probe-based choice for the queue-broker role applies: a live role socket selects UDS; a failed UDS attempt falls back to the session-proxy route within the same call.
  2. Session-proxy route (sandbox default): the client connects to the laptop-agent session proxy’s Unix socket — $HOME/.cache/laptop-agent/broker.sock (fleet-config’s broker_socket() wins when it loads; env beats config file beats that compiled-in default). Framing: 8-byte big-endian length prefix + one JSON envelope {method:"POST", path, body, port:4801, token_file:"<home>/tools/queue-broker-token"}. The proxy, on the laptop, reads the named token file there and forwards to the broker on port 4801. Read timeout 660 s. On a failed first attempt the client auto-spawns the proxy/broker program — a sibling fleet binary (fleet proxy serve) always wins; the Python ~/tools/laptop-agent-broker.py is the fallback for standalone rollback builds — waits up to ~5 s for the socket, and retries once.

Broker-unavailable on either route is exit 3, or the fallback switch (exit 6) for the work verbs — see fleet queue: the fallback queue.

Broker envelopes are {ok:true, ...} or {ok:false, exit, error}; the client prints error and exits with exit. A broker envelope whose error carries PostgREST code 57014 (statement timeout) or PGRST002 (schema cache) is retried with exponential backoff + jitter — base 500 ms, ×2, cap 20 s, max 6 attempts. Safe for writes because a 57014 means the statement rolled back.

Broker server facts that shape client behaviour: the pre-body gate refuses from headers alone — wrong/missing token → 401 {"error":"unauthorized"}; Content-Length over the 16 MiB cap → 413 {"error":"request body too large"}. The only unauthenticated route is GET /healthz → {"service":"queue-broker"}. Non-POST → 405. Token files are read + trimmed; a missing, unreadable, empty, or whitespace-only file is a hard error naming the file. Before dispatch, the broker re-validates durations and not_before with the same ranges as the client; violations answer {ok:false, exit:2, …}. /validate and /healthz are served without the Turso backend; everything else answers exit 3 queue backend not ready: … until the backend connects.

Global parsing rules and defaults

  • Help: repo-queue with no args prints the top usage and exits 2; a single --help/-h/help exits 0. <verb> --help anywhere in the verb’s args prints that verb’s exact usage and exits 0 — help wins over every other argument, except when the help-looking token is the value of a value-flag (fail 5 --error help records the error text “help”; park 5 --reason -h parks with reason “-h”).
  • Parsing errors are exit 2: unknown flag, duplicate flag, a boolean given an inline value (--dry-run=false), a value flag with no value, a value flag followed by another --flag token, extra positionals past a verb’s arity (rejected before any broker contact), and non-numeric values for numeric flags (the message names the flag). Message + the verb’s usage go to stderr.
  • --worker default: repo-worker-code. Exceptions: cancel defaults its worker to fleet-monitor (see lifecycle verbs); stack record’s owner worker and the outbox owner defaults differ (see inspection and admin).
  • --queue default — the divergence. The nominal default is repo-health-code-shadow, overridable by env REPO_QUEUE_DEFAULT_QUEUE — but claim and list are unscoped when neither flag nor env is present (one-queue model: the broker works across the one fleet queue), and enqueue has no default at all. Every other verb keeps the shadow default. The help surface presents all three behaviours identically ([--queue <name>] everywhere), so the divergence is invisible from help alone. Known discrepancy: this divergence is deliberate in source (#7016, #8097) but undocumented in help.
  • --lane on the holder-checked verbs (heartbeat, checkpoint, park, release, block, fail, complete): flag, else env REPO_QUEUE_LANE, else null — the broker then checks the worker alone. All scheduled lanes share one worker id, so the lane is what tells the broker whose claim a verb acts on.
  • --progress / --progress-file are mutually exclusive (both → exit 2). The file form reads the file’s text as the progress value.
  • --execution <id> (park, fail, complete) is parsed into an execution record {lane, lane_id?, session_id, fallback_reason?}; a lane-looking value (e.g. opencode-a, any-n) is split into mode (opencode/direct) + lane_id; the mode-only values direct/opencode pass through unchanged.
  • Durations are rejected, never clamped, identically at client and broker: lease 1..=86400 (default 2700), heartbeat extend 1..=86400 (default 900), park delay 1..=604800 (no default), list limit 1..=500 (default 20). not_before must be a non-empty RFC 3339 timestamp no more than 366 days in the future.
  • Mode line: claim, heartbeat, checkpoint, complete (and the fallback-switch envelope) carry a mode_line object {verb, mode, route} selected by the routing contract from observed legs (database / replica / github-write / github-read). Modes: normal (route cloud), gh-read-degraded, gh-write-degraded, db-degraded (route github-markers).

Exit codes (the whole queue client)

Stated once here and referenced by every other queue chapter:

  • 0 — success.
  • 1 — gate / not-found: verify-disposition gate failure or unreadable GitHub readback; show task not found; fallback complete disposition rejection.
  • 2 — usage error (message + usage on stderr).
  • 3 — transport / broker-path failure: broker unreachable, HTTP 401 (token rejected), HTTP ≥400 broker error, malformed broker reply, unwritable signal file, /events-list not served by the broker (timeline/show), home unresolvable.
  • 4 — broker store failure: the default when a broker envelope {ok:false} carries no exit of its own; broker-side store/transport failures are emitted as exit 4. Also stack replay’s routed-conflict exit.
  • 5 — no-claim / no-row: the verb ran but there is no matching claimed row / no claimable task (require_row failure: “no matching claimed row (task not claimed by this worker, or already terminal)”).
  • 6 — fallback switch: a work verb’s primary-store failure switched the work to the GitHub fallback (see the fallback queue).

Sources: fleet-queue client, client support, client transport, queue broker, Turso queue store.

fleet queue validate

usage: repo-queue validate <packet-path>
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
<packet-path> (positional)file pathrequiredThe packet JSON file to validate.
(no flags)——validate has no flags at all — not even --json; output is always the JSON object below.

Behaviour. Loads the packet and validates it through the broker (/validate). An unreadable file dies exit 2 cannot read packet file: …; invalid JSON dies exit 2 packet file is not valid JSON: …. Validation failure dies with the broker’s exit code and the joined error list. On success it prints, on stdout, {"valid": true, "dedupe_key": <packet.dedupe_key|null>, "kind": <payload.kind|null>, "title": <packet.title|null>}.

The validator checks, among other things: priority on the design scale [10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 70, 90]; max_attempts 1..=1000 (design default 1000); payload size hard ceiling 16384 bytes (warn above 4096); the payload schema const "repo-task/v1"; kind one of six values the validator allows (pr_shepherd, triage, small_fix, ci_investigation, second_pass, feature_slice); repo on the validator’s 9-repo allowlist; and the identity rule — a packet must carry at least one of issue, prs (non-empty), set, or source.

Known discrepancy: the published packet schema (repo-task-v1.schema.json) allows only 4 kinds and 8 repos; the validator allows 6 kinds (adding second_pass, feature_slice) and 9 repos (adding legacy dezren39/nix, kept for in-flight dedupe keys after the rename to dezren39/darwin-nix). A packet valid to the broker can be invalid against the published schema, and vice versa. This chapter documents the validator (source) behaviour.

Exit codes: 0 valid · 2 unreadable file / invalid JSON / usage · broker’s exit code on validation failure.

$ fleet queue validate ./task.json
{"valid": true, "dedupe_key": "fix: repo-health:v1:fix:developing-today/code:issue:13165", "kind": "small_fix", "title": "Write the fleet book queue chapters"}

fleet queue enqueue

usage: repo-queue enqueue <packet-path> [--queue <name>] [--platform <p>] [--dry-run] [--shadow-intent]
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
<packet-path> (positional)file pathrequiredThe packet JSON file to enqueue.
--queuequeue namenone — required in effectTarget queue stream. Resolution: --queue flag → the packet’s own "queue" field → env REPO_QUEUE_DEFAULT_QUEUE. With none of the three: exit 2 (see Behaviour).
--platformplatform familyunsetRestricts the item to a platform family; validated client-side. Absent = unset, claimable anywhere.
--dry-runbooleanoffValidate + ask the broker to build the row, print it, file nothing.
--shadow-intentbooleanoffRequired to enqueue into a queue whose name ends in -shadow; without it, exit 2.

Behaviour. Flow: read packet (exit 2 shapes as in validate) → broker /validate (a dry run still validates, with dry_run noted) → shadow guard → POST /enqueue {packet, queue, dry_run, shadow_intent, platform}.

Queue resolution deliberately differs from every other verb: with no flag, no packet "queue" field, and no env, enqueue dies exit 2 with enqueue: no queue resolved — … (enqueue has no default queue; the old shadow default silently misrouted work).

Outputs:

  • Dry run: the would-be task row as JSON, with two extra keys: "_dry_run": true and "_rpc": "agent.enqueue_repo_task". Exit 0.
  • Real run: one human line, any warning: … lines, then the task row as JSON. Exit 0. The line is one of:
    • enqueued new task <id> (queue <q>, status <s>) — row created within 10 s skew of the call;
    • dedupe hit: existing task <id> (queue <q>, status <s>, created <ts>) — the dedupe key already has a live row; nothing was filed. Warnings are added when the holding row is in a different queue than requested, or in a terminal state;
    • revived: existing task <id> (…) — dedupe hit on a queued row whose updated_at is fresh (broker revived it in place);
    • revived: new task <id> (…), predecessor task <pid> (<pstatus>) — the envelope carried revived_from: the key’s prior task was terminal, a fresh task was created linked to it;
    • work already queued: existing task <id> (queue <q>, status <s>) holds <identity>; nothing filed (set payload.dedupe_override to file a deliberate parallel) — the envelope carried work_identity_collision: a live task already holds this work identity (repo, issue, kind family), regardless of dedupe key.

Dedupe semantics: dedupe is by (queue, dedupe_key) among live rows (the Turso backend does a read-then-insert check — its (queue, dedupe_key) index is deliberately NOT unique). A key held only by terminal rows accepts a new row. A cancelled row is revived in place by enqueue (fields reset, attempts 0, lease deleted, enqueued event flagged revived_from_cancelled); a failed row deliberately does not revive — re-enqueue of a failed identity files a new row or is an explicit operator action (the revive verb).

At enqueue the broker also: enriches a packet that names an issue but carries no labels array from the GitHub mirror in the same store; selects the stored priority from label bands (expedite → 15, next-up → 25 — stored values deliberately not on the packet priority scale); and normalizes max_attempts / required_budget_minutes from the packet copy into the payload mirror.

Exit codes: 0 enqueued / dedupe hit / revived / dry run · 2 unreadable packet, invalid JSON, no queue resolved, shadow queue without --shadow-intent, usage · 3 transport · 4 broker store failure.

$ fleet queue enqueue ./task.json --queue repo-health-code
enqueued new task 19479 (queue repo-health-code, status queued)
{"id": 19479, "queue": "repo-health-code", "status": "queued", "dedupe_key": "fix: repo-health:v1:fix:developing-today/code:issue:13165", "payload": {"schema": "repo-task/v1", "kind": "small_fix", "…": "…"}}

fleet queue list

usage: repo-queue list [--queue <name>] [--status <s>] [--limit <n>] [--not-before <ts>] [--lane <l>] [--worker <w>] [--task <id>] [--json]
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
--queuequeue nameunscopedFlag → env REPO_QUEUE_DEFAULT_QUEUE → no scope (all queues). Never the shadow default.
--statusstatus stringunsetFilter by status. Help names queued|parked|claimed|blocked as the actionable set; any status string is forwarded.
--limitinteger20Range 1..=500, rejected (never clamped) outside it, exit 2 naming --limit.
--not-beforeRFC 3339 timestampunsetFilter; validated client-side with the park/revive rule, exit 2 on garbage.
--lanelane idunsetFilter forwarded to the broker.
--workerworker idunsetFilter forwarded to the broker.
--tasktask idunsetNarrow to one task regardless of status ordering — the recovery path for verifying a just-completed task.
--json—offExact-task status form: requires --queue and --task together; see Exact form below. The bulk flags do not apply in that form.

Behaviour. A bare list prints a scope note to stderr: it shows one queue (or every queue when unscoped) in the broker’s default ordering — newest terminal rows first — “not the actionable set”, with pointers to --status, --queue, --limit. Fetching is paged at 100 rows/page with broker offsets, because a single oversized /list reply used to render as a silent “(no tasks)”. A reply with no rows array is an error (exit 3), never an empty list.

Output is a table with columns task, priority, status, age, dedupe_key, title (title truncated to 72 chars); (no tasks) when empty. When the broker reports a total: (N matching tasks), or (truncated: showing X of N matching tasks — raise --limit to see more).

Exact form (--json, #8581 pilot). With --json, --queue and --task are required together (exit 2 without both) and no other list flag applies (exit 2 naming it). The verb makes one scoped rich /list read and prints a single JSON record instead of the table: verb, mode and route actually used (the #8581 contract vocabulary), queue, task_id, as_of (when this seat observed the answer), and a result of found (the broker row rides under task, attributed to source: cloud, with the row’s own task_as_of when it carries a timestamp), not_found, partial, or unknown. Only a complete authoritative zero — ok reply, empty rows, total reported as 0, no truncation — is not_found; a truncated window, an uncertified zero, or a reply naming other tasks is partial with a detail naming why, and a transport failure, a denial, a broker error envelope, a malformed reply, or a matching row that names a different queue is unknown with its own detail. This slice attempts no replica or marker fallback: when nothing served, the record says mode: db-degraded, route: unavailable rather than naming a route it never took. Exit codes in this form: 0 found · 1 not_found · 3 partial / unknown / transport · the broker envelope’s own exit (default 4) on a broker error.

Exit codes: 0 ok · 2 usage (including out-of-range --limit, bad --not-before) · 3 transport / malformed reply · 4 broker store failure.

$ fleet queue list --status queued --limit 3
task     priority  status  age   dedupe_key                                                        title
19479    20        queued  4m    fix: repo-health:v1:fix:developing-today/code:issue:13165         Write the fleet book queue chapters
19480    30        queued  2m    triage: repo-health:v1:triage:developing-today/code:issue:13170   Triage the failing nightly
(2 matching tasks)

fleet queue claim

usage: repo-queue claim [--queue <name>] [--worker <id>] [--lease-seconds <n>] [--lane <l>] [--task <id>] [--count <n>] [--from-session <id>] [--platform <p>] [--session-id <id>] [--model-provider <p>] [--model-id <id>] [--model-variant <v>] [--filter <f>] [--pool <p>] [--launched-by <who>] [--remaining-budget-minutes <n>] [--handoff] [--bind]
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
--queuequeue nameunscopedFlag → env → unscoped across the one fleet queue, priority order.
--workerworker idrepo-worker-codeClaiming worker identity, stamped on the row + leases table. Passing it explicitly counts as claim intent even though it equals the default (see bare-claim refusal).
--lease-secondsinteger seconds2700 (45 min)Lease length. Range 1..=86400, rejected outside, exit 2. A 0/negative lease is “born expired”.
--lanelane idunsetLane identity for this claim; validated broker-side against the lane registry (unknown lane / worker mismatch / disabled lane / queue mismatch each refuse and claim nothing). Canonical lane universe: 6 families (code, any, not-code, opencode, openchamber, nix) × a..=z = 156 lanes, all enabled.
--tasktask idunsetBy-id claim: take exactly that row when the by-id predicate allows (a queued row under the ordinary predicate, or a sink/handed-off row).
--countinteger1Batch claim: the broker runs the same atomic pick n times. Range 1..=5, enforced client- and broker-side; outside → exit 2.
--from-sessionsession idunsetWith --task: session-to-session transfer. The named session must be the task’s current holder (its session mark is the capability); a mismatch refuses and leaves the claim untouched. The task never passes through queued/parked.
--platformplatform familyunsetA mark, not a filter: stamped on the row and the claimed event; a mismatched or undeclared claim claims items all the same.
--session-idsession idunsetThe claiming session’s own id, recorded as a mark on the claimed event; also enables model-stamp derivation and --bind. Session ids have the shape ses_ + alphanumerics.
--model-providerprovider nameunsetThe claiming session’s serving model provider, stamped by the broker as the row’s claim_provider.
--model-idmodel idunsetStamped as the row’s claim_model.
--model-variantvariant nameunsetStamped as the row’s claim_variant. If all model flags are absent and --session-id is given, the stamp is derived from the session’s own record; derivation failure never fails the claim.
--filterfilter expressionunsetClaimer-side boolean filter expression over task metadata (repo, queue, pool, platform, label, kind, priority, lane, model), evaluated by the broker inside the claim.
--poolpool identityunsetThe claimer’s declared pool identity; recorded like the other marks and used only to satisfy a task’s own requires.pool.
--launched-bywhoopencode-claimant (only sent with --bind)Who launched the bound session.
--remaining-budget-minutesinteger minutesunsetThe claimer’s remaining shift budget. The broker only matches requirement-bearing tasks whose required_budget_minutes fits; omitting it leaves requirement-bearing tasks unclaimed. Skips are reported (see no-claim output).
--handoffbooleanoffPick = the next recorded opencode handoff (status handed_off) from the sink; the broker picks the row, the caller names no task.
--bindbooleanoffClaim + lane-assign + session-bind in ONE broker round trip via /claim-flow. Requires --session-id, a single (non-batch) claim, and no --from-session; violations die exit 2 before broker contact. A post-claim lane/bind failure inside the flow is answered as a partial SUCCESS envelope carrying claim_flow_partial (never a retryable error) — the client prints the note on stderr and stamps claim_flow_partial onto the printed row.

Behaviour — bare-claim refusal. A claim with no task, no filter, no queue scope, no count, no handoff/bind, and no identity marks (worker, lane, session-id, pool, platform, from-session) is refused before any broker contact, exit 2: “a bare claim is never a meaningful intent and has repeatedly stolen the queue’s top task during CLI probing”.

Behaviour — the pick. One atomic conditional update (libSQL is single-writer, so the claim is one conditional UPDATE whose WHERE re-checks claimability against the picked row; a competing claim after the first lands matches no row and returns no claim, exit 5). Eligible: queued rows with attempts < max_attempts and not_before null or due, plus parked rows whose not_before is due. Order: priority ASC, created_at ASC (lowest number = highest priority). Claiming sets status claimed, worker_id, claimed_at, lease_until = now + lease_seconds, upserts the leases row, writes a claimed event — and increments attempts by 1 for a fresh (queued) claim but 0 for a parked resume (park/resume must not consume attempts; the event carries resumed_from_park). Every claim first runs lease expiry opportunistically: abandoned claims whose lease lapsed become claimable at the moment anyone looks.

Behaviour — no-double-serve guard. After a successful primary claim, the client checks the task’s issue against the GitHub fallback (see the fallback queue). If the issue is live or contested in the fallback under a different worker, the client immediately blocks the task back with reason-class fallback_held and prints {"task": null, "guard": "fallback_held", "held_by": <w>, "repo": …, "issue": …}, exit 5. If the GitHub check itself fails, the claim is served with a guard_warning key added (the guard fails open; a GitHub outage must not stall every claim). Batch claims run the same guard per row; held rows land in guard_held.

Behaviour — timeline mirroring. On a pre-#9046 broker the client appends session_bound / model_stamp events after a claim (and a session_unbound for the from-session on a transfer); a post-#9046 broker stamps in-op and its rows carry claim_session_id, making the appends a no-op. Timeline appends are fail-soft — they warn, never fail the claim.

Output. Success: the task row verbatim as JSON (the row is the contract: {id, queue, status, dedupe_key, payload, …}), exit 0, plus a mode_line. A row that arrives with a null or empty-object payload is treated as payload-less and reported as no claim. Batch output: {"tasks": […rows…], "claimed": k, "requested": n, "guard_held": […]}, exit 0 when k ≥ 1. No-claim output: {"task": null} — deliberately carrying no id/queue/status a caller could mistake for a task — plus any of budget_skipped, max_required_budget_minutes, queued, at_cap_queued, queued_not_yet_due, parked_due the broker supplied; stderr gets the diagnostic no claimable task — Q queued (A at the attempt cap, D not yet due), P parked due (with ; every queued task is at the attempt cap when that is the whole story). Exit 5.

Exit codes: 0 claimed · 2 usage / bare-claim refusal / out-of-range lease or count / --bind precondition failure · 3 transport · 4 broker store failure · 5 no claimable task, or claim held by the no-double-serve guard · 6 fallback switch on primary-store failure.

$ fleet queue claim --worker repo-worker-code --lane code-a --session-id ses_01J9EXAMPLE0000000000000
{"id": 19479, "queue": "repo-health-code", "status": "claimed", "worker_id": "repo-worker-code", "lane_id": "code-a", "lease_until": "2026-11-23T04:50:00Z", "dedupe_key": "fix: repo-health:v1:fix:developing-today/code:issue:13165", "payload": {"schema": "repo-task/v1", "kind": "small_fix"}, "mode_line": {"verb": "claim", "mode": "normal", "route": "cloud"}}
$ fleet queue claim --worker repo-worker-code --lane code-a
{"task": null, "queued": 0, "parked_due": 0}
no claimable task — 0 queued (0 at the attempt cap, 0 not yet due), 0 parked due
(exit 5)

fleet queue release

usage: repo-queue release <task-id> [--worker <id>] [--lane <id>] [--reason <text>]
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
<task-id> (positional)task idrequiredThe claimed task to release.
--workerworker idrepo-worker-codeHolder identity; the row must be claimed by this worker (and lane, when supplied).
--lanelane idenv REPO_QUEUE_LANE, else nullHolder lane check; null means the broker checks the worker alone.
--reasontextrequiredWhy this task goes back to the pool; recorded on a released event. Must be non-empty.

Behaviour. Returns the task to queued, immediately claimable; the reason is recorded on a released event. Used by dispatch for an item whose sub-task failed to launch/bind — back to the pool in the same touch instead of sitting claimed until lease expiry. Release also closes the session binding window on the timeline (session_unbound, trigger release). On success it prints the broker’s returned task row as JSON and exits 0. When no matching claimed row exists, it dies exit 5 with release: no matching claimed row (task not claimed by this worker, or already terminal).

Help: the usage writes --reason bare — it is required and non-empty — missing → exit 2 release requires --reason "<why this task goes back to the pool>" (#8217). The top-level usage line lists the same flags as the per-verb usage, [--lane <id>] included; a parity test cross-checks the two so they cannot drift apart again.

Exit codes: 0 released · 2 usage / missing or empty --reason · 3 transport · 4 broker store failure · 5 no matching claimed row.

$ fleet queue release 19479 --worker repo-worker-code --lane code-a --reason "sub-task failed to launch; returning to pool"
{"id": 19479, "queue": "repo-health-code", "status": "queued", "worker_id": null, "lease_until": null}

usage: repo-queue show <task-id> [--limit <n>] [--json]
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
<task-id> (positional)task idrequiredThe task to show.
--limitinteger10History tail length; validated with the list-limit rule (1..=500), rejected outside, exit 2.
--jsonbooleanoffPrint the details + history as JSON instead of the rendered form.

Shows one task’s current details + recent history: the rich /list row for the task is the source of truth for mutable state, plus the tail of the same 14-kind event timeline timeline reads (see inspection and admin). Task not found: stderr repo-queue show: task <id> not found, exit 1. A broker without /events-list: exit 3.

fleet queue health

usage: repo-queue health [--queue <name>] [--worker <id>]
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
--queuequeue nameunsetScopes the request body when given. Health uses the plain flag only — no env/shadow-default resolution is applied to the body.
--workerworker idrepo-worker-codeAttribution only — accepted because the claimant packet mandates --worker on every verb; it changes neither the request body nor the printed table.

Output: first line project: <netloc> (resolved via <source>) (source defaults to bitwarden), then a table whose columns are whatever keys the broker’s health rows carry (per-queue counts by status); (no queues have tasks) when empty. $ fleet queue health

queue                 queued  claimed  parked  blocked  done
repo-health-code      12      3        1       0        481

fleet queue: lifecycle verbs

The lifecycle verbs move a claimed task through its life: attribution (lane, bind), lease care (heartbeat, checkpoint), waiting (park, wake, block, unblock, dep-recheck, quarantine-recheck, repair), and the terminal/revival verbs (cancel, revive, fail, complete, verify-disposition).

Shared rules, stated in fleet queue: core verbs and not repeated in full here: the global exit-code vocabulary (0 ok, 1 gate/not-found, 2 usage, 3 transport/401, 4 broker store failure, 5 no-claim/no-row, 6 fallback switch); the --worker default repo-worker-code; the --lane resolution (flag → env REPO_QUEUE_LANE → null, broker checks worker alone); and --progress / --progress-file mutual exclusion.

Holder-checked verbs. lane, bind, heartbeat, checkpoint, park, release, block, fail, complete are holder-checked broker-side: the row must be claimed by this worker (and lane, when one is supplied) and non-terminal, else the envelope has no row and the client dies exit 5 with <verb>: no matching claimed row (task not claimed by this worker, or already terminal). On success they print the broker’s returned task row as JSON and exit 0. Several lifecycle verbs answer {task, lane_ledger} (and sometimes follow_on_task_id) instead of the bare row when the broker includes a ledger.

The person-wait guard (FDR-0013) applies to park and block and is described once under block below; park references it.

Sources: commands_lifecycle.rs, commands_query.rs, verify_disposition.rs, disposition.rs, person_wait.rs, turso_queue lifecycle.

fleet queue lane

usage: repo-queue lane <task-id> [--worker <id>] [--exclusion-reason <text>] [--opencode-reason <text>] [--limit-platform <p>] [--limit-reason <text>] [--clear-platform-limit]
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
<task-id> (positional)task idrequiredThe claimed task to report lane progress on.
--workerworker idrepo-worker-codeHolder identity.
--exclusion-reasontextunsetRecorded on the lane ledger as exclusion_reason.
--opencode-reasontextunsetRecorded on the lane ledger as opencode_reason.
--limit-platformplatform familyunsetRecord a platform limitation (platform_limit). Requires --limit-reason (see Behaviour).
--limit-reasontextunsetThe reason for the platform limitation (platform_limit_reason).
--clear-platform-limitbooleanoffClear a recorded platform limitation.

Behaviour. Reports lane progress on a task. Broker route /lane; writes the repo_task_lane_ledger row for the task: assigned_lane (the caller’s lane context), exclusion_reason, opencode_reason, platform_limit, platform_limit_reason. A platform limitation exists only with its recorded reason: the broker refuses a --limit-platform with no --limit-reason. --clear-platform-limit clears a recorded limitation. Prints the returned task row as JSON.

Exit codes: 0 ok · 2 usage / platform limit without a reason · 3 transport · 4 broker store failure · 5 no matching claimed row.

$ fleet queue lane 19479 --worker repo-worker-code --limit-platform macos --limit-reason "needs the macOS runner pool"
{"id": 19479, "status": "claimed", "lane_ledger": {"assigned_lane": "code-a", "platform_limit": "macos", "platform_limit_reason": "needs the macOS runner pool"}}

fleet queue bind

usage: repo-queue bind <task-id> [--worker <id>] --session-id <id> [--launched-by <who>] [--model-provider <p>] [--model-id <id>] [--model-variant <v>]
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning

--workerworker idrepo-worker-codeHolder identity.
--session-idsession idrequiredThe session to bind. Missing → exit 2.
--launched-bywhoopencode-claimantWho launched the bound session; recorded on the lane ledger.
--model-providerprovider nameunsetServing model provider for the model stamp.
--model-idmodel idunsetServing model id for the model stamp.
--model-variantvariant nameunsetServing model variant for the model stamp. Explicit --model-* wins; else the stamp is derived from the session’s own record.

The client also appends session_bound (and model_stamp when a stamp exists) timeline events, trigger bind. Prints the returned task row as JSON.

fleet queue heartbeat

usage: repo-queue heartbeat <task-id> [--worker <id>] [--lane <id>] [--extend-seconds <n>] [--progress <p>] [--progress-file <f>]
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
<task-id> (positional)task idrequiredThe claimed task whose lease to refresh.
--workerworker idrepo-worker-codeHolder identity.
--lanelane idenv REPO_QUEUE_LANE, else nullHolder lane check.
--extend-secondsinteger seconds900 (15 min)Minimum renewal window from now. Range 1..=86400, exit 2 outside.
--progresstext/JSONunsetProgress value merged into the row. Mutually exclusive with --progress-file.
--progress-filefile pathunsetFile whose text is read as the progress value. Mutually exclusive with --progress.

Behaviour. The Turso broker keeps the later of the current deadline and now + extend_seconds. It writes the resulting deadline to the task and its lease in one SQLite statement and refreshes heartbeat_at, including on an early heartbeat. A changed claim observed during renewal returns exit 5. Brokers built before #13553 replace the deadline with now + extend_seconds and can shorten a longer lease. Check the serving broker revision when interpreting older observations. --progress/--progress-file optionally merge a progress value into the row. Heartbeat goes through the fallback-switch path: a primary-store failure switches the work to the GitHub fallback, exit 6 (see the fallback queue). Prints the row + mode_line.

Exit codes: 0 ok · 2 usage / out-of-range --extend-seconds / both progress flags · 3 transport · 4 broker store failure · 5 no matching claimed row · 6 fallback switch.

$ fleet queue heartbeat 19479 --worker repo-worker-code --lane code-a
{"id": 19479, "status": "claimed", "lease_until": "2026-11-23T04:35:00Z", "mode_line": {"verb": "heartbeat", "mode": "normal", "route": "cloud"}}

fleet queue checkpoint

usage: repo-queue checkpoint <task-id> [--worker <id>] [--lane <id>] [--stage <s>] [--progress <p>] [--progress-file <f>]
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
<task-id> (positional)task idrequiredThe claimed task to checkpoint.
--workerworker idrepo-worker-codeHolder identity.
--lanelane idenv REPO_QUEUE_LANE, else nullHolder lane check.
--stagestage namerequiredThe checkpoint stage. Missing → exit 2.
--progresstext/JSONunsetProgress value merged into the row. Mutually exclusive with --progress-file.
--progress-filefile pathunsetFile whose text is read as the progress value. Mutually exclusive with --progress.

Behaviour. Records progress + stage without touching the lease. The broker (/checkpoint) merges the progress (default {}) into the task row with progress.last_checkpoint = {stage, at} stamped in; upserts the per-worker KV row checkpoints(worker_id, 'task:<id>') = {stage, progress, at}; writes a checkpoint event. Fallback-switch path, like heartbeat: a primary-store failure switches, exit 6. Prints row + mode_line.

Help: the usage writes --stage bare — it is required — missing → exit 2 checkpoint: --stage is required.

Exit codes: 0 ok · 2 usage / missing --stage / both progress flags · 3 transport · 4 broker store failure · 5 no matching claimed row · 6 fallback switch.

$ fleet queue checkpoint 19479 --worker repo-worker-code --lane code-a --stage drafting --progress '{"chapters": 2}'
{"id": 19479, "status": "claimed", "progress": {"last_checkpoint": {"stage": "drafting", "at": "2026-11-23T04:20:00Z"}}, "mode_line": {"verb": "checkpoint", "mode": "normal", "route": "cloud"}}

fleet queue park

usage: repo-queue park <task-id> [--worker <id>] [--lane <id>] --reason <text> [--delay-seconds <n>] [--not-before <ts>] [--progress <p>] [--progress-file <f>] [--ready-condition <c>] [--execution <id>] [--required-budget-minutes <n>] [--hands <kind> --action <text>]
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
<task-id> (positional)task idrequiredThe claimed task to park.
--workerworker idrepo-worker-codeHolder identity.
--lanelane idenv REPO_QUEUE_LANE, else nullHolder lane check.
--reasontextrequiredWhy the task is parked. Missing → exit 2.
--delay-secondsinteger secondsbroker default 1200 when neither delay nor not-before is givenRelative wait. Range 1..=604800 (7 days); 0 is rejected by design — “a park that waits zero seconds is a requeue, and a requeue already has its own verb (release)”. Mutually exclusive with --not-before.
--not-beforeRFC 3339 timestampunsetAbsolute wake time; must be non-empty and ≤366 days in the future. Mutually exclusive with --delay-seconds.
--progresstext/JSONunsetProgress merged into the row; may carry ready_condition (see Behaviour). Mutually exclusive with --progress-file.
--progress-filefile pathunsetFile whose text is read as the progress value.
--ready-conditionJSON objectderived (see Behaviour)What “done waiting” means. Non-JSON → exit 2; non-object JSON → exit 2.
--executionexecution idunsetFolded into an execution record {lane, lane_id?, session_id, fallback_reason?}.
--required-budget-minutesinteger minutesbroker-derived for capacity waits (see Behaviour)The minimum remaining shift budget a future claimer must declare. Non-positive values record no requirement.
--handsphysical|interactive-login|payment|signatureunsetHands kind for a valid person-wait (FDR-0013); must come with --action.
--actiontextunsetOne sentence a person can do in five minutes; required with --hands on a person-wait.

Behaviour. Parks a claimed task: status becomes parked, out of the claimable pool until its not_before is due, its ready-condition is released by the revalidation sweeper, or wake short-circuits the wait.

  • Ready-condition kinds the revalidation sweeper can verify from DB state: task_terminal {task_id}, task_status {task_id, status}, event_seen {task_id?, event_kind}, time {until}. External kinds (ci, pr_merged, issue_closed, person_answer, review, …) are recorded faithfully but a DB sweeper cannot verify them. With no explicit condition the broker derives one from progress.ready_condition, else {"kind":"time","until":<not_before>}.
  • wait_kind is derived from the condition kind at park time: time→timer; triage→triage; ci|ci_green|pr_merged|issue_closed|upstream_pr→ci; review|codex_review|pr_review|person_answer→review; capacity|quota_reset→capacity; anything else→external. park_kind records relative vs absolute.
  • Broker wait floors: whatever delay a lane asks for, a triage wait is held at least 6 h (21600 s) and a ci or capacity wait at least 1 h (3600 s) — a requested wake earlier than the floor is bumped to the floor; timer/review/external waits keep the caller’s delay. (Lanes re-discovering an unchanged wait every 20–25 min was the park churn this kills.) A park whose recorded stage is awaiting_triage is a triage wait whatever condition the caller attached.
  • Handoff parks / the sink: a non-triage park that is a handoff (the condition defaulted, per the broker’s rule) is routed to_sink — parked into the handed-off sink where claim --handoff / by-id claims collect it, rather than sitting as an ordinary timed park.
  • --required-budget-minutes: for a capacity wait the broker defaults it from the packet’s timebox_minutes when the flag is absent.
  • Person-wait guard (FDR-0013): a park whose ready-condition kind is person_answer, or whose reason text names the owner as the release, is refused client-side (exit 2, before broker contact) unless it is a valid hands item; a valid hands item is stamped into progress.hands = {kind, action}. See the full guard under block below.
  • Park stamps last_checked_at = now, resets check_outcome, and the park revalidation sweeper later records check_outcome ∈ confirmed (condition unmet; park untouched), released (condition met → status queued, not_before null, park_released event), or stale (cannot verify).
  • Output: row (or {task, lane_ledger[, follow_on_task_id]}); a park closes the session binding window on the timeline.

Exit codes: 0 parked · 2 usage / missing --reason / both delay flags / bad ready-condition / person-wait refusal · 3 transport · 4 broker store failure · 5 no matching claimed row.

$ fleet queue park 19479 --worker repo-worker-code --lane code-a --reason "waiting on CI for the linked PR" --ready-condition '{"kind":"ci","repo":"developing-today/code"}' --delay-seconds 600
{"id": 19479, "status": "parked", "wait_kind": "ci", "not_before": "2026-11-23T05:20:00Z"}

fleet queue wake

usage: repo-queue wake <task-id> [--worker <id>] [--reason <text>]
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
<task-id> (positional)task idrequiredThe parked task to wake.
--workerworker idrepo-worker-codeCaller identity.
--reasontextempty stringWhy the wait is over; recorded with the wake.

Behaviour. Releases a broker-held parked wait now that its condition is satisfied: the broker flips the row back to queued. Canonical caller: the triage step waking an item it just triaged. Prints the row.

Exit codes: 0 woken · 2 usage · 3 transport · 4 broker store failure · 5 no parked row the broker can wake.

$ fleet queue wake 19479 --reason "triaged; ready to work"
{"id": 19479, "status": "queued", "not_before": null}

fleet queue block

usage: repo-queue block <task-id> [--worker <id>] [--lane <id>] --reason-class <c> --blocker <b> [--progress <p>] [--progress-file <f>] [--ledger-id <id>] [--question <text>] [--context <text>] [--options-json <json>] [--links-json <json>] [--blocked-by-pr <n>] [--blocked-by-issue <n>] [--blocked-by-task <id>] [--blocked-by-ci <ref>] [--dep-recheck-seconds <n>] [--dep-max-ttl-seconds <n>] [--hands <kind> --action <text>]
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
<task-id> (positional)task idrequiredThe claimed task to block.
--workerworker idrepo-worker-codeHolder identity.
--lanelane idenv REPO_QUEUE_LANE, else nullHolder lane check.
--reason-classclass namerequiredFree-form block class (contrast fail, whose --reason-class is a closed enum). Missing → exit 2.
--blockertextrequiredWhat blocks the task. Missing → exit 2.
--progresstext/JSONunsetProgress merged into the row. Mutually exclusive with --progress-file.
--progress-filefile pathunsetFile whose text is read as the progress value.
--ledger-ididunsetNeeds-drew payload: the PM ledger id (see Behaviour).
--questiontextunsetNeeds-drew payload: the question for the owner. A hands item’s --action serves as the question when none is given.
--contexttextunsetNeeds-drew payload: optional context.
--options-jsonJSON arrayunsetNeeds-drew payload: array of {"id","label"} objects; bad shape → exit 2.
--links-jsonJSON arrayunsetNeeds-drew payload: array of strings; bad shape → exit 2.
--blocked-by-prcomma-separated owner/repo#N refsunsetTyped dependency: PRs that must land. Bad refs die client-side, exit 2.
--blocked-by-issuecomma-separated owner/repo#N refsunsetTyped dependency: issues that must close/resolve. Bad refs die client-side, exit 2.
--blocked-by-taskcomma-separated bare task idsunsetTyped dependency: queue tasks that must reach a terminal state.
--blocked-by-cicomma-separated owner/repo#N refsunsetTyped dependency: CI runs; here N is an Actions run id.
--dep-recheck-secondsinteger seconds900How often the broker re-checks the deps. Clamped broker-side to 300..=3600.
--dep-max-ttl-secondsinteger seconds259200 (3 days)Max lifetime of a dep block before TTL expiry releases it. Broker floor 60 s, ceiling 7 days (604800 s).
--handsphysical|interactive-login|payment|signatureunsetHands kind for a valid person-wait (FDR-0013); must come with --action.
--actiontextunsetOne sentence a person can do in five minutes: a single line of ≤200 chars that must not itself ask for a decision.

Behaviour. Sets status blocked; the row keeps its claim identity in progress/ledger terms but is out of the claimable pool until unblocked, dep-cleared, or TTL-expired. Output: the row, exit 0. (The claim path also uses /block internally with reason-class fallback_held for the double-serve guard — see core verbs.) After a /block, the broker fire-and-forget raises the needs-drew alert for an escalated block, mirroring the client’s own raise.

Typed dependency blocks. The parsed deps array sent to the broker is [{kind:"pr"|"issue", repo, number} | {kind:"ci", repo, run_id} | {kind:"task", task_id}] — never a prose block the broker cannot watch. The deps are stored on the task row in the blocked_deps column (TEXT, JSON) — the state the task calls dep_blocked when blocked_deps is non-empty — alongside dep_recheck_seconds, dep_next_recheck_at, and dep_blocked_until. The broker watches these deps and releases the task itself when they clear, or when the max TTL expires. Production cadence: the broker’s sweep fires the dep recheck every minute; the dep-recheck verb is the manual trigger.

Person-wait guard (FDR-0013). A block whose reason class is one of escalated-to-user, drew_decision, person-answer, or whose blocker text contains an owner-wait phrase (“awaiting drew”, “needs the owner”, “owner decision”, “waiting for the owner”, … — an 18-phrase list), waits on a person and is refused (exit 2, before broker contact) unless it is a hands item: --hands physical|interactive-login|payment|signature and --action "<one sentence a person can do in five minutes>". The refusal text tells the worker a choice is theirs to make. Passing --hands/--action on a block that does not wait on a person is also an error. A valid hands item is stamped progress.hands. The same guard applies to park.

Needs-drew payload. Only for --reason-class escalated-to-user with --ledger-id and --question. Then the client stamps progress.needs_drew.ledger_id, sends a needs_drew {ledger_id, question, context?, options, links} object in the /block body, and after the block lands posts the alert to the PM aggregator’s alerts-intake (token resolved by name through fleet-secrets; value never printed). A failed alert post only warns on stderr — the block already succeeded and the verb still exits 0. Without ledger-id + question, an escalated block behaves exactly as before.

Exit codes: 0 blocked · 2 usage / missing --reason-class or --blocker / bad dep ref / bad options/links shape / person-wait refusal / hands flags on a non-person block · 3 transport · 4 broker store failure · 5 no matching claimed row.

$ fleet queue block 19479 --worker repo-worker-code --lane code-a --reason-class dependency --blocker "waiting on PR developing-today/code#13100" --blocked-by-pr developing-today/code#13100
{"id": 19479, "status": "blocked", "blocked_deps": [{"kind": "pr", "repo": "developing-today/code", "number": 13100}], "dep_recheck_seconds": 900, "dep_blocked_until": "2026-11-26T04:20:00Z"}

fleet queue unblock

usage: repo-queue unblock <task-id> [--worker <id>] [--reason <text>] [--drop-dep <list>]
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
<task-id> (positional)task idrequiredThe blocked task to release.
--workerworker idrepo-worker-codeCaller identity; the broker audits who overrode.
--reasontextempty stringWhy the block is overridden; audited.
--drop-depcomma-separated kind:ref listunsetSurgical dep drop: issue:owner/repo#N, pr:owner/repo#N, ci:owner/repo#RUN, task:ID. Bad refs die client-side, exit 2; the broker re-validates every spec.

Behaviour. The manual override: releases a blocked task now, dep-blocked or classic. The broker audits who overrode and what dep record was discarded.

  • Without --drop-dep: clears the task’s blocked state entirely (deps discarded).
  • With --drop-dep <list>: surgical. Only the named entries are dropped from the task’s blocked_deps record. The task stays blocked on the remaining deps; dropping the last one releases it.

Quarantined rows: the full override refuses a row that is still quarantined by the claim path, naming the quarantine and pointing at fleet queue repair <id> — unblock cannot clear a packet defect; repair the packet first. The --drop-dep path is unchanged (it leaves the row blocked).

Output: the row, exit 0.

Exit codes: 0 unblocked (or last dep dropped) · 2 usage / bad --drop-dep ref · 3 transport · 4 broker store failure · 5 no blocked row matches.

$ fleet queue unblock 19479 --reason "PR merged manually; dep record is stale" --drop-dep pr:developing-today/code#13100
{"id": 19479, "status": "queued", "blocked_deps": []}

fleet queue dep-recheck

usage: repo-queue dep-recheck [--task <id>] [--limit <n>]
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
--tasktask idunsetForce one task’s recheck instead of a full pass.
--limitintegerno documented defaultPass size limit; forwarded verbatim to the broker (no default is documented in help or client source).

Behaviour. Runs the broker’s dependency recheck pass now, or forces one task’s recheck with --task. The pass re-reads each dep-blocked task’s deps (issue/PR state, CI run state, task terminality) and releases the ones that cleared; TTL-expired dep blocks are released by the same machinery. Output: the pass result row as JSON.

Exit codes: 0 ok · 2 usage · 3 transport · 4 broker store failure.

$ fleet queue dep-recheck --task 19479
{"task": 19479, "checked": 1, "released": 1, "still_blocked": 0}

fleet queue quarantine-recheck

usage: repo-queue quarantine-recheck [--task <id>] [--limit <n>]
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
--tasktask idunsetForce one task’s recheck instead of a full pass.
--limitintegerno documented defaultPass size limit; forwarded verbatim to the broker.

Behaviour. Runs the broker’s quarantine recheck pass: re-validates blocked, dep-free rows whose recorded error is a claim-path quarantine (e.g. a stored packet that fails claim-time validation) and requeues the ones whose error no longer reproduces. Production cadence is the broker sweep’s; this is the manual trigger. Output: the pass result row as JSON.

Exit codes: 0 ok · 2 usage · 3 transport · 4 broker store failure.

$ fleet queue quarantine-recheck
{"checked": 3, "requeued": 1, "still_quarantined": 2}

fleet queue repair

usage: repo-queue repair <task-id> [--worker <id>] [--reason <text>] [--dry-run]
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
<task-id> (positional)task idrequiredThe quarantined / malformed task to repair in place.
--workerworker idrepo-worker-codeCaller identity; recorded as the repair’s operator.
--reasontextempty stringWhy the task is repaired; recorded with the repair.
--dry-run—offReport the defects and the planned repairs; write nothing.

Behaviour. Repairs a stored packet that is malformed, in place — the gap the neighbouring verbs leave: the claim path quarantines such a row on every claim, quarantine-recheck can only release a row whose error no longer reproduces, and unblock refuses to clear a packet defect. (Worked example: a payload.dedupe missing its checked_at/basis stamp.) The broker re-runs the packet validators — validate_packet plus the claim-guard reason — applies the deterministic repairs whose correct value can be re-derived, re-validates the repaired packet in memory, and only then writes: one status-guarded update clears the quarantine and restores the task claimable (queued, or blocked with its deps intact when dep-blocked). A repaired timeline entry names the verb, the operator, the defects and the repairs. Output: the repaired row.

  • Eligible states: blocked, queued, parked, handed_off. claimed is refused — repair never mutates a task a worker holds. cancelled / failed point at revive first; done is refused.
  • The one repairable class today: the dedupe-stamp defect. Repair re-performs the dedupe check live — no other live task may hold the same work identity (repo, issue, kind) or the same dedupe_key among claim-guard-clean rows — and stamps checked_at plus a basis stating the re-check. A live duplicate refuses the repair: the stamp cannot be honestly re-derived. A packet carrying neither identity nor key refuses too.
  • Any other defect is unrepairable today: the broker refuses with the defect list and changes nothing.

Exit codes: 0 repaired (or the dry-run report) · 2 usage · 3 transport · 4 broker store failure · refusals exit non-zero with the reason and mutate nothing.

$ fleet queue repair 19481 --dry-run
{"task_id": 19481, "outcome": "dry_run", "defects": ["..."], "repairs": [{"field": "payload.dedupe", "action": "stamped checked_at/basis by re-performing the dedupe check live"}], "dry_run": true, "status": "blocked", "status_after": "queued"}

fleet queue cancel

usage: repo-queue cancel <task-id> [--worker <id>] [--reason <text>]
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
<task-id> (positional)task idrequiredThe task to cancel.
--workerworker idfleet-monitorCaller identity. Note: cancel is a monitor close-out verb — its worker default is NOT the global repo-worker-code.
--reasontextrequiredWhy the task will never be worked. Missing → exit 2. Recorded as result.cancel_reason.

Behaviour. For a task that will never be worked (issue closed, self-assigned elsewhere, superseded). Sets status cancelled, clears worker/lease, deletes the lease row, records result.reason_class = "cancelled" + result.cancel_reason, writes a cancelled event. The original function only accepted queued or parked rows. Output: the row; cancel closes the timeline binding window.

Help: the usage writes --reason bare — it is required (exit 2 without it) — and its description names cancel’s --worker default: fleet-monitor, not repo-worker-code.

Exit codes: 0 cancelled · 2 usage / missing --reason · 3 transport · 4 broker store failure · 5 no matching row.

$ fleet queue cancel 19481 --reason "issue closed as duplicate; superseded by task 19482"
{"id": 19481, "status": "cancelled", "result": {"reason_class": "cancelled", "cancel_reason": "issue closed as duplicate; superseded by task 19482"}}

fleet queue revive

FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning

--workerworker idrepo-worker-codeCaller identity.
--reasontextempty stringWhy the task is revived; recorded with the revive.

Behaviour. Revives a terminal task in place: a failed task, or a queued task dead at cap (attempts exhausted), gets attempts = 0 and a fresh not_before through the broker’s /revive — the supported replacement for direct-SQL resets. Output: the row.

Exit codes: 0 revived · 2 usage / bad --not-before · 3 transport · 4 broker store failure · 5 no matching row.

$ fleet queue revive 19483 --reason "transient infra failure fixed; retry the work"
{"id": 19483, "status": "queued", "attempts": 0}

FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning

--workerworker idrepo-worker-codeHolder identity.
--lanelane idenv REPO_QUEUE_LANE, else nullHolder lane check.
