fleet queue signal

usage: repo-queue signal [--queue <name>] [--reason <text>]
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
--queuequeue namerepo-health-code-shadowThe ordinary queue resolution — flag → env REPO_QUEUE_DEFAULT_QUEUE → the shadow default. (Unlike claim/list, signal is NOT unscoped; unlike enqueue, it does have a default.)
--reasontextmanual_signalReason recorded in the signal object.

Behaviour. Asks the broker /signal-count {queue} for queued_count + oldest_queued_at, then writes a wake-up signal file for the queue’s consumers: a JSON object {"queue", "generation", "queued_count", "oldest_queued_at", "updated_at", "reason"} where generation is one more than the max generation found in the existing signal/state files for that queue. Signal file path: env REPO_QUEUE_SIGNAL_PATH, else $HOME/workspace/goals/keep-the-four-repos-healthy/hidden_files/repo-queue-signal.json, with a sibling repo-queue-signal-state.json carrying {queue, generation, updated_at}. Both writes are atomic (tmp + rename); a write failure dies exit 3. The printed output is the signal object itself, exit 0.

Exit codes: 0 ok · 2 usage · 3 transport / unwritable signal file · 4 broker store failure.

$ fleet queue signal --queue repo-health-code --reason "manual wake for the book build"
{"queue": "repo-health-code", "generation": 42, "queued_count": 12, "oldest_queued_at": "2026-11-23T03:58:00Z", "updated_at": "2026-11-23T04:30:00Z", "reason": "manual wake for the book build"}

fleet queue models

usage: repo-queue models [--days <n>] [--json]
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
--daysinteger days7Rollup window. Clamped to 1..=30 (note: clamped, unlike the reject-don’t-clamp duration/limit flags elsewhere).
--jsonbooleanoffPrint an object including "days" and the per-model rows instead of the human table.

Behaviour. Rolls up serving-model stamps across tasks: which models worked which tasks, joined from claim stamps + timeline binding windows + the route ledger. Output: human table headed model rollup — last <n>d (since <ts>), or with --json an object including "days" and the per-model rows. If the broker’s /events-list doesn’t serve the cross-task kinds, it prints repo-queue models: this broker does not serve cross-task … and a 50000-row scan cap produces a warning line rather than silent truncation.

Exit codes: 0 ok · 2 usage · 3 transport / cross-task events not served · 4 broker store failure.

$ fleet queue models --days 7
model rollup — last 7d (since 2026-11-16T04:30:00Z)
model                     tasks  completed
claude-sonnet (example)   41     38

fleet queue outbox

usage: repo-queue outbox <enqueue|list|metrics|claim|resolve|drain> ...

The creation outbox is the queue for GitHub object creation (issues, PRs, comments) that must survive crashes and rate limits: producers enqueue, a single serial drainer creates through gh, verifies by read-back, and resolves. Pilot producer: new-issue-creator-code-a. There is no dual-write and no automatic fallback to direct creation — a broker failure stops the drain visibly.

State machine: kinds issue | pull_request | issue_comment | pr_comment; states pending | leased | uncertain | done | blocked. Constants: claim lease 120 s, min gap between creates 2 s, hourly create budget 300, retry backoff base 30 s cap 3600 s, circuit breaker opens after 3 consecutive rate limits for 300 s, default max attempts 8. Entries carry a fleet-outbox:<id> marker in the created object’s body so the drainer can reconcile by search/read-back.

Each subverb below follows the reference format. All outbox subverbs print the full broker envelope JSON unless noted.

fleet queue outbox enqueue

usage: repo-queue outbox enqueue [--repo <r>] [--kind <k>] [--dedup-key <d>] [--producer <p>] [--payload <json> | --payload-file <f>]
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
--reporepounsetTarget repo for the object to create.
--kindissue|pull_request|issue_comment|pr_commentunsetObject kind.
--dedup-keykeyunsetDedupe key; the broker table has a unique index on (repo, dedup_key).
--producerproducer nameunsetProducing identity (pilot: new-issue-creator-code-a).
--payloadJSONrequired (one of the two)Creation payload inline. Neither --payload nor --payload-file → exit 2.
--payload-filefile pathrequired (one of the two)Creation payload from a file.

Behaviour. POST /outbox-enqueue; prints the full broker envelope JSON. The entry lands in state pending.

Exit codes: 0 ok · 2 usage / missing payload · 3 transport · 4 broker store failure.

$ fleet queue outbox enqueue --repo developing-today/code --kind issue --dedup-key book-13165 --producer new-issue-creator-code-a --payload '{"title":"Fleet book: queue chapters","body":"… fleet-outbox:pending"}'
{"ok": true, "row": {"id": 77, "state": "pending", "kind": "issue", "repo": "developing-today/code"}}

fleet queue outbox list

usage: repo-queue outbox list [--repo <r>] [--state <s>]
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
--reporepounsetFilter by repo.
--statepending|leased|uncertain|done|blockedunsetFilter by state.

Behaviour. POST /outbox-list; prints the envelope.

Exit codes: 0 ok · 2 usage · 3 transport · 4 broker store failure.

$ fleet queue outbox list --state pending
{"ok": true, "rows": [{"id": 77, "state": "pending", "kind": "issue", "repo": "developing-today/code"}]}

fleet queue outbox metrics

usage: repo-queue outbox metrics
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
(none)——Takes no flags.

Behaviour. POST /outbox-metrics with {}; prints the envelope (counts by state/kind plus circuit-breaker state).

Exit codes: 0 ok · 2 usage · 3 transport · 4 broker store failure.

$ fleet queue outbox metrics
{"ok": true, "pending": 1, "leased": 0, "uncertain": 0, "done": 128, "blocked": 0, "circuit_open": false}

fleet queue outbox claim

usage: repo-queue outbox claim [--owner <name>]
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
--ownerowner nameoutbox-drainerClaiming drainer identity. Claim lease is 120 s.

Behaviour. Claims the oldest due entry; prints the envelope (its row is null when idle).

Exit codes: 0 ok (including idle, row: null) · 2 usage · 3 transport · 4 broker store failure.

$ fleet queue outbox claim
{"ok": true, "row": {"id": 77, "state": "leased", "kind": "issue", "repo": "developing-today/code"}}

fleet queue outbox resolve

usage: repo-queue outbox resolve <id> [--outcome done|rate_limited|uncertain|failed] [--github-number <n>] [--github-url <u>] [--retry-after <s>] [--error <text>]
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
<id> (positional)entry idrequiredThe leased entry to resolve. Missing <id> → exit 2 with the usage line.
--outcomedone|rate_limited|uncertain|failednone (see note)Resolution outcome.
--github-numberintegerunsetCreated object’s number, for done.
--github-urlURLunsetCreated object’s URL, for done.
--retry-aftersecondsunsetBackoff hint for rate_limited.
--errortextunsetError text for failed/uncertain.

Behaviour. POST /outbox-resolve for the leased entry, recording the outcome and (for done) the created object’s identity for read-back reconciliation.

Known discrepancy: --outcome has no client-side default or validation — omitted, it sends the empty string and the broker decides. The usage line presents it as a normal optional flag with a closed value set; the closed set is enforced, if at all, broker-side only. This chapter documents the source behaviour.

Exit codes: 0 ok · 2 usage / missing <id> · 3 transport · 4 broker store failure.

$ fleet queue outbox resolve 77 --outcome done --github-number 13170 --github-url https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/13170
{"ok": true, "row": {"id": 77, "state": "done", "github_number": 13170}}

fleet queue outbox drain

usage: repo-queue outbox drain [--owner <name>] [--max <n>]
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
--ownerowner nameoutbox-drainerDrainer identity used for claims.
--maxinteger20Max items to drain this run, floored at 1.

Behaviour. The pilot drainer itself. Loop: claim → if the entry is uncertain, reconcile by marker first (search + strongly-consistent list scan; a lookup that could not check keeps the entry uncertain with the error class recorded and never re-creates) → create via gh (pacing: ≥2 s between creates; the broker enforces circuit + hourly budget at claim) → verify by read-back → resolve. Per-item output lines are JSON: {"id","outcome":"done"|"uncertain"|"rate_limited"|"failed"|"reconciled"|"lookup_unchecked", …}; when the claim comes back empty it prints {"drained": k, "idle": true, "claim": <envelope>} and exits 0; after --max items, {"drained": k, "idle": false}. Create outcomes map: created+verified → done; created but read-back failed or ambiguous output → uncertain; 403/429/rate-limit → rate_limited; other failure → failed.

Exit codes: 0 drained / idle · 2 usage · 3 transport (a broker failure stops the drain visibly) · 4 broker store failure.

$ fleet queue outbox drain --max 5
{"id": 77, "outcome": "done", "github_number": 13170}
{"drained": 1, "idle": true, "claim": {"ok": true, "row": null}}

fleet queue stack

usage: repo-queue stack <record|list|transition|restack|replay> ...

A stack is a recorded, ordered set of merge intents — finished branches with their authoring lane/worker/session — stored in the broker’s merge_intents table (unique on (stack_id, position) and (repo, branch)). Intent states: intended → replaying → landed, plus conflicted and abandoned — five states in total; legality of every move is decided by the pure core’s transition table, never in SQL. A conflicted intent returns only through its recorded authoring lane.

Each subverb below follows the reference format.

fleet queue stack record

usage: repo-queue stack record --stack <id> --repo <r> --branch <b> [--base-branch <b>] [--head-sha <sha>] [--issue <n>] [--pr <n>] --lane <l> [--worker <id>] [--session-id <id>]
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
--stackstack idrequiredStack to append to. Missing → exit 2.
--reporeporequiredThe intent’s repo. Missing → exit 2.
--branchbranch namerequiredThe finished branch. Missing → exit 2.
--base-branchbranch nameunsetBase the branch was authored against.
--head-shacommit SHAunsetRecorded head SHA.
--issueissue numberunsetLinked issue.
--prPR numberunsetLinked PR.
--lanelane idrequiredAuthoring lane (the owner lane for conflict routing). Missing → exit 2.
--workerworker idcaller’s worker (repo-worker-code)Authoring worker.
--session-idsession idunsetAuthoring session.

Behaviour. The append is fail-fast validated client-side with the same pure-core rules the broker applies, and the broker additionally validates the (lane, worker) pair against the lane registry — an unregistered owner lane is refused. POST /stack-record; prints the row.

Exit codes: 0 ok · 2 usage / missing required flag / validation failure · 3 transport · 4 broker store failure / broker refusal.

$ fleet queue stack record --stack book-13165 --repo developing-today/code --branch writer/w2-queue --lane code-a
{"stack_id": "book-13165", "position": 0, "repo": "developing-today/code", "branch": "writer/w2-queue", "state": "intended"}

fleet queue stack list

usage: repo-queue stack list <stack-id> [--stack <id>] [--worker <id>]
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
<stack-id> (positional)stack idone of positional / --stack requiredThe stack to list.
--stackstack idunsetAlternative spelling of the positional. If both are given and disagree → exit 2.
--workerworker idrepo-worker-codeCaller identity.

Behaviour. POST /stack-list; prints the derived stack state (the full state is answered from the database alone).

Exit codes: 0 ok · 2 usage / disagreeing ids · 3 transport · 4 broker store failure.

$ fleet queue stack list book-13165
{"stack_id": "book-13165", "intents": [{"position": 0, "branch": "writer/w2-queue", "state": "intended"}]}

fleet queue stack transition

usage: repo-queue stack transition --stack <id> --position <n> --to <state> [--pr <n>] [--conflict-detail <text>] [--worker <id>]
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
--stackstack idrequiredThe stack. Missing → exit 2.
--positionintegerrequiredThe intent’s position. Missing → exit 2.
--tointent staterequiredTarget state; must parse as an intent state (intended, replaying, landed, conflicted, abandoned). Missing/unparseable → exit 2.
--prPR numberunsetPR associated with the move.
--conflict-detailtextrequired when --to conflictedWhat the authoring lane must resolve. A move to conflicted without it → exit 2.
--workerworker idrepo-worker-codeCaller identity.

Behaviour. An illegal move is a broker refusal, not a write. POST /stack-transition.

Exit codes: 0 ok · 2 usage / missing required flag / conflicted without detail · 3 transport · 4 broker store failure / illegal move refused.

$ fleet queue stack transition --stack book-13165 --position 0 --to replaying
{"stack_id": "book-13165", "position": 0, "state": "replaying"}

fleet queue stack restack

usage: repo-queue stack restack --stack <id> --position <n> --base <b> [--head-sha <sha>] [--worker <id>]
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
--stackstack idrequiredThe stack. Missing → exit 2.
--positionintegerrequiredThe intent’s position. Missing → exit 2.
--basebranch namerequiredThe new base branch. Missing → exit 2.
--head-shacommit SHAunsetNew head SHA after the restack.
--workerworker idrepo-worker-codeCaller identity.

Behaviour. Acknowledges that an intent’s author restacked its branch off a withdrawn base; the broker re-plans with the core’s plan_restack (taint rules bind there) and refreshes the recorded base_branch. POST /stack-restack.

Exit codes: 0 ok · 2 usage / missing required flag · 3 transport · 4 broker store failure.

$ fleet queue stack restack --stack book-13165 --position 0 --base main
{"stack_id": "book-13165", "position": 0, "base_branch": "main", "state": "intended"}

fleet queue stack replay

usage: repo-queue stack replay [--stack <id>] [--worker <id>] [--repo-dir <dir>] [--dry-run]
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
--stackstack idrequired in practiceThe stack to replay. The usage line brackets it optional, but missing → exit 2.
--workerworker idrepo-worker-codeCaller identity.
--repo-dirdirectory.Checkout to replay in.
--dry-runbooleanoffPrint the plan JSON — exactly what a live pass would do — and change nothing.

Behaviour. The replay executor: walks the stack’s recorded merge order bottom-up and lands it — rebase onto new main, push (force-with-lease pinned to the verified pre-rebase tip), open PR, merge, mark landed, post the outcome note — one intent at a time. --dry-run prints {"stack_id","dry_run":true,"plan":[{"position","branch","action"}]}. Refuses a checkout with somebody else’s rebase already in progress. Replay never resolves a conflict itself.

Exit codes: 0 landed/idle (an empty plan prints a note explaining the stack is empty, finished, or blocked at a conflicted head) · 2 usage / missing --stack · 3 any other step failure — the intent is left replaying and a later stack replay resumes it (including the case where the conflict itself could not be recorded) · 4 a rebase/merge conflict was recorded conflicted and routed to its authoring lane (the JSON carries conflict {position, detail, route {owner_lane, owner_worker, owner_session, repo, branch, base_branch, issue_number}}).

$ fleet queue stack replay --stack book-13165 --dry-run
{"stack_id": "book-13165", "dry_run": true, "plan": [{"position": 0, "branch": "writer/w2-queue", "action": "rebase+merge"}]}
$ fleet queue stack replay --stack book-13165
{"stack_id": "book-13165", "landed": [0], "state": "landed"}

fleet serve

fleet serve runs one or more fleet daemon roles in the foreground. Each role is a blocking serve loop that also exists as a leaf elsewhere in the binary; serve is the composition point a service manager (systemd) supervises.

Roles:

Role tokenCapabilityRunsSame leaf as
queue-brokerqueue-brokerthe repo work queue as a resident serviceargv0 queue-broker
secrets-brokersecrets-brokerthe Bitwarden-backed secrets cacheargv0 secrets-broker
searchsearch-servethe Atlas search servicefleet search serve, argv0 atlas-search serve
proxyproxy-servethe session proxy brokerfleet proxy serve

See also fleet proxy, fleet secrets, fleet search, and Secrets and the secrets broker.

Role-list semantics

fleet serve <role>
fleet serve <role> [<role> ...]
  • One role: fleet serve <role> runs that role in the foreground.
  • Two or more roles: fleet serve <role> [<role> ...] with two or more distinct role tokens and nothing else runs all of them in one process. The parser only engages as a list when at least the first two tokens are both role tokens; it then validates the whole tail.
  • A duplicate is a hard error: error: duplicate role 'queue-broker' in 'fleet serve' list.
  • Any non-role token is a hard error, for example: error: unexpected argument '--help' in 'fleet serve' list: a serve list is role tokens only (queue-broker, secrets-broker, search, proxy).
  • All roles are capability-checked before anything binds. If any role is not available in this invocation, the whole list stubs with exit 69 and fleet serve: role '<role>' cannot run in this invocation — there is no partial start.
  • Each role’s blocking loop runs on its own thread in the one process. Startup prints fleet serve: starting N roles in one process: <tokens>.
  • Supervision is fail-fast: the supervisor polls the threads on a 100 ms tick; the first role thread to return or panic takes the whole process down (the external supervisor restarts the unit). The process exit code is the role’s own code, except that a role exiting cleanly (code 0) is converted to exit 1 — a daemon role returning at all is abnormal — and a panic is also exit 1. The role is named on stderr either way.
  • One composition subtlety: the proxy role inside a list runs co-hosted, which disables the proxy’s idle-exit, so an idle proxy cannot exit the shared process and kill its siblings.

Help: appending --help to a two-role list prints the serve domain help and exits 0 — a list has no single role to name. Single-role --help prints that role’s own usage, for the two brokers as well (see below).

If the invocation cannot use a role at all (not in this build, narrowed out by the invocation name, or disabled by config), serve answers with the capability stub on stderr, always exit 69.

argv0 aliases

Invoking the binary as queue-broker or secrets-broker routes straight into the serve domain with that role prepended. Help, stub, and argument-rejection behaviour are identical to the spelled-out form.

fleet serve queue-broker

fleet serve queue-broker
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
———This role takes no flags and no arguments.

Behaviour

Runs the repo work queue as a resident service. Any trailing argument is rejected before the daemon starts with unexpected argument '<first>' for 'fleet serve queue-broker', exit 2 — through the serve spelling and through the argv0 alias alike. A help flag in the flag position (fleet serve queue-broker --help) is answered first with the generic serve domain help, exit 0.

  • Bind: TCP QUEUE_BROKER_BIND, default 100.99.113.103:4801 (the laptop tailnet address), plus a Unix-socket dual-bind: QUEUE_BROKER_SOCKET, default ~/.config/queue-broker/broker.sock. Routes and auth are identical on both transports. A Unix-socket bind failure degrades to “TCP only” with a log line.
  • Token: QUEUE_BROKER_TOKEN_FILE, default ~/.config/queue-broker/token; an unreadable token file is a startup error, exit 3. Requests carry X-Agent-Token; a pre-body gate refuses unauthenticated or oversized requests from headers alone (401 / 413) before any body byte is read. The only unauthenticated route is the health probe.
  • Protocol: POST /<command> with a JSON args object; response envelope {"ok": true, ...} or {"ok": false, "exit": N, "error": "..."} where exit mirrors the queue client’s codes (2 validation, 3 config, 4 HTTP, 5 no row).
  • Health: GET /healthz returns {"service": "queue-broker"}, unauthenticated.
  • Backend: Turso only, on the dedicated fleet-queue database at QUEUE_BROKER_TURSO_URL, token from QUEUE_BROKER_TURSO_TOKEN_FILE or resolved from the secrets broker. QUEUE_BROKER_BACKEND unset, empty, or turso is accepted; anything else is a startup config error, exit 3.
  • Secrets dependency: QUEUE_BROKER_SECRETS_URL (default http://100.99.113.103:4800, or unix://<path> for the secrets broker’s socket) and QUEUE_BROKER_SECRETS_TOKEN_FILE (default ~/.config/secrets-broker/token).
  • Startup ordering: the listener binds first, then the Turso backend comes up on a startup thread, so /healthz answers immediately and queue verbs answer exit 3 with a turso_pending reason until the backend is ready. A backend that cannot come up within its retry budget still exits the broker with 3 so the supervisor restarts it.

Help: fleet serve queue-broker --help prints this role’s own usage — the environment configuration surface below — and exits 0.

Exit codes

  • 0 — only via --help; a running broker returning 0 in a serve list is converted to 1 by the supervisor.
  • 2 — unexpected argument.
  • 3 — token-file or backend startup failure.
  • 69 — role not available in this invocation.

Example

$ fleet serve queue-broker

Runs the queue broker in the foreground on TCP port 4801 and its Unix socket until stopped.

fleet serve secrets-broker

fleet serve secrets-broker
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
———This role takes no flags and no arguments.

Behaviour

Runs the secrets broker in the foreground, dual-bound on TCP and a Unix socket. Any trailing argument is rejected before the daemon starts with unexpected argument '<first>' for 'fleet serve secrets-broker', exit 2. A help flag in the flag position is answered first with the generic serve domain help, exit 0.

The broker’s full semantics — the serving gate, cache-first reads, read-through on miss, refresh, and per-secret install — are covered in Secrets and the secrets broker. The client side is fleet secrets. Its configuration:

Env varDefaultMeaning
SECRETS_BROKER_BIND100.99.113.103:4800TCP bind. On the sandbox (FLEET_LOCATION=sandbox) the bind is forced to 127.0.0.1:4800 at the bind itself, whatever the env says.
SECRETS_BROKER_SOCKET~/.config/secrets-broker/broker.sockUnix-socket dual-bind; a bind failure degrades to TCP-only with a log line.
SECRETS_BROKER_TOKEN_FILE~/.config/secrets-broker/tokenDaemon token file; unreadable means startup exit 3.
SECRETS_BROKER_TTL_S900 (minimum 30)Refresh interval in seconds. Unparseable falls back to 900 with a warning; parsed but below 30 refuses to start, exit 2.

Endpoints (header X-Agent-Token required on everything except /health; identical over TCP and the Unix socket): GET /health, GET /secrets (names only, sorted), GET /secret/<name>, POST /refresh.

Help: fleet serve secrets-broker --help prints this role’s own usage — the environment configuration surface below — and exits 0.

Exit codes

  • 0 — only via --help.
  • 2 — unexpected argument, bad home, or a refused TTL.
  • 3 — token-file or bind failure.
  • 69 — role not available in this invocation.

Example

$ fleet serve secrets-broker

Runs the secrets broker in the foreground on TCP port 4800 and its Unix socket until stopped.

fleet serve search

usage: fleet serve search [options]
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
--configPATH~/.local/state/atlas-search/service.json (env ATLAS_SEARCH_SERVICE_CONFIG)Service config file.
--listenADDRfrom configListen address override (loopback only).
--job-ttl-msN600000Completed-job TTL override, milliseconds.
--hard-ttl-msN3600000Submit hard-cap override, milliseconds.
-h, --help——Print this role’s usage and exit 0.

Behaviour

This is the only flag-bearing serve role. It runs the Atlas search service in the foreground: the loopback HTTP job protocol over one shared Snowflake embedder and a read-only Turso backend — the atlas-search service rehomed into fleet, same config, same wire. The role is also reachable as fleet search serve; both spellings require the search-serve capability. See fleet search for the client.

  • The embedder is the Snowflake snowflake-arctic-embed-m-v2.0 model at a pinned snapshot revision, loaded lazily on the first vector query only — FTS-only jobs and a cold service work without it. The model directory resolves from ATLAS_MODEL_DIR / the Nix closure.
  • The backend is a read-only Turso backend; its token comes only from the service config chain, never the environment.
  • The job protocol is a bounded async queue with in-memory temp state; /health reports the embedder load state.
  • init (client table) and fetch-model deliberately stay on the standalone atlas-search artifact. Rollback is pointing the unit’s ExecStart back at atlas-search serve.

Exit codes

  • 0 — only via --help; a running service never exits 0.
  • 1 — runtime failure.
  • 2 — usage / config error.
  • 69 — role not available in this invocation.

Example

$ fleet serve search --job-ttl-ms 300000

Runs the search service with a five-minute completed-job TTL.

fleet serve proxy

fleet serve proxy
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
———This role takes no flags and no arguments.

Behaviour

Runs the session proxy (the broker) in the foreground, binding the broker socket from fleet config (FLEET_BROKER_SOCKET / [proxy] broker_socket, default ~/.cache/laptop-agent/broker.sock). It is the same leaf as fleet proxy serve; see fleet proxy for the full broker semantics — warm pools, the hello negotiation, keepalive, and idle exit. Inside a multi-role serve list the proxy runs co-hosted and its idle-exit is disabled (see Role-list semantics above). Unlike the two broker roles, this role has its own usage text: fleet serve proxy --help prints the proxy-role usage, exit 0.

Exit codes

  • 0 — clean exit (for example --help, or a live broker already owning the socket); in a serve list a clean role exit is converted to 1.
  • 2 — unexpected argument.
  • 69 — role not available in this invocation.

Example

$ fleet serve queue-broker secrets-broker proxy
fleet serve: starting 3 roles in one process: queue-broker secrets-broker proxy

Runs all three roles in one supervised process; the first role to exit takes the process down.

fleet proxy

The session proxy is the broker every sandbox seat talks through to reach the laptop’s services. The wire is 8-byte big-endian length-prefixed JSON frames. The broker persists nothing: the routing table comes from config, tunnels live in memory, and token files are read per request and never stored or logged.

The broker’s services map (port → service) is built in: 4799 laptop-agent, 4800 secrets-broker, 4801 queue-broker, 21118 rustdesk. The session broker socket defaults to ~/.cache/laptop-agent/broker.sock (FLEET_BROKER_SOCKET / [proxy] broker_socket).

The domain’s argv0 alias is laptop-agent-broker. Capabilities: proxy-serve (serve), proxy-connect (connect/init/get/put/ssh — present in every build), proxy-raw-splice (splice).

See also fleet serve and Proxy, sessions and recovery.

fleet proxy serve

fleet proxy serve
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
———Takes no arguments. --help prints the usage, exit 0; any other trailing argument is a usage error naming it, exit 2.

Behaviour

Binds the session broker Unix socket and serves in the foreground. If a live broker already owns the socket, it exits quietly; if the socket file is stale, it unlinks and binds.

  • Warm tunnel pools: per-port pools of warm CONNECT tunnels to the laptop’s services; pool size from LAPTOP_AGENT_POOL, compiled default 50. A request takes a pooled connection and on any failure retries once on a fresh one. Pool overflow policy: idle → grow (below the live ceiling) → wait briefly for a returned tunnel → grow anyway; a request never fails because of the pool.
  • Two reaches to the laptop: the Cloudflare leg is primary for the laptop-agent daemon port when its Access file exists (~/tools/laptop-agent-cf-access.json, a JSON {client_id, client_secret} file, mode 600, read per request, sent only as CF-Access-* headers, never stored or logged; no file, no leg) — TLS through the platform egress proxy to the tunnel hostname sandbox-link.security.cab, whose ingress lands on the daemon’s own listener laptop-side, token auth preserved end to end. The tailnet leg (CONNECT through the host egress proxy to the tailnet target host 100.99.113.103) is the automatic fallback, on connection failure and on a Cloudflare edge error status (502/503/530) alike. Pools and recovery gates key on (port, transport) so the legs never share a bucket.
  • Hello negotiation: sessions speak the legacy dialect (proto 0: request frames from the first frame) or negotiate a hello first (proto 1, fleet clients), decided per connection by peeking at the first frame, never by configuration. The hello response carries the services map (port → {name, version}) and the broker’s capability list. A too-old peer gets the proto-too-old frame and exit 69 on the client side.
  • Keepalive and idle exit: a keepalive thread pings the laptop-agent’s /health every 180 s. The broker exits once client requests have been idle for idle_exit_secs ([proxy] idle_exit_secs, default 3600 s; 0 is rejected at config load) — keepalive traffic does not count as use. In a multi-role serve list the idle exit is disabled (co-hosted mode).
  • Colocated brokers: for the queue/secrets broker ports, the broker first tries the role’s own Unix socket with a bounded dial (the dial is the probe; a socket that answers within the deadline is used, any other outcome selects TCP within the same attempt) before tunnelling.

Port 3130 note: port 3130 is the host egress proxy port — the CONNECT proxy named by the session’s HTTPS_PROXY environment. It is not a fleet listener. The tailnet leg’s shape is: fleet → HTTP CONNECT to the egress proxy at <egress host>:3130 → tailnet target 100.99.113.103:<service port>. Fleet contains no 3130 listener to restart; 3130 belongs to the session/host layer.

Exit codes

  • 0 — clean exit, including “a live broker already owns the socket”.
  • 2 — usage (trailing argument).
  • 69 — capability unavailable in this invocation.

Example

$ fleet proxy serve

Binds the broker socket and serves until client requests have been idle for 3600 s.

fleet proxy connect

fleet proxy connect [--print-path] [--stdio [--host H] [--port N]] [--request METHOD PATH [--service-port N] [--token-file F] [--body JSON]]
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
--print-path—offPrint the PATH shim directory and exit. Mutually exclusive with --request and --stdio.
--stdio—offRaw relay spelling (SSH’s ProxyCommand shape): relay stdin/stdout over one tunnel. Mutually exclusive with --request and --print-path.
--hostHconfig target hostTunnel destination host. Requires --stdio.
--portN22Tunnel destination port. Requires --stdio.
--requestMETHOD PATH—Issue exactly one framed request on the negotiated stream and print {"status": …, "body": …} as JSON.
--service-portNthe request’s implied route (4799)Select the laptop service port. Must follow --request.
--token-fileF—Name the token file the broker should read for this request. Must follow --request.
--bodyJSON—Request body; must be valid JSON. Must follow --request.

Each flag may be given at most once; a repeat is a usage error.

Behaviour

Connect to the session proxy: ensure a broker answers (starting one when none does), sync the PATH shims from its services map, and optionally issue one request over the negotiated stream. The ensure step spawns fleet serve proxy detached when the socket does not answer, then waits for the hello. A legacy (proto 0) answer still counts as running; its services map is the built-in table. The negotiated services map regenerates the PATH shim directory; --print-path prints that directory and exits (the shell-integration spelling).

Exit codes

  • 0 — ok.
  • 2 — usage (repeated flag, bad combination, invalid --body JSON).
  • 3 — transport failure.
  • 69 — protocol / capability unavailable (including a proto-too-old peer).

Example

$ fleet proxy connect --request GET /health --service-port 4799
{"status": 200, "body": {"ok": true}}

Ensures a broker, then issues one health request to the laptop-agent service.

fleet proxy init

fleet proxy init
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
———Takes no arguments.

Behaviour

Byte-identical to the fleet init built-in — one implementation lives in the proxy client and both spellings resolve identically. It autostarts this host’s fleet roles per the [host] manifest: on the sandbox, probe the broker socket and sync PATH shims when a broker answers (a strict no-op when one is already running — init never fights an incumbent broker), start one when none does, and probe/start the standing loopback secrets broker. An unknown location reports state, starts nothing, and exits 69.

Exit codes

  • 0 — roles running or correctly reported.
  • 2 — session initialisation error, before any role work.
  • 69 — unknown location, or this build cannot run init.

Example

$ fleet proxy init

Autostarts the sandbox roles (proxy + secrets-broker) if they are not running.

fleet proxy ssh

fleet proxy ssh -- [ssh args...]
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
--—required, firstLiteral separator. Everything after it is SSH arguments. A second -- inside the SSH arguments is an error: “the SSH destination is fixed; do not pass a second ‘–’”.

Behaviour

Runs system OpenSSH through the fleet proxy as a recovery path — the route you use when the normal laptop channel is what is broken. Everything that decides where the connection lands is pinned by fleet; the caller supplies only extra SSH options and an optional remote command. Option parsing walks clusters character-by-character so clustered forms like -vL split correctly.

The pinned argv shape:

  • Destination user@<target host> with HostName=<target host> (default 100.99.113.103), User=user.
  • Identity ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 with IdentitiesOnly=yes.
  • UserKnownHostsFile=~/.ssh/known_hosts_laptop, StrictHostKeyChecking=yes.
  • ConnectTimeout=60, ConnectionAttempts=3, ServerAliveInterval=15, ServerAliveCountMax=8.
  • ControlMaster=auto with ControlPath=~/.ssh/cm-%r@%h:%p and ControlPersist=3600.
  • ProxyCommand=<this fleet binary> proxy connect --stdio --host <target host> --port %p.

The fleet proxy credential stays in the environment and is sent only by the CONNECT relay, never in the SSH argv. The command execs the system ssh (Unix only; elsewhere exit 69). Its exit code is ssh’s own.

Exit codes

  • ssh’s own exit code on success of the exec.
  • 2 — usage (missing --, or a second -- in the SSH arguments).
  • 69 — non-Unix platform.

Example

$ fleet proxy ssh -- hostname
amd

Opens the pinned recovery SSH connection and runs hostname on the laptop.

fleet proxy get

fleet proxy get [--mode OCTAL] [--no-resume] <laptop-path> <local-path | ->
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
--modeOCTALdestination defaultFile mode for the downloaded file.
--no-resume—off (resume on)Do not resume from an existing deterministic temp; start over.
- (as destination)——Stream to stdout instead of a local path.

Behaviour

Downloads a file from the laptop over the agent channel, through the broker to the laptop-agent daemon’s file routes. Chunks are 2 MiB raw chunks, base64-encoded, carried in JSON envelopes (stat, begin, commit, abort, read). Chunks land in a deterministic local temp — .<name>.fleet-part-<sha256[..12]> beside the destination — so an interrupted transfer resumes by re-issuing begin and continuing from the temp’s size. The whole-file SHA-256 from the daemon’s stat must match before the temp is renamed over the destination. - streams to stdout (the hash is still verified at the end; a mismatch fails the command after the bytes were emitted — check stderr). Recursive get is deferred in v1: the daemon protocol has no directory-listing route.

Exit codes

  • 0 — ok, hash verified.
  • 2 — usage.
  • 3 — transport.
  • 69 — capability unavailable.

Example

$ fleet proxy get /home/user/build/result.tar ./result.tar

Downloads the file with resume support and verifies its SHA-256 before renaming it into place.

fleet proxy put

fleet proxy put [--mode OCTAL] [--no-resume] <local-path | -> <laptop-path>
fleet proxy put -r [--mode OCTAL] [--no-resume] <local-dir> <laptop-dir>
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
--modeOCTAL0644 for stdin; otherwise the local file’s modeFile mode on the laptop.
--no-resume—off (resume on)Do not resume from an existing deterministic temp; start over.
-r—offRecursive: upload a directory tree.
- (as source)——Read stdin (spooled locally first).

Behaviour

Uploads a file to the laptop over the agent channel. The file is hashed (SHA-256), uploaded in 2 MiB chunks to a deterministic temp on the laptop — .<name>.fleet-part-<sha256[..12]> beside the destination — and atomically renamed over the destination only after the daemon verifies the hash. An interrupted put resumes from the temp unless --no-resume is given. Progress and the final sha256 go to stderr.

Exit codes

  • 0 — ok, hash verified by the daemon and rename committed.
  • 2 — usage.
  • 3 — transport.
  • 69 — capability unavailable.

Example

$ fleet proxy put ./result.tar /home/user/build/result.tar

Uploads the file in 2 MiB chunks; the destination only appears once its hash verifies.

fleet proxy splice

fleet proxy splice
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
———Takes no arguments.

Behaviour

Listens on 127.0.0.1:21118 (loopback only, a pinned constant) and relays each accepted TCP stream through the fleet broker to the laptop’s RustDesk direct-access service (port 21118 laptop-side). Requires the broker to advertise raw-splice support in its hello (the proxy-raw-splice capability plus the service flag); a legacy or non-advertising broker is a transport error, not a silent fallback. This is the RustDesk direct-access path that avoids the relayed session.

Exit codes

  • 0 — clean exit.
  • 2 — usage (trailing argument).
  • 3 — transport (broker does not advertise raw-splice).
  • 69 — capability unavailable.

Example

$ fleet proxy splice

Starts the loopback splice listener on 127.0.0.1:21118 until stopped.

fleet dispatch

fleet dispatch is a thin client over pm-dispatch, the pm-stack dispatch service. The service is a working TypeScript/Bun suite that is not rewritten; this domain is verbs over its existing HTTP routes — and those routes are exactly three. Per-task status is not here: a task’s state is the repo queue itself, so per-task status reads ride the queue domain (fleet queue list).

VerbRouteAuth
statusGET /healthunauthenticated
launchPOST /v1/sessionsBearer
enqueuePOST /v1/tasksBearer

See also fleet dispatch-test and Dispatch and dispatch-test.

Connection ladder and auth (all verbs)

Transport selection, in order:

  1. Direct URL: env FLEET_DISPATCH_URL or fleet.toml [dispatch] url. It must be http://host[:port] with no path — a path is a usage error; a missing port gets the configured port appended.
  2. Loopback probe: probe 127.0.0.1:{port} with a 750 ms connect timeout; if it answers, go direct to loopback. Port: [dispatch] port, default 4879.
  3. If config proxy_direct() is set: direct to {target_host}:{port}.
  4. Proxy-egress CONNECT: a CONNECT tunnel through the fleet proxy egress to the target host’s dispatch port (the sandbox route). The client opens its own tunnel on the egress because the framed session-broker shape forwards only an X-Agent-Token header, which pm-dispatch does not accept.

Auth is Authorization: Bearer <token>, the token resolved by name through fleet-secrets: default name pm-dispatch.api-token, overridable with [dispatch] token_name. The value enters exactly one header per request and is never printed, logged, or stored. HTTP 401 is reported as a transport-class error naming the mismatch with the service’s own token env (name only).

Success bodies print to stdout as pretty JSON exactly as the service sent them; errors go to stderr, prefixed fleet dispatch: . For HTTP error bodies the error string is used, and if the body has more fields the whole body is appended in brackets (a failed launch’s 502 names its cancelled task_id); messages are truncated at 600 chars.

The argument parser is shared by launch and enqueue: --flag value and --flag=value are both accepted; duplicate value flags, unknown options, values on boolean flags, and stray positionals are all usage errors.

fleet dispatch status

fleet dispatch status
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
———Takes no arguments. Any argument is a usage error. --help/-h prints usage and succeeds without contacting the service.

Behaviour

Issues GET /health on pm-dispatch: is the service up, and which build. Prints the service’s health body as a JSON object plus an added "transport" field describing the route taken, for example "direct http://127.0.0.1:4879" or "tunnel via proxy egress to {host}:4879". A non-object health body is wrapped as {"health": <body>, "transport": …}.

Exit codes

  • 0 — ok.
  • 2 — usage.
  • 3 — transport down / credentials unresolved or rejected.
  • 4 — the service answered with an HTTP error status.

Example

$ fleet dispatch status
{"ok": true, "transport": "direct http://127.0.0.1:4879"}

fleet dispatch launch

fleet dispatch launch --repo <owner/name> --prompt <text> [options]
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
--repo<owner/name>requiredAn allowlisted fleet repo (allowlist checked service-side).
--prompt<text>required (or --prompt-file)The session prompt.
--prompt-file<path>—Read the prompt from a file. Together with --prompt is a usage error.
--title<text>service default: the prompt’s first lineTracking-issue title.
--model<provider/id>—Model hint for the session.
--directory<path>—Must be the repo’s laptop primary or inside it.
--priority<p>—Integer 10–90, or critical|high|normal|low. Sent as a JSON number when it parses as an integer, otherwise as the raw string; range validation is the service’s job.
--issue / --no-issue—service default: issueCreate the tracking issue. Both together, in either order, is a usage error. Sent only when given.
--wait / --no-wait—service default: waitWait for the launch to complete. Both together is a usage error. Sent only when given.

Behaviour

POSTs /v1/sessions — creates the tracking issue and queue task, starts the session, and assigns the task to it (all service-side). The client sends only the fields the caller set: repo and prompt always; title, model, directory, priority when given; issue: bool only when --issue/--no-issue was given; wait: bool only when --wait/--no-wait was given. The defaults named in the help (title = first prompt line, issue on, wait on) are the service’s defaults, applied because the client omits the fields.

Exit codes

  • 0 — ok.
  • 2 — usage.
  • 3 — transport down / credentials unresolved or rejected.
  • 4 — the service answered with an HTTP error status.

Example

$ fleet dispatch launch --repo developing-today/code --prompt "Fix the failing smoke test" --no-wait

Creates the tracking issue and queue task, starts a session on the laptop, and returns without waiting for the launch to complete.

fleet dispatch enqueue

fleet dispatch enqueue --repo <owner/name> --title <text> --prompt <text> [options]
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
--repo<owner/name>requiredAn allowlisted fleet repo (allowlist checked service-side).
--title<text>requiredTask title.
--prompt<text>required (or --prompt-file)The task prompt.
--prompt-file<path>—Read the prompt from a file. Together with --prompt is a usage error.
--kind<kind>service default: triageOne of triage|small_fix|pr_shepherd|ci_investigation. Validated client-side; an unknown kind is a usage error listing the four. Sent only when given.
--priority<p>—Integer 10–90, or critical|high|normal|low (same wire rule as launch).
--model<provider/id>—Stored as the payload’s model hint only.
--issue—service default: no issueCreate a tracking issue first. One-way boolean — there is no --no-issue; omitting it sends nothing. The opposite default from launch.
--issue-number<n>—Attach to this existing issue instead. Must parse as an integer; sent as issue_number.
--dedupe-key<key>service default: canonical key from the issue, else uniqueSent as dedupe_key.

Behaviour

POSTs /v1/tasks: enqueue only, no session. Wire names are snake_case (issue_number, dedupe_key); launch’s are single words.

Exit codes

  • 0 — ok.
  • 2 — usage (including an unknown --kind).
  • 3 — transport down / credentials unresolved or rejected.
  • 4 — the service answered with an HTTP error status.

Example

$ fleet dispatch enqueue --repo developing-today/code --title "Triage the red nightly" --prompt "Find why the nightly failed" --kind ci_investigation

Enqueues a CI-investigation task without launching a session.

fleet dispatch-test

fleet dispatch-test is an explicit-dispatch CI test harness: scan fleet repos for free Actions capacity, submit a job, and track its stored status. Nothing here is trigger-driven: every verb runs only when a caller invokes it, and submit dispatches a workflow_dispatch run explicitly.

See also fleet dispatch and Dispatch and dispatch-test.

Shared machinery

  • Execution homes: ONE repo — the fleet repo, config [dispatch-test] fleet_repo, default dezren39/fleet — holds the other fleet repos as git submodules and carries the generic workflow fleet-dispatch-test.yml. Eligible homes are its copies: the source repo plus its fork network, discovered per invocation by breadth-first traversal of GET /repos/{r}/forks, depth-capped at 8 levels, deduplicated, source first, then copies in API order — unless [dispatch-test] scopes pins an explicit list (pin wins; scan output reports scopes_source: "config" vs "fork-network").
  • Capacity counting: for each scope, ACTIVE = (jobs with status in_progress or queued across all in_progress runs — fetched paginated, page size 100, max 100 pages) + (number of queued runs, from total_count, counted as 1 active unit each — a queued run has not started and exposes no jobs, so it counts once regardless of its eventual fan-out).
  • Workflow presence: the repo’s workflows list (paginated) contains a workflow whose path ends with fleet-dispatch-test.yml and whose state is active (a missing state counts as active).
  • Eligible = workflow_present && active < threshold.
  • Threshold: --threshold N, else [dispatch-test] threshold, else 40. --threshold 0 is a usage error (“can never be satisfied”).
  • Pagination contract: paged reads are complete, bounded, or say so; truncation is never silent.
  • Auth, by name through fleet-secrets only: GitHub token name [dispatch-test] token_name, default github.ghcr-classic-pat; Turso token name [dispatch-test] turso_token_name, default turso.fleet-dispatch-jobs-token. Each value enters exactly one Authorization header per request. GitHub calls use User-Agent: fleet-dispatch-test against https://api.github.com.
  • Turso jobs store: endpoint [dispatch-test] turso_url, default https://fleet-dispatch-jobs-dezren39.aws-us-east-1.turso.io; requests are POST {url}/v2/pipeline. Table jobs, columns: id, created_at, name, target_repo, target_ref, script, status, run_id, run_url, exit_code, output_tail, updated_at, submodule, commands. The phase-2 migration (ALTER TABLE jobs ADD COLUMN submodule TEXT, … ADD COLUMN commands TEXT) is applied idempotently by submit and status; a “duplicate column” error means already-migrated and is ignored.

Known discrepancy: the help text understates three source behaviours — scan’s human output has a leading scopes source: … line the help omits; --threshold 0 is a usage error the help does not mention; and submit’s forced --repo also skips the eligibility checks (below).

fleet dispatch-test scan

fleet dispatch-test scan [--threshold N] [--json]
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
--thresholdNconfig, else 40Eligibility threshold: a scope is eligible when active < threshold and the workflow is present. 0 is a usage error.
--json—offPrint the facts as JSON instead of lines.

Behaviour

Scans every scope in order. Human output: a first line scopes source: {config|fork-network} (fleet repo {repo}), then one line per scope <repo> active=<n> workflow=<yes|no> eligible=<yes|no>, then chosen: <repo|none> (the first eligible scope). --json prints:

{ "threshold": 40, "fleet_repo": "dezren39/fleet", "scopes_source": "fork-network", "scopes": [{ "repo": "dezren39/fleet", "active": 3, "workflow": true, "eligible": true }], "chosen": "dezren39/fleet" }

Exit codes

  • 0 — ok (including chosen: none).
  • 2 — usage (including --threshold 0).
  • 3 — transport down / credentials unresolved / no eligible scope class failures on the scan path.
  • 4 — an HTTP error status from GitHub or Turso.

Example

$ fleet dispatch-test scan
scopes source: fork-network (fleet repo dezren39/fleet)
dezren39/fleet active=3 workflow=yes eligible=yes
chosen: dezren39/fleet

fleet dispatch-test submit

fleet dispatch-test submit --submodule NAME [--threshold N] [--repo owner/name] [--ref REF] [--name TEXT] [--commands TEXT | --commands-file PATH]
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
--submoduleNAMErequiredFleet-repo submodule to run in — a single path segment: alphanumerics, -, _, .; never empty, . or .., never a slash. Examples: code, opencode, openchamber, nix, hatch.
--thresholdNconfig, else 40Capacity threshold for the scan rule. 0 is a usage error.
--repoowner/name—Force this execution-home copy. Forcing bypasses the eligibility rule: the code scans the forced repo only to report active_at_scan; it does not check active < threshold or workflow presence.
--refREFemptyRef inside the submodule repo; empty = the submodule stays at the umbrella’s recorded SHA. Stored in the row’s target_ref.
--nameTEXT—Free-text job name recorded on the row.
--commandsTEXTtrivial smoke setShell commands run inside the submodule. Mutually exclusive with --commands-file. Default: set -eux; echo dispatch-test smoke; git rev-parse HEAD; uname -a.
--commands-filePATH—Read the commands from a file. Mutually exclusive with --commands.

Behaviour

The job id is generated client-side (time-based base36 + random hex suffix). The sequence order is load-bearing:

  1. Connect to GitHub and to the Turso jobs store; run the idempotent schema migration.
  2. INSERT the job row with status='queued', target_repo=NULL, target_ref=<ref>, script=<commands>, submodule=<name>, commands=<commands>, run_id/run_url/exit_code/output_tail=NULL, created_at/updated_at = now (RFC 3339 UTC). (script mirrors commands so MVP-era readers still see the payload.)
  3. Pick the home: forced --repo, else the scan rule over discovered/pinned scopes. No eligible scope is a transport-class error (exit 3): “no eligible scope: no execution-home copy has active < {threshold} with the generic workflow present (job {id} remains queued in the store)”.
  4. Dispatch sequence: (a) UPDATE jobs SET target_repo=? — (b) dispatch POST /repos/{repo}/actions/workflows/fleet-dispatch-test.yml/dispatches with {"ref": <that repo's default_branch>, "inputs": {"job_id": id}} — the job id is the workflow’s only input — (c) only then UPDATE jobs SET status='dispatched'. Any failure stops the sequence: a failed dispatch leaves the row queued (with its target repo recorded).
  5. Prints JSON: {job_id, repo, submodule, ref (null when empty), active_at_scan, threshold, status: "dispatched"}.

Row lifecycle: queued (insert) → dispatched (client, after the workflow POST) → running (the workflow itself writes this, with run_id/run_url, when it fetches the job) → terminal status + exit_code/output_tail written back by the workflow, always, even on failure (a cancelled run is the best-effort exception — its row stays running, which status reports honestly).

Exit codes

  • 0 — ok, row dispatched.
  • 2 — usage (bad submodule, --commands with --commands-file, --threshold 0).
  • 3 — transport down / credentials unresolved / no eligible scope.
  • 4 — an HTTP error status from GitHub or Turso.

Example

$ fleet dispatch-test submit --submodule code --name "smoke the code submodule"
{"job_id": "…", "repo": "dezren39/fleet", "submodule": "code", "ref": null, "active_at_scan": 3, "threshold": 40, "status": "dispatched"}

fleet dispatch-test status

fleet dispatch-test status <job-id>
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
<job-id> (positional)job idrequiredExactly one positional; anything else is a usage error. This verb takes no flags.

Behaviour

Prints the stored row as pretty JSON with all columns (id, created_at, name, target_repo, target_ref, submodule, commands, script, status, run_id, run_url, exit_code, output_tail, updated_at), values typed from the Turso cells. This reads the store only — it never queries GitHub for live run state.

Exit codes

  • 0 — ok.
  • 2 — usage (not exactly one positional).
  • 3 — transport down / credentials unresolved.
  • 4 — an HTTP error status, including an unknown job id: “job {id} not found in the jobs store” exits 4.

Example

$ fleet dispatch-test status <job-id>
{
  "id": "…",
  "status": "dispatched",
  "submodule": "code",
  "target_repo": "dezren39/fleet"
}

fleet secrets

fleet secrets resolves secrets by name: the secrets broker first, Bitwarden (bws) as fallback. Secret values are never printed anywhere except get’s stdout, never logged, and never written to a file by this domain. For the broker itself — its cache, refresh, and serving gate — see Secrets and the secrets broker and the secrets-broker role in fleet serve.

The platform rule is that secrets are resolved by name through the fleet-secrets chain only; no domain shells out to bws or reads a token file on its own.

Writes exist at the same library level, for one flow: fleet-secrets’ BwsStore stores a value under a name through bws secret create (replacing any existing secret of that name, then verifying by reading it back), into the Bitwarden project named by $FLEET_BWS_PROJECT_ID or [secrets] bws_project_id. Its only caller is fleet bridge exchange, putting a freshly minted per-agent credential under its name during bootstrap enrolment. There is still no fleet secrets write verb, and the broker remains a read-through cache.

The resolution chain (shared context)

get walks this chain in order:

  1. Broker leg(s) first. Where the secrets broker’s own socket answers (the laptop), a direct source speaks GET /secret/<name> over that Unix socket directly. Elsewhere (the sandbox), a broker source makes a framed exchange through the session broker to port 4800: the request names the token file ([secrets] token_file, default ~/tools/secrets-broker-token); the session broker reads the file per request and sends its contents as X-Agent-Token — fleet only ever names the file; the value never transits fleet’s own memory on this leg.
  2. bws CLI fallback — bws secret list + get, the same shape the broker itself uses to fill its cache. The fallback carries its own credential: the BWS_ACCESS_TOKEN env var when non-empty, else the on-disk machine-account token file, handed to the bws child via its environment.
  3. (Library-level, not in this domain’s headline chain) a 1Password source for seats that keep secrets there — the same names resolve without a broker or a Bitwarden token.

Retry semantics: a broker leg that cannot answer is retried before the chain moves on — the budget is sized to real restart windows (a full switch restarts broker + tunnel together; the broker is back in ~16 s) without making a genuinely dead broker a hang: the first pause doubles per attempt up to a cap, with a per-attempt ceiling on a single exchange. Exactly one broker leg owns the retry budget; when a direct leg exists, the session-broker leg behind it gets no retries. A broker 404 is definitive about the name and is not retried. If the session-broker socket file does not exist at all, the leg does not burn the retry budget. Resolved values live in a type whose Debug is redacted; chain errors count failed sources without ever carrying a value.

Known discrepancy: “the laptop secrets-broker” in the domain summary is location-relative. On the sandbox the first leg is a local loopback broker spawned by fleet init; on the laptop it is a direct Unix-socket leg; only from the sandbox-through-proxy path is it the laptop’s broker.

The three broker service tokens are published in Bitwarden Secrets Manager under the names fleet.secrets-broker-token, fleet.queue-broker-token, and fleet.laptop-agent-token, and live on a seat as mode-0600 files ~/tools/secrets-broker-token, ~/tools/queue-broker-token, and ~/tools/laptop-agent-token. Do not conflate these client-side files with the daemon-side token files in each broker’s own config dir (~/.config/secrets-broker/token, ~/.config/queue-broker/token).

fleet secrets get

fleet secrets get <name>
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
<name> (positional)secret namerequiredExactly one name, not starting with -. This verb takes no flags. Help flags are answered before arity checks, so --help is never mistaken for a secret name.

Behaviour

Resolves one secret by name through the chain above. The value goes to stdout and nowhere else; errors are value-free shapes on stderr. A broken pipe on stdout is a quiet success (the Unix-filter rule), so fleet secrets get NAME | head does not fail.

Broker response shapes this verb consumes: a cache hit answers {"key", "value", "fetched_at_unix", "age_seconds", "source": "cache"}; a read-through hit answers the same shape with "source": "bitwarden-read-through" and "age_seconds": 0; a not-loaded broker answers 503 {"error": "secrets not loaded yet"}; an absent name answers 404 {"error": "no such secret"}; a Bitwarden read-through failure answers a loud 502, never a silent 404-as-if-absent.

Exit codes

  • 0 — ok, value on stdout (including the broken-pipe case).
  • 2 — usage (missing/extra name, or a name starting with -).
  • 3 — unresolved / broker unavailable and the fallback could not resolve the name either.

Example

$ fleet secrets get fleet.secrets-broker-token > /dev/null && echo resolved
resolved

(The value itself is deliberately not shown; in real use it is piped or captured, never displayed.)

fleet secrets list

fleet secrets list
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
———Takes no arguments and no flags.

Behaviour

Lists the names in the broker’s cache, one per line — names only, never values. Source selection mirrors get’s first leg only: the direct broker source when the broker’s own socket is configured/live, else the session-broker source over the session broker socket plus the configured secrets token file.

Known discrepancy: list has no bws fallback, contradicting the symmetry the domain summary (“broker first, Bitwarden as fallback”) suggests. A broker failure is loud — stderr plus exit 3 — because a bws listing has different semantics: it enumerates the vault, not the broker’s cache, so it is never silently substituted.

Exit codes

  • 0 — ok, names on stdout.
  • 2 — usage (trailing argument).
  • 3 — broker unavailable. There is no fallback for this verb.

Example

$ fleet secrets list
fleet.laptop-agent-token
fleet.queue-broker-token
fleet.secrets-broker-token

Names only; the listing is the broker’s cache, not the vault.

fleet gh

fleet gh is the real gh CLI, passed through under a rotating fleet token. Four argument vectors are shadow subcommands (tiers, cache-serve, cache-status, closures); every other argument vector passes through to the real gh unchanged.

See also The gh passthrough.

The passthrough (any other arguments)

fleet gh <args...>
fleet gh --raw <args...>
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
--raw—off (also FLEET_GH_RAW=1)First-class bypass: exec the real gh directly with the caller’s ambient credentials; no token resolved or injected, no rotation or failover.
(all other args)——Passed to the real gh binary unchanged. FLEET_GH_BIN selects the binary, default gh.

Behaviour

Before each attempt, one token is resolved by name through the fleet secrets chain and exported as GH_TOKEN for that attempt only. Attempts are captured (piped), not streamed, because the failure text is what classifies a failover; the caller sees the final attempt’s stdout, stderr, and exit code byte-exact as gh produced them. Attempts are silent by default; FLEET_GH_TRACE=1 names each attempt’s token source (never a value) on stderr. Tokens are never printed, logged, or written to a file; provider errors name source and stage only. The audit log redacts secret-carrying arguments (gh secret set bodies, Authorization headers) in its copy only.

Rotation order (source behaviour):

  1. Fleet App installations — “developing.today fleet”, App ID 5612056 (FLEET_GH_APP_ID may override). Private key by secret name github-app.developing-today-fleet.private-key. Default owners, in order: developing-today, developing-today-forks, dezren39.
  2. developing.today App installations — App ID and key both by name (kaneo.github-app-id, kaneo.github-app-private-key). Default owners: developing-today, dezren39.
  3. developing-today-backup App installations — by name (github-app.backup-app-id, github-app.backup-private-key). Default owner: developing-today.
  4. Personal — the gh OAuth token, parsed out of the broker secret named github-cli.hosts-yml (the hosts.yml file itself, stored by name; the parser extracts its oauth_token). Tried last: the final fallback, not the first identity used.

Known discrepancy: the help summary’s “the developing.today App’s installations, then personal last” understates the source — there are three Apps in a fixed order (fleet → developing.today → backup), each expanded over its owners, with the personal token last.

Mechanics per App leg: the private key is resolved by name; an RS256 JWT is signed with the system openssl, the key passed over an inherited fd — never written to disk, never in argv; the owner’s installation is resolved live from GET /app/installations, paginated at 100/page. Hint-first: when the call names a repo or org, that owner’s installation moves to the front of each App leg, because an installation token only sees its own installation’s scope. Controls: FLEET_GH_ORDER (comma list fixing the rotation exactly: personal, app:<owner>, devtoday:<owner>, backup:<owner>), FLEET_GH_APP_OWNERS / FLEET_GH_DEVTODAY_OWNERS / FLEET_GH_BACKUP_OWNERS (comma lists replacing an App’s default owners).

Failover triggers. A failed attempt’s combined stdout+stderr is classified:

ClassTrigger strings (case-insensitive)Retry?
RateLimitrate limit, rate_limit, too many requests, http 429Yes — any call
Permissionmissing required scopes, insufficient_scopes, resource not accessible, not accessible by integration, not accessible by personal access token, this endpoint requires you to be authenticated, bad credentials, http 401Yes — any call
NodeResolutioncould not resolve to a nodeRead-only calls only
Otheranything elseRead-only calls only

The rule: a write is only repeated under a fresh token when the failure proves GitHub refused the request before processing it — rate-limit and permission/scope rejections are both pre-execution refusals. Node-resolution is explicitly not one: GraphQL executes mutation fields serially, so a batched mutation may already have run an earlier field before a later field’s node fails to resolve; replaying would duplicate the part that landed. Any other write failure is returned as-is. Reads repeat on any failure class. A token provider failure skips that source silently (named under trace) and the rotation continues; if no attempt produced output, the caller gets the provider errors and exit 3. If the last failover has no successor, the caller is shown the real gh failure, not a summary.

Two wrappers sit in front of the rotation:

  • Close guard: issue close and issue edit --add-label status:done are refused (exit 2, never reaching the rotation) when the queue broker has a claimed or parked task bound to that repo#issue, unless the bound task’s completion record (a fleet-closure/v1 record carrying its task id) is presented with the wrapper-only flag --completion-record <path>, stripped before gh runs. The queue query fails open — a broker outage must not block every close.
  • Metadata create path: issue create / pr create bodies are stamped with the fleet Metadata block before the rotation runs, and the full record is inserted into the metadata store after a successful create; a malformed caller block refuses the create before any write; a failed insert never loses the item (reported on stderr, ingestion heals it). Controls: FLEET_METADATA_DB, FLEET_GH_STAMP_KEY_ID (key material by name from the secrets broker).

Exit codes

  • The final attempt’s gh exit code, byte-exact.
  • 2 — close-guard refusal, or a malformed metadata block on a create.
  • 3 — no token source produced an attempt (provider errors reported).

Example

$ fleet gh api rate_limit --jq '.rate.remaining'

Runs the real gh under the first rotation token that succeeds, failing over on a rate-limit or permission refusal.

fleet gh tiers

fleet gh tiers
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
———Takes no flags.

Behaviour

Probes every rotation source and prints its core and GraphQL rate-limit headroom — labels and numbers only; token values never leave the provider.

Help: fleet gh tiers --help prints the verb’s own usage and exits 0; any other argument is a usage error naming it.

Exit codes

  • 0 — every source answers.
  • 3 — any source is down.

Example

$ fleet gh tiers

Prints per-source core and GraphQL headroom for all three Apps’ installations and the personal token.

fleet gh cache-serve

fleet gh cache-serve [--bind <addr>]
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
--bind<addr>FLEET_GH_CACHE_BIND, else 127.0.0.1:4802Daemon bind address. --bind beats the env, which beats the default; a bind without a port gets 4802.

Behaviour

Runs the credential/token cache daemon in the foreground (port 4802 — the next port after the queue broker’s 4801). It caches four things, memory-only, single-flight minting (concurrent requests for one key block on the in-flight mint):

Entry kindTTL
Secret resolutions60 s
App JWTswithin their expiry, minus a 60 s skew
Installation tokensuntil shortly before expires_at, minus the same 60 s skew, floored at 1 s
Per-App installation lists300 s

Nothing is written to disk; a restart is a cold cache, never a stale one. The wire is newline-delimited JSON over TCP, protocol version 1 — a daemon that does not know a request’s version answers {ok: false, …} rather than guessing. Every normal fleet gh call resolves through the localhost daemon first, then the laptop daemon (the proxy’s reach target at the same port; [gh] cache_local / cache_laptop in config, FLEET_GH_CACHE env beats both); with no daemon answering it resolves in-process over the same cache implementation and says so on stderr (“resolving in-process”).

Exit codes

  • 0 — clean exit.
  • 2 — usage.
  • 69 — capability unavailable.

Example

$ fleet gh cache-serve

Runs the cache daemon in the foreground on 127.0.0.1:4802.

fleet gh cache-status

fleet gh cache-status
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
———Takes no arguments and no flags.

Behaviour

Probes the configured cache daemons and prints each one’s snapshot — entry counts by kind, hit/miss counters, soonest expiry. Key names and values never leave the daemon; counts only.

Exit codes

  • 0 — at least one daemon answered.
  • 2 — usage (trailing argument).
  • 3 — no daemon answered.

Example

$ fleet gh cache-status

Prints counts-only snapshots for each configured cache daemon.

fleet gh closures

fleet gh closures [<item>]
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
<item> (positional, optional)item reference—Filter the closure log to one item. This verb takes no flags.

Behaviour

Reads back the closure log. The policy layer behind it: issue|pr close|reopen through the rotation must carry a --reason from the taxonomy — implemented, superseded, cancelled, started-incorrectly — enforced with the policy error “Please give a reason. This is required by policy.” The reason is written into the close comment, and every successful close or reopen appends one fleet-closure/v1 JSON-line record to closure-records.jsonl in the fleet state directory (backed up with it); closures prints the log, optionally filtered to one item.

Help: fleet gh closures --help prints the verb’s own usage and exits 0.

Exit codes

  • 0 — ok.
  • 2 — usage.

Example

$ fleet gh closures

Prints the full fleet-closure/v1 closure log, one JSON record per line.

fleet bridge

fleet bridge is the mailbox client for the message bridge (at https://bridge.security.cab). Every fleet agent has a mailbox on the bridge named after it, and registers with optional groups (muse, code-lanes, …). Central sends a message or a command to one agent, a group, or all; the agent reads its mailbox, does the work, and posts its answer back, which marks the command handled.

See also The bridge: fleet messaging.

Each verb has its own help: fleet bridge <command> --help prints that verb’s usage section plus the shared defaults-and-exit-codes footer, as the domain status line advertises. A bare fleet bridge --help prints the whole-domain usage text.

Tokens, URLs, and defaults (all verbs)

Two token families, both resolved by name through fleet-secrets; values are never printed, logged, or put in argv:

FamilySecret nameOpensURL shape
Owner token (central verbs)message-bridge.access-token (renamable via [bridge] owner_token_name)send, agents, log/api/<owner-token>/fleet/…
Fleet token (agent verbs)message-bridge.fleet-tokenhello, inbox, post, ack, work — agent routes only; it cannot send commands/fleet/<fleet-token>/…
Per-agent credentialbridge.<agent>-fleet-token (the name the agent profile records)The same agent routes, as that one agent only; its groups are the ones bound when the owner minted its bootstrap token/fleet/<credential>/…
Notes token (notes family)bridge.<agent>-token (renamable via [bridge] notes_token_name)notes send, notes inbox, notes ack for the token’s class/name identityAuthorization: Bearer header on /notes/…

Tokens travel in the URL path, so every error string is scrubbed of token values (<token>) before it is printed, and a 404 is reported as “a wrong token, an old bridge without fleet mailboxes, or a wrong URL”. Plain http URLs are accepted only to this machine; anything else must be https, because tokens ride the path.

Derivation fallback: when the fleet token’s secret is missing but the owner token resolves (the laptop seat), the fleet token is derived from the owner token exactly as the bridge derives it: base64url(HMAC-SHA256(key = owner token bytes, message = "message-bridge/fleet-token/v1")). The derived value is used in-process only; it is never written anywhere.

Defaults: the agent name defaults to $FLEET_AGENT, then [bridge] agent; groups to $FLEET_AGENT_GROUPS, then [bridge] groups; the bridge URL to $FLEET_BRIDGE_URL, then [bridge] url, then https://bridge.security.cab (env beats file throughout). Output is the bridge’s JSON, passed through.

Exit codes for every verb unless noted: 0 ok · 2 usage · 3 transport or credentials · 4 the bridge refused the request (its JSON error goes to stderr).

fleet bridge send

fleet bridge send --to <targets> [--command] [--sender NAME] <text | ->
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
--to<targets>requiredTargets: agent:<name> (or a bare name), group:<name>, all. Repeat --to or comma-separate.
--command—off (plain message)Mark the send as a command.
--senderNAME—Sender name recorded on the message.
<text | -> (positional)textrequiredMessage text; - reads it from stdin.

Behaviour

Central verb (owner token). Sends a message — or, with --command, a command — to one agent, a group, or all agents. Route: POST /api/<owner-token>/fleet/send. A command sits in the target mailboxes until an agent takes it (see inbox --take) and posts an answer back, which marks it handled.

Exit codes

0 ok · 2 usage · 3 transport or credentials · 4 the bridge refused the request.

Example

$ fleet bridge send --to group:muse --command "run the nightly triage"

Sends a command to every agent in the muse group.

———Takes no arguments and no flags.

Prints the registered agents, groups, and unread counts as the bridge’s JSON.

--directioninbound|outbound—Filter by direction.
--kindmessage|command—Filter by kind.

fleet bridge mint-enroll

fleet bridge mint-enroll --agent A [--kind K] [--groups g1,g2] [--notes-identity I] [--ttl SECS]
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
--agentArequiredThe new agent’s name; the token is bound to it and enrolls no other.
--kindKagentThe agent kind the token is bound to.
--groupsg1,g2—Groups the mailbox registers with at exchange.
--notes-identityI—A class/name notes identity to register at exchange.
--ttlSECS86400The token’s lifetime in seconds (60 to 604800).

Behaviour

Central verb (owner token). Mints a bootstrap enroll token. Route: POST /api/<owner-token>/enroll-tokens. The answer carries the token value once: the bridge stores only its SHA-256 hash and can never show it again. Hand the value to the new seat, which runs fleet agent enroll --name A --kind K --bootstrap <value>; the exchange burns the token and returns the agent’s fleet credential and notes token, likewise once. The PM console’s Agents screen mints these from its Provisioning section and shows the value and the command once, on that screen only.

Exit codes

0 ok · 2 usage · 3 transport or credentials · 4 the bridge refused the request.

Example

$ fleet bridge mint-enroll --agent scout-2 --kind muse --groups muse

Mints a day-long bootstrap token for scout-2 and prints it, once.

fleet bridge enroll-tokens

fleet bridge enroll-tokens
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
———Takes no arguments and no flags.

Behaviour

Central verb (owner token). Lists every minted bootstrap token’s state: pending, used (with the exchange’s time), expired (its TTL lapsed), or revoked (with the revocation time), each with its binding (agent, kind, groups, notes identity) and mint/expiry times. Route: GET /api/<owner-token>/enroll-tokens. State only: no hash or value is ever shown — the value existed once, in the mint answer.

Exit codes

0 ok · 2 usage · 3 transport or credentials · 4 the bridge refused the request.

Example

$ fleet bridge enroll-tokens

Shows which minted tokens are still outstanding, and how each closed one ended.

fleet bridge revoke-enroll

fleet bridge revoke-enroll (--agent A | --token-hash H)
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
--agentA—Take back every still-pending token minted for this agent; the answer counts them.
--token-hashH—Revoke the one token stored under this SHA-256 hash; the answer is {revoked: true|false}.

Behaviour

Central verb (owner token). Revokes unused bootstrap tokens. Route: POST /api/<owner-token>/enroll-tokens/revoke. Exactly one form is required. The hash is not a credential — it cannot enroll anything — so it may travel where a token value never may. Used tokens are untouched: they became credentials, revoked with fleet bridge revoke --agent. Expired tokens are already dead and keep their state.

Exit codes

0 ok · 2 usage · 3 transport or credentials · 4 the bridge refused the request.

Example

$ fleet bridge revoke-enroll --agent scout-2

Takes back every outstanding token minted for scout-2.

fleet bridge mint-credential

fleet bridge mint-credential --agent A [--scopes s1,s2] [--addr service:<name>]
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
--agentArequiredThe agent (or service) the credential belongs to; it acts only as itself.
--scopess1,s2see belowAny of inbox, send, read. Agent mints default to inbox, send; service mints to send, read.
--addrservice:<name>—Make it a service credential, bound to that address; the name must be the agent’s own.

Behaviour

Central verb (owner token). Mints a per-agent credential directly, for an agent already enrolled or for a service. Route: POST /api/<owner-token>/fleet/credentials/mint. Like the enroll mint, the answer carries the credential value once and the bridge stores only its hash. Enroll-minted credentials never carry read; that scope is for service credentials like the PM stack’s.

Exit codes

0 ok · 2 usage · 3 transport or credentials · 4 the bridge refused the request.

Example

$ fleet bridge mint-credential --agent pm-stack --addr service:pm-stack

Mints the PM stack’s service credential and prints it, once, to be stored in the vault as bridge.pm-stack-token.

fleet bridge hello

fleet bridge hello [--agent A] [--groups g1,g2]
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
--agentA$FLEET_AGENT, then [bridge] agentAgent name to register.
--groupsg1,g2$FLEET_AGENT_GROUPS, then [bridge] groupsComma-separated groups to join.

Behaviour

Agent verb (fleet token). Registers / refreshes this agent and its groups — this is the registry write: the bridge’s agent registry is exactly the set of agents that have said hello. Route: POST /fleet/<fleet-token>/hello with {agent, groups}.

Under a per-agent credential the hello only refreshes: the credential’s groups were bound when the owner minted its bootstrap token and set by the exchange, and a credentialed hello (or inbox call) cannot change them — group membership drives group:<name> addressing, so it is not the caller’s to reassign. The shared fleet token keeps caller-supplied groups.

Exit codes

0 ok · 2 usage · 3 transport or credentials · 4 the bridge refused the request.

Example

$ fleet bridge hello --agent archer --groups muse

Registers archer in the muse group (or refreshes an existing registration).

fleet bridge ack

fleet bridge ack [--agent A] (--up-to ID | ID...)
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
--agentA$FLEET_AGENT, then [bridge] agentAgent whose mailbox to ack in.
--up-toID—Mark every message up to this id read. Alternative to listing ids.
ID... (positional)ids—Mark exactly these messages read.

Behaviour

Exit codes

0 ok · 2 usage (neither --up-to nor any id) · 3 transport or credentials · 4 the bridge refused the request.

Example

$ fleet bridge ack --agent archer --up-to 412
