fleet bridge work

fleet bridge work [--agent A] --state acted|queued|done [--task ID] ID...
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
--agentA$FLEET_AGENT, then [bridge] agentAgent whose mailbox copy to mark.
--stateacted|queued|donerequiredThe lifecycle state to record.
--taskID—The fleet queue task the instruction became; required for queued.
ID... (positional)idsrequiredThe instruction rows to mark; several ids are marked one by one.

Behaviour

Agent verb (fleet token). Records the work-item lifecycle of instructions in this agent’s own mailbox. Route: POST /fleet/<fleet-token>/work with {agent, id, state, task_id?} per id. An instruction starts at received; the receiving agent moves its own copy forward — acted (handled in-session), queued (it became a fleet queue task; --task names it), then done. States move only forward (received → acted | queued → done); re-marking the current state is a no-op. Only the receiving agent can mark a row: with a per-agent credential, naming another agent or another agent’s row is the bridge’s plain 404. The owner sees every row’s state and task id in the pipeline, so an instruction that is neither acted on nor queued stays visible at received. Notes instructions carry the same lifecycle on the notes surface (POST /notes/work, same body shape); connector-channel instructions store no lifecycle fields — their read state stands in for acted in the pipeline.

The rule the lifecycle serves, carried verbatim by this book, the verb’s help text, and the woken-agent text the intake ladder hands out with a pushed command:

Task it or queue it. An instruction is a work item: do the work now, in this session, and reply — or queue it as a repo-task/v1 packet whose context_refs carry the bridge surface, the message id and the batch, and reply with the task id. Record the outcome with fleet bridge work: –state acted for work done in-session, –state queued –task for queued work, –state done when the work is finished. An instruction that is neither acted on nor queued is a defect: it stays at received, where the owner can see it stuck in the pipeline.

Exit codes

0 ok · 2 usage (including --state queued without --task) · 3 transport or credentials · 4 the bridge refused the request.

Example

$ fleet bridge work --agent archer --state queued --task 23500 412

Records that archer queued instruction 412 as fleet queue task 23500.

fleet bridge exchange

fleet bridge exchange --agent A --bootstrap TOKEN
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
--agentA$FLEET_AGENT, then [bridge] agentThe agent name the bootstrap token was minted for.
--bootstrapTOKENrequiredThe single-use bootstrap token the owner minted (console hand-off).

Behaviour

Provisioning verb (no stored token; the bootstrap token rides the request body and is scrubbed from every error). Trades the token at POST /enroll/exchange for the agent’s own credentials — a per-agent fleet credential and, when the mint carried a notes identity, a notes token. The values come back exactly once and go straight into the vault through fleet-secrets’ write path (Bitwarden, into the project named by $FLEET_BWS_PROJECT_ID or [secrets] bws_project_id) under bridge.<agent>-fleet-token and bridge.<agent>-token. The verb prints names and metadata only — never a value. A refused exchange (wrong, used, expired or revoked token, or a name that is not the minted name) stores nothing; if storing fails after a successful exchange, the error says so loudly, because the burned token cannot be replayed. fleet agent enroll --bootstrap runs this verb first, then enrols as usual.

Exit codes

0 ok · 2 usage · 3 transport, credentials or vault write · 4 the bridge refused the exchange.

Example

$ fleet bridge exchange --agent muse-9 --bootstrap <token from the console>

Stores muse-9’s credentials under bridge.muse-9-fleet-token and bridge.muse-9-token and prints the exchange’s names and metadata.

fleet bridge notes

fleet bridge notes send --to CLASS/NAME [--kind note|instruction] [--reply-to ID] <text | ->
fleet bridge notes inbox
fleet bridge notes ack (--up-to ID | ID...)
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
--toCLASS/NAME—Recipient identity; a * segment wildcards (muse/*, */archer, */*). Required unless --reply-to is given.
--kindnote|instructionnoteinstruction makes the note a work item: it lands in the recipient’s inbox without a sender (the bridge keeps the sender store-side).
--reply-toID—Answer a note in your own inbox. The reply is routed store-side to that note’s real sender — including an instruction whose sender you cannot see — and may replace --to.
--up-to (ack)ID—Acknowledge every note up to this id. Alternative to listing ids.
ID... (ack, positional)ids—Acknowledge exactly these notes.

Behaviour

The class/name notes family, authenticated by the calling identity’s own notes token as a Bearer header (routes POST /notes/send, GET /notes/inbox, POST /notes/ack). Inbox rows carry kind and reply_to; a plain note names its sender in from, an instruction’s from is null. Replying to an instruction therefore needs nothing but its id: the replier never learns who sent it, and the reply still reaches them.

Exit codes

0 ok · 2 usage · 3 transport or credentials · 4 the bridge refused the request.

Example

$ fleet bridge notes send --reply-to 41 "check done, filed as task 23101"

Answers note 41 — even if it arrived as a sender-free instruction.

fleet bridge health

fleet bridge health
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
———Takes no arguments and no flags, and no token.

Behaviour

Reads the bridge’s /healthz, unauthenticated — the only bridge verb that needs no token. It proves the service answers; it proves nothing about whether this seat holds a usable token (that is what fleet agent doctor’s bridge leg checks, with a real mailbox read).

Exit codes

0 ok · 2 usage · 3 transport · 4 the bridge refused the request.

Example

$ fleet bridge health

Prints the bridge’s health JSON.

fleet agent

fleet agent is the agent’s front door: enrol an agent of any kind, check what this seat reaches, and take the next piece of work down the intake ladder. The fleet already has the legs — bridge mailboxes, the queue, the laptop transport, GitHub, secrets by name; what a new kind of agent lacked was one place to enroll, check its seat, and take work. fleet agent is that place. Its sibling domain fleet shell rides on the same agent capability — there is no separate shell capability atom.

Every verb prints one JSON object. Exit codes for the domain: 0 ok · 2 usage · 3 a needed leg is down · 5 no work on any rung (next only).

See also Agents: enrolment, doctor and the intake ladder and fleet bridge.

Help: fleet agent <verb> --help prints that verb’s own usage — its synopsis, a short description, and the shared output/exit-code footer. An unknown verb (or no verb) falls back to the shared domain USAGE. The per-verb sections below are written from source semantics.

fleet agent kinds

fleet agent kinds
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
———Takes no arguments and no flags.

Behaviour

Prints the kind table as JSON: for each kind its name, summary, bridge groups, seat, and enrolment note, plus the three seat definitions. A kind says three things: which bridge groups it joins, how it reaches the fleet from where it runs, and what to tell it at enrolment. Adding a kind is adding a row; no verb changes. The 16 kinds:

KindGroupsSeatNote (abridged)
musemusebinaryFresh Muse gets a bridge-capable static build from scripts/muse/bootstrap.sh; older installs run the same commands on the laptop install via ~/tools/laptop-ssh.sh
opencodeopencodebinaryRuns on the laptop seat, so every leg is local
openchamberopencode, openchamberbinaryJoins opencode too, so group:opencode reaches both pipelines
openclawopenclawbinary—
claude-codeclaude-codebinaryA cloud session has no tailnet: messaging and the priority rung work over HTTPS; builds go through fleet shell
codexcodexbinary—
geminigeminibinary—
antigravityantigravitybinary—
grokgrokbinaryA bot with no shell enrolls as kind http under the same name and groups
dotdothttppkgs/dot-bridge carries its Slack and ChatGPT transports; the mailbox is the same store
duetduethttp—
claude(none)connectorFixed bridge address claude; set a wake hook for channel:claude so a send starts a session
chatgpt(none)connectorFixed address chatgpt; woken by its MCP Events subscription
laptoplaptopbinaryA job or service on the fleet laptop
http(none)httpAnything that can make an HTTPS request and nothing else
generic(none)binaryAny other agent with a shell — the fallback enroll names in its unknown-kind error

Seats: binary = has a shell and runs the fleet binary itself (enroll, then next); http = no shell of its own, speaks the bridge’s fleet routes over HTTPS (scripts/fleet/bridge-mailbox.py is the reference client) and gets work from its mailbox; connector = a chat assistant with the Message Bridge connector attached — it has a channel address, not a mailbox.

Exit codes

0 ok · 2 usage.

Example

$ fleet agent kinds

Prints all 16 kinds with their groups, seats, and enrolment notes as one JSON object.

fleet agent enroll

fleet agent enroll --kind K --name N [--groups a,b] [--dry-run] [--profile PATH]
fleet agent enroll --kind K --name N --bootstrap TOKEN
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
--kindKrequiredOne of the 16 kinds (see kinds). An unknown kind is a usage error listing all kinds, with “use generic for anything with a shell”.
--nameNrequiredThe agent’s name (its bridge mailbox name). The shared USAGE spells this --name; the domain help line abbreviates it as the enroll line’s second value.
--groupsa,bkind’s built-in groupsAdditional bridge groups; adds to the kind’s groups, never replaces them.
--dry-run—offProbe nothing and register nothing.
--profilePATHdefault profile pathWhere to save the profile.
--bootstrapTOKEN—Provision from the owner’s single-use bootstrap token instead of the shared fleet token (binary seats only; never with --dry-run — the exchange burns the token).

Behaviour

Registers an agent and saves its profile. Flow: the kind is validated; --groups adds to the kind’s built-in groups; for a binary/http seat the bridge leg is probed in Register mode — bridge hello with the name and groups, which is what actually registers the mailbox; connector kinds instead get the “attach the connector” instruction and a fixed channel address. The four legs are probed (see doctor) and the saved profile records agent, kind, groups, and leg state.

With --bootstrap, provisioning comes first: fleet bridge exchange trades the token — minted by the owner bound to this name, kind and groups — for the agent’s own credentials, which land in the vault by name (bridge.<agent>-fleet-token, bridge.<agent>-token). The mint-bound groups replace the kind/--groups set (they are the truth a credentialed hello cannot change), the profile is saved early so the probe’s hello resolves the new credential by its recorded name, and the profile records the credential names and the notes identity — never a value. For a muse seat whose mint carried a notes identity, enrolment also writes the wake hookup (the signal-poll detector under ~/hooks/scripts/ and the hook definition under ~/hooks/definitions/, the hatch-personal scripts/messages-hook/ pattern), so the agent is woken when a note lands. A refused exchange enrols nothing: no vault write, no profile, no hook.

The JSON answer carries: the profile, registered (true only when not a dry run and the bridge leg answered), the legs, the rungs map, and seat-specific next-step lines — for a binary seat the run loop (fleet agent next --agent <name>, do the task, run its then lines, repeat while the run has budget) and the fleet shell line (“runs where builds belong; never build in a limited sandbox”); for an http seat the token-by-name note and the reference-client commands; for central, the fleet bridge send --to <address> [--command] lines.

Exit codes

0 — a dry run, or any intake rung is live. 2 — usage (including an unknown kind). 3 — no intake rung is live.

Example

$ fleet agent enroll --kind generic --name worker-1

Registers worker-1, probes its four legs, and saves its profile with the run-loop instructions.

fleet agent doctor

fleet agent doctor [--agent N]
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
--agentNprofile / $FLEET_AGENTAgent name to probe the bridge leg as. With no name known, the bridge leg is reported not ok even when the service answers.

Behaviour

Checks which legs answer from this seat. The four legs are bridge, queue, github, shell — there is no secrets leg; secrets is folded into the bridge leg’s stated need (“HTTPS to the message bridge, and the fleet token by name through fleet secrets”). The four probes are independent and are issued together (one parallel call), each a real fleet verb run as this seat:

LegProbe“Up” detailWhat it needs
bridgebridge hello (enroll) / bridge inbox --agent A --limit 1 (doctor with a name) / bridge health (no name known)“registered” / “the mailbox answers”HTTPS to the bridge + the fleet token by name through fleet secrets
queuequeue health“answers”The queue broker: its socket on the laptop, or the laptop transport from elsewhere
githubgh api rate_limit via fleet gh; if that fails, plain signed-in gh api rate_limit“answers”, with route: "fleet" or "plain" recordedgh with a token: fleet gh’s rotation, or a signed-in gh
shelllaptop-agent health“the laptop answers”A route to the laptop: its broker, the Cloudflare tunnel, the tailnet or ssh

Doctor’s bridge probe with a known agent is a read that takes nothing (inbox --limit 1): service health alone proves nothing about whether this seat holds the fleet token, so only a call made as an agent counts. With no agent name, the bridge leg is reported not ok even when the service answers (“the service answers, but no agent name is known to read a mailbox with: enrol, or pass –agent”).

From the legs, doctor derives the rungs map — which intake rungs this seat still has: push = bridge leg, queue = queue leg, shortlist = always true (it is a local file), priority = github leg. The answer also reports builds: “fleet shell reaches the laptop” when the shell leg answers, else “fleet shell has no laptop route from here; it will try a codespace, then run here”.

Exit codes

0 — any intake rung is live (bridge, queue or github). 2 — usage. 3 — no intake rung is live.

Example

$ fleet agent doctor --agent archer

Probes all four legs in parallel and prints the legs, the rungs map, and the builds line as one JSON object.

fleet agent next

fleet agent next [--agent N] [--lane L] [--repo OWNER/NAME] [--low-water N] [--shortlist PATH] [--platform P] [--pool P] [--remaining-budget-minutes N] [--filter EXPR] [--queue Q] [--no-push] [--no-queue] [--no-shortlist] [--no-priority]
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
--agentNprofile / $FLEET_AGENTAgent taking the work.
--laneLderived from the agent nameQueue lane for the queue rung’s claim.
--repoOWNER/NAMEdeveloping-today/codeRepo the priority/shortlist rungs draw from.
--low-waterN3Shortlist low-water mark for this call.
--shortlistPATHprofile/state defaultShortlist file path.
--platformP—Carried into the queue claim.
--poolP—Carried into the queue claim.
--remaining-budget-minutesN—Carried into the queue claim.
--filterEXPR—Carried into the queue claim.
--queueQ—Queue name for the queue rung’s claim.
--no-push—offSkip rung 1 (recorded as skipped in tried).
--no-queue—offSkip rung 2.
--no-shortlist—offSkip rung 3.
--no-priority—offSkip rung 4.

Behaviour

Tries four rungs in order and returns the first that yields work. A rung that is down (bridge unreachable, broker not answering) is not the same as a rung that is empty: down rungs are recorded and skipped, so a seat with only HTTPS still gets work from rungs 1 and 4. Every answer is {agent, rung, task, then, tried} — tried is the per-rung log (skipped/empty/down/rejected with a why), and then is the list of follow-up commands the runner should execute for the handed-out task.

  1. Push — a command addressed to this agent on the bridge (bridge inbox --commands --take). This rung outranks everything: a command a person (or central) pushed is work already chosen.
  2. Queue — a claim on the one fleet queue (queue claim with the agent’s lane; the lane defaults from the agent name — known lane families are validated by the queue, and a lane registered to a shared queue worker is honoured). next claims with a 4-hour lease (14400 s, overriding the queue’s 45-minute default, which lapses mid-task) and the task’s then lines name the lease deadline plus the queue checkpoint / queue complete commands with the claimed worker/lane. A broker refusal that is really a lane verdict (lane bound to another queue, registration did not land) is reported as rung rejected, distinct from down.
  3. Shortlist — the top of this host’s local shortlist: entries are re-checked against GitHub before hand-out (an issue closed, assigned or owner-parked since listing is dropped with a named why), then handed out in rank order. Refill switch: if the list is at or below low-water with nobody refilling, next does not hand out a stale remnant — it returns rung refill instead, a purpose-switch task (purpose: "refill-shortlist", target 8) whose instructions and then lines are the shortlist fill / shortlist add commands. One run refills; the marker it leaves keeps the rest working.
  4. Priority — the highest-priority open issue straight from GitHub. Label queries run soonest-first over the priority label family (priority/critical, then priority/high, … — the same ordering as the shortlist ranks); candidates are filtered (owner-parked labels — user/owned, user/review, user/escalated class — are kept out), and the winner is reserved into the shortlist file as it is handed out, so two seats on one host do not take the same issue.

Exit codes

0 — a rung yielded work. 2 — usage. 3 — a needed leg is down (domain-level). 5 — no work on any rung.

Example

$ fleet agent next --agent archer
{"agent": "archer", "rung": "queue", "task": {…}, "then": […], "tried": […]}

Returns the first available work down the ladder, with the follow-up commands in then.

fleet agent shortlist status

fleet agent shortlist status [--low-water N]
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
--low-waterN3Low-water mark for the low computation.
--shortlistPATHprofile/state defaultShortlist file path (shared shortlist flag).

Behaviour

Reports the local list next draws on: a JSON file on this host, guarded by a lock file (stale after 30 s). Entries are {repo, issue, title, rank, why, added_at} plus handed-out records and an optional refill marker. status prints the list, its count, low (count ≤ low-water — so a list of exactly 3 is already low), and the refill state. Defaults: low-water 3, target 8.

Ranks (lower is sooner): expedite → 0, priority/critical → 1, now → 2, priority/high → 3, next → 4, priority/normal → 5, anything else unranked = 6. Hand-out order is lowest rank, then oldest added_at, then lowest issue number.

Exit codes

0 ok · 2 usage · 3 a needed leg is down.

Example

$ fleet agent shortlist status

Prints the entries, the count, whether the list is low, and the refill state.

fleet agent shortlist take

fleet agent shortlist take
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
--shortlistPATHprofile/state defaultShortlist file path (shared shortlist flag). This verb takes no verb-specific flags.

Behaviour

Hands out the soonest entry to this agent — the same selection next rung 3 uses (lowest rank, then oldest, then lowest issue number). A handed-out issue is kept from being handed out again on this host for 2 h (7200 s); pruning drops expired handed records and expired refill markers.

Exit codes

0 ok · 2 usage · 3 a needed leg is down · 5 no work (empty list) by the domain’s next-family convention.

Example

$ fleet agent shortlist take

Hands out the soonest shortlist entry as one JSON object.

fleet agent shortlist clear

fleet agent shortlist clear
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
--shortlistPATHprofile/state defaultShortlist file path (shared shortlist flag). This verb takes no verb-specific flags.

Behaviour

Empties the list and clears the refill marker.

Exit codes

0 ok · 2 usage.

Example

$ fleet agent shortlist clear

Empties the local shortlist and clears any live refill marker.

fleet agent shortlist add

fleet agent shortlist add --issue N --title T [--repo R] [--rank N] [--why TEXT]
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
--issueNrequiredIssue number to add.
--titleTrequiredIssue title recorded on the entry.
--repoRdeveloping-today/codeRepository the issue belongs to.
--rankN6 (unranked)Rank for hand-out order (see status for the rank table).
--whyTEXT—Why this entry was listed.
--shortlistPATHprofile/state defaultShortlist file path (shared shortlist flag).

Behaviour

Adds one entry {repo, issue, title, rank, why, added_at}. Duplicates (same repo+issue already listed) are refused — the add returns false rather than listing the issue twice.

Exit codes

0 ok · 2 usage.

Example

$ fleet agent shortlist add --issue 13165 --title "Write the fleet book" --rank 1

Adds issue 13165 at rank 1 (priority/critical rank).

fleet agent shortlist fill

fleet agent shortlist fill [--repo R] [--target N]
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
--repoRdeveloping-today/codeRepository to draw candidates from.
--targetN8 (clamped 1–50)Top the list up to this many entries.
--shortlistPATHprofile/state defaultShortlist file path (shared shortlist flag).

Behaviour

Tops the list up to target from the priority candidates: it fetches 2× target candidates from GitHub (the same candidate scan as next rung 4), adds them in rank order until the target is met, records the fill (so a just-filled list suppresses an immediate second refill), and clears the refill marker. Refill bookkeeping: a refill marker (by, at) lasts 30 min (1800 s); a list needs refill when it is low, no marker is live, and no fill finished within the window.

Exit codes

0 ok · 2 usage · 3 a needed leg is down (GitHub unreachable).

Example

$ fleet agent shortlist fill

Tops the local shortlist up to 8 entries from the priority candidates.

fleet shell

fleet shell runs a command, or opens a shell, where builds belong: the laptop, a codespace, or here. A limited sandbox is the wrong place to compile. It adds no transport; it builds the argv for the verb that already knows how to get there. The domain rides on the agent capability.

Help: fleet shell --help prints the shell’s own usage, with every flag below. (The registry’s domain help — fleet help shell — names only the targets subcommand; the flags live in the shell usage.) A standing discrepancy: the --detach usage error for local/codespace says “it needs –target laptop”, but the actions target also accepts --detach with different semantics — the error string predates the actions target.

See also fleet agent and fleet laptop-agent.

fleet shell

fleet shell [options] [-- COMMAND...]
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
--targetauto|laptop|codespace|actions|localautoWhere to run. An explicit target is used as given and never falls back — a caller that asked for the laptop does not silently build in a sandbox.
--codespaceNAMEthe first availableWhich codespace (codespace target).
--repoOWNER/NAMEthis checkout’s originThe repository an actions run executes in.
--cwdDIR—Directory to run in (the Cargo workspace for the shared target lane). A usage error on the actions target (“the command runs in the runner’s checkout of the repository”).
--build—offA heavy build: take a fleet-build-lock slot; Cargo workspaces use a shared target lane (see Behaviour). A usage error on the actions target (“dispatches through placement instead — drop –build”). Requires a command after --.
--timeoutSECSlaptop non-build 120; laptop build 3600; actions wait 3600How long a laptop command may run; on the actions target, how long to wait for the run. Must be a u64. Requires a command after --.
--detach—offLaptop: start it as a laptop job and return its id (follow with fleet laptop-agent poll JOB --wait N). Actions: dispatch and return the session handle instead of waiting. A usage error on local/codespace. Requires a command after --.
--print—offPrint the plan as JSON instead of running it: {target, codespace (name|null), repo (actions repo|null), program, args, because}.
-h, --help——Print the full usage (the only place the flags are listed).

Positionals before --: only the single word targets is allowed; anything else is a usage error “unexpected argument ‘{x}’: put the command after --”. --build, --detach, and --timeout all require a command after --; with no command they are a usage error.

Behaviour

Targets: auto (default), laptop, codespace, actions, local.

Auto resolution, in order:

  1. Env FLEET_SHELL_TARGET (parsed with the same validator; an invalid value is a usage error) — only when --target was left at auto; an explicit --target X beats the env.
  2. Here, if this seat is the laptop: seat signal = env FLEET_LOCATION or fleet.toml host location, trimmed, equal to "laptop".
  3. The laptop, if it answers: probe = running fleet laptop-agent health successfully.
  4. A codespace, if one exists: the first codespace from gh codespace list --json name,repository,state.
  5. Here (local), with because-string “neither the laptop nor a codespace answered; running here”.

Auto never picks actions. Actions is reachable only by explicit --target actions (or FLEET_SHELL_TARGET=actions).

Per-target execution plan:

  • local: interactive (no command) → sh -l. With a command → sh -lc <line> where the line is the command, prefixed cd {cwd} && when --cwd was given, or the build line when --build. --detach on local is a usage error.
  • laptop: interactive → fleet proxy ssh -- (the pinned ssh leaf). With a command → fleet laptop-agent exec --shell -- <command>, with --cwd DIR when given and --timeout N. With --detach → fleet laptop-agent run --shell -- <command> instead (no --timeout is passed in detach mode), returning the laptop job id.
  • codespace: gh codespace ssh -c NAME [-- <line>]; NAME from --codespace, else the first available (preferring state == "Available", else the first listed). Interactive = no -- part. --detach on codespace is a usage error.
  • actions: the plan is a placement dispatch: fleet queue dispatch --repo {repo} --command {command} --dispatch --json. --repo defaults to this checkout’s origin remote parsed for github.com/ / github.com: shapes; with neither a flag nor a GitHub origin it errors “the actions target needs a repository”. Interactive use is a usage error (“it cannot open a shell”).

Command quoting: the words after -- are joined by shell-string rules — a single word is taken as shell text verbatim; multiple words are POSIX-quoted word by word (left bare only if [A-Za-z0-9_\-./:=,+@%], else single-quoted).

--build: the build lock and the Cargo target broker. On laptop/local/codespace, a --build command is wrapped by the build lock: ~/tools/fleet-build-lock <command> (one slot). If the host has no executable lock, local/codespace fall back with a stderr note “fleet shell: this host has no build lock; running without one”. If the command may invoke Cargo (a cargo invocation followed — after skipping toolchain/flag words — by a compiling subcommand build|check|test|bench|clippy|run|install|doc|rustc|nextest|fix|package|publish, and conservatively any just or make invocation), the locked command is instead a broker-aware shell script that: locates the Cargo workspace (honouring --manifest-path/--path), derives a repo key (the path segment after pkgs/, else the workspace root basename, sanitised), and leases a shared target dir from ~/tools/cargo-target-broker checkout --repo {key} --profile {dev|test|release} --wait 900 --json (profile: test if the command mentions test/bench, release for --release or a non---debug install, else dev; --workspace-cwd added when the caller’s cwd is outside the workspace). It exports the leased CARGO_TARGET_DIR, runs the command in its own process group with signal-forwarding traps, and checks the lease in on exit. If the broker/lease fails, it falls back to CARGO_TARGET_DIR=$HOME/build-cache/{repo} with the stderr note “fleet shell: broker unavailable; using shared fallback …”. Non-Cargo builds under the lock run as fleet-build-lock sh -c '<command>'.

Detach behaviour, per target:

  • laptop + --detach: runs fleet laptop-agent run … and returns its job id immediately; follow up with fleet laptop-agent poll JOB --wait N. No timeout is forwarded.
  • actions + --detach: dispatches through placement (a “patient” call — dispatch is not cut short, “cutting it short would orphan the run”), extracts handle from the JSON (missing handle or non-JSON is a Down error), prints {target: "actions", repo, handle, state, run_url, because, note: "dispatched, not waited on; reconnect with: fleet queue session result {handle}"} and exits 0.
  • actions without --detach: polls fleet queue session result {handle} --json every 15 s until terminal is true or the budget (default 3600 s, or --timeout) expires. On terminal it prints {target, repo, handle, state, run_url, because} and exits 0 iff state == “succeeded”, else 1 (failed and cancelled both give 1). On budget expiry it errors “run {handle} still {state} after {budget}s; reconnect with: fleet queue session result {handle}”. The run’s own output is not streamed: “the run’s own output lives on that page (gh run view –log)”.
  • local / codespace + --detach: usage error — “–detach starts a laptop job; it needs –target laptop”.

Exit codes

  • The executed command’s / leaf verb’s exit code, in general.
  • Actions target: 0 iff the run succeeded, else 1 (and 0 for a successful --detach dispatch).
  • 2 — usage (bad target, missing command for --build/--detach/--timeout, detach on local/codespace, interactive/--build/--cwd on actions, invalid FLEET_SHELL_TARGET).

Example

$ fleet shell --target laptop --build -- cargo test

Takes a build-lock slot on the laptop, leases a shared Cargo target dir, and runs cargo test there with the 3600 s build timeout.

fleet shell targets

fleet shell targets
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
———Takes no arguments; anything after -- with targets is a usage error.

Behaviour

Prints a JSON reachability report:

{
  "targets": [
    { "target": "laptop", "reachable": true, "how": "…" },
    { "target": "codespace", "reachable": false, "codespace": null },
    { "target": "actions", "reachable": true, "how": "…" },
    { "target": "local", "reachable": true, "how": "this machine" }
  ],
  "auto_would_pick": { "target": "laptop", "because": "…" }
}

The how strings: laptop = “this seat is the laptop” or “fleet laptop-agent (broker, Cloudflare tunnel, tailnet, ssh)”; codespace = “gh codespace ssh”; actions = “fleet queue dispatch (placement over the registered Actions surfaces)”; actions reachability = fleet queue surfaces parses and contains at least one github-actions or blacksmith surface (of any status).

Known discrepancy: because reachability ignores surface status, a registry whose only Actions surface were a standby surface would still report actions reachable even though placement could never pick it.

Exit codes

  • 0 — report printed.
  • 2 — usage.

Example

$ fleet shell targets

Prints which targets answer from this seat and which one auto would pick, with the reason.

fleet search

fleet search is the atlas-search client surface over the live Atlas service contract: hybrid FTS+vector search over the Atlas corpus, with classification filters. Search “joins unchanged” after the service cutover; the service role itself is fleet serve search (see fleet serve). Two verbs: search (the default) and get-chunk. init and fetch-model are usage errors naming the standalone artifact — they stay on the standalone atlas-search artifact.

See also Search: the Atlas corpus.

Invocation shapes:

fleet search <query> [options]
fleet search search <query> [options]   (atlas-search's own shape — the leading `search` token is stripped)
fleet search get-chunk <chunk-id> [options]

Routing (both verbs)

  • Via-service route: an in-process client speaking the Atlas service’s loopback HTTP job protocol to the service at --service-url (default http://127.0.0.1:18760): submit a search job, wait for it (unless --no-wait, which prints the job handle), render the result so output matches atlas-search in shape. The backend behind the service is a read-only Turso corpus store with one shared Snowflake embedder.
  • Standalone route: there is no second embedder/backend in the fleet workspace — the client delegates to the kept standalone atlas-search binary on PATH, passing the caller’s arguments in atlas-search’s own shape (with --via-service/--standalone stripped, and ATLAS_SEARCH_VIA removed from the child’s environment so an ambient value can’t silently re-route it), inheriting its stdout byte-for-byte. A missing artifact is exit 3 with a message naming it as “the search domain’s kept standalone”.
  • Precedence: explicit --via-service / --standalone first; then env ATLAS_SEARCH_VIA=service|standalone; then fleet.toml [search] via; then the seat default:
    • Sandbox seat → via-service, with a loud standalone fallback (stderr: “fleet search: warning: –via-service: {detail}; falling back to standalone”). The via-service client reaches the laptop’s loopback service through the loopback forward on the shared laptop-ssh control connection.
    • Laptop seat → standalone. The seat signal is the service’s own config file ~/.local/state/atlas-search/service.json: only the serving host has one.
  • Provisioning / sensitivity ceilings: the via-service client presents a per-seat bearer token — env ATLAS_SEARCH_TOKEN, else the JSON file at ~/.config/atlas-search/client.json (a JSON object with one token string field, file mode 0600). Identities are named in the service config; the server clamps --max-sensitivity to the identity’s ceiling: identity drew-cli → secret-bearing, identity sandbox-scripts → personal. The fleet verb adds no ceiling logic of its own. A seat with no client.json cannot use the service route and falls back to standalone.

fleet search search

fleet search <query> [options]
fleet search search <query> [options]
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
<query> (positional)textrequiredThe search query (a single positional).
--kN10Final result count.
--poolN100Per-branch candidates, validated 1..=400.
--modeMODEhybridhybrid | fts | vector.
--kindCSV—Classification kind filter.
--topicCSV—Topic filter.
--projectCSV—Project filter.
--clientCSV—Client filter.
--sinceYYYY-MM-DD—Sessions created on/after (inclusive).
--untilYYYY-MM-DD—Sessions created on/before (inclusive).
--max-sensitivityLVpersonalshareable | personal | local-only | secret-bearing. A request; the server clamps it to the client identity’s ceiling.
--group-by-session—offRoll chunk hits up to sessions.
--expandN0Include N neighbouring chunks around each hit (validated 0..=100).
--with-message—offInclude the parent message text.
--no-cache—offBypass service cache reads; the fresh result still lands in the cache.
--no-wait—offDo not block: print the service job handle and return. (The one-shot default waits for the job.)
--hydrateN0Hydrate the top N results to full content (validated ≤ 1000).
--raw-rows[=branches]optional =branches—Ungrouped rows: bare = flat fused rows; =branches = pre-fusion branch rows.
--text—offHuman-readable output instead of JSON (default output is JSON).
--modelNAMESnowflake/snowflake-arctic-embed-m-v2.0Embedding model.
--embedderNAMEautoauto | fastembed | st.
--truncN0Truncate vectors to N dims (0 = full).
--vector-backendBscanscan | index-fill | index-fixed.
--via-service—seat defaultPrefer the Atlas service (job protocol). Mutually exclusive with --standalone (usage error).

--service-urlURLhttp://127.0.0.1:18760Service base URL; env ATLAS_SEARCH_URL, then fleet.toml [search] url, override it.

Standalone-only engine knobs (--backend, --db) are deliberately not part of this surface.

Behaviour

The search is hybrid FTS+vector over the Atlas corpus with the classification filters above — the subset of atlas-search search’s flags that translates to the wire request or to routing. Both --flag value and --flag=value spellings are accepted. Default output is JSON; --text renders human-readable output. With --no-wait on the service route, the command prints the service job handle and returns instead of blocking for the result.

Exit codes

  • 0 — ok.
  • 1 — service-job/backend failure surfaced without a fallback.
  • 2 — usage/validation (including --via-service with --standalone, or --pool outside 1..=400).
  • 3 — routing unavailable (no service and no standalone artifact).

Example

$ fleet search 'queue broker lease' --k 5 --text

Runs a hybrid search for “queue broker lease” and prints the top 5 hits as text.

fleet search get-chunk

fleet search get-chunk <chunk-id> [--neighbors N] [--text]
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
<chunk-id> (positional)chunk idrequiredThe chunk to fetch.
--neighborsN0Include N chunks either side in the same message.
--text—offHuman-readable output instead of JSON.
-h, --help——Print this verb’s own usage.

Behaviour

Fetches one chunk with its provenance (session, client, sensitivity). The verb parses nothing beyond answering --help itself: every other argument is forwarded verbatim to the standalone atlas-search artifact, so atlas-search get-chunk’s own options (--context, --backend, --db, --vecdb, --via-service, --service-url) work through this verb unchanged. get-chunk always runs standalone — it is job-scoped in the service protocol, so it cannot ride the service route; when via-service was requested (flag/env/config — the seat default doesn’t count) it prints the loud fallback note first, then delegates to the standalone artifact.

Exit codes

  • 0 — ok.
  • 1 — backend failure surfaced without a fallback.
  • 2 — usage/validation.
  • 3 — routing unavailable (no standalone artifact).

Example

$ fleet search get-chunk 112081 --neighbors 2 --text

Fetches chunk 112081 with two neighbouring chunks on each side, rendered as text.

fleet orgs

fleet orgs maintains and reads the Turso-backed registry of GitHub Apps, organizations and installations. The registry is populated using each configured fleet App’s own GitHub App JWT; it does not use OAuth-token organization reads as a substitute for installation coverage.

fleet orgs list [--app SLUG] [--org LOGIN] [--permission NAME[=LEVEL]] [--json]
fleet orgs sync

list

Reads the stored registry and prints one row per installation: organization, App, installation ID, repository selection and permissions. Output includes the last successful sync time. Options may be combined:

OptionMeaning
--app SLUGMatch the GitHub App slug.
--org LOGINMatch the account login.
--permission NAMEMatch installations granting that permission at any level.
--permission NAME=LEVELMatch a permission at the specified level.
--jsonEmit the same filtered rows as JSON.

sync

Records a sync run, then for each fleet App (app, devtoday, backup) calls GET /app and paginated GET /app/installations with that App’s JWT. It upserts the Apps, organizations and installations; installations no longer returned by GitHub are removed. A successful command prints the sync-run ID and per-App counts. Missing configuration, unresolved secrets, or GitHub/ database failures are operational errors (exit 69); unknown verbs and invalid options are usage errors (exit 2).

Configuration

NamePurpose
FLEET_ORGS_TURSO_URLHTTP URL of the registry database.
turso.fleet-orgs-tokenSecret name resolved for the Turso auth token.
App-specific secretsPrivate keys (and IDs where not public) used to mint each App JWT.

The command is implemented by fleet-orgs; see The crates for the storage model and sync details. The binary must include the orgs capability for these verbs to be available.

fleet cert

fleet cert (alias fleet pki) is the CLI over the library-first fleet-cert PKI/X.509 API. It manages CA hierarchy material, leaf certificates, chains, bundles and read-only inventory. The built surface is:

fleet cert <group> <verb> [options]
fleet pki  <group> <verb> [options]

root       create | inspect | list | validate
issuer     create | inspect | list
leaf       issue | inspect | list
ocsp       sign | inspect | test
chain      build | test
bundle     inspect
inventory  list | show | search | audit
key        generate | inspect
publish    plan | verify
profile    list | show
algorithms list | describe
explain    [topic]
doctor

Use fleet cert --help for the usage summary, fleet cert explain <topic> for a topic, and fleet cert doctor to distinguish implemented capabilities from deferred ones. Unknown groups, verbs, options or malformed values are usage errors (exit 2); operational, validation and policy failures exit 1.

Common options and signing policy

OptionMeaning
--jsonEmit one JSON value instead of text.
--not-before RFC3339Set validity start; defaults to now.
--not-after RFC3339Set an exact validity end; mutually exclusive with --valid-for.
--valid-for DURATIONSet lifetime from not-before (for example 20y, 90d, or 15 years 7 days).

Signing never discovers keys from ambient locations. Root and issuer creation must name their key destination/source explicitly; issuer creation also names its root and root key directory, and leaf issuance names an issuer key directory. Consult fleet cert explain signer-source for the exact rule.

Group guide

  • root creates, inspects, lists and validates root sets, including their cross-signing graph.
  • issuer creates, inspects and lists issuer sets under a named root.
  • leaf issues, inspects and lists leaves for the built-in server, client, saml-signing and oidc-signing profiles.
  • ocsp signs, inspects and tests RFC 6960 responses. Signing can use an issuer directly or a delegated ocsp-responder leaf.
  • chain builds and tests signature-verified certificate paths under selected trust sets.
  • bundle inspect verifies and reads a bundle manifest and its indexed artifacts.
  • inventory provides read-only list, show, search and audit across certificate bundles. Audit reports drift, missing/orphaned material and upcoming expiries; it exits 1 when expired material or drift is found.
  • key generates or inspects keys. Import/export, escrow, restore and rotation are not part of the currently built surface.
  • publish plan|verify are read-only publication planning and verification. apply and status remain production-gated/deferred.
  • profile and algorithms list/show profiles and list/describe supported signature algorithms.

Validity uses RFC 3339 instants and Gregorian calendar arithmetic. The crate clamps issuer/leaf validity to the signer’s validity window and records the clamp as a manifest warning. Bundle manifests index artifacts with SHA-256; tampering is rejected on load. See the fleet-cert crate record for supported algorithms, bundle layout, deferred verbs and crate-level test evidence.

fleet laptop-agent

fleet laptop-agent is the client for the laptop-agent daemon — the Python service on the laptop at 100.99.113.103:4799. The client speaks HTTP JSON to it; the token is the laptop-agent token file (~/tools/laptop-agent-token), read per request and sent as X-Agent-Token on the direct legs; on the broker leg the token rides in the framed request’s named token file instead. The domain’s argv0 alias is laptop-agent itself.

See also fleet proxy and fleet shell.

Help: a help token anywhere before the -- separator — and not swallowed as an option’s value — prints the domain’s shared USAGE and exits 0, before any transport is touched: poll --help asks for help; it does not poll a job named --help (#13175).

Shared behaviour (all verbs)

Strict parsing: anything unaccounted for is a usage error (exit 2) before any transport is touched. Job ids are restricted to the characters the daemon mints ([A-Za-z0-9_-]), because a job id goes into a URL path.

Each call gets a fresh trip id (sent as the X-Trip-Id header on HTTP legs / the trip field on the broker leg, and used for exec cancellation and log correlation). The default call deadline is 660 s, overridable via LAPTOP_AGENT_DEADLINE_S. Failures print laptop-agent: <error> and exit 1, except the timeout and usage cases noted per verb.

The transport ladder

Every verb’s call goes down a four-leg ladder, in order; the first leg that answers wins, and when an earlier leg failed the client prints one line: laptop-agent: note: answered by <leg> after <legs> failed.

  1. Broker — the warm session-broker socket (default ~/.cache/laptop-agent/broker.sock): the framed protocol (8-byte big-endian length + JSON {method, path, body, trip}; reply framed the same way, {status, body}). Absent when no socket file exists.
  2. Cloudflare — TLS through the egress proxy to the tunnel hostname, with the Access service token resolved by name (secret name cloudflare.access-laptop-agent) only when this leg is tried, so a healthy broker never pays for the resolution; a resolution failure is cached 60 s.
  3. Tailscale — HTTP CONNECT through the egress proxy at port 3130 to 100.99.113.103:4799.
  4. SSH — a named stub: always absent (“ssh leg not implemented”). The ladder’s fourth leg exists in the ordering but never carries traffic in this build.

Replay rules: each leg classifies its failures as absent (not configured here), unsent (failed before the request was written), or sent (failed after). A request may fall through to the next leg freely when absent/unsent, but a sent failure replays only for idempotent calls — non-idempotent calls (exec, run submits) are never replayed on a leg that may already have sent them, so a submitted job or an exec is never duplicated by the ladder.

The USAGE block (printed only inside error messages) is:

usage: fleet laptop-agent <command>
  health
  jobs
  kill JOB
  exec [--cwd DIR] [--timeout SECS] [--shell] -- CMD...
  run  [--cwd DIR] [--shell] -- CMD...
  poll JOB [--wait SECS]
  fetch REMOTE_PATH LOCAL_PATH

fleet laptop-agent health

fleet laptop-agent health
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
———Takes no arguments. Any trailing argument is a usage error, exit 2.

Behaviour

Issues GET /health to the daemon (via the ladder) and prints the daemon’s health JSON verbatim.

Exit codes

  • 0 — the daemon answered.
  • 1 — no leg answered.
  • 2 — usage.

Example

$ fleet laptop-agent health

Prints the daemon’s health JSON.

fleet laptop-agent exec

fleet laptop-agent exec [--cwd DIR] [--timeout SECS] [--shell] -- CMD...
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
--cwdDIRdaemon defaultWorking directory for the command (sent as the spec’s cwd).
--timeoutSECS120Daemon-side timeout in seconds. The client deadline is timeout + 15 s transport grace.
--shell—offRun the joined command string as a shell command ({cwd, shell: "cmd string"}) instead of an argv spec ({cwd, argv}).
--—requiredSeparator; everything after it is the command. No command is a usage error (“no command given (use – cmd…)”).

Behaviour

Synchronous run: POST /exec with body {cmds: [spec], timeout_s}. Prints the first result’s stdout to stdout and stderr to stderr, and returns the command’s own exit code. Output capture is capped at 1 MiB per stream (tail kept) with a truncation warning on stderr. On client-deadline expiry it best-effort cancels by trip (POST /exec/<trip>/cancel, 3 s budget) and exits 124; a daemon-reported timeout also exits 124. exec is non-idempotent for the ladder: it is never replayed after a sent failure.

Exit codes

  • The command’s own exit code.
  • 1 — transport failure.
  • 2 — usage.
  • 124 — timeout (client deadline or daemon-reported).

Example

$ fleet laptop-agent exec --timeout 300 -- cargo build

Runs cargo build synchronously on the laptop with a 300 s timeout and returns its exit code.

fleet laptop-agent run

fleet laptop-agent run [--cwd DIR] [--shell] -- CMD...
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
--cwdDIRdaemon defaultWorking directory for the job.
--shell—offRun the joined command string as a shell command instead of an argv spec.
--—requiredSeparator; everything after it is the command.
--timeout——Not accepted — passing it is an unknown-option error. Detached jobs have no client-side timeout; use poll --wait to bound waiting.

Behaviour

Detached submit: POST /jobs. Prints the returned job_id and exits 0. Follow up with poll. run is non-idempotent for the ladder: it is never replayed after a sent failure.

Exit codes

  • 0 — job submitted, job_id printed.
  • 1 — transport failure.
  • 2 — usage (including --timeout).

Example

$ fleet laptop-agent run -- ./long-build.sh
job_…

Submits a detached job and prints its job id.

fleet laptop-agent poll

fleet laptop-agent poll JOB [--wait SECS]
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
JOB (positional)job idrequiredJob id ([A-Za-z0-9_-] only).
--waitSECS—How long to keep polling before reporting still-running.

Behaviour

Incremental output streaming: GET /jobs/<job>?out_off=N&err_off=M. The client persists per-job output offsets in a local offsets file (<job>.json in the laptop-agent state dir), sends them on each poll, appends only the new stdout/stderr, and saves the returned out_next/err_next. It polls every ≤3 s until the job’s state is done — then prints [laptop-agent] job <job> done exit=<e> duration_ms=<d> on stderr and returns the job’s exit code — or until the wait deadline passes, printing still running and returning 0 (still-running is not a failure). A reply without offsets is an error, exit 1.

Exit codes

  • The job’s exit code, once the job is done.
  • 0 — still running at the wait deadline.
  • 1 — transport failure, or a reply without offsets.
  • 2 — usage.

Example

$ fleet laptop-agent poll job_… --wait 600

Streams new output every ≤3 s for up to 600 s, then returns the job’s exit code (or 0 with “still running”).

fleet laptop-agent jobs

fleet laptop-agent jobs
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
———Takes no arguments. Any trailing argument is an unknown-command error, exit 2.

Behaviour

Issues GET /jobs and prints the job list pretty-printed.

Exit codes

  • 0 — ok.
  • 1 — transport failure.
  • 2 — usage.

Example

$ fleet laptop-agent jobs

Prints the daemon’s job list as pretty JSON.

fleet laptop-agent kill

fleet laptop-agent kill JOB
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
JOB (positional)job idrequiredExactly one job id ([A-Za-z0-9_-] only).

Behaviour

Issues POST /jobs/<job>/kill with {} and prints the reply.

Exit codes

  • 0 — ok.
  • 1 — transport failure.
  • 2 — usage.

Example

$ fleet laptop-agent kill job_…

Kills the named job and prints the daemon’s reply.

fleet laptop-agent fetch

fleet laptop-agent fetch REMOTE_PATH LOCAL_PATH
FlagArgumentDefaultMeaning
REMOTE_PATH (positional)pathrequiredFile path on the laptop.
LOCAL_PATH (positional)pathrequiredDestination path on this host. This verb takes no flags.

Behaviour

Hash-checked copy. First it hashes the remote file on the laptop by running shasum -a 256 through /exec, then pulls the file in 1 MiB raw ranges via GET /file?path=…&off=…&len=1048576 until an empty chunk, verifies the assembled bytes’ SHA-256 against the remote hash, and only then writes the destination — a mismatch writes nothing and exits 1.

Exit codes

  • 0 — ok, hash verified and destination written.
  • 1 — transport failure, or a SHA-256 mismatch (nothing written).
  • 2 — usage.

Example

$ fleet laptop-agent fetch /home/user/build/result.tar ./result.tar

Copies the file in 1 MiB ranges and writes it locally only after its SHA-256 matches the remote hash.

fleet laptop route forms

The four Fleet domains that reach the laptop, codified as one matrix by #13717: tier 0 (fleet laptop), the generic tiered command; T1 (fleet commander), the Desktop Commander MCP endpoint; T2 (fleet http), the laptop-agent daemon’s HTTP API; T3 (fleet ssh), real SSH. Outside the binary, the same methods exist as raw commands (T4–T6, literal recipes in the laptop mechanics doc) and the laptop-ssh script is T7 — the fallback / simplified tier.

Why forms at all: the platform’s execution-risk behaviour keys on the literal command shape an agent runs, so each form stays a first-class, separately invocable command, and every result names the form that served it. Circumstance decides the form; there is no single blessed invocation.

fleet laptop — tier T0

fleet laptop tiers prints the matrix. fleet laptop exec [--form T1|T2|T3] [--timeout SECS] [--cwd DIR] -- CMD... walks T1 → T2 → T3 in order (or attempts one pinned tier), each attempt a literal invocation of that tier’s own implementation. It advances only when a tier fails to serve — transport, auth or connect failure, or a tier-level timeout — never on a served result, whatever its exit code, and it reports the serving tier on stderr (fleet: served by form T1 commander/fleet). The per-attempt --timeout always applies (default 120 s). Tier 0 deliberately does not fall through to the laptop-ssh wrapper: reaching T7 is the caller’s own final step.

One recorded casualty of the walk rule: ssh’s own failure exit is 255, so the walker reads a remote command that itself exits 255 over ssh as a tier failure. Standalone fleet ssh propagates 255 untouched.

fleet commander — tier T1

A client for the self-hosted Desktop Commander MCP endpoint (#13404, #13654). The bearer is resolved from the secrets broker by name (desktop-commander.machine-bearer) at call time and never stored; requests carry a browser user agent (the edge 1010-blocks non-browser agents). One MCP session per invocation. exec starts the command via start_process (the schema’s timeout_ms is always sent), polls read_process_output to completion, and propagates the remote exit code from the endpoint’s own completion line; on the deadline (default 120 s) it force-terminates the process and exits 124 — an exec never leaves a running process behind on the laptop. health initializes a session, runs hostname, and reports {"ok":true,"form":"T1 commander/fleet",...}.

fleet http — tier T2

The laptop-agent daemon’s HTTP API as a route-form surface: the same verbs as fleet laptop-agent, over a ladder built from the client’s HTTP legs only (http_ladder: broker socket → Cloudflare tunnel → Tailscale CONNECT). The SSH leg is excluded by construction, so this tier can never silently become the ssh tier. The primary-checkout guard is applied before anything is sent; a guard refusal is a served result (exit 1), never something tier 0 may route around. Timeouts always apply: the daemon’s timeout_s (default 300) plus the transport grace as the local deadline; a daemon-side timeout exits 124.

fleet ssh — tier T3

SSH’s endpoint-grade shape is a binary-owned client contract: the binary constructs the ssh invocation itself — pinned host key (~/.ssh/known_hosts_laptop, StrictHostKeyChecking=yes), proxy CONNECT helper, IdentitiesOnly, ConnectTimeout — instead of delegating to a shell script, and enforces a mandatory overall deadline (default 300 s; the ssh child is killed on expiry, exit 124). Connections multiplex over a fleet-owned ControlMaster socket (~/.ssh/cm-fleet-…, persist 600 s, separate from laptop-ssh’s master); fleet ssh close tears it down. The honest limit: sshd owns the remote process, so a client-side kill ends the session but cannot cancel the remote command protocol-side.

fleet actions

Live short-lived exec sessions inside GitHub Actions runners (#13774), coordinator-handed-off. A seat opens a session at the queue broker (the coordinator), dispatches the fleet-exec.yml workflow in dezren39/fleet, and binds the resulting run — the handoff is the session handle plus the portable OWNER/REPO#RUN_ID form and the run attempt. Commands then run on the runner with their IO streamed back through the broker; files leave through the workflow artifact and, when configured, R2. Nothing connection-shaped is ever printed: the workflow inputs carry only the handle and non-secret parameters, and the runner proves its run membership to the broker with the job’s GitHub OIDC token, verified against GitHub’s JWKS with its repository, job_workflow_ref, run_id and run_attempt claims bound to the session row.

The lease

Every session carries two clocks, both enforced by the broker and by the runner-side agent (which exits at expiry even if partitioned from the broker):

  • the lease — set by start --timeout, required, no default; renewable through the coordinator, clamped at the max;
  • the max lifespan — --max-lifespan, default 30 min, ceiling 2 h (the fleet leg cap). Past it, only an emergency extension helps: exec extend records the request and the broker raises a needs-drew alert (source fleet-actions-exec); Drew’s approve/deny returns through exec decide, and approval adds up to +30 min to the max and the lease. While a decision is pending the session holds a 300 s grace past its lease.

Commands

  • fleet actions exec start --repo OWNER/REPO --timeout S [--max-lifespan S] [--ref R] [--target-repo OWNER/REPO] [--hide-logs] [--detach] [--broker-url URL] — open, claim (the #13765 coordinator claim is attempted first; while those verbs are not live the session proceeds on the singular path and the output names it via placement_path), dispatch, bind, print the handoff, then attach unless --detach. --repo is the workflow host repo (default dezren39/fleet); sessions are recorded in the local store under the state dir so the portable form resolves later.
  • fleet actions exec run <ref> [--timeout S] -- <command...> — enqueue one command, stream its output, exit with its code.
  • fleet actions exec attach <ref> / watch <ref> — stream the session’s IO after handoff; watch also reports the run and session status.
  • fleet actions exec renew <ref> --timeout S — extend the lease within the max.
  • fleet actions exec extend <ref> [--minutes M] [--reason T] — request the emergency extension (raises the alert).
  • fleet actions exec decide <ref> --approve|--deny — record Drew’s answer.
  • fleet actions exec close <ref> — close the session.
  • fleet actions agent … — the runner half, invoked by the fleet-exec-session composite action in dezren39/fleet: it registers with the OIDC token, long-polls the broker, executes commands in the workdir, streams IO back, installs fleet-exec-put on the session PATH, and enforces the lease locally.
  • fleet actions put <file> — the egress helper: copy the file into the session outbox (uploaded as the run’s fleet-exec-out artifact) and, when the workflow populated the FLEET_EXEC_R2_* environment from masked repo secrets, PUT it to R2 under fleet-exec/<handle>/ with a SigV4 signature.

Log visibility

The agent echoes command IO to its own stdout by default, so it lands in the public Actions run log; start --hide-logs turns the echo off. Either way the broker is the transport — its IO chunk store is the cache of record — and the seat’s run, attach and watch read from it. The OIDC token and the R2 credentials are never written to any log; the log audit is part of the mode’s acceptance bar.

The broker surface

The verbs live in crates/fleet-queue/src/turso_queue/ actions_exec.rs beside placement’s: /actions-exec-open, -bind, -command, -stream, -renew, -extend-request, -extend-decide, -close (seat side, broker token) and /actions-exec-register, -poll, -io, -result (agent side, OIDC through the public door at exec.security.cab, which is path-scoped to these verbs). Session state lives in the actions_exec_sessions / actions_exec_commands / actions_exec_io tables; every transition is a conditional UPDATE, so two actors racing a session resolve to exactly one winner.

Tutorial: enrol a new seat

This tutorial takes a fresh seat — a new agent instance on a new sandbox or machine — from nothing to taking work. It assumes the fleet binary is already installed on the seat. If it is not, install it first by following Installation and bootstrap, then come back here.

By the end, the seat will have its three broker token files, a registered bridge mailbox, a saved agent profile, and a checked answer from every leg of fleet agent doctor. Names, kinds and groups in the examples are illustrative: pick your own agent name, and use a kind from Step 4.

Secrets in this tutorial are handled by name only. You never type, print or paste a secret value; the bootstrap fetches token files for you, and every later command resolves the values it needs by name.

Step 1: Run the seat bootstrap

On a Muse sandbox seat, the bootstrap script rebuilds the whole seat — tools, tokens, the tailnet link, the binary, and the local init stack — from the pinned release. It is idempotent: re-running it skips work that is already done.

bash scripts/muse/bootstrap.sh

What the output means: the script runs named phases in order — tools token restore tailnet fleet persist init check. Each phase either reports that its work was already present or does it and moves on. The final check phase verifies the binary (including that the bridge domain is available), the laptop link, secret resolution by name, and a bridge hello/inbox probe as your agent.

What can go wrong, and the fix:

  • A phase fails and the script stops, naming the phase. Exit 1 means “a phase failed”; exit 2 means the command line itself was wrong. Fix the named phase’s cause (usually a missing download or a tailnet join that needs attention) and re-run the whole script — completed phases skip themselves.
  • The check phase reports a missing token name. That is not fatal to enrolment itself, but the affected legs will fail in Step 5. Note which name is missing and continue to Step 2 to check the token files directly.

Seats that are not Muse sandboxes do not run this script. If your seat was provisioned another way, continue at Step 2 and make sure the token files and the binary are in place by your provisioning route instead.

Step 2: Confirm the three token files appeared

The bootstrap’s token phase fetches three Bitwarden Secrets Manager secrets — by the names fleet.secrets-broker-token, fleet.queue-broker-token and fleet.laptop-agent-token — into three files under ~/tools/. These are client-side files the seat’s commands name when they talk to the brokers; the brokers read the files per request and never store or log their contents.

ls -l ~/tools/secrets-broker-token ~/tools/queue-broker-token ~/tools/laptop-agent-token

What the output means: three regular files, each with owner-only permissions (-rw-------, mode 0600). Their contents are secret values — do not open, print or copy them anywhere. Only their presence, names and permissions matter here.

What can go wrong, and the fix:

  • A file is missing. The seat can still enrol (the bridge leg works over HTTPS with a by-name secret), but the queue, secrets and shell legs will fail with synthesised transport errors, because those legs read these shared files. Re-run the bootstrap’s token provisioning; if the missing Bitwarden name itself does not resolve, that is a provisioning problem to raise with whoever stood the seat up — do not substitute another secret’s value, and do not reuse the older, different name secrets-broker.token, which is a different value.
  • Permissions are wider than 0600. Tighten them:
chmod 600 ~/tools/secrets-broker-token ~/tools/queue-broker-token ~/tools/laptop-agent-token

Do not confuse these client-side ~/tools/*-token files with the daemon-side token files under ~/.config/secrets-broker/token and ~/.config/queue-broker/token. The daemon-side files belong to the brokers themselves (see Tutorial: run the brokers); a working seat needs its own ~/tools/ set.

Step 3: Say hello on the bridge

Registering on the bridge is a single command. The bridge’s agent registry is exactly the set of agents that have said hello: name, groups and last-seen time all come from this call.

fleet bridge hello --agent <your-agent-name> --groups muse

Replace <your-agent-name> with the name you will enrol under in Step 4, and the groups with the groups your kind carries (Step 4 shows where groups come from; --groups here takes a comma-separated list). The command prints the bridge’s JSON answer.

What the output means: your mailbox now exists on the bridge at https://bridge.security.cab, and central can address you as agent:<your-agent-name> or through any group you named. Re-running hello refreshes the registration and its groups; it is safe to repeat.

What can go wrong, and the fix:

  • Exit 3 — transport or credentials. The fleet token (secret name message-bridge.fleet-token) could not be resolved by name, or the bridge could not be reached. Check that secret resolution works at all by following Tutorial: resolve a secret, then retry.
  • Exit 4 — the bridge refused the request; its JSON error is printed on stderr. A 404 here is reported as a wrong token, an old bridge without fleet mailboxes, or a wrong URL — check the bridge URL resolution ($FLEET_BRIDGE_URL, then [bridge] url in the fleet config, then the default above).
  • Exit 2 — a usage error; fix the flags and retry. Note that fleet bridge has one shared usage text for the whole domain, so read the hello line in it carefully.

If you omit --agent, the name defaults to $FLEET_AGENT, then [bridge] agent in the fleet config; groups default the same way via $FLEET_AGENT_GROUPS and [bridge] groups. For a first enrolment, pass both explicitly so the registration is the one you intend.

Step 4: Enrol the agent

Enrolment validates the kind, adds any extra groups, probes the bridge in register mode (the hello from Step 3 is what actually registers the mailbox), probes the remaining legs, and saves a profile recording the agent, kind, groups and leg state.

fleet agent enroll --kind muse --name <your-agent-name> --groups muse

--kind and --name are required. --groups a,b adds to the kind’s built-in groups. If you do not know which kind fits, list the table first:

fleet agent kinds

That prints one JSON object describing every kind: its name, summary, bridge groups, seat type (binary, http or connector) and enrolment note. Sixteen kinds are registered, including muse, opencode, openchamber, openclaw, claude-code, codex, gemini, antigravity, grok and the fallback kind generic for any other agent with a shell. Adding a kind is adding a row to that table; no verb changes.

What the output means: one JSON object carrying the saved profile, registered (true only when this was not a dry run and the bridge leg answered), the four legs, the intake rungs this seat still has, and seat-specific next-step lines — for a binary seat, the run loop (fleet agent next --agent <name>, do the task, run its then lines, repeat) and the fleet shell line. Exit 0 means a dry run, or that at least one intake rung is live; exit 3 means no intake rung is live.

What can go wrong, and the fix:

  • Unknown kind: a usage error (exit 2) listing all kinds. Pick one from the list, or use generic for anything with a shell.
  • registered is false even though enrolment exited 0: the bridge leg did not answer, so the mailbox was not registered by this call. Re-run Step 3, fix what it reports, then enrol again.
  • You only want to preview: add --dry-run. A dry run probes nothing and registers nothing, and always exits 0.
  • To save the profile somewhere other than the default path, pass --profile PATH.

Step 5: Read all four legs with doctor

Doctor probes four legs in parallel, each with a real fleet verb run as this seat. The four legs are bridge, queue, github and shell. There is no separate secrets leg: secret resolution is folded into the bridge leg’s stated need.

fleet agent doctor --agent <your-agent-name>

Read the answer leg by leg:

LegProbe“Up” meansIt needs
bridgebridge inbox --agent <name> --limit 1“the mailbox answers”HTTPS to the bridge, and the fleet token by name through fleet secrets
queuequeue health“answers”The queue broker: its socket on the laptop, or the laptop transport from elsewhere
githubgh api rate_limit via fleet gh, falling back to a signed-in plain gh“answers”, with route: "fleet" or "plain" recordedA gh token: the fleet rotation, or a signed-in gh
shelllaptop-agent health“the laptop answers”A route to the laptop: its broker, the Cloudflare tunnel, the tailnet, or ssh

Two details matter when reading the result:

  • Doctor’s bridge probe with a known agent is a read that takes nothing (inbox --limit 1). Service health alone proves nothing about whether this seat holds the fleet token, so only a call made as an agent counts. With no agent name known, the bridge leg is reported not ok even when the service answers — enrol, or pass --agent.
  • From the legs, doctor derives the rungs map: push follows the bridge leg, queue follows the queue leg, priority follows the github leg, and shortlist is always true because it is a local file. The answer also reports builds: whether fleet shell reaches the laptop from here, or will try a codespace and then run locally.

Exit 0 means at least one intake rung (bridge, queue or github) is live; exit 3 means none is.

What can go wrong, and the fix:

  • queue down while bridge is up: the classic missing-token-file shape. Go back to Step 2 — a seat whose bootstrap skipped the token phase enrols fine and then fails exactly here.
  • github down: neither the fleet rotation nor a signed-in gh answered. Sign gh in on the seat, or check secret resolution by name as in Tutorial: resolve a secret.
  • shell down but the other legs up: the seat can still take work; builds will fall back as the builds line describes. Fix the laptop route when you need laptop builds.

Step 6: Take the first piece of work

fleet agent next walks the intake ladder in order — a pushed bridge command, a queue claim, the local shortlist, then the highest-priority open issue from GitHub — and returns the first rung that yields work. A rung that is down is recorded and skipped; a rung that is empty is different, and the answer’s tried log says which was which.

fleet agent next --agent <your-agent-name>

What the output means: one JSON object, {agent, rung, task, then, tried}. Do the task, then run the commands in then — for a queue task those lines name the lease deadline and the exact fleet queue checkpoint / fleet queue complete commands for the claim. The queue rung claims with a four-hour lease, overriding the queue’s 45-minute default, which would lapse mid-task. The full claim-and-complete flow is Tutorial: claim and complete a queue task.

What can go wrong, and the fix:

  • Exit 5: no rung had work. This is a normal, healthy answer for an idle fleet — the seat is enrolled and reachable, there is simply nothing to hand out right now. Read tried to confirm each rung was empty or skipped rather than down; a down rung points back at the matching doctor leg in Step 5.
  • Exit 3: a needed leg is down before the ladder could run. Fix it via Step 5.
  • Exit 2: a usage error in the flags.

You are done when

All of the following hold:

  • ls -l ~/tools/*-token shows the three token files, each mode 0600.
  • fleet bridge hello --agent <your-agent-name> exits 0.
  • fleet agent enroll --kind <kind> --name <your-agent-name> printed a profile with registered: true.
  • fleet agent doctor --agent <your-agent-name> exits 0, and you have read all four legs — bridge, queue, github, shell — and know which rungs they give you.
  • fleet agent next --agent <your-agent-name> either handed you a task with its then lines, or exited 5 with every rung empty or skipped in tried — never down for a reason you have not fixed.

Tutorial: claim and complete a queue task

This tutorial works one queue task from claim to a verified completion: claim it (through fleet agent next), keep the lease alive with heartbeats, record progress with checkpoints, build the completion’s evidence with verify-disposition, and complete — including what the evidence gate’s rejection looks like and how to recover from it.

It assumes the fleet binary is installed (see Installation and bootstrap) and the seat is enrolled (see Tutorial: enrol a new seat).

One warning before Step 1, because it decides whether Step 6 works at all: a claim taken through fleet agent next may be registered under the worker and lane agent-next-05, not under your agent name and not under the queue client’s defaults. Every holder verb after the claim — heartbeat, checkpoint and complete — is checked by the broker against the worker (and the lane, when you supply one). Completing with the wrong worker or lane does not complete the wrong task; it finds no matching claimed row at all. Step 2 shows how to read the real worker and lane out of the claim, and Step 6 uses them exactly: --worker agent-next-05 --lane agent-next-05.

Step 1: Claim through fleet agent next

fleet agent next --agent <your-agent-name>

What the output means: one JSON object, {agent, rung, task, then, tried}. For queue work, rung is "queue" and task is the claimed task row. The claim behind this rung is an ordinary queue claim with a four-hour lease (14400 seconds, overriding the queue client’s 45-minute default). The then lines are part of the contract: they name the lease deadline and the exact checkpoint and complete commands for this claim, with the right task id, worker and lane already filled in. Prefer those lines over retyping flags from memory.

Exit 5 from next means no rung had work — there is nothing to claim right now, and this tutorial ends there until work exists. Exit 2 is a usage error; exit 3 is a leg down (run fleet agent doctor --agent <your-agent-name> and fix the leg).

You can also claim directly with the queue client:

fleet queue claim --worker <id> --lane <l>

A direct claim prints the task row verbatim as JSON — {id, queue, status, dedupe_key, payload, …} — and exits 0. Two direct-claim rules surprise people:

  • A bare claim is refused before any broker contact, exit 2: a claim with no task, no filter, no queue scope, no count, no handoff/bind and no identity marks (worker, lane, session-id, pool, platform, from-session) “is never a meaningful intent”. Passing --worker explicitly counts as intent even when it equals the default.
  • No claimable task prints {"task": null} — deliberately carrying no id, queue or status a caller could mistake for a task — plus a diagnostic on stderr of the form no claimable task — Q queued (A at the attempt cap, D not yet due), P parked due, and exits 5.

Keep the claimed row. Everything below needs its id, and Steps 2–6 need the worker and lane the claim was stamped with.

Step 2: Read the claim’s worker and lane

fleet queue show <task-id>

What the output means: the task’s current details, sourced from the broker’s rich row for the task, plus the tail of its event timeline. Confirm the row is claimed, and note the worker and lane recorded on it. When the claim came from fleet agent next, expect the worker/lane pair agent-next-05 / agent-next-05 — the shared identity the agent ladder claims under. All scheduled lanes share related worker ids, which is exactly why the lane matters: it is what tells the broker whose claim a later verb acts on.

What can go wrong, and the fix:

  • repo-queue show: task <id> not found, exit 1: the id is wrong, or it never was a broker task id. Go back to the claim output from Step 1 and copy the id from the row itself.
  • Exit 3: the broker path failed (unreachable, token rejected, or a broker that does not serve the event routes). The claim itself is unaffected; fix the transport and retry the read.

From here on, this tutorial writes the holder flags as --worker agent-next-05 --lane agent-next-05. If your Step 1 claim was a direct claim under a different worker/lane, substitute the pair your claim actually used, everywhere, unchanged.

Step 3: Heartbeat to keep the lease

A claim is a lease. If it lapses, the task returns to the pool and another worker may take it. A heartbeat sets the lease to now plus the extend on both the task row and the lease record.

fleet queue heartbeat <task-id> --worker agent-next-05 --lane agent-next-05

What the output means: the broker’s updated task row as JSON, plus a mode_line describing the route the verb took. The default extend is 900 seconds (15 minutes) — note the asymmetry: a claim’s default lease is 2700 seconds, but a heartbeat only adds 900 unless told otherwise. For a long stretch of work, say so:

fleet queue heartbeat <task-id> --worker agent-next-05 --lane agent-next-05 --extend-seconds 3600 --progress "halfway through the fix"

--extend-seconds must be in 1..=86400; values are rejected, never clamped, and 0 or a negative value would lapse your own claim, so it dies with exit 2. --progress <p> (or --progress-file <f> — the two are mutually exclusive, both together is exit 2) merges a progress value into the row.

What can go wrong, and the fix:

  • Exit 5 with heartbeat: no matching claimed row (task not claimed by this worker, or already terminal): the broker does not believe you hold this task. The usual causes are a wrong --worker/--lane pair (re-read Step 2), a lease that already lapsed and was re-claimed by someone else, or a task that is already terminal. Do not retry blindly — check fleet queue show <task-id> first.
  • Exit 6: the primary queue store failed and the verb switched this work to the GitHub fallback. The output is one JSON object naming the switch, with a hint of the form continue this work with: fleet queue fallback scan|claim|heartbeat|release|unblock. Follow it: from here the task is worked through the fallback verbs until the primary store returns. Setting REPO_QUEUE_NO_FALLBACK_SWITCH=1 disables the switch and restores plain die-on-error, if you ever need the raw failure.

Step 4: Checkpoint progress

A checkpoint records where the work has got to, without touching the lease. The broker merges the progress into the task row, stamps progress.last_checkpoint = {stage, at}, stores a per-worker checkpoint record, and writes a checkpoint event.

fleet queue checkpoint <task-id> --worker agent-next-05 --lane agent-next-05 --stage implementing --progress "fix written; tests running"

--stage is required. The help line brackets it as optional; the client does not — omitting it dies with checkpoint: --stage is required, exit 2. The output is the updated row plus a mode_line, exit 0.

What can go wrong, and the fix:

  • Exit 5: the same no-matching-claimed-row shape as the heartbeat. Same diagnosis: worker/lane pair, lapsed lease, or terminal task.
  • Exit 6: the fallback switch, exactly as in Step 3.

Checkpoint at meaningful boundaries — claim taken, fix written, tests green, PR opened — not on a timer. A later reader (or a later you, after a crash) reconstructs the work from these stages.

Step 5: Build the completion evidence with verify-disposition

A completion whose work is verifiable on GitHub must carry a disposition: a fresh, live readback of the issue and its linked PRs, produced by verify-disposition. It reads GitHub live — never a remembered claim — and prints the record the completion gate will check.

fleet queue verify-disposition <issue-number> --repo <owner/name> --json

--repo is required (exit 2 without it). Save the --json output to a file; Step 6 feeds it to complete as the result’s disposition.

What the output means: a record of the form {"checked_at", "source", "issue": {number, state, state_reason, closed_at, closed_by}, "pulls": [{number, state, is_draft, merged_at}], "verdict", "follow_up"}. The verb then runs the offline gate on its own record before returning:

  • Exit 0: the record would pass the broker’s gate.
  • Exit 1: the gate would reject it, or the issue/PR list could not be read from GitHub at all.
  • Exit 2: a usage error.

The verdict is one of exactly five:

VerdictMeans
merged_verifiedSome pull in the readback is merged
closed_verifiedThe issue is closed and no unfinished pulls remain
open_draft_with_followupUnfinished pulls exist, nothing merged, and a follow-up is on record
