open_draft_supersededOperator-asserted variant of the above, also requiring a follow-up
invalid_no_workNo merged pull, issue open, no unfinished pull

When the honest verdict needs a follow-up — typically open_draft_with_followup, because a draft PR still carries work — name exactly one follow-up target and give a reason (any follow-up target requires --reason, exit 2 without it):

fleet queue verify-disposition <issue-number> --repo <owner/name> --follow-up-pr <n> --reason "the remaining work moved to the successor PR" --json

The alternatives are --follow-up-task <id> (checked by the broker at completion time — only the queue knows whether that task is live) and --follow-up-issue <n|url> (same repo only; its own readback is embedded and checked: it must be open, must not be the issue being completed, and must link the completed issue and every unfinished PR with an explicit marker such as Refs #n). A successor PR must be in the readback and must be merged.

Two freshness facts to plan around: the record goes stale after 1800 seconds (30 minutes) by default (--staleness-seconds changes it for this verb), and a record more than 300 seconds in the future is unreadable clock skew. Run this step immediately before completing, not at the start of the work.

Step 6: Complete — with the evidence gate

fleet queue complete <task-id> --worker agent-next-05 --lane agent-next-05 --result-file result.json

where result.json is a JSON object carrying, for a verifiable completion, the disposition record from Step 5 under the key disposition, plus any pr / pr_url / merged_pr fields naming the PRs the completion claims. (--result <json> passes the object inline instead; when both are given, --result-file wins. A result that is not a JSON object dies with exit 2.)

What the output means on success: the task row — or {task, lane_ledger}, and for a triage completion possibly a follow_on_task_id — with the task now in the terminal status done. Exit 0.

The evidence gate is pure (no network): before accepting the completion, the broker parses the disposition record and checks its freshness, that it describes this task’s issue, that the verdict matches the readback, that every PR the result links appears in the readback, and any follow-up. A completion that requires a disposition and does not carry one is rejected the same way.

What a gate rejection looks like, and how to recover

A rejection names the defect and ends with the sentence that matters: “…; the task remains claimed”. The completion did not land, nothing terminal was written, and your claim — worker, lane and lease — is exactly where it was. Recovery is therefore always the same shape:

  1. Read the named defect literally. The common ones: the record is stale (older than 1800 s); the verdict does not match the readback (for example claiming merged_verified with no merged pull in it); a linked PR is missing from the readback; unfinished pulls remain with no follow-up on record; a follow-up issue does not link the completed issue or is itself closed.
  2. Fix the underlying fact, not the wording. Merge the PR, close the issue properly, file and link the follow-up, or correct the result’s PR fields so they name only PRs the readback contains.
  3. Re-run Step 5 to mint a fresh disposition against the corrected reality — never edit a stale record by hand; its checked_at is part of what the gate checks.
  4. Re-run this step’s complete with the same worker and lane. Keep heartbeating (Step 3) while you work through a rejection, so the lease does not lapse mid-recovery.

What else can go wrong here:

  • Exit 5, no matching claimed row: wrong worker/lane (see Step 2) or the lease lapsed during a long recovery. If the task was re-claimed by another worker, it is theirs now — do not complete over them.
  • Exit 6: the fallback switch. In the fallback, completion is fleet queue fallback complete <repo> <issue-number> --worker <id> --summary <text> --result <path>, where --result is the same verify-disposition --json record; it must pass the same offline gate before anything is posted, and a rejection there also posts nothing, leaves the claim live, and exits 1.
  • --telemetry <json>, if you pass it, may only carry the keys pool, model, effort, cost_usd; an unknown field dies with exit 2 listing the allowed set.

You are done when

  • fleet queue show <task-id> reports the task with status done.
  • The completion you submitted carried a disposition record that fleet queue verify-disposition <issue-number> --repo <owner/name> itself exited 0 on, minted within the staleness window before the completion.
  • No gate rejection is outstanding: if complete ever answered “…; the task remains claimed”, you fixed the named defect, re-minted the disposition, and completed again — under the same --worker and --lane the claim was taken with.

Tutorial: dispatch a build remotely

This tutorial runs a build (or any command) in a target repository on a fleet runner instead of on your own machine: first as a dry run, so you read the placement decision before anything runs; then for real, so you get a session handle; then polling that handle to a terminal result. It also covers chaining a follow-up run onto the same host, pushing the Nix cache, and the raw gh fallback for when no fleet binary is available.

It assumes the fleet binary is installed (see Installation and bootstrap). The placement model behind this tutorial — surfaces, tiers and the registry as data — is covered in Placement and surfaces as data.

The verb is fleet queue dispatch. Despite living under queue, it is not a broker verb: it is the placement engine absorbed into the queue client. It decides where a job runs across the fleet’s GitHub Actions copies and runner providers, and dispatches the fleet-command.yml workflow there. It is unrelated to the top-level fleet dispatch domain.

Step 1: Dry-run first, and read the placement decision

Without --dispatch, the verb is a dry run: it loads the surface registry, computes live capacity, picks a surface, prints the decision — and writes nothing, dispatches nothing.

fleet queue dispatch --repo <owner/name> --command '<cmd>'

For example, a test run in this repository:

fleet queue dispatch --repo developing-today/code --command 'cargo test --workspace'

--repo and --command are both required, and --repo must be a valid owner/name (exactly one /, characters [A-Za-z0-9._-]); anything else is a fatal usage error, exit 2. Every error in this verb family prints repo-queue: <message> on stderr and exits 2.

What the output means (human form):

decision: <surface-id | queued>
  - <reasoning line>
  - …
dry-run (no session written; pass --dispatch to submit)

Read the reasoning lines — they are the decision, not decoration. The cascade that produced them, in order:

  1. A hard pin (--surface ID), if you gave one: that surface or a fatal error, never a fall-through.
  2. Follow-up affinity, if you gave --followup (Step 5).
  3. Tier 1 — free GitHub-hosted Actions: every github-actions surface that is eligible and has free slots, sorted least-loaded owner first, then least-recently-used owner, then the registry’s selection_priority, then per-surface recency, then surface id.
  4. Tier 2 — Blacksmith, in registry order, within its minute budget.
  5. Tier 3 — Codespaces, only when the laptop is marked busy or the surface was explicitly selected.

If every tier is exhausted, the decision is queued with the reasoning “all tiers exhausted — job stays queued (recorded, never dropped; repo-queue remains its system of record)”.

For machine-readable output, add --json. A dry run’s object carries job, decision, reasoning and "mode": "dry-run (no session written; pass --dispatch to submit)", plus a note when a testing override was used, load_read_errors when any load read failed, and owner_load_coverage — per owner: whether its load was measured, partial, unknown, or simulated, the known subtotal, the cap, and which reads are missing. Load failures are soft, but an owner whose load could not be read is reported as unknown capacity, never as an idle zero.

What can go wrong, and the fix:

  • pinned surface <id> is ineligible: <why>, exit 2: a --surface pin is a placement choice, not an override of eligibility. Read the <why> — a common one is pinning the org-run surface, whose registry status is standby, not active, so it can never be selected or pinned. Drop the pin or pick an eligible surface.
  • --surface <id>: no such surface in the registry: the id is not in the registry (including surfaces whose kind has no adapter). List the registry with fleet queue surfaces and copy an id exactly.
  • A macOS job (--platform macos) is ineligible on surfaces without platform_input: true, and counts against the owner’s macOS sub-cap (5 for every shipped owner). If the decision surprises you, the reasoning lines name the surface that failed and why.

Step 2: Dispatch for real, and read the fp_ handle

Add --dispatch (and --json, so the handle is unambiguous):

fleet queue dispatch --repo developing-today/code --command 'cargo test --workspace' --dispatch --json

What the output means: the job object, the decision, the full reasoning array, and then the session fields — handle, run_id, run_url, and (when known) runner_repo and portable_id. The handle has the form fp_ followed by 32 lowercase hex characters, for example:

fp_d0a842c9bd33aa2999f5a12393397ab9

Keep the handle. Use it to poll (Step 3) and to submit a follow-up (Step 5). Dispatch records it in ~/.local/state/fleet-place/sessions.json (override the directory with FLEET_PLACE_STATE) and mirrors it to the queue broker. On a second seat with access to that broker, inspect the same handle:

fleet queue session status <handle> --json

How dispatch actually happens, so the output makes sense: for the chosen surface’s host repo, the client snapshots existing workflow runs, POSTs the workflow dispatch (anything but HTTP 204 is fatal), then polls the run list for up to about 40 seconds to correlate the new run — exactly, when the surface declares a dispatch_id input, by matching a fresh fp_… dispatch id placed in the run title.

What can go wrong, and the fix:

  • The dispatch succeeds but no run correlates in time: the session is still written, with run_id: null, state dispatched, and the note “dispatch accepted (HTTP 204) but the run did not appear within ~40s; resolve it from the workflow’s run list”. This is not a failed dispatch — do not re-dispatch. Resolve the run from the host repo’s workflow run list, then refer to it by its portable reference <host-owner>/<host-repo>#<run-id> (Step 4).
  • The all-tiers-exhausted case with --dispatch: a session record is still written — surface, run_id and run_url all null, state queued — and its handle is printed (the JSON gains handle and state, but no run_id/run_url keys). The job is recorded, never dropped; nothing is running yet.

Step 3: Poll the session to a terminal result

fleet queue session status <handle>

What the output means: the stored record is refreshed from GitHub first (if it has a run and a registered host surface), then printed in the form:

<handle>: state=<state> surface=<surface-id> run=<run-url>

States are queued, dispatched, running, succeeded, failed and cancelled, mapped from the GitHub run’s status and conclusion. Add --json to print the whole refreshed record instead of the one line.

When you need the verdict rather than the state:

fleet queue session result <handle>

That prints <handle>: <state> (terminal=<bool>) run=<run-url>, where terminal is true exactly when the state is succeeded, failed or cancelled. While it is not terminal, the record carries the note “not terminal yet — reconnect with the same handle”. Poll result on your own cadence; there is no streaming form, and the run’s own output is not streamed either — it lives on the run page (gh run view --log).

Two neighbouring forms worth knowing:

fleet queue session list
fleet queue session list --mine

list merges the local store with up to 200 broker records and shows their stored state, newest first. --mine keeps only records whose submitted_by is the current user on this host.

What can go wrong, and the fix:

  • repo-queue: no session with handle <h> in <store path>, exit 2: neither the local store nor the broker supplied the session. Check broker access on both seats. Once the run ID is known, use the portable reference (Step 4) to read the run directly from GitHub.
  • Passing --help to session status or session result is safe: a help flag after the subcommand prints the session usage and exits 0 — it is never taken as a handle.

Step 4: Refer to a run portably

Anywhere a handle is accepted, a portable reference OWNER/REPO#RUN_ID is accepted too — where OWNER/REPO is the runner-host repo of a registered github-actions or blacksmith surface (for example developing-today/fleet), not the target repo:

fleet queue session result developing-today/fleet#45146933211

What the output means: the reference is resolved directly against the GitHub API with that surface’s token, producing a synthetic record with the same state mapping as Step 3. This is the form that survives moving between seats and workspaces, and the form a follow-up takes when you do not have the original handle.

Step 5: Chain a follow-up that sticks to the host

A follow-up downloads the previous run’s fleet-output artifact and, by preference, stays on the same host surface — which also keeps it in the same Actions cache scope, since caches are per host repo.

fleet queue dispatch --repo developing-today/code --command '<cmd>' --followup <handle-or-portable-ref> --dispatch

Dry-run it first (drop --dispatch) and read the affinity line in the reasoning. The preferred surface is kept only while all of these hold: its adapter exists and is eligible; it has capacity; and the owner’s queued count is strictly below the surface’s sticky_queue_threshold — 2 on every shipped surface. With two or more runs already queued on that owner, stickiness is released, and the reasoning records exactly why: followup affinity released from <id>: eligible=<…>, capacity=<…>, queued=<n> (threshold 2); …. On a keep, the line reads followup affinity keeps <id>: <capacity summary>.

What can go wrong, and the fix:

  • With --dispatch, a previous run that is not yet terminal is fatal: “previous run is still <state>; wait for a terminal result before downloading its output”. Wait for Step 3’s result to report terminal=true first.
  • A previous dispatch with no correlated run yet is likewise fatal: “previous dispatch has no correlated run yet; resolve its status before continuing”. Resolve it via Step 4, then chain from the portable reference.
  • In dry-run mode neither guard fires, and a local previous record is read without refreshing — so a dry run can show an affinity a real dispatch would refuse. Treat the dry run as a placement preview, not a promise.

Step 6: The --push-nix-cache variant

fleet queue dispatch --repo <owner/name> --command 'nix build' --push-nix-cache --dispatch

What changes: placement sends the workflow input push_nix_cache: true. On success, the workflow’s action signs ./result and copies it to the shared Fleet R2 cache — resolving ./result, signing with the key from the host repo’s secret named NIX_CACHE_SIGNING_KEY, and uploading to the URL in the secret named NIX_CACHE_UPLOAD_URL (names only; the endpoint is secret-configured, not hardcoded).

What can go wrong, and the fix:

  • “cache push requested but signing/upload secrets are not configured; skipping”: the run still succeeds; only the push is skipped. The host surface you landed on does not carry the NIX_CACHE_* secrets — the fleet-personal registry note names them for that surface. Pin or follow up onto a surface whose host repo has them, or accept the skip.
  • No ./result in the target checkout: also a notice-and-skip. Build something that leaves a ./result link, or drop the flag.
  • A related variant: --actions-cache KEY:PATH binds one extra Actions cache path under the key prefix KEY (default namespace prefix fleet-deps-v1), with --actions-cache-restore-key PREFIX (repeatable, and it requires --actions-cache) adding restore prefixes.

Step 7: The raw gh workflow run fallback

When no fleet binary is available — a foreign host, a broken install — the same workflow can be dispatched directly. You give up placement (you choose the host repo yourself), session records, and correlation; you keep the identical workflow contract.

gh workflow run fleet-command.yml --repo developing-today/fleet --field repo=developing-today/code --field command='cargo test --workspace'

The workflow is fleet-command.yml in a fleet host repo (dezren39/fleet, developing-today/fleet or developing-today-forks/fleet). Its inputs include repo and command (both required), plus optional ref, runner (github or blacksmith), platform (linux or macos), container_image, actions_cache_key (default fleet-deps-v1), actions_cache_path, actions_cache_restore_keys, previous_run_id, previous_run_repo, push_nix_cache and timeout_minutes (5–120, default 60 — an input placement itself never sends, so placement dispatches always get the 60-minute default). Follow the run with gh run list --repo <host-repo> --workflow fleet-command.yml and gh run view --log.

What can go wrong, and the fix:

  • Dispatching in the target repo instead of a host repo: there is no fleet-command.yml in developing-today/code — it lives only in the fleet host repos. Re-run against a host repo, with the target named in the repo field.
  • runner=blacksmith from any host repo other than developing-today/fleet, or with platform=macos: the workflow’s normalize job rejects both. Use the developing-today/fleet host for Blacksmith, on Linux.

You are done when

  • A dry run printed a decision whose reasoning lines you can explain: which tier picked the surface, or why the pin/affinity held or was released.
  • The real dispatch printed an fp_… handle (or a portable OWNER/REPO#RUN_ID reference you resolved from the run list).
  • fleet queue session result <handle> reports terminal=true with the state you expected — succeeded for a good build — and you know the run’s own log lives on its run page, not in the session record.

Tutorial: resolve a secret

This tutorial resolves a secret by name through fleet secrets: first through the secrets broker, then by observing the Bitwarden fallback, then listing what the broker holds — and finally reading the three failure shapes (502, 404, exit 3) correctly and checking the broker’s health when resolution fails.

It assumes the fleet binary is installed (see Installation and bootstrap).

The standing rule for this whole surface: secrets are resolved by name through fleet secrets only. No fleet domain shells out to bws itself or reads a token file on its own, and no command in this tutorial ever prints a secret value anywhere except the one place get is specified to put it — its own stdout. The examples below use the placeholder name example.api-token; substitute a real secret name (never a value) from your own vault.

Step 1: Resolve a name through the broker path

fleet secrets get example.api-token

What the output means: the secret’s value, on stdout and nowhere else, and exit 0. Nothing else is printed — no source label, no age, no log line. That silence is deliberate: the command is built to sit in a pipeline, and a broken pipe on stdout (for example piping into head) is a quiet success, not an error.

The resolution chain behind that one line (Resolver::default_chain in the fleet-secrets crate):

  1. Broker leg first. Where the secrets broker’s own socket answers (the laptop), the client speaks GET /secret/<name> over that Unix socket directly. Elsewhere (a sandbox seat), it makes a framed exchange through the session broker to port 4800. On that leg the request names the token file (config [secrets] token_file, default ~/tools/secrets-broker-token); the session broker reads the file per request and sends its contents as the auth header — the client only ever names the file, and the value never transits the client’s own memory on this leg.
  2. bws CLI fallback (Step 3), only when the broker leg cannot answer.
  3. At library level there is also a 1Password source for seats that keep secrets there; the fleet secrets default chain’s headline shape is broker, then bws.

What the broker does with the request: a cache hit answers immediately with the cached value. A miss on a loaded cache is not final — the broker reads through to Bitwarden for that one name and serves what it finds, so a secret minted moments ago is visible immediately instead of at the next refresh tick. The broker refreshes its whole cache from Bitwarden at startup and then on a TTL (default 900 seconds), serving stale values while a refresh runs.

What can go wrong, and the fix:

  • Exit 2: a usage error — get takes exactly one name, and the name must not start with -.
  • Exit 3: unresolved — no source in the chain could produce the value. Work through Steps 4 and 5 before concluding the name is wrong.
  • The value looks stale after a rotation: the broker serves cached values with their fetch time, and a rotation lands within one TTL of the edit. Wait out the TTL, or ask for a broker refresh (Step 5); do not “fix” it by reading Bitwarden directly in your own scripts — the by-name chain is the platform rule.

Step 2: Know which names exist — list

fleet secrets list

What the output means: the names in the broker’s cache, one per line, names only, never values. Exit 0.

What can go wrong, and the fix — one deliberate asymmetry to memorise: list has no bws fallback. A broker failure here is loud (an error on stderr, exit 3), because a bws listing has different semantics — it enumerates the vault, not the broker’s cache — so it is never silently substituted. If list fails but get works, you are seeing exactly that asymmetry, not an inconsistency: get fell back, list refused to. Fix the broker (Step 5) rather than working around the listing.

Step 3: Force and observe the bws fallback

There is no --force-bws flag. The fallback is a property of the chain: when the broker leg reports itself unavailable, the leg is retried first — the retry budget is sized to real restart windows (a full switch restarts broker and tunnel together, and the broker is back in about 16 seconds), with pauses doubling per attempt up to a cap — and only then does the chain move on to bws. One exception: if the session-broker socket file does not exist at all, the leg does not burn its retry budget — no broker on this box is not a broker mid-restart.

To force the fallback in a test, make the broker leg genuinely unavailable on a seat where that is safe — for example on a sandbox seat, before fleet init has started the local loopback secrets broker (see Tutorial: run the brokers for what init starts), or while the laptop broker is stopped for maintenance — then run Step 1 again:

fleet secrets get example.api-token

What the output means: the same contract as the broker path — the value on stdout, exit 0, nothing else. The fallback runs bws secret list plus bws secret get, the same shape the broker itself uses to fill its cache, with the bws credential resolved the way the broker resolves its own (the BWS_ACCESS_TOKEN environment variable when non-empty, else the on-disk machine-account token file, handed to the bws child through its environment).

How you observe which path answered, since the output deliberately does not say: by the broker’s state, not by the value. Check the broker’s health (Step 5) at the same moment — if it was not serving, the value came from bws; if it was serving, it came from the broker. Latency is a secondary hint only: the per-call bws fetch the broker exists to replace cost 10–40 seconds per invocation, against an immediate cache hit. Never treat latency alone as proof.

What can go wrong, and the fix:

  • The fallback also fails, exit 3: bws is missing, its credential does not resolve, or the name is absent from the vault as well as unreachable through the broker. Distinguish “absent” from “unreachable” with Step 4.
  • A broker 404 is definitive and is not retried, and does not fall back: the broker has a loaded cache and read-through, and the name is not in Bitwarden. That is Step 4’s 404, not a fallback trigger.

Step 4: Read the failure shapes — 502 vs 404 vs exit 3

These three answers mean three different things. Confusing them sends you fixing the wrong layer.

404 — the name does not exist. From the broker: {"error": "no such secret"}. The broker’s cache was loaded, the read-through to Bitwarden ran, and Bitwarden definitely does not hold that name. Fix the name: check spelling against Step 2’s list. Do not retry, and do not restart anything — nothing is down.

502 — the source behind the broker failed. From the broker: {"error": "bitwarden read-through failed"}. The name was a cache miss, the broker tried to read through, and Bitwarden itself failed (the bws call behind the broker errored). This is loud precisely so it is never mistaken for a 404: the secret may well exist; the broker could not check. Fix the broker’s Bitwarden leg (Step 5), then retry.

503 — the broker is up but not serving yet. Before its first successful refresh, the broker answers GET /secret/<name> with {"error": "secrets not loaded yet"}, and its health endpoint answers 503 too. A live process whose bws cannot run is not serving, and health says so. This is a wait-or-fix-the-refresh state, not a missing secret.

Exit 3 — the client could not resolve the name at all. The fleet secrets client-side shape: the broker leg was unavailable (after its retries), and the fallback also failed or the name was unresolved through it. Exit 3 is about the path, where 404/502/503 are answers from a broker that was reached. (For completeness: the client’s other exits are 0 for success and 2 for usage.)

Step 5: Check the broker’s health when it fails

The broker’s health endpoint is unauthenticated and reports the serving gate directly. On the laptop, where the broker binds its tailnet address on port 4800:

curl -s http://100.99.113.103:4800/health

Read the answer field by field: {ok, serving, secrets, last_refresh_unix, refreshing, oldest_secret_age_seconds}.

  • serving: true with a recent last_refresh_unix: the broker is healthy; secrets is the cached name count and oldest_secret_age_seconds tells you the stalest value it can serve. A resolution failure against a serving broker is a 404 problem (Step 4), not a health problem.
  • HTTP 503 with serving: false: no refresh has succeeded yet. Check refreshing and last_refresh_unix. A failed authenticated secret read during startup can include refresh_error in its 503 response. Use that diagnostic when available.
  • No answer at all: the broker process is not running, or this seat cannot reach it. On a sandbox seat, run fleet init (it starts the local loopback broker copy the sandbox uses) or see Tutorial: run the brokers to run one in the foreground and watch it start. On the laptop, check the service that runs fleet serve secrets-broker.

To kick a refresh on a running broker without restarting it, POST to /refresh on the same address. Unlike /health, that endpoint requires the broker’s X-Agent-Token header — supply the token through your normal operator tooling for the daemon-side token file (~/.config/secrets-broker/token on the laptop), without printing its contents or placing them in a command line. It answers 202 {"ok": true, "refresh": "started"}. This acknowledges the request. If a refresh is already running, the worker skips the overlapping sweep. Then re-read /health: a successful refresh sets last_refresh_unix and clears the recorded refresh error.

Note the sandbox shape: on a sandbox seat (FLEET_LOCATION=sandbox) the local broker’s bind is forced to 127.0.0.1:4800 at the bind itself, whatever its environment says — the same health checks apply against loopback there.

You are done when

  • fleet secrets get example.api-token (with a real name substituted) exits 0 and prints the value on stdout only.
  • fleet secrets list exits 0 and lists names — proving the broker leg, since list never falls back.
  • You can state, for a failure you induced or observed, which of 404 (name absent), 502 (Bitwarden read-through failed), 503 (broker not serving yet) or exit 3 (client could not resolve at all) it was, and which layer you fixed.
  • The broker’s /health reports serving: true.

Tutorial: bridge messaging

This tutorial exercises the whole bridge loop: an agent says hello and registers its mailbox, central sends it a message and a command, the agent reads its inbox, posts a reply, and acknowledges what it has handled — and central reads the log to confirm the exchange.

It assumes the fleet binary is installed (see Installation and bootstrap).

The model in one paragraph: every fleet agent has a mailbox on the message bridge (live at https://bridge.security.cab) named after it, and registers with optional groups. Central sends a message or a command to one agent, a group, or all; the agent reads its mailbox, does the work, and posts its answer back, which marks the command handled. The bridge’s agent registry is exactly the set of agents that have said hello.

There are two credential classes, both resolved by name through fleet secrets — never typed or printed:

  • Central verbs (send, agents, log) use the owner token, secret name message-bridge.access-token.
  • Agent verbs (hello, inbox, post, ack) use the fleet token, secret name message-bridge.fleet-token, which opens only the agent routes and cannot send commands.

Every verb’s output is the bridge’s JSON, passed through. Exits for the whole domain: 0 ok, 2 usage, 3 transport or credentials, 4 the bridge refused the request (its JSON error goes to stderr). Every verb has its own help: fleet bridge <command> --help prints that verb’s usage section plus the shared defaults-and-exit-codes footer, and a bare fleet bridge --help prints the whole-domain usage text.

The agent name defaults to $FLEET_AGENT, then [bridge] agent in the fleet config; groups default to $FLEET_AGENT_GROUPS, then [bridge] groups; the bridge URL to $FLEET_BRIDGE_URL, then [bridge] url, then the default above. The steps below pass --agent explicitly so the flow is unambiguous.

Step 1: Say hello — register the mailbox

fleet bridge hello --agent <your-agent-name> --groups muse,code-lanes

What the output means: the bridge’s JSON answer to the registration. Your agent now appears in the registry with the groups you named and a last-seen time from this call. hello is both the first registration and the refresh: re-running it updates groups and last-seen. This is also the call fleet agent enroll makes for its bridge leg (see Tutorial: enrol a new seat).

What can go wrong, and the fix:

  • Exit 3: the fleet token could not be resolved by name, or the bridge is unreachable. Verify secret resolution with Tutorial: resolve a secret. One special case: on a seat where the fleet token’s secret is missing but the owner token resolves (the laptop seat), the fleet token is derived from the owner token in-process, exactly as the bridge derives it — it is never written anywhere. If hello works on the laptop without the fleet-token secret present, that derivation is why.
  • Exit 4 with a 404 shape: reported as a wrong token, an old bridge without fleet mailboxes, or a wrong URL. Check the URL resolution order above before suspecting the token.

Step 2: Send to an agent, a group, and all (as central)

Central sends with --to. Targets are agent:<name> (or a bare name), group:<name>, or all; repeat --to or comma-separate several.

A plain message to one agent:

fleet bridge send --to agent:<your-agent-name> "standup notes are in the shared doc"

The same message to a whole group:

fleet bridge send --to group:muse "standup notes are in the shared doc"

And to every registered agent:

fleet bridge send --to all "standup notes are in the shared doc"

A command — work the agent is expected to do and answer — adds --command (without it, the default is a plain message):

fleet bridge send --to agent:<your-agent-name> --command "run the queue health check and report back"

Long text can come from stdin by passing - as the text argument. --sender NAME overrides the recorded sender name.

What the output means: the bridge’s JSON answer for the send. The message is now in each target mailbox as an unread row; for a command, it will sit as an unhandled command until the agent posts its answer (Step 4).

What can go wrong, and the fix:

  • Exit 3 as central: the owner token (secret name message-bridge.access-token) did not resolve. Central verbs cannot use the fleet token, and the fleet token cannot send commands — using the wrong class is a credentials failure, not a partial send.
  • Exit 4: the bridge refused — read its JSON error on stderr; a mistyped target is refused here rather than silently dropped.

Step 3: Read the inbox (as the agent)

fleet bridge inbox --agent <your-agent-name>

What the output means: your unread rows as JSON. Useful filters, all from the verb’s own --help:

  • --commands or --messages: only that kind. The intake ladder’s push rung reads with --commands --take, because a pushed command outranks every other source of work.
  • --all: include rows already read.
  • --take: mark what this call returns as read, as it returns it.
  • --since-id N, --limit N: page the mailbox.
  • --wait SECS (with --interval SECS, default interval 15 s): poll until something arrives or the seconds pass. The wait is capped at 24 hours in the client.
  • --groups g1,g2: refresh this agent’s registered groups (the same groups hello records). There are no group mailboxes: a group send lands as one row in each member agent’s own mailbox at send time.

Note the id of the command row from Step 2 — Step 4 replies to it, and Step 5 acknowledges up to it.

What can go wrong, and the fix:

  • An empty inbox right after a send: check the target spelling (a bare name and agent:<name> are the same target; a group send lands as one row in each registered member’s own mailbox, so an agent that joins the group later never sees it), and whether a previous --take read already marked the rows read — re-read with --all to see them.
  • Exit 3 / exit 4: same credential and refusal shapes as Step 1.

Step 4: Post a reply

A bare post sends a message to central. With --reply-to, it answers that specific row and marks it read — for a command, that answer is what marks the command handled.

fleet bridge post --agent <your-agent-name> --reply-to <id> "queue health: all queues answering; details in the log"

As with send, - reads the text from stdin.

post can also address others directly with --to: drew, claude, chatgpt, connectors, agent:<name> (or a bare name), group:<name>, agents, or all, repeated or comma-separated:

fleet bridge post --agent <your-agent-name> --to group:muse "health check done — summary posted to central"

Adding --instruction (or --kind instruction) makes the post an instruction, which requires --to.

What can go wrong, and the fix:

  • Replying without --reply-to when you meant to answer a command: the post lands as a new message to central, and the command stays unhandled. Re-post with the row’s id.
  • Exit 2: an instruction without --to, or other flag misuse — the the verb’s own --help text is the reference.

Step 5: Acknowledge what you have handled

Reading with --take marks rows read as they are returned; ack is the explicit form, for rows you read earlier or handled out of band. It takes either explicit ids or one --up-to boundary:

fleet bridge ack --agent <your-agent-name> --up-to <id>

fleet bridge ack --agent <your-agent-name> <id> <id>

What the output means: the bridge’s JSON answer; the named rows (or every row up to the boundary) are now read, so they no longer count in your unread total and no longer appear in a default inbox read.

What can go wrong, and the fix:

  • Acking rows you have not actually handled: ack is a state change, not a receipt you can retract. Prefer --take on the read that does the handling, and use explicit ack only for rows you can name.

Step 6: Read the log as central

Central’s view of the whole exchange is the log:

fleet bridge log

What the output means: the central message log as JSON — both directions, messages and commands. Filters: --agent A, --direction inbound|outbound, --kind message|command, --since-id N, --before-id N, --limit N, --order asc|desc. The send from Step 2, the reply from Step 4 and the resulting handled state are all visible here; this is the audit view the mailbox verbs do not give you.

The companion central verb is the registry view:

fleet bridge agents

It prints the registered agents, their groups and unread counts — the quick check that a Step 1 hello landed and that Step 5’s ack drained the unread count.

Finally, the token-free health probe, useful before blaming credentials for a failure in any step:

fleet bridge health

It answers the bridge’s /healthz with no token at all.

What can go wrong, and the fix:

  • log and agents are central verbs: they need the owner token. An exit 3 here with working agent verbs means the owner token’s name (message-bridge.access-token) is the one that does not resolve on this seat — the two token classes fail independently.

You are done when

  • fleet bridge agents (as central) lists your agent with the groups from Step 1.
  • A command sent in Step 2 appears in the agent’s Step 3 inbox, is answered by a Step 4 post --reply-to, and shows as handled in the Step 6 log.
  • The agent’s unread count in fleet bridge agents is back to zero after Step 5’s ack.
  • You can state which token class each verb you ran used — owner token for send/agents/log, fleet token for hello/inbox/post/ ack — and neither value was ever printed.

Tutorial: run the brokers

This tutorial runs the queue broker in the foreground, proves it healthy two different ways, adds the secrets broker beside it in the same process, and stops everything cleanly. It is the manual form of what a service manager runs in production — useful on a new host, in a test environment, and whenever you want a broker’s startup output in front of you instead of in a log.

It assumes the fleet binary is installed (see Installation and bootstrap).

Two facts frame everything below:

  • The broker roles take no arguments. Through fleet serve, any trailing argument to queue-broker or secrets-broker is rejected before the daemon starts (unexpected argument '<first>' for 'fleet serve <role>', exit 2) — through the spelled-out form and through the queue-broker / secrets-broker argv0 aliases alike. There is no per-role help for the two brokers either: fleet serve queue-broker --help answers with the generic serve domain help, exit 0.
  • In production these roles are supervised (systemd on the laptop), and the supervisor restarts them. In this tutorial you are the supervisor: the process runs until you stop it.

Step 1: Run the queue broker in the foreground

fleet serve queue-broker

(The argv0 spelling queue-broker, invoked as its own program name, lands in exactly the same place.)

What happens, in order:

  1. The broker loads its token from its token file — QUEUE_BROKER_TOKEN_FILE, default ~/.config/queue-broker/token. Requests carry that token in the X-Agent-Token header; an unreadable token file is a startup error, exit 3. Token files are loaded by reading and trimming the file; a missing, unreadable, empty or whitespace-only file is a hard error naming the file, and the broker refuses to start.
  2. It binds two listeners with identical routes and auth: TCP on QUEUE_BROKER_BIND (default 100.99.113.103:4801, the laptop’s tailnet address; port 4801 is the queue broker’s fleet-wide port), and a Unix socket on QUEUE_BROKER_SOCKET (default ~/.config/queue-broker/broker.sock). If the socket bind fails, the broker degrades to TCP-only with a log line rather than dying.
  3. The listener comes up before the backend: the Turso backend connects on a startup thread, so the health probe and validation answer immediately while queue verbs answer exit 3 with a turso_pending reason until the backend is ready. A backend that cannot come up within its retry budget exits the broker with 3, so a supervisor restarts it.

The process now blocks in the foreground. Leave it running and work from a second terminal for the next steps.

What can go wrong, and the fix:

  • Exit 3 at startup: the token file, the bind, or the backend config. The backend accepts only Turso: QUEUE_BROKER_BACKEND unset, empty or turso is fine; anything else is a startup config error, exit 3. The backend’s credential comes from QUEUE_BROKER_TURSO_TOKEN_FILE, or is resolved through the secrets broker by the secret name turso.fleet-queue-rw-token; its URL is QUEUE_BROKER_TURSO_URL, defaulting to the dedicated fleet-queue database.
  • The broker also needs the secrets broker for some resolutions: it reads QUEUE_BROKER_SECRETS_URL (default http://100.99.113.103:4800, or unix://<path> for the secrets broker’s socket) and QUEUE_BROKER_SECRETS_TOKEN_FILE (default ~/.config/secrets-broker/token). Step 3 runs that broker too.
  • Sandbox clients never reach this process directly: they reach it through the session proxy, which forwards to port 4801. A broker that is healthy locally (Step 2) but unreachable from a sandbox has a proxy problem, not a broker problem.

Step 2: Health-check the queue broker — two different checks

These two commands answer different questions. Do not substitute one for the other.

The unauthenticated probe, which any monitor can call:

curl -s http://100.99.113.103:4801/healthz

It answers {"service":"queue-broker"}. /healthz is the broker’s only unauthenticated route, and it is served without the Turso backend — so it proves the process is up and listening, not that the backend is ready. (Everything else on the broker is a POST with the token header; a non-POST request gets 405 {"error":"POST only"}, a wrong or missing token 401 {"error":"unauthorized"}, and an oversized body 413 — the pre-body gate refuses from headers alone, before any body byte is read. The body cap is 16 MiB.)

The queue-level health verb, which goes through the broker’s real request path:

fleet queue health

What the output means: a first line project: <netloc> (resolved via <source>), then a table of per-queue task counts by status, built from whatever keys the broker’s health rows carry — or (no queues have tasks) when the store is empty. Exit 0 means the broker and its backend answered a real queue request. If /healthz answers but this verb exits 3 in the first moments after startup, the backend is still connecting (turso_pending); give it its retry window before treating it as a failure. Note that fleet queue health is itself on the fallback-switch path: a dead primary store switches the verb to the GitHub fallback with exit 6 rather than a plain failure.

Step 3: Add the secrets broker

Stop the Step 1 process (Step 5 shows the clean way) and start both roles in one process, as a serve list:

fleet serve queue-broker secrets-broker

What the output means: fleet serve: starting 2 roles in one process: queue-broker secrets-broker. A serve list is role tokens only, two or more distinct ones, and nothing else:

  • A duplicate is a hard error: error: duplicate role 'queue-broker' in 'fleet serve' list.
  • Any non-role token is a hard error — including --help. A serve list has no --help form at all.
  • All roles are capability-checked before anything binds. If any role cannot run in this invocation, the whole list stubs with exit 69 and no partial start.
  • Each role’s blocking loop runs on its own thread. Supervision is fail-fast: the first role thread to return or panic takes the whole process down, naming the role on stderr. A role exiting cleanly (code 0) is converted to process exit 1 — a daemon role returning at all is abnormal — and a panic is also exit 1.

The secrets broker in this list behaves exactly as it does alone (fleet serve secrets-broker in its own terminal works too, as does the secrets-broker argv0 alias):

  • It binds TCP on SECRETS_BROKER_BIND (default 100.99.113.103:4800) plus its Unix socket (SECRETS_BROKER_SOCKET, default ~/.config/secrets-broker/broker.sock), with its token from SECRETS_BROKER_TOKEN_FILE (default ~/.config/secrets-broker/token; unreadable is a startup exit 3). On a sandbox seat (FLEET_LOCATION=sandbox) the bind is forced to 127.0.0.1:4800 at the bind itself, whatever the environment says.
  • It is a resident Bitwarden Secrets Manager cache: at startup a background thread runs a full refresh (bws secret list, then one bws secret get per name, fetched 8-way parallel), then repeats on the TTL — SECRETS_BROKER_TTL_S, default 900 seconds, minimum 30. An unparseable TTL falls back to 900 with a warning naming the value; a parsed TTL below 30 makes startup refuse to run, exit 2, because one interval costs a full vault refresh and 0 would spin that loop with no sleep at all.
  • Until the first refresh succeeds, the broker is up but not serving: its health endpoint answers 503. That gate is the subject of Step 4.

What can go wrong, and the fix:

  • The whole list stubs at exit 69 naming a role: this invocation cannot run that role (a narrowed build such as fleet-connect, or the domain disabled in the fleet config). Nothing bound — fix the invocation, not the roles.
  • One role’s startup failure (for example the secrets broker’s token file) takes the list down by design. Read the stderr line naming the role, fix that role’s cause, and start the list again.

Step 4: Health-check the secrets broker

curl -s http://100.99.113.103:4800/health

What the output means: {ok, serving, secrets, last_refresh_unix, refreshing, oldest_secret_age_seconds}.

  • serving: true: at least one refresh has succeeded. secrets is the cached name count; oldest_secret_age_seconds is the stalest value the broker can currently serve; reads are cache-first, with a read-through to Bitwarden on a miss.
  • HTTP 503 with serving: false means the first successful refresh is pending. Follow refreshing and last_refresh_unix on public health. An authenticated secret read while unready can return a 503 with refresh_error when a refresh has failed.
  • The client-side cross-check is fleet secrets list, which lists the broker cache’s names and never falls back (see Tutorial: resolve a secret).

Step 5: Know where state lives, then stop cleanly

Broker state is mostly not in local files, which is what makes stopping and restarting these processes safe:

  • Queue state lives in the dedicated Turso database fleet-queue (org dezren39, group great-star-lord) — the broker’s only backend. The broker process itself holds connections and in-flight requests, not the queue. Tasks, leases, lanes, events, the creation outbox and merge-intent stacks are all rows in that store.
  • Secrets state is a cache, held in memory: the authoritative copy is Bitwarden itself, and a restarted broker rebuilds its cache from bws on its first refresh. Nothing is lost by stopping it — only freshness, until the first refresh lands.
  • Local files are configuration and credentials only: the token files (~/.config/queue-broker/token, ~/.config/secrets-broker/token), the sockets (~/.config/queue-broker/broker.sock, ~/.config/secrets-broker/broker.sock), and the fleet config that resolved them. The placement session store (~/.local/state/fleet-place/sessions.json) belongs to the dispatch client, not to either broker.

To stop: send the foreground process Ctrl-C (or SIGTERM to its process group under your own supervisor). A clean stop is simply the process exiting — there is no drain protocol to run, no state to flush, and no shutdown verb. In a serve list, stopping the process stops every role in it together; remember the fail-fast rule in reverse: if one role dies on its own, the process exit you observe (the role’s own code, or 1 for a clean/panic exit) names that role on stderr, and the correct response is to fix the named role and restart the list — exactly what systemd does with the production units.

What can go wrong, and the fix:

  • A restarted queue broker answers /healthz but queue verbs exit 3: the backend is still connecting. This is the designed startup ordering, not a wedge — unless the backend’s retry budget expires, at which point the broker exits 3 and your supervisor (or you) restarts it.
  • A restarted secrets broker serves 503 longer than a refresh should take: check the readiness fields in Step 4 and the most recent refresh failure in the broker logs or the authenticated not-loaded response.

You are done when

  • curl -s http://100.99.113.103:4801/healthz answers {"service":"queue-broker"} and fleet queue health exits 0 with a counts table — both checks, not just the probe.
  • fleet serve queue-broker secrets-broker starts both roles in one process, and the secrets broker’s /health reports serving: true with a set last_refresh_unix.
  • You can name where each piece of state lives — queue rows in the Turso fleet-queue database, secrets as an in-memory cache over Bitwarden, only tokens/sockets/config as local files — and you have stopped the foreground process cleanly with no state lost.

The crates

The fleet binary is one Rust workspace, pkgs/fleet/, with 16 crates: 15 library crates and the one binary crate that assembles them. The workspace is self-contained — its own Cargo.toml, Cargo.lock and rust-toolchain.toml, no workspace relationship to the repository root — at version 0.1.0, edition 2024, rust-version 1.85, licensed MIT OR Apache-2.0. Shared externals are pinned once at the workspace level (serde 1 with derive, serde_json 1, sha2 0.11, toml 1.2); the fleet crates depend on each other by path only. The release profile is a size contract, not a speed profile: opt-level = "z", lto = true, codegen-units = 1, strip = true, sized for the connect variant’s budget (target ≤ 1.5 MiB, hard ≤ 2 MiB, stripped).

This chapter names every crate by its exact package name, gives its purpose in the crate’s own words (the description line of its Cargo.toml, quoted verbatim), and maps which crate owns which domain. The chapters after this one go deep on the three library surfaces an embedder touches most: The queue client, Placement and surfaces as data, and Registry, config and capabilities.

The 16 crates

fleet

“One multicall binary for the fleet’s tools: search, queue, dispatch, proxy — with compile-time capability-selected variants (epic developing-today/code#5412).”

The bin crate: [[bin]] name = "fleet", and no lib.rs. Its src/main.rs is the multicall entrypoint — argv0 routing, the capability surface, the stub machinery, root built-ins — and it also carries two domains as bin-crate modules rather than library crates: secrets (the fleet secrets verbs, over fleet-secrets) and gh (the fleet gh passthrough, with its gh_cache, gh_closure, gh_guard and gh_metadata modules). Unconditional modules include invocation_ledger, session_state and derived_version (the last also included by path from build.rs, which bakes the source revision and the derived version into the binary).

fleet-agent

“The fleet agent domain: one front door for any agent. Enrol a named agent of any kind, check what this seat can reach, ask for the next piece of work down the intake ladder (pushed command, queue claim, local shortlist, highest priority), and open a shell where builds belong.”

Owns the agent domain (kinds, enroll, doctor, next, shortlist) and the shell domain (run_shell entry): one crate, two registry domains, both riding the single agent capability. It links only fleet-config among the fleet crates: it runs the other domains’ verbs through the same binary rather than linking their crates.

fleet-bridge

“The fleet bridge domain: send and receive through the message bridge’s fleet mailboxes — central commands one agent, a group or all; agents read, answer and ack.”

Owns the bridge domain. Essentially a single src/lib.rs plus its tests: the mailbox client for the bridge service, with the two token classes (owner token for central verbs, fleet token for agent verbs) resolved by name through fleet-secrets.

fleet-cert

“The fleet cert domain: PKI/X.509 roots, issuers, leaves, chains and bundles over a library-first Rust API (developing-today/code#9157, spec doc/2026-11-13T01-34-11Z_design_fleet_ca_credentials_secrets).”

Owns the cert domain (fleet cert, alias fleet pki), entry point fleet_cert::run, with the domain’s own usage text in fleet_cert::cli. The verb surface covers roots, issuers, leaves, chains, bundles and profiles; the OCSP verb group (sign, inspect, test) and the ocsp-responder profile landed in #13722.

fleet-config

“fleet configuration: ~/.config/fleet/fleet.toml + env resolution, the [domains] enable/disable table, and state-dir paths.”

A platform crate, not a domain: the one place configuration resolves. Environment overrides, then the config file (${XDG_CONFIG_HOME:-~/.config}/fleet/fleet.toml unless $FLEET_CONFIG names another), then compiled-in defaults. A missing file is not an error; a malformed file — including unknown sections or keys — is a loud error on every path, never a silent fallback. It also owns the fleet’s path, port and socket constants. Covered in depth in Registry, config and capabilities.

fleet-dispatch

“The fleet dispatch domain: a thin client over pm-stack’s pm-dispatch service — status, launch, and enqueue verbs (epic developing-today/code#5412, step 4 #5432).”

Owns the dispatch domain: a single-file client over pm-dispatch’s existing HTTP routes — exactly three (GET /health, POST /v1/sessions, POST /v1/tasks). pm-stack itself is a working TypeScript/Bun service suite that is deliberately not rewritten; per-task status is not here, because that state is the repo queue itself.

fleet-dispatch-test

“The fleet dispatch-test domain: explicit-dispatch CI test — scan fleet repos for free GitHub Actions capacity, submit a job to the Turso-backed jobs store, dispatch the pilot workflow, and track the job’s stored status.”

Owns the dispatch-test domain (scan, submit, status). Nothing in it is trigger-driven: every verb runs only when a caller invokes it, and submit dispatches a workflow_dispatch run explicitly.

fleet-kv

“Identity-scoped local SQLite storage for fleet-kv.”

A platform crate, not a domain: the identity-scoped SQLite storage core (#13362) that other fleet surfaces build on.

fleet-laptop-agent

“The fleet laptop-agent domain: the transport ladder (broker, Cloudflare, Tailscale, SSH) and the verbs over the laptop-agent daemon (epic developing-today/code#5412, issue #10796).”

Owns the laptop-agent domain (health, jobs, kill, exec, run, poll, fetch): the client for the laptop-agent daemon on port 4799, with a four-leg transport ladder — broker, Cloudflare, Tailscale, and an SSH leg that exists in the ordering as a stub and never carries traffic in this build.

fleet-orgs

“The fleet orgs domain: the Turso-backed org/App registry, synced from each GitHub App’s own JWT (developing-today/code#8884).”

Owns the orgs domain, entry point fleet_orgs::run. The registry tables are sync_runs, apps, orgs and installations, with idempotent upserts; sync uses each App’s JWT against GET /app and GET /app/installations. fleet orgs list prints the table or --json, with --app, --org and --permission filters, and shows the last successful sync time. The Turso URL comes from FLEET_ORGS_TURSO_URL; its token is the secret turso.fleet-orgs-token.

fleet-proxy

“The fleet session proxy domain: proxy serve (the broker) and proxy connect/init (the client) — design note §4, epic developing-today/code#5412.”

Owns the proxy domain: the session broker (proxy serve), the client verbs (connect, init, ssh, splice, get, put), warm tunnel pools to the laptop’s services, and file transfer over the agent channel. The crate is a non-optional dependency of the bin crate with its own features split: the client is in every variant; only the broker half (serve) is feature-gated. It also carries two extra binaries (fleet-connect-udp, fleet-udp-forward).

fleet-proxy-proto

“The fleet proxy wire contract: length-prefixed JSON framing plus the hello/capability frame types. The contract lives here and nowhere else.”

A platform crate: the session-broker wire protocol and nothing else — 8-byte big-endian length-prefixed JSON frames, the hello/capability handshake, and the major-version window (N / N−1, plus the legacy proto 0 dialect). (The design note’s “4-byte” framing was a census error; the live wire is 8-byte, and the crate README records the erratum.)

fleet-queue

“The fleet queue domain: the repo-queue client surface plus the queue-broker and secrets-broker server roles (epic developing-today/code#5412, step 2 #5430).”

By far the largest crate, and the owner of three registry surfaces at once: the queue domain (the client, including the GitHub fallback queue and the placement module), and — under the serve domain — the queue-broker and secrets-broker roles. It also builds three standalone binaries from src/bin/ (repo-queue, queue-broker, secrets-broker), the migration’s rollback inventory: they retire only at the epic’s close, not before. Its internal split — client surface, broker surface, and the feature gates between them — is the subject of The queue client and Placement and surfaces as data.

fleet-registry

“The full fleet domain registry: names, one-line descriptions, argv0 aliases, capabilities and variant profiles. Std-only; compiled into every fleet variant.”

A platform crate with a hard constraint: dependency-free (std only, strings and tables, no I/O), so it can be compiled into every variant — including the size-gated connect build — and --help is always complete. It owns the 22 capability atoms, the 19 domains, the three build variants and the argv0 alias map. Covered in depth in Registry, config and capabilities.

fleet-search

“The fleet search domain: the atlas-search client surface over the live Atlas service (job protocol), with the Q3 host defaults — via-service with loud standalone fallback on the sandbox seat, standalone on the laptop seat (epic developing-today/code#5412, step 5 #5433) — and the serve search role, the Atlas service itself rehomed from the atlas-search bin crate (#5604).”

Owns the search domain (the Atlas client) and the search serve role (the Atlas service itself, behind the crate’s serve feature). It is the one workspace member that consumes crates outside the workspace: atlas-core / atlas-embed / atlas-proto by relative path from pkgs/atlas-search. The serve role’s engine is a verbatim copy of atlas-search’s service, held byte-for-byte by a parity-guard workflow.

fleet-secrets

“The one secrets-by-name path for fleet: secrets-broker protocol first, bws CLI fallback. Values are never stored, never logged, and redacted in Debug.”

A platform crate, not a domain: the resolver every domain uses to turn a secret name into a value. The resolution chain is broker first (direct socket where the broker is local, framed through the session broker elsewhere), then the bws CLI fallback, then a 1Password source where a vault is named. Resolved values live in a type whose Debug is redacted; chain errors count failed sources without ever carrying a value.

Dependency shape

Three rules describe the whole graph:

  1. fleet-registry depends on nothing — not even on the workspace’s shared externals. That is what lets every variant, however small, know every domain name, summary, alias and required capability, whether or not it can run it.
  2. Platform crates sit at the bottom: fleet-registry, fleet-config, fleet-secrets and fleet-proxy-proto own the contracts (registry, configuration, secret resolution, wire framing) that domain crates consume. Domain crates do not shell out around them — no domain resolves its own config file, fetches its own Bitwarden secret, or invents its own framing.
  3. The bin crate assembles. crates/fleet wires the domain crates behind Cargo features, reconstructs its compiled capability set from those features at runtime (see Registry, config and capabilities), and routes argv0 → domain → capability check → handler or stub. Domain crates generally do not depend on each other; where one domain needs another’s verbs (fleet-agent running queue or bridge verbs), it goes through the assembled binary, not a crate edge.

Feature wiring mirrors the capability set one level down. On the bin crate, for example, queue = ["dep:fleet-secrets", "dep:fleet-queue", "fleet-queue/client"] and queue-broker = ["dep:fleet-secrets", "dep:fleet-queue", "fleet-queue/queue-broker"]: enabling a capability enables exactly the matching feature surface of the owning crate. proxy-connect is not a feature at all — it is compiled into every variant unconditionally.

Which crate owns which domain

Registry domainPrimary capabilityOwning crateEntry point
queuequeuefleet-queuefleet_queue::client::run
serve (roles queue-broker, secrets-broker)queue-brokerfleet-queue (bin-crate glue routes the roles)fleet_queue::queue_broker::run, fleet_queue::secrets_broker::run
serve (role search)search-servefleet-searchfleet_search::serve::run
serve (role proxy)proxy-servefleet-proxythe proxy serve loop, via bin-crate glue
proxyproxy-connectfleet-proxy (+ fleet-proxy-proto)bin-crate glue over fleet-proxy client/serve
dispatchdispatchfleet-dispatchfleet_dispatch::run
dispatch-testdispatch-testfleet-dispatch-testfleet_dispatch_test::run
secretssecretsbin crate, over fleet-secretscrates/fleet/src/secrets.rs
ghghbin cratecrates/fleet/src/gh.rs and siblings
bridgebridgefleet-bridgefleet_bridge::run
agentagentfleet-agentfleet_agent::run
shellagentfleet-agentfleet_agent::run_shell
searchsearchfleet-searchfleet_search::run
laptop-agentlaptop-agentfleet-laptop-agentfleet_laptop_agent::cli::run
orgsorgsfleet-orgsfleet_orgs::run
certcertfleet-certfleet_cert::run

Note the two irregular rows, because embedders trip on both: shell has no capability atom of its own — it rides the agent capability — and secrets and gh are domains without library crates, living as modules in the bin crate (over fleet-secrets, in the secrets case).

Example: depending on the platform layer

The smallest useful embedding is the dependency-free registry: any crate, tool or test can ask what the fleet’s surface is without linking a single domain. This example is illustrative — it follows the researched API (fleet_registry::DOMAINS, fleet_registry::domain) but the exact return type of the lookup helper was not verified against the source signature in this pass.

# Cargo.toml
[dependencies]
fleet-registry = { path = "../fleet-registry" }

// Print the registered summary for the queue domain, if it exists.
fn main() {
    for d in fleet_registry::DOMAINS {
        println!("{} — {}", d.name, d.summary);
    }
    // fleet_registry::domain(name: &str) -> Option<&'static Domain>
    if let Some(d) = fleet_registry::domain("queue") {
        println!("queue aliases: {:?}", d.aliases);
    }
}

The queue client

fleet-queue is three surfaces in one crate — a client, a queue broker and a secrets broker — and Cargo features are the walls between them. This chapter is about embedding the client surface: what the client feature turns on, how a verb call travels to the broker (the call() path), the argument-parsing helpers every verb is built on, the fallback module’s feature gate, the two transport routes, and how token files are handled on each side.

For the crate’s place in the workspace, see The crates. For the verbs themselves, the tutorials Tutorial: claim and complete a queue task and Tutorial: run the brokers cover the operator’s view.

The feature gates

fleet-queue’s features, and the modules each one gates in lib.rs:

FeatureDependencies it addsModules it gates
clientfleet-config, ureqclient, fallback, needs_drew, placement
queue-brokerclient, plus tiny_http, ureq, fleet-config, libc, rusqlitequeue_broker, turso_queue, validate
secrets-brokertiny_http, fleet-config, libcsecrets_broker

Either broker also gates uds_http; disposition is gated on client or queue-broker (the completion gate is needed on both sides). Unconditional modules include backoff, bin_args, creation_outbox, log, merge_intent, token_file, work and person_wait.

Two consequences an embedder must internalise:

  • queue-broker includes client. A broker build carries the whole client surface with it; there is no broker-only build of this crate without the client.
  • The fallback module sits behind the client feature — #[cfg(feature = "client")] pub mod fallback;. The GitHub-issues fallback transport is client surface, not broker surface. A test run under --features queue-broker alone would not even compile the fallback’s tests; they run only under a client-carrying feature set (the Nix fleet-brokers build and the full-variant check phase both carry it).

The bin crate maps capabilities onto these features exactly: queue = […, "fleet-queue/client"], queue-broker = […, "fleet-queue/queue-broker"], and the standalone fleet-brokers package builds -p fleet-queue --features client,queue-broker,secrets-broker --bins, producing repo-queue, queue-broker and secrets-broker as separate artifacts.

The entry point

The client’s single public entry is the same function the multicall binary and the standalone repo-queue binary both call:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn run(args: &[String]) -> i32   // fleet_queue::client::run
}

args is the argument vector after the domain name (fleet queue <args…> / repo-queue <args…>), and the return is the process exit code. Inside, run is one match over 32 verb names — the same 32 names the registry lists as the queue domain’s subcommands — dispatching to a cmd_<verb> handler in the client modules (commands_lifecycle.rs for lifecycle verbs, commands_query.rs for query verbs, fallback_stack.rs for the outbox/stack groups), with fallback routed to crate::fallback::run and dispatch / session / surfaces routed to the placement module (see Placement and surfaces as data).

Bare invocation and help follow the client’s own contract: no args prints the top usage and returns 2; a single --help / -h / help returns 0; an unknown verb prints repo-queue: unknown command … plus the top usage and returns 2.

The call() path

Every broker-backed verb handler is the same five moves:

  1. Declare its flags and parse (next section).
  2. Validate positionals and build a JSON request body.
  3. POST the body to the verb’s broker route via the transport’s call helper — call("/unblock", &body) for the unblock verb, and so on. Every client verb is one POST route on the broker (/validate, /enqueue, /list, /claim, /claim-flow, /heartbeat, /checkpoint, /complete, /unblock, … plus the event, outbox and stack families).
  4. Unwrap the broker envelope: success is {ok: true, …}; failure is {ok: false, exit, error} — the client prints error and exits with exit (defaulting to 4 when the envelope carries no exit of its own).
  5. Print the returned row (most verbs) as JSON and return 0.

Two transport behaviours sit inside step 3 and are part of the client’s contract, not accidents:

  • Retry on transient store errors. A broker envelope whose error carries PostgREST code 57014 (statement timeout) or PGRST002 (schema cache) is retried with exponential backoff and jitter — base 500 ms, doubling, capped at 20 s, at most 6 attempts. This is safe for writes because a 57014 means the statement rolled back.
  • The fallback switch. For the work verbs — claim, heartbeat, checkpoint, complete, health — any primary-store failure (broker unreachable, or an {ok: false} envelope) switches the caller to the GitHub fallback for that work instead of dying: a diagnostic on stderr, one JSON object on stdout naming the switch ({"ok": false, "fallback": true, "switch_to": "github-fallback", …} with a mode_line of mode db-degraded, route github-markers), and exit 6. The environment variable REPO_QUEUE_NO_FALLBACK_SWITCH=1 is the escape hatch that restores plain die-on-error.

The client’s exit-code vocabulary follows from this: 0 success, 1 gate/not-found failures on specific verbs, 2 usage, 3 transport or broker-path failure (unreachable, HTTP 401, HTTP ≥ 400, malformed reply), 4 a broker envelope failure with no exit of its own, 5 “the verb ran but there is no matching claimed row / no claimable task”, 6 the fallback switch.

Verb argument parsing helpers

All queue verbs parse through one hand-rolled parser in client/support.rs — there is no clap anywhere in the workspace, by design. The pure core is parse_args_inner; parse_verb_args is the wrapper handlers call:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
// Shape of a handler's first moves (from cmd_unblock):
let args = parse_verb_args("unblock", rest, &["worker", "reason", "drop-dep"], &[]);
reject_extra_pos("unblock", &args, 1);
}

The signature pattern is parse_verb_args(verb, rest, value_flags, bool_flags): the handler declares exactly the flags it accepts, value flags in the first slice and booleans in the second. The result is an Args value — { pos: Vec<String>, opts: Map<String, Value> } — with accessors get, has, get_i64 and pos_i64.

The parser’s rules are the client’s usage contract, and they are strict:

  • A help token anywhere in a verb’s args prints that verb’s exact usage and exits 0 — help wins over every other argument, except when the help-looking token is the value of a value-flag (fail 5 --error help records the error text “help”).
  • Unknown flags, duplicate value flags (never silent last-wins), a boolean given an inline value (--dry-run=false), a value flag with no value, a value flag followed by another --flag token, extra positionals past the verb’s arity, and non-numeric values for numeric flags are all usage errors: message plus the verb’s usage on stderr, exit 2 — and for the arity and flag-shape errors, all of this happens before any broker contact.
  • Durations and limits are rejected, never clamped, identically at client and broker: claim lease 1..=86400 (default 2700), heartbeat extend 1..=86400 (default 900), park delay 1..=604800, list limit 1..=500 (default 20).

Two hand-maintained usage strings per verb live beside the parser (the one-line synopsis in TOP_USAGE and the long form in usage(verb)), and a machine test — every_verb_usage_matches_its_parser — asserts every verb’s usage names exactly the flags its parser accepts. An embedder adding a verb gets that test as a free oracle; see the worked example in the crates’ contributor documentation.

Shared resolution helpers sit on top of Args: opt_worker (flag, else the default worker repo-worker-code), opt_queue (flag, else REPO_QUEUE_DEFAULT_QUEUE, else the shadow default repo-health-code-shadow — with claim and list deliberately unscoped when neither flag nor env is present, and enqueue having no default at all), and the lane resolution for holder verbs (flag, else REPO_QUEUE_LANE, else null, in which case the broker checks the worker alone). These helpers are crate-internal (pub(super) / pub(crate)): an embedder outside the crate uses client::run, not the helpers.

Transport routes

The client never touches the database and never fetches from Bitwarden. It POSTs JSON to the queue broker, which is the only process that talks to the Turso store. Route selection, in order:

1. The direct route (on-laptop)

Chosen when a broker URL is configured: the environment variable REPO_QUEUE_BROKER_URL, else the file ~/.config/repo-queue/broker-url. A unix://<path> value selects the broker’s Unix socket; anything else is read as http://host:port TCP. With no configured URL, fleet-config’s probe-based choice for the queue-broker role applies: a live role socket selects the Unix socket, otherwise the client falls through to route 2 — and a failed Unix-socket attempt falls back to the session-proxy route within the same call.

On the wire this is raw HTTP/1.1: POST <path>, header X-Agent-Token: <token>, Content-Type: application/json, Connection: close. Read timeout 300 s, write timeout 60 s. Chunked and Content-Length responses are both decoded strictly; HTTP 401 and HTTP ≥ 400 die with exit 3 (a ≥ 400 surfaces the body’s error field).

2. The session-proxy route (sandbox default)

The client connects to the laptop-agent session proxy’s Unix socket — fleet-config’s broker_socket() when it loads, else $HOME/.cache/laptop-agent/broker.sock (environment beats config file beats that compiled-in default). Framing is the proxy protocol: an 8-byte big-endian length prefix plus one JSON envelope:

{ "method": "POST", "path": "/claim", "body": {}, "port": 4801, "token_file": "<home>/tools/queue-broker-token" }

The proxy, on the laptop, reads the named token file there and forwards to the broker on port 4801. Read timeout 660 s. On a failed first attempt the client auto-spawns the proxy/broker program — a sibling fleet binary (fleet proxy serve) always wins; the Python ~/tools/laptop-agent-broker.py is the fallback for standalone rollback builds — waits up to about 5 seconds for the socket, and retries once.

Broker-unavailable on either route is exit 3, or the fallback switch (exit 6) for the work verbs.

Token file handling

One loader serves every side: token_file::load_token_file reads the file and trims it, and a missing, unreadable, empty or whitespace-only file is a hard error naming the file — a broker refuses to start and a client refuses to send. (Before this rule, an empty token file authenticated any empty-token client, including to the secrets broker.)

Which file, on which route (names and paths only — values are never read by the client code that names them, and never printed):

SideSource
Session-proxy envelopeNames the file <home>/tools/queue-broker-token; the proxy reads it on the laptop, per request
Direct route, client tokenREPO_QUEUE_TOKEN_FILE, else ~/.config/queue-broker/token
Broker’s own tokenQUEUE_BROKER_TOKEN_FILE, default ~/.config/queue-broker/token — compared against the request’s X-Agent-Token header
Broker’s Turso credentialQUEUE_BROKER_TURSO_TOKEN_FILE, else resolved through the secrets broker by the secret name turso.fleet-queue-rw-token

The broker side mirrors the client’s strictness: its pre-body gate refuses from headers alone — wrong or missing token gets 401 {"error":"unauthorized"}, a Content-Length over the 16 MiB cap gets 413 — before any body byte is read. The only unauthenticated route is GET /healthz.

Example: embedding the client

This example is illustrative: it uses the verified entry point (fleet_queue::client::run, taking the post-domain argument vector and returning the exit code) to run one verb from an embedding binary.

# Cargo.toml — the client surface only; no broker code is compiled.
[dependencies]
fleet-queue = { path = "../fleet-queue", features = ["client"] }

// Run `fleet queue health` from inside another binary and propagate
// its exit code (0 ok, 3 broker path down, 6 fallback switch, ...).
fn main() -> std::process::ExitCode {
    let args: Vec<String> = std::env::args().skip(1).collect();
    let code = fleet_queue::client::run(&args);
    std::process::ExitCode::from(code as u8)
}

With the queue-broker feature instead, the same crate additionally exposes fleet_queue::queue_broker::run() and fleet_queue::secrets_broker::run() — both argument-free serve loops (the standalone broker binaries accept no arguments at all: -h / --help prints usage with exit 0, anything else is a usage error at exit 2, classified by the crate’s bin_args helper).

There is no public transport-level helper for embedders: the call() family in client/transport.rs (call, call_result, call_fb) is pub(super) — visible only inside the client module. client::run is the only public entry point, which is why the example above goes through it.

Placement and surfaces as data

Placement — deciding where a build job runs — is data, not code. The surface registry is a JSON file; adding a location is adding an entry; no surface is hardcoded in the engine. This chapter documents that file field by field, how the registry is resolved and extended, the decision types the engine works with, the local session store format, and how another crate uses placement.

The live engine is Rust: the placement module of fleet-queue (gated behind the crate’s client feature), exposed as the fleet queue dispatch, fleet queue session and fleet queue surfaces verbs. It is the absorption of the fleet-place reference implementation into the queue client. The operator’s walkthrough is Tutorial: dispatch a build remotely.

Do not confuse this engine with pkgs/fleet/placement/. That directory is a different, unrelated Go proof-of-concept (a placement-record package for a policy framework) that is deliberately not wired into the live queue client or any dispatcher. Two placement systems share one name; only the Rust module over fleet-surfaces.json dispatches anything.

The surface registry: fleet-surfaces.json

The registry lives at pkgs/fleet/fleet-surfaces.json and is compiled into the binary (include_str!). Resolution at runtime, in order:

  1. An explicit override — the --registry PATH flag or the FLEET_PLACE_REGISTRY environment variable — is strict: a bad path is a fatal error, never a silent fallback. The file must parse as JSON and contain a surfaces array, or the error is registry {path} has no surfaces array.
  2. Without an override, $HOME/git/code/pkgs/fleet/fleet-surfaces.json wins if it exists (a live checkout can carry a newer registry).
  3. Then the cwd-relative pkgs/fleet/fleet-surfaces.json, if it exists.
  4. Finally, the embedded copy.

Top-level shape:

{
  "comment": "Fleet placement registry. …",
  "version": 2,
  "laptop": { "busy": false, "busy_source": "manual-flag", "note": "…" },
  "owners": { "<owner>": { "…": "…" } },
  "surfaces": [{ "…": "…" }]
}
  • comment: human documentation of the format; never read by code.
  • version: 2 in the shipped registry.
  • laptop.busy (bool), laptop.busy_source (string, shipped value "manual-flag"), laptop.note (string): the saturation signal for the codespace tier. It is set from queue depth where a caller can read it, else flipped by hand or overridden per-dispatch with --laptop-busy. Deliberately not scraped telemetry.
  • owners: per-owner caps, below.
  • surfaces: the surface entries, below. fleet queue surfaces prints the resolved registry verbatim as pretty JSON — that output is this file, which is the quickest way to read the registry a given binary will use.

Every field of a surface entry

The union of fields across the shipped entries, with the code that consumes each:

FieldTypeConsumed by / meaning
idstringSurface identity: the --surface ID pin, the session record’s surface, and the sort tie-break
kindstringAdapter selector: github-actions, blacksmith, codespace or laptop. Any other value gets no adapter — the surface is invisible to the cascade and cannot be pinned either
statusstringEligibility requires exactly "active" for github-actions/blacksmith surfaces. Shipped values: active, standby (org-run), pending-scope (codespace-overflow), handoff-only (laptop). The codespace and laptop adapters do not apply this check
ownerstringThe account whose cap, load and budget the surface draws on; load is aggregated per owner, not per surface
repostring or nullThe runner-host repo the workflow is dispatched in (not the target repo). null for codespace-overflow and laptop. Used for token minting, load counting, run correlation, and the session record’s runner_repo / portable_id
