workflowstring or nullThe workflow file dispatched; "fleet-command.yml" for all Actions/Blacksmith surfaces, null for codespace/laptop
targetsstring arrayTarget-repo patterns: exact owner/repo, owner/*, or * (see matching rules below)
notesstringHuman documentation only; never read by code
app_installationinteger or nullGitHub App installation id for that host repo. Documentation/record only in the Rust code — nothing in the engine reads it; token minting goes through a separate helper
dispatch_asstring, optional"user" dispatches with the signed-in user’s token; absent or "app" uses an App installation token. Any other value fails eligibility
dispatch_id_inputboolThe workflow declares a dispatch_id input. When true, dispatch mints a fresh fp_… handle (separate from the session handle) and sends it as that input; the workflow puts it in the run title, enabling exact run correlation. When absent/false, correlation falls back to pre-dispatch snapshot exclusion
platform_inputboolThe workflow declares a platform input. Gates macOS: a platform=macos job is ineligible on a surface where this is not true
previous_run_id_inputboolThe workflow accepts previous_run_id / previous_run_repo inputs (follow-up output download)
container_inputboolThe workflow accepts container_image; a --container value is only sent when this is true
sticky_queue_thresholdintegerFollow-up stickiness threshold. Code default if absent: 2, clamped to at least 1. All shipped surfaces: 2
selection_priorityintegerTier-1 sort key (third position). Code default if absent: 50. Shipped: 10 everywhere except org-run at 20. Lower sorts first
public_targets_onlybool, optionalOnly fleet-forks (true). Eligibility does a live GET /repos/{target} and requires "private": false
host_surfacestring, optionalOnly fleet-org-blacksmith ("fleet-org"): records which github-actions surface hosts this Blacksmith variant. Documentation-level linkage; the Blacksmith adapter dispatches its own surface’s repo/workflow directly
budgetobject, optionalBlacksmith: {free_minutes_monthly, paid_cap_minutes, rate_note}. Codespace: {core_hours_monthly, note}
max_liveinteger, optionalOnly codespace-overflow (3). Printed in the capacity summary only; never enforced

The seven shipped surfaces

idkindstatusOwner / host repodispatch_asNotable
fleet-personalgithub-actionsactivedezren39 / dezren39/fleet(app)Its repo secrets include GHCR_ORG_PAT and NIX_CACHE_* (names only) for private checkouts, cross-run artifacts and Nix cache pushes
fleet-orggithub-actionsactivedeveloping-today / developing-today/fleetuserCanonical org runner; also the Blacksmith host
fleet-forksgithub-actionsactivedeveloping-today-forks / developing-today-forks/fleetuserpublic_targets_only: true — private targets are rejected because this host has no GHCR_ORG_PAT secret
org-rungithub-actionsstandbydeveloping-today / developing-today/code(app)platform_input, previous_run_id_input, container_input all false; priority 20. Because eligibility requires "active", it can never be selected or pinned — retained for manual workflow use
fleet-org-blacksmithblacksmithactivedeveloping-today / developing-today/fleetuserhost_surface: fleet-org; budget below
codespace-overflowcodespacepending-scopedezren39 / no repo—Budget 180 core-hours/month; max_live: 3; never creates codespaces
laptoplaptophandoff-onlydezren39 / no repo—Targets ["*"]; a placement record only — this adapter never runs shell commands on the laptop

All Actions/Blacksmith surfaces target ["dezren39/*", "developing-today/*", "developing-today-forks/*"] except org-run, which targets only ["developing-today/*"].

Per-owner caps

From the shipped owners object:

Ownerconcurrent_jobs_capconcurrent_macos_capplanprivate_minutes_monthly
developing-today205free-org2000
developing-today-forks205free-org (assumed - confirm)2000
dezren39405pro3000

Only concurrent_jobs_cap is read as the cap: an owner missing from owners, or a missing field, yields cap 0 — zero free slots, so the surface is unusable in Tier 1. plan and private_minutes_monthly are never read by the placement code; they are registry documentation. For a macOS job the effective cap is min(concurrent_jobs_cap, concurrent_macos_cap) — 5 for every shipped owner — and the adapter deliberately counts all of the owner’s active host runs against that minimum, so macOS headroom is max(0, 5 − (running + queued on that owner's hosts)).

Target matching

A repo string is valid (valid_owner_repo) when it has exactly one /, both parts non-empty and not ./.., with characters [A-Za-z0-9._-] only; a --repo failing this is a fatal usage error (exit 2). A pattern matches a repo when: "*" matches any valid owner/name; "owner/*" matches when the owner is exactly equal and the name is a single non-empty segment; anything else is exact string equality. A surface targets a job iff any of its targets matches the job’s repo.

Budgets that are, and are not, enforced

Blacksmith’s registry budget is real: free_minutes_monthly: 3000, paid_cap_minutes: 0, with a rate_note recording that Blacksmith is orgs-only, free for 3,000 minutes a month, then paid per minute — and that paid_cap_minutes is the knob to raise. Eligibility computes remaining = free + paid_cap + this job's --allow-paid-blacksmith − used, where used is reconciled from the local store’s ledger of Blacksmith dispatch durations for the current UTC month. The --allow-paid-blacksmith MINUTES value (a float, default 0.0) is an eligibility allowance for this one decision only — not a per-run spending cap, not a workflow input, not persisted.

By contrast, the codespace budget numbers (core_hours_monthly: 180, max_live: 3) appear only in a capacity summary string. Neither is measured or enforced anywhere; dispatch does not count live codespaces.

Reading and extending the registry

Read the registry the way the binary does:

fleet queue surfaces

That prints the resolved registry as pretty JSON (a --registry PATH flag reads a different file). To extend placement:

  1. Add a surface entry to fleet-surfaces.json with a unique id, a kind that has an adapter, the owner whose caps it draws on (add the owner to owners first if it is new — a missing owner means cap 0), its host repo and workflow, and its targets.
  2. Add a compatible workflow to the host repo: the entry’s capability flags (dispatch_id_input, platform_input, previous_run_id_input, container_input) are promises about that workflow’s declared inputs. Declaring a flag the workflow does not implement sends inputs into the void; omitting one the workflow supports disables the feature silently.
  3. Set status: "active" only when the surface should really be picked. standby is a supported, deliberate state: registered, documented, and unpickable.

No code change is needed for a new surface of an existing kind. A new kind is a code change: one adapter implementing the trait below.

Placement decision types

The engine’s vocabulary, as researched from the module:

  • The job: {repo, command, ref, runner, platform, container, surface_pin, preferred_surface, previous_run_id, previous_run_repo, push_nix_cache, actions_cache, actions_cache_restore_keys, allow_paid_blacksmith} — exactly the fields a session record stores under job (below). runner is auto | github | blacksmith; platform is linux | macos. A job pinning runner=blacksmith makes every github-actions adapter ineligible, and vice versa for runner=github.
  • The adapter trait: each registry kind is served by one adapter implementing eligible(job, ctx, gh) -> (bool, reason), capacity(job, ctx) -> {summary, free_slots, remaining_total_minutes}, dispatch(job, gh) -> DispatchResult, and status(session, gh) (defaulting to the stored state). free_slots and remaining_total_minutes are both optional in a capacity report: a summary-only adapter (codespace) reports neither. For the GitHub Actions adapter, free_slots is present only when the owner’s load coverage is measured or simulated — or when a partial known subtotal already proves saturation, yielding a proven 0; an unreadable owner reports no estimate rather than a false zero.
  • DispatchResult: {run_id, run_url, note, codespace, terminal_state} — what a dispatch attempt hands back to be recorded as a session.
  • The decision: decide(registry, job, ctx, gh) returns the chosen adapter (or none, for the all-tiers-exhausted case) together with the reasoning array — one human string per skip, candidate and pick, which is part of the dispatch verb’s output, not a debug log.
  • The context (ctx): built per decision from the GitHub API and the local store — per-owner load (running, queued) counted only over that owner’s fleet runner-host repos (two total_count reads per host repo, in_progress and queued; failures are soft and recorded in load_read_errors), per-owner load coverage (status measured/partial/unknown/simulated, known subtotal, cap, read time, source, and missing reads — also emitted as the decision output’s owner_load_coverage), per-owner and per-surface last-dispatch epochs from the session store, the month’s Blacksmith minutes used, and the laptop-busy flag (--laptop-busy or the registry’s laptop.busy).

The cascade itself — hard pin, follow-up affinity (kept only while the preferred surface is eligible, has capacity, and its owner’s queued count is strictly below its sticky_queue_threshold), Tier 1 free Actions sorted by (load, owner_last_dispatch, selection_priority, surface_last_dispatch, surface_id) — with a deterministic unknown-capacity fallback, named in the reasoning, when no eligible surface has measured headroom — Tier 2 Blacksmith in registry order, Tier 3 Codespaces, then exhaustion — is walked step by step in Tutorial: dispatch a build remotely.

The session store format

The local store at $FLEET_PLACE_STATE/sessions.json defaults to ~/.local/state/fleet-place/sessions.json. Its existing record shape remains readable. Dispatch commits locally before its best-effort mirror write to the broker’s placement_sessions table. Listing merges local records with up to 200 broker records and attempts to insert missing local records into the mirror. Status, result and follow-up prefer the record with the newer updated_at and select the broker copy on ties.

Store shape:

{
  "sessions": { "<fp_handle>": { "…": "…" } },
  "blacksmith_dispatches": [{ "…": "…" }]
}

A missing or unparseable store loads as {"sessions": {}, "blacksmith_dispatches": []}. Writes are pretty-printed JSON with recursively sorted keys, written to a per-process temp file and renamed over the store, under a lock directory (sessions.lockdir beside the store; waiters poll every 50 ms up to a 15-second deadline; a lock older than 120 seconds is stale and is broken). New sessions are committed under the lock by re-loading the on-disk store and merging, so concurrent processes do not drop each other’s records.

A session record (dispatched case):

{
  "handle": "fp_…",
  "job": { "repo": "…", "command": "…", "ref": "…", "runner": "…", "platform": "…", "container": "…", "surface_pin": "…", "preferred_surface": "…", "previous_run_id": "…", "previous_run_repo": "…", "push_nix_cache": false, "actions_cache": "…", "actions_cache_restore_keys": [], "allow_paid_blacksmith": 0.0 },
  "surface": "fleet-org",
  "surface_kind": "github-actions",
  "runner_repo": "developing-today/fleet",
  "portable_id": "developing-today/fleet#45146933211",
  "decision_reasoning": ["…"],
  "run_id": 45146933211,
  "run_url": "https://github.com/developing-today/fleet/actions/runs/45146933211",
  "state": "queued|dispatched|running|succeeded|failed|cancelled",
  "submitted_by": "<USER>@<hostname>",
  "actor": "developing-today[bot] (GitHub App dispatch)",
  "created_at": "YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SSZ",
  "updated_at": "YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SSZ",
  "note": "…",
  "codespace": "…"
}

Field notes an embedder must know:

  • handle is fp_ plus 16 random bytes from /dev/urandom, hex-encoded — 35 characters total, 128 bits.
  • surface_kind is omitted in the all-tiers-exhausted record, which has surface / run_id / run_url null, state: "queued", and no runner_repo / portable_id. runner_repo appears only when the surface has a repo; portable_id only when a run id is known; note only when the adapter supplied one; codespace only on codespace dispatches.
  • Initial state: the adapter’s terminal_state if set (codespace dispatches are created already-terminal), else queued if a run was correlated, else dispatched.
  • actor is hardcoded to the App string even for dispatch_as: "user" surfaces — a known inaccuracy in the record for the majority of shipped surfaces. Do not build attribution on it.
  • blacksmith_dispatches entries are {handle, month, minutes, run_id, note, reconciled}: appended with minutes: 0.0 at dispatch, then reconciled to the run’s real duration (rounded to 2 dp) when the session reaches a terminal state, or before the next real dispatch decision.
  • Refresh: session status / session result (and follow-up resolution, and Blacksmith reconciliation) re-read the GitHub run and update state + updated_at on change. session list does not refresh — it prints stored state as-is. A portable reference OWNER/REPO#RUN_ID bypasses the store entirely and resolves live, as described in the tutorial.

Using placement from another crate

Placement is a module of fleet-queue behind the client feature, and its researched public surface is the verb entry points the queue client dispatches to: cmd_dispatch, cmd_session and cmd_surfaces in fleet_queue::placement. The supported embedding today is therefore the same one the binary uses — depend on fleet-queue with the client feature and drive the verbs, either through fleet_queue::client::run with a dispatch-shaped argument vector, or through the placement entry points directly.

This example is illustrative: the client::run route uses the verified entry point from The queue client; the exact signatures of the individual cmd_* placement functions were not verified in this pass, so they are not presented as checked signatures here.

# Cargo.toml
[dependencies]
fleet-queue = { path = "../fleet-queue", features = ["client"] }

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
// Ask placement for a dry-run decision (no --dispatch flag) and let
// the placement module print its decision + reasoning, exactly as
// `fleet queue dispatch` would.
fn dry_run_decision() -> i32 {
    let args: Vec<String> = [
        "dispatch",
        "--repo", "developing-today/code",
        "--command", "cargo test --workspace",
        "--json",
    ]
    .iter()
    .map(|s| s.to_string())
    .collect();
    fleet_queue::client::run(&args)
}
}

The verb entry points share the standard signature, verified against the source: placement::cmd_dispatch(args: &[String]) -> i32, and likewise cmd_session and cmd_surfaces. The engine itself is pub fn decide(registry: &serde_json::Value, job: &Job, ctx: &Ctx, gh: &dyn Gh) -> R<(Option<Box<dyn Adapter>>, Vec<String>)> — it returns the chosen adapter (or None when the job stays queued) plus the reasoning lines. Job is a public struct, and the adapter types (Adapter, Capacity, DispatchResult, and the concrete adapters) are re-exported publicly from fleet_queue::placement (pub use adapters::{...}), so embedders can name them.

Registry, config and capabilities

Two platform crates decide what a given fleet invocation is: fleet-registry says what exists — every domain, capability and build variant, in every build — and fleet-config says what this host allows and where everything lives. On top of them, the binary computes an invocation surface: compiled capabilities, narrowed by the name it was invoked under and by the host’s config, with every unusable domain answering through the same stub. This chapter covers all three layers and the gating rules an embedder must respect.

For the crate map, see The crates.

fleet-registry: the inventory is the registry

fleet-registry is dependency-free — std only, strings and tables, no I/O — and is compiled into every variant, including the size-gated connect build, so --help is always complete. It owns four things.

The 22 capabilities

enum Capability, with stable string ids in Capability::ALL, in registry order:

proxy-connect, proxy-serve, proxy-raw-splice, queue, queue-broker,
secrets-broker, search, search-serve, dispatch, dispatch-test,
laptop-agent, secrets, gh, bridge, agent, commander, laptop-http,
laptop-ssh, laptop, cert, actions, orgs

CapabilitySet is a BTreeSet<Capability>, built with capability_set(&[…]); the crate provides full_capabilities(), serve_capabilities() and connect_capabilities() for the three variant sets below.

The 19 domains

pub const DOMAINS: &[Domain] — the full registry in help order: queue, serve, proxy, dispatch, dispatch-test, secrets, gh, bridge, orgs, agent, shell, search, cert, laptop-agent, commander, http, ssh, laptop, actions.

struct Domain is the unit that help lists, stubs name, and config disables:

FieldMeaning
name: &'static strThe domain’s invocation name
summary: &'static strThe one-line description help prints
capabilities: &'static [Capability]Every capability the domain spans
primary: CapabilityThe capability headline availability keys on
aliases: &'static [&str]Its argv0 aliases
subcommands: &'static [&str]The top-level verb inventory rendered by domain help

The primary rule has a visible consequence: on the fleet-serve build, the search domain is marked absent because its headline capability is the search client, even though the search-serve role exists under serve. And shell’s capability list is ["agent"] — there is no shell capability atom; shell rides on the agent capability.

pub fn domain(name) looks a domain up by name (a linear find over DOMAINS).

The 3 variants

enum Variant { Full, Serve, Connect } — a property of the artifact, whose names double as invocation profiles:

VariantInstalled nameCompiled capabilities
FullfleetAll 22
Servefleet-serveproxy-connect, proxy-serve, proxy-raw-splice, queue-broker, secrets-broker, search-serve, secrets (7) — daemon roles plus proxy, no working-seat clients
Connectfleet-connectproxy-connect, proxy-raw-splice (2)

Variant::name() gives the installed side-by-side name; wherever a variant is actually used, the binary is renamed plain fleet and the hyphenated names survive as argv0 personalities (symlinks to the one binary, created at install time). Variant::capabilities() is the profile ceiling. Variant::from_invocation_name() recognises only fleet-serve / fleet-connect; plain fleet selects no profile. The profiles nest — connect ⊂ serve ⊂ full, and full equals Capability::ALL — an invariant the crate’s own tests assert, along with unique/stable capability ids, every domain’s primary being in its own surface, aliases routing to real domains, and the domain alias table matching the argv0 map.

The argv0 alias map

struct AliasRoute { domain, implied_arg } and pub fn alias_route(argv0) give the multicall names; anything not listed is not a multicall name:

argv0Routes to domainImplied argument
repo-queuequeue—
queue-brokerservequeue-broker
secrets-brokerservesecrets-broker
laptop-agent-brokerproxyserve
atlas-searchsearch—
laptop-agentlaptop-agent—

An alias route constructs the surface with no profile (aliases do not narrow), prepends the implied argument, and dispatches straight to the domain. is_known_invocation_name(name) is true for fleet, a variant name, or an alias; any other invocation name is a usage error (exit 2) naming the expected names.

CapState: the four answers a domain can give

The binary’s Surface (in the bin crate) holds the invocation’s whole effective surface: the compiled set, the optional profile, their intersection as the effective set, and the loaded config. Surface::cap_state(cap, domain_name) checks in order and yields enum CapState:

CapStateMeaningStub wording (first line)
AvailableCompiled in, in profile, not config-disabled— (the domain runs; the fourth form below is its skeleton variant)
NotInBuildThis build was compiled without itfleet: this build does not include '<domain>'.
NarrowedByNameThe invocation name (fleet-serve / fleet-connect) scoped it awayfleet: invoked as '<name>', this build does not include '<domain>'.
DisabledByConfigThe [domains] table in this host’s fleet config set the domain to falsefleet: '<domain>' is disabled by config on this host.

Every stub goes to stderr and returns exit 69 (EX_UNAVAILABLE). Its second line is always Enabled capabilities: <comma list> — the usable set: the effective set minus every capability of every config-disabled domain — and its third line names the build. There is also a not-implemented form for a capability that is Available but has nothing behind it yet: “included in this build but not implemented yet”, with the build named on the third line. Help renders the same four states inline ([not in this build], [narrowed out by this name], [disabled by config]), and renders them on every variant — help never stubs.

fleet capabilities prints the whole picture as JSON: the build block (name, version, derived version, source revision, invoked-as, profile), two capability lists — capabilities (what this invocation can use) and compiled_capabilities (what the binary was built with); their difference is exactly the profile/config narrowing — and one entry per domain with its state (available, not-in-build, narrowed-by-name, disabled-by-config) and available boolean.

compiled_capabilities(): the binary reports its own variant

Capabilities are compiled in through Cargo features on the bin crate, and reconstructed at runtime — the binary derives its variant from its feature set; it does not trust a baked-in name.

  • The feature sets: default = ["full"], where full enables every domain feature; serve enables the serve set as one feature for the Nix build; the connect build is --no-default-features with nothing optional on. Each feature wires its optional dependencies and the owning crate’s matching feature (for example queue = ["dep:fleet-secrets", "dep:fleet-queue", "fleet-queue/client"]).
  • proxy-connect is not a feature: it is compiled into every variant unconditionally. fleet-proxy itself is a non-optional dependency with default features off — the client is in every variant; only the broker half (fleet-proxy/serve) is gated. fleet-secrets is optional for the same reason in reverse: the connect variant must not carry it.
  • fn compiled_capabilities() starts from {ProxyConnect, ProxyRawSplice} unconditionally and inserts one Capability per cfg!(feature = "…"). build_variant(compiled) then matches the set against the three variant sets — Full, Serve, Connect, or None, which renders as the build name fleet-custom in fleet version.

Dispatch order, end to end: argv0 alias → domain route; argv0 variant name → root dispatch with that profile as a ceiling; argv0 fleet → root dispatch; then per domain — capability compiled in? in profile? not config-disabled? → the domain handler, else the stub; an unknown name is a usage error, exit 2. The dispatch is hand-rolled, explicitly not clap, because it must behave identically in every variant — including the tiny connect build, where the full registry and the stub machinery are the product.

fleet-config: one place config resolves

Config::load() / Config::file_path() resolve, in order: environment overrides (FLEET_CONFIG, FLEET_BROKER_SOCKET, …), then the config file ($FLEET_CONFIG, else ${XDG_CONFIG_HOME:-~/.config}/fleet/fleet.toml), then compiled-in defaults. The crate owns the [domains] enable/disable table (domain_enabled(name) — the per-host shaping and incident lever behind DisabledByConfig), the [proxy], [secrets], [queue-broker], [secrets-broker] and [dispatch] sections, and the fleet’s constants: ports (4799 laptop-agent, 4800 secrets-broker, 4801 queue-broker, 4802 gh cache, 4879 pm-dispatch, 3130 egress proxy) and role sockets (environment beats [<role>] socket in the file beats the runtime-dir/home defaults).

The [host] manifest: FLEET_HOST_CONFIG and FLEET_LOCATION

fleet init — autostart this host’s roles per the manifest — resolves the manifest in this order:

  1. FLEET_HOST_CONFIG: a complete inline [host] manifest. It wins outright. A manifest with no location is a loud error.
  2. FLEET_LOCATION: names the location; roles come from the config file’s [host] section only if the file’s location matches, else from the built-in map.
  3. The config file’s [host] section: location, init_mode, and [host.roles] — the role set is exactly the key set of the roles table, and an unknown role name is a loud parse error, never silently ignored.

The built-in location map has two locations today (a future lab node provisions its own [host] section instead of growing the table):

Locationinit_modeRoles
sandboxspawnproxy, secrets-broker
laptopsystemdlaptop-agent, queue-broker, search, secrets-broker

The full [host] role vocabulary is five names — proxy, queue-broker, secrets-broker, search, laptop-agent — a superset of the serve roles (it includes laptop-agent, which is not a serve role). Behaviour that follows from the manifest rules:

  • An unknown location (no manifest from any source, or a location with no roles) makes init report state — every source consulted, plus detected hostname/OS/systemd for the report only, since detection never selects roles — start nothing, and exit 69. Never guess-start a role.
  • Roles the manifest itself disables (enabled = false) are reported as skipped with their reason; then the [domains] gate is applied and wins over the manifest.
  • In spawn mode (sandbox), v1 spawn semantics exist for exactly the two sandbox roles; any other role in a spawn manifest is reported and skipped, never spawned. In systemd mode (laptop), init never detached-spawns a daemon systemd owns: it reports each unit’s state, starts an inactive-but-existing unit, and reports a missing unit as skipped.

Capability gating rules for embedders

These are the rules the narrowing-only design imposes on anyone embedding or wrapping the binary:

  1. Profiles only narrow, never widen. Invoking under fleet-serve or fleet-connect sets a capability ceiling: the effective surface is compiled ∩ profile. No invocation name, config file or environment variable can give an invocation a capability its binary was not compiled with.
  2. Config only disables. The [domains] table can remove a domain on a host (the incident lever), and that gate wins even over the [host] manifest’s role list — but it cannot enable what the build or profile lacks.
  3. Aliases do not narrow. An argv0 alias (repo-queue, queue-broker, …) routes straight to its domain with no profile. Only the two hyphenated variant names narrow.
  4. Check state, don’t assume. An embedder that depends on a domain must handle all four CapState outcomes — or, from outside the process, exit 69 with the stub’s wording — and should read fleet capabilities (the JSON census) rather than hardcoding which build it hopes it is running. The two lists in that output exist precisely so a wrapper can tell “this binary can’t” (compiled set) from “this invocation can’t” (usable set).
  5. Help is not evidence of availability. The full registry renders on every variant by design. Availability is the domain’s state in the capabilities census, or the stub you get when you invoke it.

Example: reading the registry and the config

This example is illustrative — it follows the researched API shapes (fleet_registry::DOMAINS, Capability::ALL, fleet_config::Config::load) but the exact signatures were not all verified against source in this pass, and two spots are marked for the coordinator rather than presented as checked signatures.

// List every registered domain with its primary capability, then ask
// the loaded config whether the queue domain is enabled on this host.
fn main() {
    for cap in fleet_registry::Capability::ALL {
        println!("capability: {}", cap.id());
    }
    for d in fleet_registry::DOMAINS {
        println!("domain {} (primary: {})", d.name, d.primary.id());
    }

    // Config::load() -> Result<Config, ConfigError>; a malformed
    // file is a loud error on every path, never a silent default.
    let config = fleet_config::Config::load().expect("fleet config must load");
    println!("queue enabled: {}", config.domain_enabled("queue"));
}

Signatures verified against the source: Capability::id(self) -> &'static str is the accessor for the stable string ids used above, and fleet_registry::domain(name: &str) -> Option<&'static Domain> is the by-name lookup. fleet_config also offers Config::load_from(path: &Path) -> Result<Config, ConfigError> for an explicit manifest path.

Repository layout

Fleet lives in pkgs/fleet/ in the developing-today/code repository. It is a self-contained Cargo workspace on the pkgs/atlas-search pattern: its own Cargo.toml, Cargo.lock, and rust-toolchain.toml, with no workspace relationship to the repository root. The design of record is epic developing-today/code#5412.

This chapter is the map. For how the pieces are built, see Building fleet. For how they are tested, see Testing.

The 13-crate workspace

pkgs/fleet/Cargo.toml declares 13 members, resolver = "2", workspace version 0.1.0, edition 2024, rust-version 1.85, licence MIT OR Apache-2.0. Shared external dependencies are pinned once in [workspace.dependencies] (serde 1 with derive, serde_json 1, sha2 0.11, toml 1.2); the 12 library crates are path dependencies of the binary crate.

CrateWhat lives there
crates/fleetThe binary crate. [[bin]] name = "fleet", entry point src/main.rs. It has no lib.rs. It also holds the bin-crate-only domains: src/secrets.rs, and the gh domain in src/gh.rs with src/gh_cache.rs, src/gh_closure.rs, src/gh_guard.rs, src/gh_metadata.rs, plus src/session_state.rs, src/invocation_ledger.rs, src/derived_version.rs, and build.rs.
crates/fleet-registryThe full domain registry: names, one-line descriptions, argv0 aliases, capabilities, and variant profiles. Standard-library only, strings and tables only, no I/O. Compiled into every variant so --help is always complete. Single file: src/lib.rs.
crates/fleet-configConfiguration: ~/.config/fleet/fleet.toml plus environment resolution, the [domains] enable/disable table, and state-directory paths. Single large src/lib.rs.
crates/fleet-secretsThe one secrets-by-name path: secrets-broker protocol first, bws CLI fallback, op CLI where a vault is named. Values are never stored, never logged, and redacted in Debug. Single src/lib.rs.
crates/fleet-proxy-protoThe session-proxy wire contract: length-prefixed JSON framing (an 8-byte big-endian length prefix plus JSON) and the hello/capability frame types. The contract lives here and nowhere else.
crates/fleet-queueThe queue domain: the repo-queue client surface plus the queue-broker and secrets-broker server roles. By far the largest crate. Key files: src/client.rs and its submodules under src/client/ (commands_lifecycle.rs, commands_query.rs, fallback_stack.rs, mode_report.rs, support.rs, transport.rs, verify_disposition.rs), src/fallback.rs, src/placement.rs, src/validate.rs, src/turso_queue.rs and src/turso_queue/, src/queue_broker.rs, src/secrets_broker.rs. Standalone binaries in src/bin/: repo-queue, queue-broker, secrets-broker.
crates/fleet-dispatchThe dispatch domain: a thin client over the pm-stack pm-dispatch service — status, launch, and enqueue verbs. Exactly three routes: GET /health, POST /v1/sessions, POST /v1/tasks. Single src/lib.rs.
crates/fleet-dispatch-testThe dispatch-test domain: scan fleet repositories for free GitHub Actions capacity, submit a job to the Turso-backed jobs store, dispatch the pilot workflow, and track the stored status. Single src/lib.rs.
crates/fleet-proxyThe session proxy domain: proxy serve (the broker) and proxy connect / proxy init (the client). Files include src/serve.rs, src/client.rs, src/http.rs, src/tunnel.rs, src/connect_udp.rs, src/files.rs, plus extra binaries fleet-connect-udp and fleet-udp-forward.
crates/fleet-laptop-agentThe laptop-agent domain: the transport ladder (broker, Cloudflare, Tailscale, SSH) and the verbs over the laptop-agent daemon. Files: src/lib.rs, src/cli.rs, src/client.rs, src/guard.rs, src/ladder.rs, src/legs.rs.
crates/fleet-searchThe search domain: the atlas-search client surface over the live Atlas service, and the serve search role — the Atlas service itself, rehomed from the atlas-search bin crate. Files include src/cli.rs, src/client.rs, src/proto.rs, src/serve.rs, src/server.rs. Feature-split into client and serve. It is the one member that consumes crates outside the workspace (atlas-core, atlas-embed, atlas-proto by relative path under ../atlas-search/crates/).
crates/fleet-bridgeThe bridge domain: send and receive through the message bridge’s fleet mailboxes. Single src/lib.rs plus src/tests.rs.
crates/fleet-agentThe agent domain: enrol a named agent of any kind, check what a seat can reach (doctor), ask for the next piece of work down the intake ladder (next), and open a shell where builds belong. Files: src/lib.rs, src/enroll.rs, src/kinds.rs, src/next.rs, src/shell.rs, src/shortlist.rs, src/tests.rs. The shell domain is served by this crate’s run_shell entry point.

Where each domain lives, in one rule: a domain’s client surface, parser, and usage strings live in its owning crate (or, for secrets and gh, in the binary crate); the registry entry that names it lives in fleet-registry; the dispatch arm that reaches it lives in crates/fleet/src/main.rs. See Register a domain or capability for what a new domain must add in each of those places.

Supporting files at pkgs/fleet/

  • default.nix — the Nix builder for all fleet packages. See Building fleet.
  • fleet-surfaces.json — the placement registry: the execution surfaces placement may choose between, the owners they draw capacity from, and the laptop saturation flag. It is compiled into the binary (include_str!) and rendered by fleet queue surfaces. Add a surface by adding a registry entry and a compatible workflow.
  • migrations/ — the fleet database migrations, numbered SQL files from 0001_agent.sql through 0026_ainventory_interpretation.sql, including their test, check, and rollback companions.
  • repo-task-v1.schema.json — the task packet schema that fleet queue validate checks a task packet against.
  • smoke.sh — the hermetic, per-variant, post-build smoke suite. See Testing.
  • fleet-build-lock — the bash helper that serialises heavy builds fleet-wide to a small number of slots. See Building fleet.
  • rust-toolchain.toml — the pinned toolchain. See Building fleet.
  • README.md — the package’s own long-form document, including the operator and contributor contract (DOC-01). See Keeping this book current.
  • Helper scripts: fleet-fetch.py (deterministic repository snapshot fetcher writing into the fleet-queue database), lane-claim.sh and lane-handoff.sh (pilot lane claim one-shots), enqueue-when-green.sh (enqueue a pull request into the merge queue the moment its required check goes green), turso-exec.py, and the Python predecessors and peers of the Rust laptop-agent surface, laptop-agent.py and laptop-agent-broker.py.
  • Subtrees that are not part of the Rust workspace: archer-slack/ (Python Slack collector/puller), hosted-worker/ (the TypeScript/Cloudflare Worker edition of the queue and gh surfaces), placement/ (a small Go module: policy.go, evaluate.go, cmd/placement-record/ — a proof of concept, not the live placement engine, which is the Rust code in fleet-queue), and runtime-db-export/ (Python export/load tooling).

The doc/ versus docs/ split

Fleet’s documentation predates this book and is split three ways. Do not merge the directories; each has a distinct job.

  1. pkgs/fleet/docs/ — long-form operator documents that ship with the package. Exactly two files today:
    • docs/verbs.md — the canonical command reference. The repository-root AGENTS.md points contributors at it, and the DOC-01 contract requires it to change with every command change.
    • docs/fleet-gh-credentials.md — the fleet gh credential lifecycle.
  2. pkgs/fleet/doc/ — agent-facing runbooks inside the package. Exactly one file today: doc/agents/remote-build-and-test.md (dispatch builds and tests remotely; do not compile on the sandbox or the laptop).
  3. Repository-root doc/ — the fleet-wide record that lives outside the package: doc/agents/ runbooks (including fleet-command-channel.md and onboarding-an-agent.md, which the fleet README cites by paths that look fleet-local) and doc/decisions/, the fleet decision records (FDR-0001 onwards, with an index in doc/decisions/README.md).

Two consequences to know before you go looking:

  • Source files cite a design of record at doc/2026-11-04T11-45-48Z_design_fleet_multicall_binary/. That directory is not under pkgs/fleet/doc/; a reader who starts there will not find it.
  • This book is a fourth home, and it does not replace the other three. docs/verbs.md remains the canonical verb reference, the FDRs remain the decision record, and this book is the narrative and procedural layer over both. The rule that keeps all of them in step is in Keeping this book current.

Building fleet

Fleet is one Rust workspace that produces one binary. Capability variants are selected by Cargo features; the installed binary is always named fleet, and hyphenated names (fleet-serve, fleet-connect, repo-queue, and so on) are argv0 personalities of that one binary, not separate artefacts. See Repository layout for the workspace map and Register a domain or capability for how features, capabilities, and profiles fit together.

Build with Nix (the normal route)

  1. From the repository root, build the package you need:

    nix build .#fleet

  2. To build the full smoke set in one go:

    nix build .#fleet .#fleet-serve .#fleet-connect .#fleet-connect-static

  3. Run the smoke suite over the results (see Testing):

    ./pkgs/fleet/smoke.sh ./result ./result-1 ./result-2 ./result-3

The builder is pkgs/fleet/default.nix. Its internal mkFleet function takes a package name, a Cargo feature set, an optional argv0 alias, an optional size gate, a platform, and a static flag. Cargo flags are always -p fleet, plus --no-default-features when the feature set is not the default, plus --features <comma-joined> when the set is non-empty — so the Nix attribute is the Cargo feature set.

The six attributes

default.nix returns six attributes:

AttributeCargo featuresPlatformAlias linkSize gate
fleetdefault (= full)glibc—no
fleet-serveserveglibcfleet-serveno
fleet-connectnone (--no-default-features)glibcfleet-connectyes
fleet-brokersseparate build, see belowglibc—no
fleet-staticdefault (= full)musl (pkgsStatic.rustPlatform)—no
fleet-connect-staticnonemusl (pkgsStatic.rustPlatform)fleet-connectyes

Notes on each:

  • fleet is the full build: every domain and every serve role in the registry runs for real in it.
  • fleet-serve and fleet-connect install side by side under their hyphenated names as a symlink to the same binary (ln -s fleet $out/bin/<alias> in postInstall). Invoking through that name narrows the surface to that variant’s profile — narrowing only, never widening.
  • fleet-static is the full profile linked for foreign soil: the artefact non-Nix hosts install, and the artefact publish-fleet.sh ships. See Release and rollout. A glibc-dynamic build names Nix store paths a foreign host does not have, which is why the static exists.
  • fleet-connect-static is the same idea for the connect profile.
  • fleet-brokers is a separate buildRustPackage invocation on -p fleet-queue --features client,queue-broker,secrets-broker --bins. It produces the three standalone artefacts repo-queue, queue-broker, and secrets-broker from fleet-queue/src/bin/*.rs (each binary declares its required-features in fleet-queue’s Cargo.toml). Its header calls it the migration’s rollback inventory: the standalone brokers retire only at the epic’s close, not before.

There is no deploy package in pkgs/fleet/default.nix. Deployment tooling is its own package tree, pkgs/deploy/. See Release and rollout.

The D7 2 MiB connect gate

Size, not speed, is the release profile’s job. pkgs/fleet/Cargo.toml sets [profile.release] to opt-level = "z", lto = true, codegen-units = 1, strip = true, against a design budget for the connect variant of target ≤ 1.5 MiB and hard ≤ 2 MiB, stripped.

The hard bound is enforced in the build. For size-gated attributes, postFixup in default.nix:

  1. Strips explicitly and fully with ${binutils}/bin/strip (the nixpkgs fixup phase only strips debug symbols, leaving the symbol table behind).
  2. Reads the binary size with stat -c %s.
  3. Fails the build if the size exceeds connectMaxBytes = 2 * 1024 * 1024 (2,097,152 bytes).

The gate is enforced a second time in smoke.sh, which runs both connect flavours under env -i and checks them against the same bound. Anything that would push the connect build over the gate — for example the opencode-probe feature, whose ureq + rustls stack would break it, or the optional fleet-secrets dependency — is kept out of the connect feature set by construction.

The crane deps split, and why the statics stay monolithic

When the root flake’s make-fleet passes a craneLib, default.nix splits the build: dependencies are built once via crane’s buildDepsOnly, keyed on the manifests and the lockfile, so a source change rebuilds only the workspace crates instead of the whole dependency tree.

Three attributes deliberately stay on the monolithic buildRustPackage path:

  • fleet-static and fleet-connect-static — under pkgsStatic, crane applies crt-static to host build scripts, and a libc build script then fails to link.
  • fleet-brokers — its --bins build and its lib-tests check split do not map onto crane’s single cargoExtraArgs.

The build source is the whole pkgs/ tree (a fileset union of pkgs/fleet, ../atlas-search/Cargo.toml, ../atlas-search/crates, and ../atlas-search/schema), because fleet-search consumes the atlas crates by path. sourceRoot is the fleet directory inside it and cargoLock is ./Cargo.lock.

The check phase runs cargoWithProfile test --locked — deliberately flagless and workspace-wide. Crane’s default would append -p fleet and narrow the run to the binary crate’s tests alone. preCheck points HOME at a build-temporary directory because some atlas-search server tests write under $HOME/.local/state/atlas-search and the sandbox HOME is not writable.

One environment detail: non-static, non-connect builds bake ATLAS_SEARCH_ORT_LIB_DEFAULT to the pinned ONNX Runtime library (ONNX Runtime is dlopen’d at runtime). The statics get no such default — a glibc libonnxruntime cannot be dlopen’d from a static binary — so the search-serve role in a static binary needs ATLAS_ORT_LIB supplied at runtime.

Build with Cargo (inside the workspace)

  1. Change into pkgs/fleet/.

  2. Build the default (full) variant:

    cargo build --release

  3. Build a narrowed variant by selecting features exactly as default.nix does. For the connect variant:

    cargo build --release -p fleet --no-default-features

    For the serve variant:

    cargo build --release -p fleet --no-default-features --features serve

  4. Run the workspace tests the same way CI and the Nix check phase do:

    cargo test --workspace

Feature sets are defined in crates/fleet/Cargo.toml under [features]: default = ["full"]; full lists every domain feature plus opencode-probe; serve is the broker-side subset shipped as one feature for the Nix build. proxy-connect is not a feature at all — it is compiled into every variant.

The toolchain pin

pkgs/fleet/rust-toolchain.toml pins channel 1.99.1 with components rustfmt and clippy and profile default. Its header warns: do not delete the file — it is required for Nix builds — and a channel bump may cause rustc itself to build, so check that nixpkgs has the new channel cached before committing a bump. The nightly CI workflow installs this same pin; see Testing.

crates/fleet/build.rs bakes the version facts into the binary: FLEET_SOURCE_REV (from the environment, else git rev-parse, else the honest string unknown — the Nix sandbox has no .git) and FLEET_DERIVED_VERSION (derived, never hand-maintained, from git describe over fleet/v* tags via the shared derivation in src/derived_version.rs, with fallbacks).

Serialising heavy builds: fleet-build-lock

pkgs/fleet/fleet-build-lock serialises heavy builds (Cargo, Nix) so a host is never running more of them than it can bear. It implements the fleet build policy of at most FLEET_BUILD_SLOTS heavy builds at once on the host running it — 2 slots by default — using flock slot files under FLEET_BUILD_LOCKDIR (default ~/.fleet-build-locks).

Properties that matter:

  • A build waits for a free slot. Load alone never parks work; the lock queues, it does not reject.
  • It sets CARGO_BUILD_JOBS to half the host’s cores unless that variable is already set.
  • Usage is fleet-build-lock [--] command [args…], run on the building host (the laptop), for example via the laptop agent. fleet shell --build takes a slot through it automatically.
fleet-build-lock -- nix build .#fleet
fleet-build-lock -- cargo test --workspace

Testing

Fleet’s testing doctrine comes from the repository’s standing rules: property-based tests where code has meaningful invariants, model-based tests where a spec or model exists, and every automated test names its oracle — in practice, test names and comments carry the issue number and the invariant they check (Oracle (#7598): …, #12777 oracle: the unblock marker is audit-only…). proptest 1.12 is a dev-dependency of the binary crate (for the gh read classifier) and of fleet-queue (for the client parser invariants).

Run the whole suite from pkgs/fleet/:

cargo test --workspace

Inline, oracle-named tests per crate

Tests are overwhelmingly inline #[cfg(test)] mod tests in the file they test. The shape per crate:

CrateWhere the tests live
fleet (bin)Inline tests in src/main.rs (serve-list parsing, proxy-ssh argv building, help-flag positions, broker-role argument rejection) plus integration targets in tests/: invocation_ledger.rs, proxy_ssh.rs, search_serve.rs.
fleet-registryIn-file invariant tests (capability_ids_are_unique_and_stable, variant_profiles_nest, every_domain_primary_is_in_its_surface, aliases_route_to_real_domains, domain_aliases_match_the_argv0_map) plus the integration target tests/pmo_operator_docs.rs — the DOC-01 machine check described in Keeping this book current.
fleet-queueA very large inline test module in src/client.rs (parser invariants, the usage↔parser parity test below, timeline rendering), marker-fold oracles in src/fallback.rs, tests in the src/client/ command modules, and integration targets gated by feature (next section). Two Python SQL regressions ship as test data: implementation_repo_sql.py and quarantine_atomic_sql.py.
fleet-configA large inline suite (around fifty tests) plus proptest.
fleet-secretsA large inline suite (around thirty-five tests).
fleet-searchtests/serve_contract.rs for the serve-role contract. The server is a parity-guarded copy of the atlas-search service, also guarded by the fleet-search-parity-guard workflow.
fleet-agentInline src/tests.rs; proptest regression seeds are checked in at proptest-regressions/tests.txt.
fleet-dispatch, fleet-laptop-agent, fleet-bridgeInline tests in src/lib.rs / src/tests.rs and module tests.

Feature-gated integration tests: [[test]] required-features

Because the workspace is feature-split (see Register a domain or capability), a test target declares the features it needs, and Cargo only builds it when that surface is compiled. In fleet-queue’s Cargo.toml:

  • tests/broker_bin_args.rs — required-features = ["queue-broker", "secrets-broker"]
  • tests/chunked_list.rs — required-features = ["client"]
  • tests/person_wait_cli.rs — required-features = ["client"]

The consequence to remember: the fallback module sits behind the client feature (#[cfg(feature = "client")] pub mod fallback; in crates/fleet-queue/src/lib.rs), so a broker-only test run does not compile the fallback tests at all. The fallback oracles run only under a client-carrying feature set. The Nix fleet-brokers test flags and the full-variant check phase both carry client; a local cargo test --features queue-broker run silently skips them. When you change fallback behaviour, run a client-carrying test set explicitly.

pkgs/fleet/tests/ — the one Python test

pkgs/fleet/tests/ contains exactly one file, and it is not a Cargo integration test: test_tailnet_proxy_env.py, a Python test of the tailnet proxy environment contract for the Python-side tooling that shares the tree.

Other test-bearing corners outside the crates: pkgs/fleet/archer-slack/ Python tests, pkgs/fleet/hosted-worker/test/ TypeScript tests for the hosted Worker edition (including stamp-sig.test.ts, the golden-vector conformance surface the Rust gh domain’s Ed25519 signing must reproduce byte-exact), pkgs/fleet/placement/evaluate_test.go for the Go placement proof of concept, and pkgs/fleet/migrations/*_test.sql.

smoke.sh — the hermetic post-build suite

pkgs/fleet/smoke.sh is the per-variant, post-build smoke suite. It is hermetic by contract: no network, no installs, no state outside a mktemp directory, and it exits non-zero if any check fails.

  1. Build the four outputs (see Building fleet).

  2. Invoke it with the four Nix package output paths; each argument’s bin/fleet is the artefact under test:

    ./pkgs/fleet/smoke.sh ./result ./result-1 ./result-2 ./result-3

What it covers:

  • Variants — for each of full, serve, connect, and static: --help renders the full registry with unavailable domains marked, and version lists exactly that variant’s capability set.
  • Stubs — a missing domain stubs with exit 69 and the right wording, reached three ways: fleet <domain>, an argv0 alias symlink, and a hyphenated variant name (which narrows). A config-disabled domain stubs at 69 with the config wording.
  • Connect hygiene — both connect flavours run under env -i and are within the D7 size gate (≤ 2 MiB).
  • Search serve role — reaches the real role rather than a stub; hermetically it stops at config load (exit 2) before any token is needed.
  • Proxy domain end to end — broker auto-start, round-trips, shim materialisation and stale-shim removal on a services-map change, init no-op, location-aware init cases (an unknown location reports and exits 69 with no broker spawned), legacy proto-0 interop, idle exit, pool default rendering, a 32-concurrent burst, and the identity stamp.
  • Queue domain — the secrets-broker role binds and /health answers (in the hermetic world, 503 with serving=false is the pass shape); the queue-broker /healthz answers; client-to-broker wiring (a credential failure surfaces as exit 3 with broker wording); the fallback switch (one JSON object, exit 6) and the operator escape hatch underneath it; client --help / --version through the argv0 route.
  • Dispatch domain — the thin client against a stub pm-dispatch and a stub bws on PATH: the token is resolved by name, presented as Authorization: Bearer, the service JSON is printed verbatim, and a deliberate 409 is passed through.
  • Secrets domain — the broker-first chain against a stub session broker speaking the framed protocol, with the bws fallback behind it.

CI: main only

Repository policy: CI runs only on main. There are no pull-request runs, required status checks are disabled, and formatting is not a merge gate (it is auto-fixed on main). The fleet-relevant workflows:

WorkflowTriggerWhat it runs
fleet-rust-tests.ymlNightly cron (17 7 * * *) plus workflow_dispatch onlyA contract check (check-fleet-rust-tests.sh, plus that script’s own test), installs toolchain 1.99.1 via rustup (the rust-toolchain.toml pin), then cargo +1.99.1 test --manifest-path pkgs/fleet/Cargo.toml --workspace --all-targets --locked. Its header records why it exists: before it, the workspace’s tests ran in no CI venue at all, and the baseline run found a stale dep-wiring oracle and a parallel-spawn flake in fleet-queue.
fleet-smoke.ymlPush to main with paths under pkgs/fleet/**, the atlas-search manifests/crates, the workflow, and its check scripts; plus workflow_dispatchContract checks, the fleet Cargo.lock versus atlas manifests check (check-fleet-lock.sh — it fails by name instead of deep inside a derivation when the lockfile has drifted from the atlas-search path dependencies), Nix-builds the four outputs .#fleet .#fleet-serve .#fleet-connect .#fleet-connect-static, runs pkgs/fleet/smoke.sh on them, and greps the log for ^smoke: [1-9][0-9]* passed, 0 failed$ so a silently skipped suite cannot report green. Timeout 150 minutes (a cold cache compiles ONNX Runtime from source; warm is roughly 40 minutes).
fleet-search-parity-guard.ymlPer its own triggersGuards the “verbatim copy” claim of fleet-search’s server.rs against the atlas-search service.

Each fleet workflow carries a contract step — a shell check script and that script’s own test run before the real work — so a workflow edited out of sync with the test-suite registry fails by name.

Discrepancy note (workflow text): fleet-rust-tests.yml’s concurrency comment speaks of push-to-main runs, but the workflow has no push trigger at all — nightly plus dispatch only, by a deliberate ruling. The header’s nightly note is the true statement; the comment is leftover boilerplate.

The usage↔parser parity test — and what it does not check

Queue usage text is hand-maintained in two strings per verb, both in crates/fleet-queue/src/client/support.rs: the one-line synopsis in TOP_USAGE and the long text returned by usage(verb). The parser is hand-rolled (parse_verb_args / parse_args_inner in the same file). The machine check that keeps them honest is every_verb_usage_matches_its_parser in the client.rs test module: it asserts that every verb’s usage names exactly the flags its parser accepts. Companion tests are usage_covers_the_acceptance_verbs and usage_never_prints_nothing (an unknown verb falls back to TOP_USAGE).

What it does not cross-check: TOP_USAGE. The parity test checks each verb’s own usage() text against its parser; it does not check the TOP_USAGE synopsis lines against either. That drift is real today: for release, heartbeat, checkpoint, fail, and complete, the per-verb usage() text carries [--lane <id>] while the TOP_USAGE synopsis omits --lane. The parser is the authority on which spelling is right for each verb. Until a cross-check exists, anyone editing a verb’s flags must update both strings by hand — the procedure in Add a flag says exactly that.

Add a subcommand

There is no clap anywhere in the fleet workspace — no clap dependency in any fleet Cargo.toml, no derive macros. Every layer is hand-rolled by design: the top-level dispatch in crates/fleet/src/main.rs must behave identically in every variant, including the tiny connect build where the registry and the stub machinery are the product, and multicall routing happens before any per-domain parsing exists. Domains adopt their own parsers as they land.

This chapter traces one real verb end to end — fleet queue unblock — and then gives the step-by-step for adding a new one. For adding a flag to an existing verb instead, see Add a flag.

The worked trace: queue unblock

unblock is a good trace because it arrived later (#8276) and then grew a flag (#12777), so every seam shows.

1. The registry entry

In crates/fleet-registry/src/lib.rs, the queue entry of pub const DOMAINS lists "unblock" as one string in its subcommands array. That alone puts the verb in fleet --help, fleet queue --help, and fleet capabilities on every variant — including builds where the queue client is not compiled, which then answer the verb with the capability stub at exit 69.

2. The client dispatch arm

In crates/fleet-queue/src/client.rs, pub fn run(args: &[String]) -> i32 is one match over the verb name. The arm is:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
"unblock" => cmd_unblock(rest)
}

where rest = &args[1..]. Bare invocation and --help are handled above the match (bare prints TOP_USAGE and exits 2; a lone help argument exits 0). An unknown verb prints repo-queue: unknown command {:?} plus TOP_USAGE and returns 2. The registry’s 32 queue subcommands match the 32 arms of this match.

3. The handler: cmd_unblock

The handler is pub(super) fn cmd_unblock(rest: &[String]) -> i32 in crates/fleet-queue/src/client/commands_lifecycle.rs — the module for lifecycle verbs (claim, lane, bind, heartbeat, checkpoint, park, wake, block/unblock, the dependency and quarantine rechecks, cancel, revive, fail, complete, health, signal, and the small outbox verbs). Query verbs live in the sibling module commands_query.rs.

Its shape is the canonical shape for a broker-backed verb:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
let args = parse_verb_args("unblock", rest, &["worker", "reason", "drop-dep"], &[]);
reject_extra_pos("unblock", &args, 1);
let mut body = json!({
    "task_id": args.pos_i64(0, "task_id"),
    "worker":  opt_worker(&args),
    "reason":  args.get("reason").unwrap_or_default(),
});
let drops = drop_dep_flags(&args);
if !drops.is_empty() { body["drop_deps"] = json!(drops); }
let resp = unwrap_ok(call("/unblock", &body));
print_json(&require_row(&resp, "unblock_task"));
0
}

Five moves: declare the flags, validate the positionals, build the JSON body, call the broker, print the returned row. The helpers live in crates/fleet-queue/src/client/support.rs:

  • parse_verb_args(verb, rest, flags, bools) — flags are value flags, bools are boolean flags. Its pure core is parse_args_inner: duplicate value flags are errors (never silent last-wins), a boolean given --flag=value is an error, a value flag followed by another --flag token is an error, and an unknown flag is unrecognized argument: --<name>. A help token that is not a flag value prints the verb’s usage and exits 0; any shape rejection exits 2 with the message plus usage.
  • Args — the parsed result, with get, has, get_i64, and pos_i64 accessors.
  • call("/unblock", &body) — the transport in src/client/transport.rs: session-proxy Unix socket from the sandbox, direct HTTP on the laptop, probe-selected. Exit 3 means the broker path was unavailable.
  • unwrap_ok / require_row(resp, "unblock_task") / print_json — envelope handling: a broker envelope is {ok: true, …} or {ok: false, exit, error}; the client prints error and exits with exit.

Help text is two hand-maintained strings in support.rs, both keyed by verb name: the TOP_USAGE synopsis line (unblock <task-id> [--worker <id>] [--reason <text>] [--drop-dep <list>]) and the usage(verb) match arm (synopsis plus the long explanation). The parity test every_verb_usage_matches_its_parser fails the suite if they drift from the parser — with one known gap for TOP_USAGE, documented in Testing.

4. The broker verb

The client is not the end of the verb. Queue-broker routing in crates/fleet-queue/src/queue_broker.rs maps POST /unblock to pub(crate) fn verb_unblock(t: &TursoBackend, req: &Value) -> Value in crates/fleet-queue/src/turso_queue/admin.rs. It refuses a missing task and any task whose status is not blocked (unblock_task: task <id> is <status>, not blocked); otherwise it flips the task to queued, writes the audit events (unblocked, and dep_unblock_override with via: "unblock_task_turso", worker and reason recorded), and returns the row the client prints as unblock_task. The surgical dependency-dropping path is fn unblock_drop(...) in the same file.

5. The fallback twin

A queue verb that must work while the broker is down also lands in crates/fleet-queue/src/fallback.rs (compiled only under the client feature — see Testing). The fallback is the GitHub-issues transport of the same queue. For unblock it has:

  • its own dispatch arm, "unblock" => cmd_unblock(rest);
  • its own fn cmd_unblock, whose grammar is narrower — flags &["worker", "reason"] only; --drop-dep was deliberately not added to the fallback grammar;
  • its own usage arm in fallback_help;
  • the guard fn unblock_refusal(open, labels, &ClaimState), which the comments require to mirror the broker’s verb_unblock refusal rules;
  • a marker discipline: the GitHub side records the override as an audit-only marker comment (<!-- fleet-claim v1 kind=unblock worker=<id> ts=<rfc3339-utc> -->, MarkerKind::Unblock) that does not fold claim state.

Fallback switching itself: a work verb that hits a primary-store failure switches to the GitHub fallback with exit 6 and one JSON object naming the switch.

Step by step: add a new verb

The queue domain is written out in full; other domains follow the same shape minus the broker and fallback steps.

  1. Registry entry. Add the verb name to the domain’s subcommands array in crates/fleet-registry/src/lib.rs. Do this only for a top-level verb of the domain — nested leaves such as outbox claim live only in the handler and the usage strings, not in the registry.
  2. Usage strings, both of them. In crates/fleet-queue/src/client/support.rs, add the one-line synopsis to TOP_USAGE and the long-text arm to usage(verb). The parity test checks the second; nothing checks the first, so review it by eye (see the discrepancy note in Testing).
  3. Parser and handler. Add the match arm in the domain’s run (queue: crates/fleet-queue/src/client.rs) and write cmd_<verb> in the domain’s commands module — lifecycle verbs in client/commands_lifecycle.rs, query verbs in client/commands_query.rs. Build it on parse_verb_args and, for a broker verb, on call("/<verb>", body) followed by unwrap_ok / require_row / print_json.
  4. Broker verb, if it mutates state. Implement verb_<verb> in the appropriate crates/fleet-queue/src/turso_queue/*.rs module and route POST /<verb> to it from src/queue_broker.rs. The broker re-validates everything the client validated; the client-side checks are for fast, legible failure at the caller’s terminal, not for safety.
  5. Fallback twin, if it must work broker-down. Mirror the verb in src/fallback.rs: dispatch arm, handler, fallback_help arm, and a guard that mirrors the broker’s refusal rules. Decide deliberately which flags the fallback grammar carries — parity with the primary grammar is not automatic, as --drop-dep shows.
  6. Tests. Add oracle-named tests next to the code (see Testing): parser invariants in the client tests, guard-mirror tests in fallback.rs where a twin exists, broker behaviour where the verb mutates state. Every test names its oracle and its issue.
  7. Docs in the same change (DOC-01). Update pkgs/fleet/docs/verbs.md and the matching chapter of this book in the same change — the same pull request, not a follow-up. The full contract is in Keeping this book current.
  8. Ship it. A merged verb is not shipped until both live installs report it. Follow Release and rollout and verify by verb surface (fleet queue --help, the new verb’s own --help), not by version string alone.

Add a flag

Adding a flag to an existing verb is a small change with more touch points than it looks like. This chapter uses the one fully traced example — --drop-dep on fleet queue unblock (#12777) — which took exactly five touches. Treat that list as the checklist for any flag; the parity test at the end is the gate that catches most misses.

For adding a whole verb, see Add a subcommand. For the parser and usage machinery referenced throughout, see Testing for the parity test and its known gap.

The case study: --drop-dep on unblock

unblock clears a task’s block. --drop-dep <list> additionally drops named dependencies in the same operation, surgically, instead of leaving the task blocked on a dependency that will never land. The list grammar is comma-separated kind:ref entries: issue:, pr:, or ci: followed by owner/repo#N, or task:ID.

Touch 1 — the parser declaration slice

In the handler cmd_unblock (crates/fleet-queue/src/client/commands_lifecycle.rs), the flag is declared by adding one string to the flags slice of the existing parse_verb_args call:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
parse_verb_args("unblock", rest, &["worker", "reason", "drop-dep"], &[])
}

The first slice is value flags; the second, empty here, is boolean flags — a boolean flag goes there instead. Nothing else about parsing changes: duplicates, missing values, and the --drop-dep=<list> inline form all inherit the rules of parse_args_inner in crates/fleet-queue/src/client/support.rs (duplicate value flags are errors, a value flag followed by another --flag token is an error, unknown flags are unrecognized argument: --<name>).

Touch 2 — the value parser

A flag with a non-trivial value grammar gets a dedicated parser next to the handler:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub(super) fn parse_drop_dep_list(list: &str) -> Result<Vec<Value>, String>
}

in commands_lifecycle.rs. It parses the comma-separated kind:ref grammar and returns an error string on a bad reference. The accessor drop_dep_flags(&args) calls it and dies at the caller’s terminal with exit 2 (unblock: --drop-dep expects …) on error. The handler then wires the result into the broker body only when it is non-empty:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
let drops = drop_dep_flags(&args);
if !drops.is_empty() { body["drop_deps"] = json!(drops); }
}

That conditional is deliberate: when the flag is absent, the body keeps exactly the old shape, so an older broker sees a request it already understands.

Touch 3 — both usage strings

Both hand-maintained usage surfaces in crates/fleet-queue/src/client/support.rs gain the flag:

  • the TOP_USAGE synopsis line becomes unblock <task-id> [--worker <id>] [--reason <text>] [--drop-dep <list>];
  • the usage("unblock") arm gains the synopsis plus the long explanation of --drop-dep semantics.

Updating only one is the classic miss. The parity test (touch 5) enforces the second; the first is on you — see the discrepancy note in Testing.

Touch 4 — broker re-validation

The broker does not trust the client’s parse. verb_unblock in crates/fleet-queue/src/turso_queue/admin.rs reads drop_deps from the request body and routes to fn unblock_drop(...), which re-validates every spec. The client’s own comment states the contract: the broker re-validates every spec; a bad reference dies there first, at the caller’s terminal. Client-side validation exists for fast, legible errors; broker-side validation is the authority, because the broker is the component that mutates state and other clients exist.

Touch 5 — docs and tests

  • pkgs/fleet/docs/verbs.md gains the flag in the verb’s prose where it is user-facing, and this book’s matching chapter is updated in the same change (DOC-01 — see Keeping this book current).
  • Oracle-named tests cover the new behaviour. For --drop-dep, the fallback-side oracles from #12777 assert that the unblock marker stays audit-only and does not fold claim state.

One deliberate non-touch: the flag was not added to the fallback grammar. Fallback unblock in crates/fleet-queue/src/fallback.rs still takes only --worker and --reason. A flag does not automatically exist in both transports; decide for each one, and record the decision in the change.

Step by step: add a flag

  1. Add the flag name to the correct slice of the handler’s parse_verb_args call — value flags in the first slice, booleans in the second (bools).
  2. If the value has a grammar, write a dedicated value parser next to the handler, returning Result<_, String>, and an accessor that dies with exit 2 and a message naming the expected shape. Wire the parsed value into the request body, conditionally if omitting it preserves the old body shape for older brokers.
  3. Update both usage strings in client/support.rs: the TOP_USAGE synopsis and the usage(verb) long text.
  4. Re-validate on the broker side if the flag reaches a broker verb. Never let a client parse be the only validation of a value that mutates state.
  5. Decide the fallback grammar explicitly: add the flag to the fallback.rs twin, or record that it is primary-only.
  6. Update docs/verbs.md and this book in the same change, and add oracle-named tests.

Defaults discipline

  • A new flag is optional unless the verb is meaningless without it. Adding a required flag to a shipped verb is a breaking change to every script that calls it; that needs its own justification, not a ride-along.
  • An omitted flag must reproduce the old behaviour exactly — including the old request-body shape where a broker is involved, as the drop_deps conditional above does.
  • Defaults that already exist are part of the contract: for example --worker defaults to repo-worker-code (with named exceptions such as cancel, whose worker defaults to fleet-monitor), and --queue defaults are verb-specific (see the queue chapters). Do not quietly change a default while adding an unrelated flag.
  • Numeric flags die with exit 2 naming the flag when given a non-numeric value. Follow that shape for any new validated value.

Hidden flags: the --reason-class precedent

Not every flag belongs in the usage strings. fail carries --reason-class, a hidden flag: it is accepted by the parser, it is a closed enum, and it defaults to transient — but it is not advertised in the verb’s help. It exists so automated callers can classify a failure for the broker’s retry and reporting logic without turning an internal taxonomy into a user-facing promise.

Use the hidden-flag shape only when all three hold:

  1. The value set is a closed enum with a safe default, so omitting the flag is always correct for a human caller.
  2. The intended callers are programs, not people reading --help.
  3. The flag is still declared in the parser slice like any other — hidden means unadvertised, not unparsed or unvalidated.

The parity test is the gate

every_verb_usage_matches_its_parser (in the client.rs test module) asserts that every verb’s usage() text names exactly the flags its parser accepts. Add a flag to the parser without the usage text — or to the usage text without the parser — and the workspace test suite fails. Run it before you push:

cargo test --workspace

Remember its one blind spot: it does not cross-check TOP_USAGE. Check that line yourself.

Register a domain or capability

A domain exists in fleet because three things agree: the registry names it, a Cargo feature compiles it in, and the runtime reconstructs the same fact from the compiled binary. This chapter explains that machinery and lists everything a new domain must add. For the crate map, see Repository layout; for the build attributes that select feature sets, see Building fleet.

The registry: crates/fleet-registry/src/lib.rs

fleet-registry is a dependency-free crate of strings and tables — no I/O — compiled into every variant, including fleet-connect, so that --help is always complete. It owns three things.

Domains

pub const DOMAINS: &[Domain] is the full registry, in help order, with 19 entries: queue, serve, proxy, dispatch, dispatch-test, secrets, gh, bridge, orgs, agent, shell, search, cert, laptop-agent, commander, http, ssh, laptop, actions. pub fn domain(name) is a linear find over it.

struct Domain is the unit that help lists, stubs name, and config disables:

FieldMeaning
name: &'static strThe domain’s invocation name.
summary: &'static strThe one-line description help renders.
capabilities: &'static [Capability]Every capability the domain spans.
primary: CapabilityThe headline capability availability keys on. Example: on fleet-serve the search domain is marked absent because its headline is the client, even though the search-serve capability exists under serve.
aliases: &'static [&str]The domain’s argv0 aliases.
subcommands: &'static [&str]The top-level verb inventory, rendered by domain help and checked by the DOC-01 machine test.

struct AliasRoute { domain, implied_arg } and pub fn alias_route(argv0) define the argv0 map. The shipped aliases are: repo-queue → queue; queue-broker → serve with implied arg queue-broker; secrets-broker → serve with implied arg secrets-broker; laptop-agent-broker → proxy with implied arg serve; atlas-search → search; laptop-agent → laptop-agent. An argv0 that is none of {fleet, a variant name, an alias} is a usage error at exit 2 naming the expected names. is_known_invocation_name(name) is fleet ∨ variant name ∨ alias.

Capabilities: the 22 atoms

enum Capability has 22 variants with stable string ids (Capability::id, Capability::ALL):

proxy-connect, proxy-serve, proxy-raw-splice, queue, queue-broker, secrets-broker, search, search-serve, dispatch, dispatch-test, laptop-agent, secrets, gh, bridge, agent, commander, laptop-http, laptop-ssh, laptop, cert, actions, orgs.

Note there is no shell capability atom: the shell domain rides on the agent capability.

CapabilitySet is a BTreeSet<Capability>, built with capability_set(&[…]). Named sets: full_capabilities() (all 22), serve_capabilities() = {ProxyConnect, ProxyServe, ProxyRawSplice, QueueBroker, SecretsBroker, SearchServe, Secrets}, and connect_capabilities() = {ProxyConnect, ProxyRawSplice}.

CapState: the four availability states

At dispatch, Surface::cap_state(cap, domain_name) checks in order and yields enum CapState:

StateMeaning
AvailableCompiled in, in profile, not config-disabled. The domain handler runs.
NotInBuildThe Cargo feature was not compiled into this build.
NarrowedByNameCompiled in, but the argv0 profile (below) narrowed it out.
DisabledByConfigThe [domains] table in fleet.toml disabled it on this host.

Any non-Available state falls through to the stub (exit 69 — see the stub wordings below). Surface itself is the invocation’s whole effective surface: compiled (from Cargo features), profile (from the hyphenated invocation name), effective (= compiled ∩ profile.capabilities(), or compiled when there is no profile), and the loaded fleet_config::Config.

The registry’s own tests are invariant oracles: capability_ids_are_unique_and_stable, variant_profiles_nest (connect ⊂ serve ⊂ full, and full == ALL), every_domain_primary_is_in_its_surface, aliases_route_to_real_domains, domain_aliases_match_the_argv0_map.

How capabilities are compiled in: compiled_capabilities() and bin-crate features

Two layers, and both must agree.

Layer 1 — Cargo features on the binary crate (crates/fleet/Cargo.toml, [features]):

  • default = ["full"].
  • full = [proxy-serve, queue, queue-broker, secrets-broker, search, search-serve, dispatch, dispatch-test, laptop-agent, secrets, gh, bridge, agent, opencode-probe].
  • serve = [proxy-serve, queue-broker, secrets-broker, search-serve, secrets, opencode-probe] — the broker-side subset, shipped as one feature for the Nix build.
  • The connect build is --no-default-features with nothing optional on.
  • proxy-connect is not a feature: it is compiled into every variant.
  • Each feature wires optional dependencies, for example queue = ["dep:fleet-secrets", "dep:fleet-queue", "fleet-queue/client"] and search-serve = ["dep:fleet-search", "fleet-search/serve"]. fleet-proxy is a non-optional dependency with default-features = false: the proxy client is in every variant, only the broker half (fleet-proxy/serve) is gated.
  • Two things are kept out of connect on purpose: opencode-probe (its ureq + rustls stack would break the D7 2 MiB gate — see Building fleet) and fleet-secrets (the connect variant carries nothing else).

Domain crates mirror the discipline one level down. In fleet-queue, the features are client, queue-broker, and secrets-broker, and src/lib.rs gates modules on them: client, fallback, needs_drew, placement under client; queue_broker, turso_queue, validate under queue-broker; secrets_broker under secrets-broker; uds_http under either broker. In fleet-search, client and serve split the client surface from the Atlas service role.

Layer 2 — runtime reconstruction. fn compiled_capabilities() in crates/fleet/src/main.rs starts from {ProxyConnect, ProxyRawSplice} unconditionally and inserts one Capability per cfg!(feature = "…"). build_variant(compiled) then re-derives which shipped Variant the set equals — Full, Serve, or Connect; an unrecognised set reports its build name as fleet-custom. The binary reports its variant from its feature set; it does not trust a baked-in name. fleet capabilities prints both lists: capabilities (what this invocation can use) and compiled_capabilities (what the binary was built with) — their difference is exactly the profile and config narrowing.

argv0 profiles narrow only

enum Variant { Full, Serve, Connect } is a property of the artefact whose names double as invocation profiles: Variant::name() is fleet / fleet-serve / fleet-connect. Variant::from_invocation_name() recognises only the two hyphenated names; plain fleet selects no profile.

The rule is narrowing only: a profile is a capability ceiling (compiled ∩ profile.capabilities()), never a widening. Invoking the full binary as fleet-connect gives you the connect surface; invoking the connect binary as fleet gives you nothing extra, because the capabilities were never compiled in (NotInBuild, not NarrowedByName). An alias route, by contrast, constructs the surface with no profile at all and prepends its implied argument.

The stub wordings

When a domain is not Available, fn stub(...) in main.rs prints to stderr and returns exit 69 (EXIT_UNAVAILABLE, EX_UNAVAILABLE from sysexits.h). The first line names the domain and the reason class; the second line lists what this invocation can do (Enabled capabilities: <usable caps>.); the third names the build. One form per CapState:

  • NotInBuild: fleet: this build does not include '<domain>'. plus This is the <build> build (<VERSION>)., and The full build is 'fleet'. when the build is not full.
  • NarrowedByName: fleet: invoked as '<invoked_as>', this build does not include '<domain>'. plus the explanation that the invocation is name-scoped to the profile and that invoked as fleet it carries the full surface.
  • DisabledByConfig: fleet: '<domain>' is disabled by config on this host. plus the instruction to re-enable the domain under [domains] in the named fleet.toml path.
  • Available (for a surface compiled in with nothing behind it): fleet: '<domain>' is included in this build but not implemented yet. plus the line naming the build and the not-implemented state.

Help renders the same states without stubbing: domain help is registry data and is always available, even where the domain is not. Help marks each domain included in this build, not in this build — invoking it prints the capability stub (exit 69), narrowed out by this invocation name — … (exit 69), or disabled by config on this host (exit 69 if invoked), and top-level help closes with: “A domain this invocation cannot use answers with a stub and exit code 69.”

Step by step: what a new domain must add

  1. Registry entry. A Domain in DOMAINS in crates/fleet-registry/src/lib.rs, in help order, with name, summary, capabilities, primary (which must be a member of its own capabilities — the registry tests enforce this), aliases, and subcommands. If the domain needs a new capability atom, add the Capability variant with a stable string id and place it in ALL and in the named sets it belongs to.
  2. Crate. A new library crate under pkgs/fleet/crates/, added to the workspace members in pkgs/fleet/Cargo.toml and to [workspace.dependencies] by path, exposing a run entry point with the domain’s argument and config shape. Follow the existing crates’ feature discipline: gate server roles and heavy dependencies behind features so the connect build stays clean.
  3. Bin-crate wiring. An optional dependency plus a feature in crates/fleet/Cargo.toml; the feature added to full (and to serve if the domain has a broker-side role); one cfg!(feature = "…") insertion in compiled_capabilities() in main.rs.
