  4. Dispatch arm. In run_domain in main.rs, a #[cfg(feature = …)] arm under the CapState::Available path calling the crate’s run. Subcommand-sensitive capability requirements (the way serve maps its role token to QueueBroker / SecretsBroker / SearchServe / ProxyServe) go in required_capability(...). An argv0 alias, if the domain needs one, goes in alias_route() in the registry — and the registry test domain_aliases_match_the_argv0_map must still pass.
  5. Help. The registry entry is the top-level help. The domain’s own --help, per-verb usage strings, and parser live in the domain crate, hand-rolled — see Add a subcommand.
  6. Capabilities JSON. Nothing extra to write: fleet capabilities is generated from the registry plus compiled_capabilities(), so a correctly registered domain appears in it automatically, with its per-domain state one of available, not-in-build, narrowed-by-name, disabled-by-config. Verify it does, on both a full build and a narrowed build.
  7. Build and smoke coverage. A Nix attribute only if the domain needs a new variant (rare — variants are profiles, not domains). Smoke coverage in pkgs/fleet/smoke.sh that the domain renders in help on every variant and stubs at 69 where it is unavailable.
  8. Docs in the same change (DOC-01). pkgs/fleet/docs/verbs.md and this book in the same change — see Keeping this book current. The DOC-01 machine test (pmo_operator_docs_match_registered_help_inventory) ties the README’s operator contract to the registered inventory, so a registry entry without its contract docs fails the workspace suite.

Release and rollout

Fleet has three distinct release motions, and confusing them is the classic rollout mistake:

  1. Publish — build the static binary and upload it as a GitHub release asset (scripts/muse/publish-fleet.sh).
  2. Bootstrap pin — point fresh-seat provisioning at that asset (scripts/muse/bootstrap.sh).
  3. Deploy — roll broker services on the laptop through generation-based profiles (pkgs/deploy/deploy.py), and update the two live installs of the binary itself.

The governing rule, from the fleet README’s Deploy section: a verb is not shipped when it merges — it is shipped when both live installs report it. That rule exists because of a real failure (#6728): fleet queue fallback was merged as source and docs while the installed binaries answered repo-queue: unknown command "fallback" for a full day.

1. Publish: scripts/muse/publish-fleet.sh

The script builds the static fleet binary and uploads it as a GitHub release asset on developing-today/code, then prints the tag and sha256 to pin in bootstrap.sh.

Contract: at most one positional argument, REV (default origin/main); no flags; -h / --help prints the header; anything else exits 2 before any subprocess runs (the operator-script argument contract: a script declares its whole command line and parses strictly against that declaration before any subprocess, network, file write, lock, or deploy step).

Steps:

  1. Fetch origin main and resolve the revision. The tag is derived from it: short is the 7-character revision prefix and tag = "fleet-static-$short".

  2. Create a throwaway detached git worktree at that revision (removed by an exit trap) and build inside it:

    nix build "$work/src#fleet-static"

    Building in a detached worktree, not the primary clone, keeps the primary on main and clean.

  3. Gate the artefact, twice:

    • Static-linkage gate — file -L on the binary must report statically linked or static-pie. A non-static build is refused.
    • Bridge-capability gate — the binary’s capabilities output, checked programmatically, must show a domain named bridge with available true. The Muse seat’s bootstrap requires the bridge-capable full profile; a build without it is fatal.

  4. Copy the binary to the asset name fleet-x86_64-linux-musl and write its checksum file fleet-x86_64-linux-musl.sha256 (<sum> <asset>).

  5. Publish idempotently: if the release fleet-static-<short> already exists, download its existing .sha256 and re-upload with --clobber only when the checksum differs; otherwise create the release as a prerelease targeted at the revision, with notes naming the build command and the bootstrap consumer.

  6. Read the two output lines — they are the pin values for the next step:

    tag=fleet-static-<short>
sha256=<sum>

2. The bootstrap pin: scripts/muse/bootstrap.sh

bootstrap.sh rebuilds a Muse sandbox seat from nothing — tools, config, laptop link — with every phase idempotent and skipping work already done. It runs in 8 phases: tools token restore tailnet fleet persist init check, selectable with --only <list> / --skip <list>; --all also restores ~/git and ~/agents. Exit 0 means ok, exit 1 names the failed phase, exit 2 is a usage error.

The fleet pin is a pair of lines near the top of the script, under the comment “pinned artifacts (update together; sha256 of the downloaded file)”:

FLEET_URL="${FLEET_URL:-https://github.com/developing-today/code/releases/download/fleet-static-<short>/fleet-x86_64-linux-musl}"
FLEET_SHA256="${FLEET_SHA256:-<sha256 of the downloaded file>}"

Both are environment-overridable. The URL is exactly the publish step’s tag scheme plus the asset name. To move the pin:

  1. Run publish-fleet.sh for the revision you intend to ship and note its tag= and sha256= lines.
  2. Edit both FLEET_URL (the tag segment) and FLEET_SHA256 in bootstrap.sh, together, in the same change. Updating one without the other makes every fresh bootstrap fail its checksum.
  3. Commit and merge through the normal worktree-and-pull-request flow.

How the pin is consumed: in the tools phase, a sha256-verifying fetch downloads the pinned binary into $HOME/.local/share/muse-bootstrap/fleet/fleet — kept under the plain name fleet in its own off-PATH directory, because fleet picks its verb set from argv0 — and only when the existing copy is missing or fails the same has_bridge capability probe publish used. fetch dies on a sha256 mismatch. In the fleet phase, that download becomes the seat’s install at ~/tools/fleet: if the existing file is not writable it is moved aside to ~/tools/fleet.old; the new binary is installed atomically (install -m 755 to ~/tools/fleet.tmp, then mv -f over ~/tools/fleet) and only when the bytes differ; then ~/tools/bin/fleet and ~/tools/bin/repo-queue are symlinked to ~/tools/fleet — the repo-queue link is the argv0 alias doing the work, not a second binary.

The other phases, briefly: token obtains the seat’s Bitwarden Secrets Manager access token; restore restores the seat’s files and provisions the shared broker token files by name from Bitwarden Secrets Manager; tailnet joins the tailnet and writes the [host] config into ~/.config/fleet/fleet.toml; persist saves a boot hook that re-runs --only tailnet,fleet after a sandbox recycle; init brings up the seat’s init stack (see Running the brokers as services); check verifies the install — fleet version and capabilities including the bridge capability, laptop-link reachability the way fleet dials it, secret resolution by name, and a bridge hello/inbox probe as the seat’s agent.

3. Deploy the brokers: deploy.py profiles and generations

Broker services on the laptop are deployed with pkgs/deploy/deploy.py — a registry-validating deployment CLI (stdlib-only Python). Service definitions live in pkgs/deploy/services.nix; the registry the CLI consumes is baked into its package at build time. A valid definition carries exactly the fields package, entryPoint, args, environment, secrets, user, ports, restart, healthCheck, targets (plus optional healthTimeoutSeconds and timer), and a class — for the laptop brokers, systemd. Secrets in a definition are names only, resolved by the secrets broker at activation time; a definition never carries a value.

The three fleet profiles:

ProfilePackage / entry pointArgsPortHealth check
queue-brokerfleet, bin/fleetserve queue-broker4801 (PORT=4801, QUEUE_BROKER_BACKEND=turso)GET /healthz on the laptop tailnet address, port 4801
secrets-brokerfleet, bin/fleetserve secrets-broker4800 (PORT=4800)GET /health on the laptop tailnet address, port 4800
laptop-agentlaptopAgent, bin/laptop-agentnone4799 (LAPTOP_AGENT_PORT=4799)none — /health requires the daemon token, so health is verified through the authenticated client after activation

queue-broker names one secret by name (the Turso fleet-queue read-write token); secrets-broker names none, because it is the resolver. laptop-agent restarts always rather than on-failure: a clean SIGTERM/success exit does not restart under on-failure, and a past daemon-death episode showed that gap is real.

Profiles, generations, and the generation log

Each target owns a per-service Nix profile. The system-scope default base is /nix/var/nix/profiles/per-service; sandbox targets default to ~/.local/share/deploy/profiles (home survives a sandbox recycle; /etc does not). --profile-base / $DEPLOY_PROFILE_BASE relocates the base.

The rendered systemd unit’s ExecStart points at the profile’s current link (<base>/<name>/current/<entryPoint>), never at a bare store path — so a generation flip is a profile repoint, not a unit rewrite, and the unit file itself does not change between generations. A flip is one atomic symlink repoint at the generation directory (<base>/.generations/<name>/<id>/).

Every deploy and rollback appends to an append-only JSONL generation log, one file per target at <state-dir>/generations/<name>.jsonl (state dir via --state-dir / $DEPLOY_STATE_DIR). Each event records the generation id, source revision, artefact, timestamp, and actor. The log is never truncated; the current and previous generations are derived by folding it in order — a deploy event makes its generation current, a rollback event makes the generation it repointed to current, and previous is the last distinct generation before current.

Activation and rollback

  1. Preview with no side effects:

    deploy <target> --dry-run

    This prints the ordered activation plan, which is the oracle for what a real activation will do.

  2. Activate. The real run, in plan order: build → install the next generation into the profile → write the unit → daemon-reload → restart only that unit → health-check (the definition’s healthCheck URL, within healthTimeoutSeconds). On any failure, the profile flips back to the previous generation and the unit restarts on it.

  3. Roll back when a generation is bad. Rollback is a repoint, never a rebuild: repoint the profile at the previous distinct generation → restart → health-check → on failure, flip back to the generation you came from → append a rollback event to the log. Rollback refuses when no generations are recorded or only one is (“rollback needs a previous generation”). deploy status folds the log and reports current and previous with their source revisions plus health.

4. The two live installs of the binary

Separate from deploy.py, the fleet binary itself has two live installs, and both must move for a change to count as shipped:

  1. Build one artefact from current main and record its version:

    nix build .#fleet
./result/bin/fleet version

    Both installs must match that build’s source revision.

  2. Laptop install — a plain binary copy over the laptop’s ~/.local/bin/fleet. Verify in place.

  3. Sandbox install — ~/tools/fleet, reached through the ~/tools/bin/fleet and ~/tools/bin/repo-queue symlinks. This install is root-owned provisioning, read-only to lanes: a lane that cannot redeploy it files or updates the tracking issue instead of working around it. In practice it moves through the bootstrap path of section 2.

One warning from the same README section: a vendor-step failure naming an atlas crate means pkgs/fleet/Cargo.lock has drifted from the atlas-search path dependencies. bash .github/scripts/check-fleet-lock.sh names the drift in seconds; regenerate with (cd pkgs/fleet && cargo update --workspace) before building. The same check runs in CI — see Testing.

5. Seat rollout order and verification

Roll a new binary out to seats in this order:

  1. Publish the static artefact and move the bootstrap pin (sections 1–2), so any seat rebuilt from scratch lands on the new build.

  2. Deploy the laptop brokers through deploy.py if the change touches a broker role, and verify each profile’s health check.

  3. Update the laptop install (~/.local/bin/fleet), then the sandbox install (~/tools/fleet).

  4. Verify per seat, by surface, not by version string alone:

    fleet version
fleet capabilities
fleet queue --help

    fleet version on each seat must report the same source revision as the artefact you built, and the verb surface you shipped must be present — for a new verb, run the verb’s own --help on each seat. A seat still answering unknown command for a merged verb is not rolled out, whatever its version line says.

Keeping this book current

A book that drifts from the binary is worse than no book: operators script against what it says. Fleet already had a documentation contract before this book existed — DOC-01, in the fleet README — and this chapter states that contract, then extends it to the book itself.

The DOC-01 contract

DOC-01 is the “Operator and contributor contract” section of pkgs/fleet/README.md (#10728). Its contributor paragraph, in substance:

Keep the command contract together: update crates/fleet-registry/src/lib.rs when a top-level help inventory changes, and update docs/verbs.md for every changed or added command, including nested leaves and examples, in the same change. Docs must not present a designed spelling as shipped: the runtime dispatch is the authority on what a binary can run. And a change to any settled semantic the section records (claim/park/resume, supervision and stop authority, cap policy, attribution/logging) requires a decision record in the same body of work.

The supporting rules in the same section:

  • The inventory is the registry. fleet --help renders the full registry on every variant and fleet capabilities prints it as JSON. The registered inventory lives in one place — crates/fleet-registry/src/lib.rs — so no build can know a domain another build forgot. See Register a domain or capability.
  • Designed-versus-shipped discipline. Spellings that are designed but not yet shipped are documented as contract, not surface, explicitly marked as not in the registered inventory and not dispatchable today, each with its shipped equivalent. Invoking one answers unknown command. Never write a designed spelling into a procedure as if it works.
  • Decision records for settled semantics. A change to claim/park/resume semantics, supervision or stop authority, cap policy, or attribution/logging requires a fleet decision record (FDR, in repository-root doc/decisions/, indexed by doc/decisions/README.md) in the same body of work — the same pull request, or the same run for non-PR work.
  • A machine check enforces the inventory half. The test pmo_operator_docs_match_registered_help_inventory in crates/fleet-registry/tests/pmo_operator_docs.rs ties the README’s operator contract to the registered help inventory: a verb added to the registry without its contract docs, or vice versa, fails the workspace test suite. The companion test published_queue_reference_matches_registered_help_inventory compares fleet queue --help’s registered commands with command headings in the reference chapters linked from SUMMARY.md. A group can appear as a leaf heading, such as fleet queue session status. The test names missing and obsolete top-level commands. Review nested leaves, flags, defaults and procedures against the matching handlers and help output. See Testing.

The extension: the book is part of the same change

This book is now one of the surfaces DOC-01 covers. The rule:

Any change to a command, a flag, a default, a capability, a surface, or an operational procedure updates the matching chapter of this book in the same pull request.

Concretely, in the same change as the code:

  1. A new or changed verb or flag → its command-reference chapter, plus Add a subcommand or Add a flag if the change alters the pattern those chapters teach, plus pkgs/fleet/docs/verbs.md per DOC-01.
  2. A new domain or capability → Register a domain or capability and Repository layout.
  3. A changed default → every chapter that states the old default. Search the book for the value; defaults are stated in more places than you remember.
  4. A changed operational procedure (ports, profile names, heal order, rollout order) → the matching operations chapter: Running the brokers as services, Health checks and the heal stack, or Release and rollout.
  5. A changed deployment of the book itself → Deploying this book.

“Same change” means same pull request. A follow-up issue promising to update the book later does not satisfy the rule — that is exactly how the pre-book docs drifted into the disagreements the research for this book catalogued (a README package count that no longer matched default.nix, usage strings that disagreed with each other, help text describing an earlier epic step as current). If you find such a disagreement while writing, fix the stale side if it is in your change’s scope; otherwise file an issue in the owning repository in the same pass and note it in your change.

The two build gates

Two mechanical gates keep the book honest:

  1. create-missing = false. The book’s book.toml sets create-missing = false, with the standing rule inherited from the mcpx exemplar: every chapter in SUMMARY.md must exist on disk; never invent stubs. Adding a SUMMARY.md entry without the file fails the build instead of silently publishing an empty page.
  2. The Nix build. The book builds as the .#fleet-docs package (see Deploying this book). The build-only workflow fleet-docs.yml runs that build on main, and the combined Pages deploy rebuilds it again. A chapter that breaks mdBook — a bad link target, a missing file — fails the build by name rather than shipping broken.

Internal links in this book are relative .md links only, and every file starts with its exact chapter title as its single # heading. Both are part of the contract: relative links keep the book readable in the repository as well as on the rendered site, and the title rule keeps SUMMARY.md, the file, and the rendered page in agreement.

Where the rule is recorded

The rule lives in three places, which must agree:

  1. pkgs/fleet/README.md — the DOC-01 contract itself, the source of truth for the registry and verbs.md halves.
  2. pkgs/fleet/doc/agents/documentation.md — the agent-facing documentation rules inside the package, which carry the book rule for sessions working in this tree.
  3. This chapter — the book stating its own maintenance rule, so a reader who arrived here first can find the whole contract.

If the three disagree, the README’s DOC-01 text wins for command-contract questions and this chapter wins for book-scope questions — and the disagreement itself gets fixed in the same pass it is noticed.

Build and preview the book locally

  1. From pkgs/fleet/, with mdBook available, build in place:

    mdbook build

    The rendered site lands in the build directory named by book.toml. Open its index.html to preview.

  2. Or build the packaged form, exactly as CI does, from the repository root:

    nix build .#fleet-docs

    The result is the rendered site; serve or open result/index.html to check links, search, and chapter order before merging.

Either route is a valid pre-merge check. The Nix route is the stronger one: it is the same derivation the deploy uses, with the same mdBook version.

Fleet research and implementation roadmap

Fleet lets a seat find work, claim it, move the work to a suitable executor, and show what finished. Its brokers, agents and providers answer different questions. A successful claim identifies the current holder. A completed run identifies one provider attempt. A merged change establishes repository completion. A deployment needs a separate receipt from the serving process. The archived charter records the governing rules. Program tracker

Preserve existing owners and dependency holds.Per-task event and status readback, an isolated early-renewal regression, and a separate decision about independent holds. Production repair cohort · Renewal defect
2Correct stale placement, install and readiness instructions with the active DOC-01 owner. Retain the repair chapter already merged.Published operator instructions agree with supported lookup, provider result, release pin and observed cold/warm behavior. Book correction · Repair chapter
3Separate image publication, dependency fetch, cache export, image pull and workload results. Resolve the first failed boundary before proposing an executor change.Source run and attempt, first failed step, tag/digest and the consumer’s actual pull where observable. Each held container item keeps its individual approval requirement. Publication · Gated workflow
4Establish live recovery and rollout evidence with the active service owner. Measure cold refresh and rollback on an isolated installation.No healthy refresh interrupted, cold-to-ready time measured, previous generation serving after induced candidate failure. Cold restart incident

A claim, open PR or current approval hold takes precedence over this ordering. A blocked label alone gives no authority to release work. Inspect the live issue and its newest comments immediately before claiming and again before merging. Explicit task model and capability requirements remain in force. The PM orchestration subprogram retains its own design ordering.

Reading a dated receipt

The November 23 queue ledger names 37 production applications. A bounded audit of those task IDs through 18:02 UTC found one repair event per ID in the application window. At readback 18 were done, 15 blocked, three claimed and one parked. All 15 blocked rows had dependency entries. Preservation of every historical manual hold remains unknown. The queue broker reported generation 6 at bcc8043b59ab. An interactive AMD seat reported 22ec90b9c29d. Capture both when investigating a new report. Repair ledger · AMD audit

The first qualifying production S3 history record was at 2026-11-23 02:30:06.420 UTC. Through 17:45:11.740 UTC, 63 qualifying records occupied 61 of 62 quarter-hour buckets. Two buckets contained two observations and one was empty. A seven-day interval can first elapse on November 30 at 02:30:06.420 UTC. Acceptance still requires coverage and scoring. The gatherer user timer was active, while the weekly-review user timer and service were absent on AMD at inspection. The first posted weekly result and periodic activation have independent evidence. The S7 installation follow-up tracks the first scheduled invocation during the normal AMD rollout. Production tick and timer audit · S3 record format and acceptance discussion · First weekly review

Record a new baseline when any named authority changes. For a build, keep workflow, attempt, checkout, execution route, workload outcome and artifact identity. For a repair, keep the deterministic proposed edit, actual committed receipt and subsequent readback. For a release, keep source, binary, bootstrap pin, broker generation and published book revision. Leave unavailable fields unknown.

Queue, placement and seat contracts

These designs extend the queue, placement and agent contracts. Acceptance criteria below describe proposed improvements unless a source records a completed proof.

Claim, renewal and recovery

One successful conditional update can grant one holder at a time. It cannot prevent an expired worker from continuing to execute. Define the durable grant as task ID, lease epoch, authenticated worker instance, issue time and broker-authoritative deadline. Every lifecycle mutation must check the current epoch, holder and state. Increment the epoch on reassignment. Give a claim request a stable retry ID. Commit grant, receipt and event together; after an ambiguous response retrieve the committed receipt before seeking another grant.

For an external effect, keep a logical operation ID across lease epochs. Where the sink supports it, enforce fencing or idempotency at the sink. If an irreversible sink cannot prove whether an operation happened, park for reconciliation. Promotion of a Turso writer requires evidence that acknowledged grants survive failover. A replica that can serve reads is insufficient proof of write authority.

The intake lease has a different purpose from the general 45-minute default. Preserve intentional long execution while measuring abandonment delay. A successful early heartbeat must not shorten an active lease. Use a controlled clock to compare default renewal at minute five of a four-hour lease against its existing expiry. Test expiry, wrong holder and late completion separately. Queue reliability · Lease design

Repair and wake behavior

The six-queue census inspected 449 blocked or parked rows. Of 37 repairable candidates, the operator subsequently reported 37 successful writes. Six unrepairable rows, two concurrently moved rows and 404 schema-clean rows accounted for the rest of the census. The semantic packet-defect tags overlapped those classifications. Do not replay the dated drain. Census · Write ledger

The release code checked live holders, updated by task ID and status, then wrote an event in a separate execution. A concurrent edit keeping the same status could be overwritten. Repairing packet shape should preserve unrelated holds, unresolved dependencies and active claims. Proposed write boundary: verify row revision and quarantine provenance, recheck duplicates at the writer, perform the allowed field update and append its receipt inside one transaction. A rejected attempt must leave the row untouched. Reconcile audit events against the ledger before attributing any subsequent movement to repair. Atomic repair and independent holds · Inspected update

A wake has a cause. Time-based parks may expire at their timestamp. Task status, specific event, terminal task or human-answer conditions require the corresponding observation. Test the original double-serve against completed holders under equal and different keys, a valid timer wake, a deliberate override and cancelled or failed revival. Include an independent eligible task to catch a fix that suppresses all work. For scale, use isolated fixtures sampled from observed task/status distributions at 1× and 10× volume. Race 1, 8, 16 and 32 lanes on both one item and independent items. Record successful grants/s, attempts/s, deadline failures, wake lag, broker/tailnet latency, rows read/written and p50/p95/p99. Compare lost replies and restarts against durable grants. Production failover and the managed-database version of this experiment require explicit resource headroom. Fix

Placement policy

Cross-seat status retrieval from an empty local store was demonstrated with generation 6. The recorded status was dispatched. The provider run/attempt, terminal status, image used and billed minutes are independent receipts. A handle locates a session; access should require the reader’s repository grant. Bounded mirror failure must leave locally known, approved dispatch routes usable. Cross-seat proof

For each eligible surface, estimate time to finish using repo, command class, platform, image and verified cache affinity. Exclude unsupported visibility, platform, runner and quota modes before scoring. Count actual pool occupancy and pending reservations without double counting them. Treat macOS as a sublimit within the parent pool. A shared free-minute allowance needs atomic reservations or nonoverlapping seat allocations with expiry. Fall back to a known included route if the reservation authority is unavailable. Never infer free minutes from a successful workflow submission.

Use the same evaluator for explain and dispatch. Return input ages, exclusions, expected waits, cache savings, budget basis and tie-break. Stamp provider attempt and monotonic observation revision so a delayed running event cannot reverse completion. Distinguish the queue before assignment, provider wait, execution and result collection. Preserve stickiness while cache savings exceed predicted extra wait. Verify released decisions by replaying retained inputs and comparing outcomes by command class. Placement records

Enrolment, handoff and the shortlist

Maintain broker-bound seat identity, granted capabilities and policy revision separately from kind, display name, installation, boot ID, probe results and last seen. A shared service token establishes group membership; a verified per-seat principal is needed to enforce a per-seat permission. Enrolment retries for one installation should return the same seat. Alias collisions must preserve existing work. Keep first-claim lane registration and retain active-owner protection; a stale display name alone cannot hold a lane indefinitely. Test simultaneous claims using equal worker names and distinct authenticated instances.

Retain bridge, queue, GitHub and shell probes for ordinary enrolment. Add a metadata-only scoped check for roles needing secret access. A broker read, observed commit and successful bridge send each prove different facts. Record lifecycle events with a stable observation time and source. Test revocation on an older client at the broker.

For the shortlist, treat eight entries and a low-water mark of three as the control. Record task revision and timestamps at candidate observation, handout and claim. Separate already-dispositioned entries from races between handout and claim. In shadow evaluate host-local and per-seat lists on identical snapshots. Compare valid handouts per refresh, latency to claim, duplicate recommendations and depletion at peak load. Intake program

Bind a proposed single-use 15-minute handoff to sender, receiving seat, checkpoint digest and current lease. Redeem and transfer atomically, returning the previous result for a retry of the same operation. An expired offer preserves the original holder until ordinary lease policy applies. Keep grouping, reply threading, delivery and acceptance as distinct bridge fields. Retried delivery must not transfer a lease twice. Oracles include competing redemptions, late heartbeats, wrong recipient, expired offer, lost acknowledgement, and a duplicate notification after completion.

Brokers, remote builds and the release train

D. Secrets broker and credential distribution

At the November 23 review, #13081 was open and Xaltha owned the active correction. PR #13125 remained unmerged. The implicated heal script repeatedly restarted a cold broker before its first refresh completed. Xaltha’s later two successful heal invocations used an already-warm broker. The recorded sandbox change still permits restarting a refresh after its progress counter stalls. Its propagation and a cold activation need separate evidence. Incident and ownership · PR #13125

The inspected broker serializes refreshes, bounds each provider child to 60 seconds, and performs a list followed by eight-way parallel gets. Its default full-refresh interval is 900 seconds. Its health handler derives serving readiness from a previous successful refresh. At 221 entries a full sweep therefore models 222 child starts, or 2,211 at 2,210 entries, excluding retries and read-through misses. These are subprocess counts. Provider request counts and elapsed times require separate measurement. Broker source

Proposed refresh experiment. Use synthetic projects of those two sizes and revisions changing 0%, 1% and 100% of entries. Verify which fields a project-scoped list returns in the installed CLI. If it supplies complete values and revisions, parse once in memory. Otherwise reuse unchanged entries by immutable item ID and revision, and fetch changed entries only. Instrument child starts, provider calls, peak memory, throttles and p95 cold/warm duration. Partial or unauthorized enumeration must never implicitly delete the cache. An authoritative scope revocation must prevent serving its entries. Tag writes by refresh epoch so a late response cannot reinstate an older value. Choose freshness by the consuming service’s revocation requirement. Provider CLI contract

Proposed distribution contract. A manifest binds a provider project and immutable item ID to a specific service principal, audience, seat capability, destination and file mode. Existing daemon/client token names that look similar cannot substitute for each other. Install atomically with the intended owner and mode 0600. Require an encrypted private local copy for approved credentials and verify it with revision metadata and an isolated restore canary. Report only the outcome. Privileged issuance and deployment require current authorization. Designated continuity credentials may serve a prior value only within an explicit audience, expiry and maximum stale age. Denial or known revocation ends every fallback; a transport error is a separate outcome. Enrolment precedent · Scoping work

E. Channel recovery and broker generations

Proposed health reports expose liveness, readiness, observation time, dependency status, serving generation and operation progress. A dependency failure should never fan out into a series of downstream restarts.

LegDiscriminating observationRecovery owner
TailnetLocal daemon available; expected peer reachableHost service manager handles absent daemon. A peer outage has its own disposition.
RelayListener accepts and completes its upstream handshakeRelay supervisor reconnects once transport is ready.
Session brokerExpected protocol version and framed health responseBroker supervisor repairs a failed listener or handshake.
Secrets brokerFirst successful refresh, current activity and scoped canaryRefresh worker times out provider calls and retries. While refreshing:true, heal reports slowness and leaves the process running.
GitHubAuthenticated read succeeds for the intended repositoryCredential owner handles denial; rate limits get bounded backoff.

Cutover contract. Size each gate from the slowest supported legitimate cold operation including allowed retries and probe delay. A child timeout bounds one fetch, not the entire inventory. Deploy through the registered per-service generation path. Proposed hardening serializes deploy and heal per service, journals the candidate and prior closure before switching, then records the serving executable digest after readiness. Reconcile interrupted switches at both journal boundaries. A test with two generations on the same port must demonstrate that rollback restores the former listener’s executable identity, the pointer and journal, and a successful authenticated canary. Generation machinery

Cold-recovery oracle. In a disposable stack, pause the second synthetic fetch across two normal heal decisions. The broker PID must survive both, finish the sweep and serve the delayed entry. Test two concurrent healers and verify at most one recovery. Place an executable with an incompatible loader before a working binary; the version/protocol test-exec must select the latter. Terminate all five disposable legs, restore them from their registered inputs, then invoke recovery again and require zero restarts. The production cutover needs the measured window and an available rollback generation. Cold-start incident

F. Remote verification and caching

The executor image, run environment and workload have separate acceptance records. Upstream #105 added root-compatible runtime preparation. Publication attempt 45193636584 built the images and passed all five warm exports; its smoke job, step 8 failed the offline root warmed-shell check at 14:50:01 UTC. The preceding vscode step owned the flake tree. #106 restored root ownership before that check. The fix-branch publication passed. A subsequent main publication, run 45228189518 at merge SHA 95d6c5da7c9e, completed successfully at 17:58:39 UTC on November 23. All eight jobs passed, including the five warm exports, full build and smoke. Quota, operator visibility and integration contracts

Fleet and pm-stack share work, but each fact needs an owner. The quota gatherer observes a provider’s plan window. A queue broker can grant a lease. A runner can attest that a command exited successfully. An operator needs to connect those records without giving any one of them more authority than it has. This chapter records the inspected implementation and proposes the contracts that still need engineering and acceptance.

H. Plan quota and admission

What the projection already decides

The pm-stack admission projection consumes observations for an exact provider binding and window. At the inspected revision a missing, retained, failed, conflicting or stale observation can yield unknown. The freshness cutoff is the smaller of the window’s policy limit and 60 minutes. A prior wall in the same period is an independent input. A measured 100% walls a window. A reading of at least 99.5% requires a preceding, consistent reading at or above that threshold, using the same denominator and at least the collection interval between them. This is a decision about admission to a window. Disabling a provider also requires less than 1% remaining in its binding window and corroborating plan-limit failures under the program’s operating policy. Admission projection · Program ruling

The S4 projection accepts a fresh, scoped wall-time forecast. It can return pace_hold for an otherwise eligible window when predicted exhaustion precedes reset by the configured margin. The default is off. Enabling it requires a single named pool and a positive integer margin. The S4 implementation merged in #13271. Its live trial remains a separate acceptance gate on #12698. Keep the decision function in pm-stack so changes to freshness, window interpretation or failure handling have one implementation and one fixture set. Flag parser · S4 acceptance

Evidence for enabling a forecast

The S3 history format carries the observed live and shadow orderings and the inputs behind their differences. A rollout needs the deployed build, first and last qualifying production ticks, missing or duplicated ticks, and outcomes scored against S2. On November 23 an operator reported 56 history lines covering 02:30–16:00 UTC. The observation establishes an initial interval. An uninterrupted week starting at its reported first timestamp would reach November 30 at 02:30 UTC. The later on-host audit dates the first qualifying record and quantifies duplicate and missing quarter-hour buckets. Post the difference rate and realized outcomes to the existing epic. Then calibrate the margin for the designated S4 pool, run its own live week, and exercise the flag-only rollback. History format · Operator observation and remaining gates

S7 has produced a weekly review. The first report scored 1,213 forecasts across a table of 17 pools, including pools with zero scored forecasts. One report proves an invocation. Repeated timer invocations, S3 history and S4 live outcomes each need their own evidence. The epic also tracks a second weekly result. First S7 report · S7 closure

Proposed Fleet interface and acceptance

Publish a versioned decision containing the pool binding, billing mode, plan window, reset time, last attempted read, last genuine measurement, quality, verdict, policy revision and evidence IDs. On expiry attempt a bounded refresh. A failed refresh records its own time and leaves the genuine observation timestamp intact. Unknown capacity leaves an established plan-only route eligible. Fresh evidence is required to rank a pool by remaining quota or to introduce a new wall. Exclude funds-backed or unknown-billing routes. Prefer eligible nonreserve pools by binding expiry; keep OpenAI in reserve. A 402 ends the attempt. Allow at most one safe retry across plan-only routes under one logical request ID. A repeated failure for that same request cannot independently confirm provider-wide disablement.

Use a fixed-clock test for fresh versus stale reads at exactly 3,600 and 3,601 seconds, an intervening failed observation between high readings, reset rollover, and 1.00% versus 0.99% remaining. The oracle is the projected verdict, reason, evidence IDs and selected billing mode. Record retries at the provider-call boundary. Add per-section coverage and error by completed reset period to the weekly report. Send allowlisted, idempotent decision and observation summaries to Atlas. Preserve unallocated shared-plan burn explicitly and keep zero-sample rows visible.

I. An operator’s cross-system read

Fleet already has queue inspection and placement session reads. The PM work inspection design has its own issue and verification history. The following is a proposal for an aggregated operator view. Check registered verbs before assigning it a command name. Existing read contracts expose authorities with different clocks, outages and access scopes. Queue inspection · Placement sessions · PM work inspection

Operator questionPrimary evidenceBehavior when evidence is incomplete
Which work can run?Queue counts and unmet requirements at one broker watermark, with current lease and eligibility reasonCount quarantined work once in its stored status and expose its defect class. A failed read yields unknown depth.
Which runs are executing?Placement session, dispatch receipt, provider run ID and attemptExpose submitted, queued, running and terminal observations separately. Keep uncorrelated submissions visible.
Which seat and build answered?Authenticated seat principal and observed instance, generation registry, running executable identityShow reported aliases and verified identity separately. An available endpoint alone cannot establish a source revision.
What is waiting?Append-only task events, last substantive checkpoint, recorded blocker and declared wake conditionAt 48 hours without progress show the item, age and blocker. Separate a deliberate future wake from an overdue one. Heartbeats measure liveness.
What capacity did it consume?Provider billing scope, run attempt, observed plan window and task allocationDeduplicate reruns and reports by their correct identities. Expose unknown attribution and distinguish included minutes, forecasts and measured usage.

Implement the proposed aggregator as bounded, independently failing reads. Every section returns source, scope, observation time, watermark and freshness. Authorize each source before aggregation. A denied source must reveal neither counts nor identifiers. Generate a redacted report from the same records for Atlas ingestion. Its export watermark and schema revision make replay deterministic. Preserve a link to restricted source evidence for authorized operators. Coordinate with the existing work on queue figures and lane attribution. Queue-health provenance · Lane attribution

The first acceptance fixture holds one source offline while another legitimately returns zero. A second fixture supplies terminal and late running observations in reverse order, followed by a provider rerun; independently score each attempt. A third advances the clock over 48 hours with background heartbeats and compares a scheduled sleep with an overdue wake. A fourth divides a single included run between two tasks; attributable shares plus unknown must equal provider total. Re-run the export from the same watermark and require identical record identities.

J. Atlas, ID and mcpx

Atlas search and freshness

The Fleet search crate exposes a CLI client entry point. Serving is gated separately. The existing Atlas client parity work supplies an independent backend oracle for chunk identity and ranking. Preserve that oracle as a typed client is extracted. Atlas owns index freshness. Fleet owns authorization context, request semantics, timeout, cache identity and the age shown to the caller. Search crate · Client completion record · Atlas program

Key reusable results on normalized query, filters, result bound, index generation, ranking revision and authorization scope. A bounded batch returns a typed result or error for each request. Offline reads require an authorized local corpus, a known watermark and an explicit maximum age. Test scope changes, invalidated generations, mixed-success batches and attempted use after offline expiry. Compare IDs and scores under an immutable snapshot, then test metadata age independently. Use allowlisted query templates and explicit relevance judgments to propose additions to the Atlas golden set.

ID as a library consumer

A Rust library target proves that code compiles as a library only after a consumer actually builds it. Stable embedding also requires explicit configuration, source scope, cancellation, versioned behavior and control over process effects. The queue’s client feature exposes queue client and placement modules. Broker functions have separate gates. Fleet’s secrets resolver exposes source and retry types that support explicit injection. The pm-dispatch entry accepts CLI-style arguments and returns an exit code. Preserve the distinction between pm-dispatch and remote-build placement in a library API. Queue library · Secrets resolver · PM dispatch · ID program

Start with an external ID fixture using a synthetic, scope-limited secret source and a fake clock. Require a redacted error on denial, bounded timeout and no implicit ambient source. Extend to queue and remote-build session reads using a pinned fixture and the public CLI as a parity oracle. Admit claim and completion after stale-owner fencing and lost-reply recovery pass through both the library and broker.

mcpx and rollout

Propose an initial MCP tier for scoped queue summaries, individual task inspection, session status and bounded audit pages. Bind the caller’s authenticated principal to broker policy. Enforce row, byte, time and concurrency ceilings in the server; return a scoped continuation cursor when a page is incomplete. Compare two independent client implementations with the same broker snapshot. Test revocation, a cursor copied across principals, replay, timeout and partial reads. Evaluate a mutation tier only after idempotency, lease fencing and protocol negotiation are proven. Keep command execution and secret-value export outside that interface.

MilestoneDeliverableRelease criterion
V1 — observationsSerialize existing quota and status evidence; add read-only external consumer fixturesFixed-clock policy fixtures and CLI/library parity pass at an immutable ref.
V2 — shared readsAdd authorized aggregation, page bounds, Atlas generation-aware caching and MCP read adaptersA denied caller cannot recover identifiers from counts, cursors, cache entries or errors. A single-source outage yields partial evidence.
V3 — operationsPublish scoped report exports and measured S4 acceptance; consider queue mutation interfaces separatelyExport replay is idempotent, measured trials have dated receipts, and losing a response never creates duplicate effects.

All milestones alter shared contracts. Tie the published chapter, command inventory, supported wire revision and named test oracle to the same reviewed change. Keep the existing PM, Atlas and ID tracking issues responsible for their own acceptance.

Match exact body markers. Check the comments for operational gates and corrections. Treat container membership and runtime-only references separately from hard design edges.
