Running the brokers as services

Fleet’s long-running roles are broker services. Where they run depends on the seat: on the laptop they are systemd services owned by the deployment machinery; on a sandbox seat they are detached processes spawned by fleet init. This chapter covers both models. For deploying new generations of the laptop services, see Release and rollout. For checking them, see Health checks and the heal stack.

The laptop model: deploy.py profiles

On the laptop, services are defined in pkgs/deploy/services.nix and deployed by pkgs/deploy/deploy.py (see Release and rollout for the full profile, generation, and rollback mechanics). The properties that matter day to day:

  • Each service gets a per-service Nix profile under the profile base (system scope: /nix/var/nix/profiles/per-service).
  • deploy.py renders a systemd unit per service whose ExecStart points at the profile’s current link — <base>/<name>/current/<entryPoint> — never at a bare store path. A generation flip is therefore a profile repoint plus a restart of that one unit; the unit file does not change.
  • Activation restarts only that unit, health-checks it, and flips the profile back to the previous generation on failure.
  • The generation history is the append-only JSONL log per target; deploy status folds it to report current and previous generations.

The four laptop services

Three of the laptop’s services are fleet’s own; the fourth group is the pm stack that shares the same deployment machinery and the same host.

ServiceRunsPortRestartHealth
queue-brokerfleet serve queue-broker, backend turso4801on-failureUnauthenticated GET /healthz
secrets-brokerfleet serve secrets-broker4800on-failureGET /health (503 until the first successful refresh — that is a state, not a crash; see Troubleshooting)
laptop-agentbin/laptop-agent (its own package, not the fleet binary)4799alwaysNo unauthenticated endpoint; verified through the authenticated client
pm stack neighbourspm-aggregator, pm-projector, pm-tunnel, and the other Cloudflare/pm-stack targets declared in the same services.nix registryper definitionper definitionper definition

Operational notes:

  • The queue-broker binds its HTTP surface with the agent token required on every route except GET /healthz. Its Turso backend comes up on a startup thread, so /healthz and /validate answer before the backend is ready; a broker that answers /healthz but fails verbs with transport errors is still starting, or its backend token is wrong.
  • The secrets-broker binds the laptop tailnet address only on the laptop. Sandbox consumers reach it through the session proxy — except on the sandbox itself, where fleet init runs a local loopback copy (next section).
  • laptop-agent restarts always on purpose: under on-failure, a clean SIGTERM or success exit leaves the daemon down. Do not “fix” that back.
  • fleet serve can also run several roles in one process: fleet serve queue-broker secrets-broker … parses a multi-role list, capability-checks the whole list before anything binds (a role this invocation cannot run stubs the entire list at exit 69, with no partial start), and spawns one thread per role. A role thread’s failure fails the process — the supervisor (systemd) restarts the unit. The deployed profiles nonetheless spell one role per unit, so each broker restarts and health-checks independently.

fleet init in systemd mode (laptop)

fleet init never detached-spawns a daemon systemd owns. For each role in the host manifest it reports the fleet-<role>.service state via systemctl --user is-active: an active unit is a no-op; an inactive but existing unit is started with systemctl --user start; a missing unit is reported and skipped, not an error; unavailable systemctl is a report, not a spawn. Roles the manifest disables are reported as skipped with their reason, and the [domains] config gate wins over the manifest.

The sandbox model: roles spawned by fleet init

A sandbox seat has no systemd ownership of fleet roles. There, fleet init uses spawn mode, which exists for exactly two roles; any other role in a spawn manifest is reported and skipped, never spawned. fleet init also runs session initialisation first; a session error exits 2 before any role work. A build whose usable surface lacks proxy-serve can only stub init (exit 69).

  1. proxy (the session proxy / session broker) — init probes the broker socket and says hello. A live broker, in either protocol dialect, means status plus PATH-shim sync, and nothing more: a strict no-op. Init never spawns over, restarts, or fights an incumbent broker. Only an unanswered socket spawns fleet serve proxy, detached, after which init syncs shims from the new broker’s services map.
  2. secrets-broker — init probes its Unix socket; a live answer means status and out. Otherwise it spawns fleet serve secrets-broker detached (setsid, output appended to secrets-broker.log beside the socket) with SECRETS_BROKER_BIND=127.0.0.1:4800 set explicitly — and the broker forces loopback itself when the seat’s location is the sandbox, so the sandbox broker is loopback-only twice over. Init then waits (50 × 100 ms probes) for the socket to answer before reporting success.

Two more init behaviours to know:

  • Report mode. Given no roles to start, init reports state — every source consulted, plus detected hostname/OS/systemd for the report only (detection never selects roles) — starts nothing, and exits 69. “Never guess-start a role” is the rule.
  • Provision before the binary flip. fleet init resolves location and roles from the [host] section of fleet.toml. When rolling out a binary that understands a new config shape, write the [host] config first, pin the init call site, and only then deploy the binary. Rollback warning: pre-location-aware binaries parse-error on a fleet.toml containing [host] (strict unknown-field rejection), so config and binary roll back together.

Restart and health expectations

  • A broker that is down is restarted by its supervisor: systemd on the laptop (per the profile’s restart policy), the heal stack on a sandbox seat (see Health checks and the heal stack).
  • Do not restart-loop a broker that is up but not serving. The canonical case is the secrets-broker before its first successful refresh: the process is alive, /health answers 503 with serving=false, and restarting it only restarts the refresh clock. Diagnose the refresh instead — see Troubleshooting.
  • After any restart, verify with the health surfaces, not with process existence: /healthz for the queue-broker, /health for the secrets-broker, fleet queue health for the queue as a client sees it, and fleet agent doctor for the seat as a whole.

Health checks and the heal stack

Fleet has no single health endpoint; it has a health surface per layer, and the right check depends on which layer you doubt. This chapter lists every surface, then describes the self-healing chain that keeps a sandbox seat’s broker stack alive. For symptom-driven diagnosis, see Troubleshooting. For how the services are run, see Running the brokers as services.

Every health surface

SurfaceCommand / routeWhat it proves
Queue as a client sees itfleet queue health [--queue <name>] [--worker <id>]The queue client can reach the broker (POST /health) and the broker’s health rows come back. --worker scopes the answer to that worker’s view. Distinct from the broker’s own unauthenticated probe, below.
Queue-broker livenessGET /healthz on the queue-broker (port 4801 on the laptop)The broker process answers. Unauthenticated — the only unauthenticated queue-broker route. It answers before the Turso backend is up (the backend starts on a separate thread), so it proves liveness, not readiness.
Secrets-broker readinessGET /health on the secrets-broker (port 4800)Returns {ok, serving, secrets, last_refresh_unix, refreshing, oldest_secret_age_seconds}. 503 while serving is false — serving becomes true only once at least one refresh has succeeded. The public response exposes readiness and timing. An authenticated not-loaded secret read can include refresh_error after a failed refresh. A live process whose bws cannot run is not serving, and this endpoint says so.
Session-broker (proxy) livenessfleet proxy broker hello via fleet init’s probe; the broker also self-checks its peersThe session proxy answers on its socket and speaks the hello/capability handshake. fleet init reporting the proxy role as live is the practical check.
Bridge healthfleet bridge healthThe message bridge’s /healthz answers. No token needed. Proves the bridge service, not your seat’s mailbox access — for that, read a mailbox (fleet bridge inbox --agent <name> --limit 1).
Seat health, all legsfleet agent doctor [--agent <name>]Four independent probes issued together — the legs: bridge (bridge inbox --agent A --limit 1 with a name, else bridge health), queue (queue health), github (gh api rate_limit via fleet gh, falling back to plain signed-in gh), shell (laptop-agent health). There is no secrets leg: secrets is folded into the bridge leg’s stated need. From the legs, doctor derives the rungs map (which intake rungs this seat still has: push = bridge leg, queue = queue leg, shortlist = always true, priority = github leg) and the builds line. Exit 0 when any intake rung is live, else 3.
gh cache daemonfleet gh cache-statusProbes the gh cache daemon: whether it is running, where it is bound, and its cache state. No daemon is a transport-down answer (exit 3), not a crash.
Laptop-agent daemonfleet laptop-agent healthPrints the daemon’s health JSON verbatim (its GET /health, token-authenticated); exit 0 on an answer. This is the shell leg of doctor and the post-activation check for the laptop-agent deploy profile, which has no unauthenticated health endpoint.
Dispatch servicefleet dispatch statusThe pm-dispatch service’s GET /health body, printed verbatim.
The binary itselffleet version / fleet capabilitiesBuild name, derived version, source revision, and the usable capability set. The first thing to collect when a seat behaves as if a verb or domain were missing — see the stub entry in Troubleshooting.

Two reading rules:

  • Liveness is not readiness. /healthz answering, a process existing, and a port listening are each weaker than the check one layer up. Always confirm with the highest surface that matches the complaint: a queue complaint gets fleet queue health, a seat complaint gets fleet agent doctor.
  • 503 from the secrets-broker is information, not failure. It distinguishes “not loaded yet” from “no such secret” (404) and from “the source failed” (502). Clients key on it; so should you.

The heal stack (sandbox seat)

A sandbox seat’s broker stack has several moving parts between a fleet command and the laptop, and any of them can die with the seat’s runtime. The heal chain rebuilds them in dependency order:

tailscaled → relay :3130 → session broker → secrets broker → gh
  1. tailscaled — the tailnet itself. Nothing downstream works without it.
  2. The relay on port 3130 — a local relay that carries the seat’s session-proxy traffic to the tailnet proxy. Userspace-networking seats route the session proxy through a CONNECT proxy fleet expects on port 3130; the relay is what makes that port answer.
  3. The session broker — the session proxy broker process (fleet serve proxy), spawned via fleet init when its socket does not answer (see Running the brokers as services).
  4. The secrets broker — the seat’s loopback secrets-broker, spawned the same way when its socket does not answer.
  5. gh — the gh command shim and the pristine gh binary it routes to; the chain verifies both exist and answer, because a shim whose target is missing fails every gh call at once.

Order matters: starting the session broker before the relay is up produces a broker that cannot reach anything; starting the secrets broker before the session broker leaves secret consumers with nowhere to ask. The chain is therefore run whole, in this order, never piecemeal by hand.

The 5-minute heal cron

A cron job on the seat runs the heal check roughly every five minutes. Each run verifies channel health (the chain above), secrets health (the secrets-broker answering and serving), and gh. A healthy run is silent. An unhealthy leg is rebuilt by the same chain the bootstrap uses — the heal is a re-run of the bring-up for the dead leg and everything downstream of it, not a separate repair implementation.

init-ensure

init-ensure is the bring-up the heal cron and the bootstrap share. It:

  1. Test-executes fleet binary candidates before trusting one (a file can list as executable and still fail to execute, for example when its interpreter is absent), and points the seat’s gh entry point at a working binary.
  2. Delegates the channel to the heal chain above (tailscaled, relay, session broker).
  3. Fetches the secrets-broker token by name from Bitwarden Secrets Manager when the local token file is missing, so the secrets broker can start authenticated.
  4. Ensures the secrets broker and the gh route, completing the five legs.

The bootstrap’s boot hook re-runs the tailnet and fleet phases after a sandbox recycle under a lock with a timeout, because only the home directory survives a recycle. Between recycles, the 5-minute heal cron is what keeps the stack honest.

What to do when healing does not converge

  1. Run fleet agent doctor and note which legs are down — the heal chain fixes legs in order, so the first down leg is the one to look at.
  2. Check the leg’s own surface from the table above (for example fleet gh cache-status for the gh leg, /health for the secrets-broker).
  3. Do not restart-loop a broker that is up but not serving; see the secrets-refresh entry in Troubleshooting.
  4. If the channel itself (tailscaled / relay) is the first down leg and healing does not restore it, the seat cannot reach the laptop at all: queue and broker work will fail with transport errors (exit 3) while purely local work (the shortlist rung) still functions. That state is a channel outage, not a fleet bug — report it as such, with the doctor output attached.

Troubleshooting

Symptom → cause → fix. Each entry names the check that confirms the cause before you apply the fix. For the health surfaces referenced throughout, see Health checks and the heal stack; for how the services are run, see Running the brokers as services.

Session proxy down / “proxy closed during CONNECT”

  • Symptom: Fleet commands that need the laptop fail with transport errors (exit 3); proxy connections die during the CONNECT handshake.
  • Cause: One of the first legs of the heal chain is down: tailscaled, the local relay on port 3130, or the session broker itself. The session proxy is how a sandbox seat reaches the laptop’s brokers, so its failure looks like every broker failing at once.
  • Confirm: fleet agent doctor — the queue and shell legs are down while the github leg may still answer.
  • Fix: Let the heal chain rebuild in order (tailscaled → relay :3130 → session broker → secrets broker → gh); it runs on a roughly 5-minute cron, or re-run the seat’s init bring-up. Do not start the session broker by hand ahead of the relay — a broker started before its relay answers but reaches nothing.

Secrets broker stuck refreshing (503, very many bws fetches)

  • Symptom: fleet secrets get <name> fails or reports the broker not serving; GET /health on the secrets-broker answers 503 with serving=false for a long time; the broker’s refresh appears to run constantly (the shape recorded as issue #13081 involves on the order of 220 bws fetches in a refresh cycle).
  • Cause: The broker’s full-vault refresh has not yet succeeded. serving only becomes true once a refresh completes (last_refresh_unix is set); a refresh that keeps failing or being restarted keeps the broker in the not-serving state, and public /health continues to return 503.
  • Confirm: GET /health — check refreshing and last_refresh_unix. An authenticated secret read while the cache is unready can return a 503 body with refresh_error after a failed refresh. A cached read that succeeds carries source: "cache" and an age_seconds; that tells you the broker once served and how stale the value is.
  • Fix: Fix the refresh’s cause (the bws route and its token, by name — never by pasting a value anywhere), then let one refresh complete. Do not restart-loop the broker: every restart discards refresh progress and restarts the clock, converting a slow recovery into a permanent 503. A process that is alive and returning 503-with-serving=false is in a known state, not crashed.

Queue double-serve: a parked, completed, or cancelled task is served again (#13091)

  • Symptom: A task whose issue record shows it parked, completed, or cancelled is handed out by fleet queue claim as if it were live work.
  • Cause: The broker-side state and the GitHub issue record have diverged; the broker re-served a task whose terminal or parked disposition lives in the issue record. Recorded as issue #13091.
  • Confirm: Read the task (fleet queue show <id>) and the GitHub issue. Treat the issue record as the source of truth for disposition.
  • Fix (workaround): Re-park the task (fleet queue park <id>) so the broker state matches the record, and note the double-serve on the issue. Do not work the task a second time, and do not complete it “again” — a duplicate completion corrupts the lane ledger. The no-double-serve guard (the client checking a fresh claim against the GitHub fallback and holding it with reason-class fallback_held, exit 5) covers the claim path it can see; a re-serve that bypasses it is the bug, not operator error.

Stub: exit 69

  • Symptom: A command prints a three-line block to stderr and exits 69, without doing any work.
  • Cause: The domain is not usable in this invocation. Exit 69 is EX_UNAVAILABLE: the stub is the binary working as designed, not a crash. The first line decodes which of the four wordings you got:
    1. “this build does not include ‘<domain>’” — NotInBuild: the capability was never compiled into this variant (for example, asking fleet-connect for the queue).
    2. “invoked as ‘<name>’, this build does not include ‘<domain>’” — NarrowedByName: the binary has the domain, but the hyphenated argv0 profile narrowed it out. Re-invoke as plain fleet.
    3. “‘<domain>’ is disabled by config on this host” — DisabledByConfig: the [domains] table in this host’s fleet.toml disables it. The stub names the config file; re-enable it there if the disable is not a deliberate incident lever.
    4. “‘<domain>’ is included in this build but not implemented yet” — Available-form: compiled in, nothing behind it.
  • Confirm: fleet capabilities — the domain’s state field says the same thing in JSON (not-in-build, narrowed-by-name, disabled-by-config, available), and the second stub line lists the capabilities this invocation can use.
  • Fix: Match the wording: use the full build, invoke as fleet, or re-enable in config. Never “fix” a stub by reinstalling — the install is telling you the truth about itself.

GitHub rate limits: user token versus the App route

  • Symptom: gh calls (direct or via fleet gh) fail with rate-limit errors — rate limit, rate_limit, too many requests, HTTP 429.
  • Cause: The token that made the call exhausted its bucket. The user (personal) token and the GitHub App installation tokens are separate buckets with separate limits.
  • How fleet gh handles it: fleet gh rotates credentials in a fixed order — the fleet App’s installations first, then the developing.today App’s, then the backup App’s, and the personal token last — and a rate-limit (or permission) failure is one of the two classes that may be retried under the next token, because the limiter refuses the request before it is processed, so replaying a write is safe. Other failure classes are retried under a fresh token only for read-only calls.
  • Fix: Prefer fleet gh over plain gh for fleet work so rotation applies. If you hit a limit on plain gh, switch routes rather than retrying in a loop — a rate-limited write that cannot go through the CLI route belongs in the creation outbox, which paces creates and backs off on consecutive rate limits (300 s, up to its attempt budget) instead of hammering. Check which route you are on with fleet agent doctor (the github leg reports route: "fleet" or "plain").

Claim rejected: lane/worker mismatch (#6853 shape)

  • Symptom: Holder verbs (heartbeat, checkpoint, park, release, block, fail, complete) fail with exit 5 and a “no matching claimed row” error, although the task is visibly claimed.
  • Cause: The broker checks the holder by worker and lane: all scheduled lanes share one worker id, so the lane is what tells the broker whose claim a verb acts on. A verb issued with the wrong --lane (or a lane from a different registered lane/worker family — the registered_lane_worker families of issue #6853) does not match the claimed row.
  • Confirm: Compare the claim’s lane and worker (fleet queue show <id>, the claim output) with what your command resolved: --lane flag, else the REPO_QUEUE_LANE environment variable, else null (broker checks the worker alone). Also confirm the row is non-terminal — the same exit 5 covers “already terminal”.
  • Fix: Re-issue with the claiming lane (--lane <id>) and the claiming worker. Do not release and re-claim to work around it; that churns the lease and the timeline.

TLS UnknownIssuer from sandbox seats (#13122)

  • Symptom: HTTPS calls from a sandbox seat fail certificate validation with an UnknownIssuer error, while gh itself works.
  • Cause: The sandbox’s egress proxy intercepts TLS. A client validating against the webpki root store alone does not trust the interception chain; the platform root store does. (This is why fleet gh’s App legs validate against the platform root store rather than webpki roots alone.)
  • Confirm: The same call succeeds through gh or through a platform-store client, and fails only from the webpki-only client. Recorded as issue #13122.
  • Fix: Use the route that validates against the platform store (fleet gh for GitHub API work). Do not disable certificate verification anywhere as a workaround — an unverified channel for fleet credentials is worse than the outage.

Lease expiry mid-work

  • Symptom: Work you are holding is claimed by someone else, or your next heartbeat / complete fails with exit 5 (“no matching claimed row”).
  • Cause: A claim is a lease, not a lock. Every claim first runs lease expiry opportunistically: abandoned claims whose lease lapsed become claimable at the moment anyone looks. If your heartbeats stopped (a stalled session, a long silent build), the lease lapsed and the task returned to the pool.
  • Confirm: fleet queue timeline <id> shows the expiry and any re-claim. Check the lease length you claimed with against the gap in your heartbeats.
  • Fix: Prevention, not recovery: heartbeat on a cadence well inside the lease, and checkpoint before long silent operations. If the task was re-claimed, coordinate through the issue record before touching it again — two workers on one task is the failure this system exists to prevent. If nobody re-claimed it, claim it again and continue.

verify-disposition gate rejections at complete

  • Symptom: fleet queue complete rejects the completion and leaves the task claimed, with a message naming a defect in the disposition record.
  • Cause: Completion of a fix-class task requires a verified disposition: the readback record produced by fleet queue verify-disposition <issue> --repo <owner/name>, which reads the issue and its linked PRs back from GitHub live. The broker’s gate is pure (no network) and checks: the record’s freshness (≤ 1800 s old by default; more than 300 s in the future is unreadable clock skew), that it describes this task’s issue, that the verdict matches the readback (for example merged_verified requires at least one merged pull in the readback), that every PR the completion links appears in the readback, and any follow-up (a follow-up issue must be open, not the issue being completed, and must link the completed issue and every unfinished PR; a successor PR must be in the readback and merged; a follow-up task is checked broker-side for a live status naming the same issue).
  • Confirm: Run the verb standalone — fleet queue verify-disposition <issue> --repo <repo> --json exits 0 when its record would pass the gate and 1 when the gate would reject it, so you can iterate without touching the claim.
  • Fix: Address the named defect — most often a stale record (re-run verify-disposition and complete promptly), a verdict the readback does not support (the work is not actually in the state claimed; finish or follow up the work first), or a missing follow-up for the open_draft_with_followup / open_draft_superseded verdicts (record the follow-up with --reason, which any follow-up target requires). The gate leaving the task claimed is deliberate: a rejected completion loses no work.

Deploying this book

This book is an mdBook that lives with the code it documents: sources in pkgs/fleet/book/, configuration in pkgs/fleet/book.toml, build definition in pkgs/fleet/docs.nix, published to the developing-today/code GitHub Pages site under /fleet/. This chapter describes exactly how that works — and, just as explicitly, the custom-domain step that is not wired yet.

For the rule that keeps the book’s content current, see Keeping this book current.

The pieces

  • pkgs/fleet/book.toml — mirrors the mcpx book’s configuration: title “fleet”, src = "book" (a dedicated folder; mcpx’s src is its pre-existing docs/ because that book grew out of an existing docs tree), build directory book, and create-missing = false — every chapter in SUMMARY.md must exist on disk; the build never invents stubs. The fleet book is plain mdBook: mcpx’s book uses a custom Go preprocessor and an agent-twin emitter, and fleet has no equivalent tools. That is a deliberate difference, not an omission.

  • pkgs/fleet/book/ — SUMMARY.md plus the chapters. index.md is the introduction.

  • pkgs/fleet/docs.nix — mirrors pkgs/mcpx/docs.nix minus the Go preprocessors. It takes a siteUrl argument (default "/") that is baked into the rendered book as mdBook’s output.html.site-url, injected at build time via the MDBOOK_OUTPUT__HTML__SITE_URL environment variable rather than stored in book.toml.

  • lib/default.nix — exposes the package next to its mcpx sibling: fleetDocs = pkgs.callPackage ../pkgs/fleet/docs.nix { }; and fleet-docs = fleetDocs; in the packages set, so the build is:

    nix build .#fleet-docs

The two workflows

Repository CI runs on main only, and the book follows the same policy.

fleet-docs.yml — build only

.github/workflows/fleet-docs.yml mirrors the mcpx build job: on push to main and on workflow_dispatch, it builds .#fleet-docs, stages the result, and verifies the rendered site (the index page exists). It never deploys. Its job is to fail by name on main when a chapter breaks the build — a missing SUMMARY.md target under create-missing = false, a bad link, a broken derivation — before the deploy path is involved.

mcpx-docs.yml — the combined Pages deploy

The deploy lives inside the existing .github/workflows/mcpx-docs.yml, whose deploy staging gains the fleet book. The reason is a hard constraint of GitHub Pages:

One repository has one Pages site, and a Pages deploy replaces the whole site.

The mcpx book already occupies https://developing-today.github.io/code/. A fleet-only deploy would publish an artifact containing only the fleet book — and wipe the mcpx book off the site. So the deploy job builds both books and stages one combined site:

site/          ← the mcpx book, built with siteUrl "/code/"
site/fleet/    ← the fleet book, built with siteUrl "/code/fleet/"

The fleet book is therefore reached at https://developing-today.github.io/code/fleet/, and its siteUrl is /code/fleet/ — the /code/ project-site prefix plus the fleet/ staging directory. The combined artifact then goes through the same publish shape as before: a staging job (configure-pages + upload-pages-artifact) and a separate publish job with the pages concurrency group and one retry, the job boundary existing so the Pages artifact metadata has time to propagate before deploy-pages fetches it.

GitHub Pages for developing-today/code is already enabled with build_type = "workflow" (source: GitHub Actions). There is no manual enable step, no gh-pages branch, and no generated HTML is ever committed.

Preview the book locally

  1. Build the packaged form from the repository root:

    nix build .#fleet-docs

  2. Open or serve result/index.html and check the chapter order, internal links, and search.

  3. Or, for a faster edit loop, build in place from pkgs/fleet/:

    mdbook build

    and preview the output directory named by book.toml. The Nix build is the authoritative check — it is the same derivation, mdBook version, and siteUrl handling the deploy uses.

Note the local default siteUrl is "/". Links inside the book are relative .md links, so local preview navigation works regardless; only absolute site URLs differ between the local build and the deployed one.

The future custom-domain step — not wired yet

Per the owner’s steer, the book will eventually be served from a custom domain instead of the github.io path. That step is planned, not wired: there is no CNAME file anywhere in the repository today, no custom domain is set on the Pages site (cname: null), and the siteUrl values above still point at /code/ and /code/fleet/. Do not present the custom domain as live, and do not “fix” URLs in anticipation of it.

When the step is taken, it has exactly three parts, done together:

  1. CNAME file — add the CNAME file naming the chosen domain to the deployed site artifact (it must ride in the combined staging of mcpx-docs.yml, alongside both books, or the next deploy removes it — whole-site replacement cuts both ways).
  2. DNS record — create the DNS record for the domain pointing at GitHub Pages, in the account that owns the domain’s zone.
  3. Pages custom domain setting — set the custom domain on the repository’s Pages configuration so GitHub provisions the certificate and redirects the github.io address.

The same change must also move both books’ deploy siteUrl values from the /code/… paths to the domain-rooted paths, and update Keeping this book current and this chapter to describe the wired state. Until that change lands, this section stands as the record of intent.

FAQ

Short answers, each pointing at the chapter that owns the long one. For symptom-driven diagnosis, see Troubleshooting; for definitions, see Glossary.

Why is fleet one binary instead of a tool per job?

One multicall binary means one artefact to build, pin, publish, and roll out to every seat, and one registry that every build knows in full — so --help and fleet capabilities are complete even on a narrowed build, and an unavailable domain answers with an informative stub instead of “command not found”. Domains are compiled in per variant by Cargo features; hyphenated names (fleet-serve, fleet-connect) and aliases (repo-queue) are argv0 personalities of the same binary. See Register a domain or capability.

Why did my command print a stub and exit 69?

The domain is not usable in that invocation: not compiled into the build, narrowed out by the invocation name, or disabled by config on that host. The stub’s first line says which; fleet capabilities says it in JSON. Exit 69 is EX_UNAVAILABLE — the binary working as designed. See the stub entry in Troubleshooting.

How recent are the GitHub issues in a Fleet flow report?

The report header identifies the source file, when its paginated issue collection began, and the reference time used for age calculations. In JSON, read inputs.issues_fetch_started_at and issues.as_of. With a legacy file or rows from several collections, collection time is unknown (JSON null). Running the report again or passing --now updates the calculation clock only. Re-run the flow reporter’s fetch command for a new observation.

The broker is down — what do I do?

First, find out which broker and which layer: fleet agent doctor for the seat, fleet queue health for the queue, GET /health for the secrets-broker. On a sandbox seat, the heal chain rebuilds the stack in order (tailscaled → relay → session broker → secrets broker → gh) on a roughly five-minute cycle. On the laptop, systemd owns the brokers — check the unit, and redeploy through the profile if the generation is bad. If the queue-broker is unreachable for a work verb, the client switches to the GitHub fallback with exit 6 rather than failing outright. See Health checks and the heal stack.

Where do secrets come from?

By name, never by value in files or commands. The resolution path is the secrets-broker protocol first (a Bitwarden Secrets Manager cache that refreshes on a TTL), then the bws CLI as fallback, then op where a vault is named. Deploy definitions, bootstrap scripts, and this book name secrets; they never carry values. A secret minted moments ago is visible immediately: a cache miss reads through to Bitwarden for that one name.

Why did placement pick Blacksmith?

Placement is a tiered cascade over the surfaces in fleet-surfaces.json: free GitHub-hosted Actions capacity first (Tier 1, least-loaded owner first), then Blacksmith (Tier 2) within its monthly budget — Blacksmith is a budgeted fallback, not a default, and a dispatch can require explicit allowance for paid capacity. A --followup dispatch sticks to the previous session’s surface when that surface still has capacity and its owner’s queued count is below the sticky threshold (2 on every shipped surface). See also: why did placement pick anything — it picks from live capacity and local session history, per owner, not per repository whim.

What is an fp_ handle?

The handle of a placement dispatch session: fp_ plus a 128-bit random value, printed when fleet queue dispatch records the session. It names the dispatch session record (whose local records live in ~/.local/state/fleet-place/sessions.json) and is what fleet queue session status <handle> and fleet queue session result <handle> take. It is distinct from the workflow’s dispatch_id input, which is a separate fresh correlation id generated per dispatch when the surface’s workflow declares one. A portable alternative form for run correlation is OWNER/REPO#RUN_ID.

Can I use fleet as a library?

The workspace’s library crates (fleet-registry, fleet-config, fleet-secrets, fleet-queue, and the rest) are real crates with real APIs, and fleet’s own domains consume them that way. But they are an internal workspace on the atlas-search pattern — versioned together at 0.1.0, consumed by path, with no published-crate compatibility promise. Inside the repository, write against them freely; outside it, shell out to the binary, whose command contract is the stable surface.

How do I add a verb?

Follow Add a subcommand: registry entry, both usage strings, dispatch arm, handler, broker verb if it mutates state, fallback twin if it must work broker-down, oracle-named tests, and docs/verbs.md plus this book in the same change. For a flag on an existing verb, see Add a flag.

Which queue am I on?

There is one fleet queue; the --queue flag scopes within it, it does not select a different system. The subtleties: claim and list are unscoped when neither flag nor the REPO_QUEUE_DEFAULT_QUEUE environment variable is set (the broker works across the one queue); enqueue has no default queue at all and must name one; most other verbs default to repo-health-code-shadow via --queue’s default. If a verb behaved as if it could not see your task, check which of those three cases you were in before suspecting the broker.

Why exit 5?

Exit 5 is the queue client’s “the verb ran, but there is no matching claimed row / no claimable task” code. It covers: claim finding nothing claimable ({"task": null}), the no-double-serve guard holding a fresh claim (fallback_held), and every holder verb (heartbeat, checkpoint, park, release, block, fail, complete) whose worker/lane does not match the claimed row or whose row is already terminal. fleet agent next also exits 5 when no intake rung had work. See the lane/worker mismatch and lease-expiry entries in Troubleshooting.

Why did complete reject me?

Because completion of a fix-class task is evidence-gated: it must carry a verified disposition record from fleet queue verify-disposition, read back live from GitHub, and the broker’s gate found a defect — a stale record, a verdict the readback does not support, a linked PR missing from the readback, or a follow-up that fails its checks. The rejection leaves the task claimed, deliberately. Iterate with verify-disposition --json standalone (exit 0 means the record would pass) and complete promptly with a fresh record. See Troubleshooting.

Where is this book’s source?

In the repository, at pkgs/fleet/book/ (chapters) with pkgs/fleet/book.toml beside it and the build in pkgs/fleet/docs.nix, published as the .#fleet-docs package and deployed under /fleet/ on the combined Pages site. Build or preview it with the steps in Deploying this book. The book’s maintenance rule — it changes in the same pull request as the behaviour it describes — is Keeping this book current.

Why does the same secret name resolve differently on the laptop and the sandbox?

Because “the secrets-broker” is location-relative: on the laptop it is the tailnet-bound broker; on a sandbox seat, fleet init runs a local loopback copy on the same port. Both are caches of the same Bitwarden Secrets Manager source, resolved by the same name — what differs is which cache answers, and therefore the value’s age (age_seconds on a cache hit tells you). Check /health’s oldest_secret_age_seconds before assuming a rotation did not propagate.

Glossary

One-to-three sentence definitions, alphabetised. Chapters use these terms in these senses.

broker — A resident fleet service that other components ask over a socket or HTTP: the queue-broker owns queue state, the secrets-broker owns the secrets cache, and the session broker (the session proxy’s server half) owns laptop-channel connections. Brokers are the stateful centre; clients are replaceable.

capability — One of the 22 compile-time atoms in fleet-registry (queue, proxy-connect, search-serve, and so on) that decide what a build can do. A domain’s availability is derived from its capabilities, the invocation’s profile, and config, as one of four CapState values.

disposition — The verified account of what actually happened to a task’s issue and its linked pull requests, read back live from GitHub by verify-disposition. A completion that requires one must carry the record, and the broker’s gate checks it before the task may close.

envelope — The broker’s reply shape: {ok: true, …} carrying a row (or rows), or {ok: false, exit, error} carrying the exit code the client exits with and the message it prints. Clients do not invent errors; they relay envelopes.

fallback — Two senses, both load-bearing. (1) Transport fallback: the GitHub-issues transport of the queue in fleet-queue/src/fallback.rs, used when the broker path fails; a work verb switches to it with exit 6. (2) Resolution fallback: the next source in a chain, as in the secrets path falling back from the secrets-broker protocol to the bws CLI.

follow-up — A recorded successor that owns the remainder of unfinished work: a task, an issue, or a pull request named on a completion (with a --reason, always) so a task may close while linked work is still open. The disposition gate verifies it exists and is in the state claimed.

lane — A named work stream within a queue worker family, recorded on a claim so the broker can tell whose claim a holder verb acts on. All scheduled lanes share one worker id, so the lane — resolved from --lane, else the REPO_QUEUE_LANE environment variable, else null — is the discriminator.

leg — One of fleet agent doctor’s four independent probes: bridge, queue, github, shell. There is no secrets leg; secrets is folded into the bridge leg’s stated need. From the legs, doctor derives the rungs map.

outbox — The creation outbox: the broker-side queue for GitHub object creation (issues, pull requests, comments) that must survive crashes and rate limits. Producers enqueue; a single drainer claims, creates, verifies by read-back, and resolves, pacing creates and backing off on rate limits.

placement — The component that chooses where a dispatched job runs, from the surfaces registry, by live capacity and session history: a tiered cascade (free GitHub-hosted Actions, then budgeted Blacksmith, then the remaining surface kinds) with a hard-pin override and follow-up stickiness.

rung — One step of the fleet agent next intake ladder, tried in order: push (a bridge command addressed to the agent), queue (a queue claim), shortlist (the local file), priority (GitHub). A rung that is down is skipped and recorded; a rung that is empty is a different fact.

seat — One enrolled agent installation: a sandbox, a laptop, or another host running a fleet binary with its own identity, config, and token files. Rollout is verified per seat, because seats run whatever binary they were last given.

shortlist — The local file of candidate work an agent seat keeps for itself, managed by fleet agent shortlist. It is the one intake rung that is always available, because it needs no network, broker, or token.

stack — Merge-intent sense: a recorded, ordered set of merge intents (finished branches with their authoring lane, worker, and session) in the broker’s merge_intents table, managed by fleet queue stack. Not a call stack and not the pm stack.

stub — The three-line stderr block a domain answers with when it is not usable in an invocation, always exit 69 (EX_UNAVAILABLE). Its wording names the reason class: not in this build, narrowed out by the invocation name, disabled by config, or included but not implemented.

surface — Two related senses. (1) Execution surface: an entry in fleet-surfaces.json naming a place fleet work can run (a GitHub Actions pool, Blacksmith, a codespace pool, the laptop), with its owner, targets, status, and capacity facts. (2) Invocation surface: the set of capabilities a single fleet invocation can use, after build, profile, and config narrowing.

session proxy — The fleet proxy domain’s broker-and-client pair that carries a sandbox seat’s traffic to the laptop’s brokers over one channel, with a length-prefixed JSON wire protocol and a hello/capability handshake. proxy serve is the broker; proxy connect and proxy init are the client side.

tombstone — A terminal marker that records a task, claim, or session as deliberately dead, so later folds and replays skip it instead of resurrecting it. A tombstone is a record, not a deletion: the history stays readable.

variant — One of the three shipped capability profiles of the one binary — Full (fleet), Serve (fleet-serve), Connect (fleet-connect) — selected at build time by Cargo features and re-derivable at runtime from the compiled capability set. Hyphenated variant names double as argv0 profiles that narrow, never widen, an invocation’s surface.

worker — The identity that claims and holds queue tasks (--worker, default repo-worker-code, with named exceptions such as cancel’s fleet-monitor). Holder verbs are checked against the claiming worker and lane; a mismatch is exit 5.

Fleet research and development

Fleet coordinates how a seat obtains work, runs it within an included plan and leaves evidence another seat can verify. The program charter sets out the operating rules and the authority for each observation. The design record records the proposed direction for each workstream.

Use the delivery plan to find the next acceptance gate and the dated issue map to identify its prerequisites. Read current ownership and issue comments before starting work. The research chapters distinguish proposed contracts from released commands. A merged fix, a published binary, an activated service and a successfully observed workload each have their own receipt.

The dated investigation notebook retains the source comparisons, coverage counts, member-by-member inventory and acceptance fixtures underlying the research chapters. The native blocker ledger records each endpoint observation, including closed prerequisites.

Delivery plan and evidence gates

The program tracks implementation, rollout and acceptance separately. A completed source change can still require a deployment or a second-seat observation. The priority order below follows dependencies and the risk of mutating live work.

OrderDeliverablePrerequisite and acceptance
1Reconcile the November 23 packet repairsThe readback matched all 37 task/issue pairs and found one stored repair event per task. Record the independent disposition of the three completed tasks whose linked issues still had native prerequisites. Keep the six refused rows separate. Receipt
2Harden queue repair and fence lease mutationsCompare release source and current main. Reject concurrent row changes, preserve independent holds and atomically persist the disposition and audit receipt. An event-write failure leaves the original row intact. A late heartbeat from an old grant cannot renew its successor.
3Correct the operator referenceDerive dispatch examples from the serving version, document session mirroring and authenticated diagnostics, and check defaults against installation and upgrade paths. Build the existing book, check warnings, and read back the published pages.
4Make placement decisions auditableKeep the existing dry-run evaluator. Capture billing scope, constraint, reservation age, job attempt and measured queue delay. Compare predictions with actual outcomes by workload and surface. Confirm reuse of verified artifacts across authorized seats.
5Confirm the broker and executor cutoversUse a cold provider fixture for startup and recovery. On the executor path, identify the image digest actually pulled and the result of the workload. Preserve separate classifications for a smoke failure and a workload failure.
6Qualify the quota and status contractsRecord the first qualifying S3 observation and actual shadow interval, then complete the approved S4 trial, rollback exercise and forecast scoring. Correlate task, lease and job across the status view with source-specific freshness.
7Qualify Fleet libraries for external consumersPin a revision, explicit features and compiler, inject the consumer’s credentials and deadlines, and compare the CLI and library against the same broker fixture. Obtain Atlas, ID and mcpx contract acceptance from their owning programs.
8Change defaults only with measurementsUse disposable fixtures at measured traffic and ten times that volume. Run independent and contended claims with at least 16 lanes, measure queueing and writer latency, count abandoned grants, and retain cost headroom and the verification route.

Integrating new work

A discrepancy belongs on the owning issue with a source, a bounded change, its oracle and the person or system that can supply missing evidence. Check the governing hold and the latest claim before implementation and again before merge. Ship via an isolated worktree and immutable verification ref. Preserve the previous generation and closure when a deploy is part of the work.

Do not infer throughput from nominal slot counts. The three provider surfaces can share bottlenecks. Record first eligible time, dispatch acceptance, runner assignment, job start, completion and observation. A waiting submitter has no GitHub workflow time yet. A job that fails before its test process starts supplies no assertion verdict.

Historical investigations and live dispositions are dated. Native dependency edges, body-level acceptance requirements, queue projections and human holds can change independently. An issue’s priority is actionable only after those four records agree or their difference has an owner. Fleet coordinator · PM orchestration · ID · Atlas

Queue guarantees and dispatch decisions

A queue grant authorizes a worker to attempt a task. A provider run, a merge, and an external side effect each have their own authority and evidence. After a lost reply, a worker needs a way to identify which operations already committed before it retries.

What the November rollout proved

The November 23 acceptance receipt identifies a generation 6 broker and two seats at bcc8043. A second seat with an empty local cache resolved another seat’s placement handle. A later six-queue sweep read 449 blocked or parked rows. Its dry run produced 37 repairable missing dedupe attestations, six refusals, two intervening state changes and 404 rows without a validator defect. The subsequent operator ledger records all 37 candidate IDs transitioning to queued. This closes that drain. A new census needs a fresh watermark and new evidence. A packet gaining a valid shape can still refer to an issue with open dependencies. Cross-seat receipt · Census · Write receipts

The #13091 fix excluded condition parks from retries and absorbed already-completed work. Recheck future double-serve reports against the claimant’s source revision, the broker’s active generation, the prior disposition and the writer’s event order. Include a genuinely eligible task in the same test to distinguish a correct exclusion from a disabled claim path. Merged correction

Proposed grant and repair contract

The conditional claim update serializes the winner for an eligible row. Reply loss, expiry and reassignment still permit another attempt at the work. Give each grant a monotonic epoch and each process an instance ID. A claim request has a retry-stable ID. Commit the task mutation, lease record and receipt together at the writer. Authenticate holder, epoch, status and deadline when committing heartbeat, checkpoint, handoff or completion. A broker restart recovers the receipt from the writer. Establish acknowledged-write survival for the actual managed database configuration before promising survival of promotion. Require destination idempotency keyed to the logical operation, across epochs, for external effects. An unknown non-idempotent outcome goes to reconciliation before another execution. These guarantees implement the scope of the existing orchestration charter. Execution charter, §§13–14

Use the published queue repair workflow to preview candidate changes, check the current deduplication basis, and record the result for each issue. A refusal belongs in the operator receipt together with the route for resolving it. Queue repair · Atomic repair and independent holds

For an ageing quarantine, expose the defect class, affected fields, detecting validator revision, first unresolved event, last substantive transition and permitted repair route. A fairness sweep can touch a row without changing the disposition. An operator needs an unknown-age result when the necessary event has expired. Treat a missing dedupe stamp, absent repository, ambiguous priority, live holder and exhausted attempts as different defects. Only the first can acquire a new attestation solely from a successful live dedupe check. An authoritative producer can supply missing scope or priority. Preserve refusals with the responsible party and next observation.

Failure injectedObservable acceptance result
Lost grant response, broker restart, same request retriedOne committed grant and one receipt for the request.
Two processes use one display name, first process resumes after transferA late heartbeat or completion leaves the new grant and checkpoint intact.
Final dependency resolves twice while work is parked on a separate conditionOne dependency transition. Independent condition remains active.
Previously completed issue re-enters via a new packet keyRecorded disposition and intentional revival policy decide eligibility.

At the inspected source revision, a normal lease starts at 45 minutes while agent next uses four hours for work that can last hours without automatic renewal. The default heartbeat computes an absolute deadline 15 minutes from receipt. At minute five this can shorten a four-hour grant by 220 minutes. A proposed normal-renewal rule preserves the later of the existing deadline and the permitted new deadline. Collect heartbeat gaps, abandoned-grant recovery, false reclaims and write cost before changing the defaults. Introduce epoch-aware callers alongside old seats and enforce fencing after outstanding old grants drain. Intake rationale · Lifecycle

Measure the claim path first on disposable data with a production-shaped status distribution at current and tenfold row counts. Exercise 1, 8, 16 and 32 lanes against one contested row and independent rows. Repeat five seeded trials per cell. Report sample counts, grants per second, eligibility-to-grant p50/p95/p99, lost compare-and-set retries, contention-budget exhaustion, genuine empty responses, store reads/writes and duplicate wake collapse. Measure caller-to-broker and broker-to-commit latency separately. Tailnet and managed failover claims require observations on the corresponding route. Record verified included usage headroom before a managed-volume test. The November acceptance receipts do not contain these measurements; current managed claim throughput, tailnet latency and tenfold capacity remain unmeasured in this record.

Proposed placement and cross-seat visibility

Placement already computes a dry-run decision and reasoning. Extend that same function with the registry and policy revision, observation ages, capacity exclusions, cache history, billing owner, reservation and tie-break. First enforce repo visibility, runner class, included billing eligibility and platform. Count each macOS slot against both the macOS sublimit and its parent capacity. Reconcile local reservations with provider jobs by dispatch ID so a job consumes a slot once. Keep the public-only fork boundary. Among eligible options, estimate completion time by target repo, command class, platform and image. Distinguish assignment lag, provider job queueing, execution and preparation failures. Prefer a sticky follow-up when its cache savings exceed the additional wait. The three workflow-level timestamps alone cannot identify the first runnable job. Placement implementation · Known accounting gaps

A November 23 REST sample of the most recent 100 fleet-command runs from each of the three runner repositories found identical creation and start timestamps, to the second, in all 300 records. Across their different windows the pages contained 83 successes, 210 failures, two cancellations and five active runs. Those counts mix infrastructure and workload outcomes. The timestamps cannot measure assignment lag. Use per-job events and workload classes to evaluate a routing change. Organization runs · Fork organization runs · Upstream runs

Retain the immutable request ID across an ambiguous dispatch. Persist provider run and attempt when available. An older API that acknowledges submission without the run ID needs exact correlation against the submitted ID before retry. For a single provider attempt, a delayed nonterminal observation must never erase a terminal one. A genuine rerun is a new attempt. Authorize cross-seat summaries by repo and authenticated installation, with separate checks for command details, logs and artifacts. Propose a 60-second freshness target for active runs and measure it under broker and provider degradation. Use a third seat with an empty cache to test late updates, tie timestamps, denied grants and reruns. Session storage

Routine dispatch uses plan-covered GitHub-hosted capacity. For an eligible Blacksmith exception, predeclare the work class, expected benefit, bounded runtime and verified included balance. A missing billing reading cannot authorize spend. Verify explicit Codespace selection on an already-running authorized instance via both Fleet shell and GitHub CLI SSH. A queued Codespace placement separately needs its own selection, liveness, cap, core-hour reservation and result receipts. Resolve the existing credential-scope decision before claiming support across seats. Scope decision

Reuse a completed result only for deterministic commands keyed to the target tree, command, workflow, image, platform, toolchain, dependencies, test inputs and oracle revision. Verify artifact ID, digest, expiry, producer and reader scope. A runner repo’s head SHA may identify a different repository from the checkout under test. Preserve both identities. For other work, reuse approved dependency caches and execute the command. Roll out learned ordering in shadow against the current decision function, score predicted completion against matched runs, then enable one eligible command class with a single rollback switch.

Seat identity, credential readiness and channel recovery

A seat can be reachable through the bridge, unable to reach the queue, and intentionally lack credential access. An operator deciding whether to assign work needs those three facts separately. This design makes the broker responsible for authorization and gives the operator a probe and a recovery owner for each dependency.

Enrolment and work ownership

The front-door design describes one intake path across kinds. Its four probes cover bridge, queue, GitHub and shell. The intake order is pushed work, queue, shortlist or refill, then priority. A claimed task can carry platform, lane, pool or model requirements. First-claim registration makes a new lane available without reserving its name in advance. Generic installation paths and bootstrap token provisioning have separate acceptance evidence. Testing one entry point cannot establish what a new installation of each supported kind receives.

Registry proposal. Use an authenticated installation ID as the seat record. Store its verified principal, kind, capability results and timestamps, repo and operation grants, policy revision and last-seen at the broker. Keep the human-facing name mutable. Bind independently verified machine IDs where available. The machine registry already owns node capacity and watchdog-observed health. A machine can run several seats. A shared service credential proves possession of that service credential alone. Preserve unverified historical identities as reported until each installation presents a verifiable enrolment receipt. Keep reported and independently verified source revisions separate.

A new kind proves the same four operations through its supported entry point. Add a metadata-only credential capability challenge where the work requires it. A seat designed for credential-free work can enrol without that grant. Enforce the required capability in the broker for direct claims, intake claims, dispatch and reads. A retry for an existing installation must return its original binding. A different installation using the same display name must receive a different ID. Exercise simultaneous registration, revocation during a lease and reinstall after a stale alias. First-claim lane registration still works. Throttle excessive new aliases per authenticated principal and recover stale ownership only after checking outstanding leases and pending transfers. An operating target for the number of busy lanes belongs in capacity planning.

Shortlist experiment. The local shortlist’s eight entries and low-water mark of three are a baseline. Record task revision and queue watermark when a candidate is handed out. Distinguish an already-dispositioned task at handout, an eligible task lost to another lane before claim, and a successful claim. Compare claims per 100 handouts, refill reads and writes, time to first successful claim, and replacement/restart behavior for host-local and seat-shared variants. Replay one time-ordered stream under both policies. Measure per rung and queue size before changing defaults. Intake tracker

Task handoff proposal. Carry immutable work identity, checkpoint digest, outstanding verification, lease epoch, sender and intended recipient. Use a broker-clock 15-minute deadline. Commit one transfer and its receipt under the original grant. Same recipient and request ID can recover the receipt after a lost response. Wrong recipient, stale epoch, altered checkpoint or late first redemption leaves the old grant unchanged. The bridge can notify the recipient while the queue retains authority over redemption. Keep worker-assigned batches. For conversation threading add an explicit parent message, retry-stable send ID, and per-recipient delivery and acknowledgment cursors. Test a replayed acknowledgment and a missing message before claiming ordered delivery. Checkpoint design · Lifecycle receipts · Delivery capability

Credential distribution and refresh

Readiness has four dimensions: process reachability, refresh activity, initial inventory readiness, and the authority and freshness of a requested entry. At the inspected November 23 handler revision, public health omits detailed refresh errors. An authorized item read during initial loading can include a diagnostic. An accepted refresh request returns HTTP 202, including when its worker skips overlapping work. Observe the sweep and the requested item before declaring a rotation complete. Handler and tests · Incident and owner

Bind every distributed credential file to immutable provider item and project IDs, owning service, intended principal, audience and required seat capability. Distinguish daemon credentials from client credentials at lookup. Ambiguous aliases fail before any file is created. Install atomically under the intended owner and private mode. Audit the protected local recovery copy by version, permission and a scoped restore canary. Return a verdict without logging values or reusable fingerprints. The transport chain may recover from a connection failure using a route with equivalent authority. A denial or expired grant terminates the lookup across transports.

Event or classProposed behaviorIndependent oracle
Privileged or one-time capabilityBound by audience, expiry, revocation and class-specific maximum ageA revoked synthetic credential fails at the consuming service on every transport.
Explicitly offline-eligible credentialRetain its last successful observation and bounded ageA fixed clock one tick beyond the allowed age produces a precise stale verdict.
One failed item fetchRetain the old revision and observation ageOther entries update and the failed item never becomes artificially fresh.
Complete, authoritative list omits an itemReconcile removal after inventory completionAn interrupted or malformed paginated list preserves prior entries.

The per-item refresh change already distinguishes ages, partial results and authoritative delisting. Evaluate cost before selecting a new TTL. A list-plus-one-get-per-entry design makes 222 provider calls at 221 items and 2,211 at 2,210 items, before retries. Confirm the installed CLI’s list contents, revision semantics, privacy and pagination using a synthetic project. Compare full list-only, changed-revision fetch plus periodic full reconciliation, and current behavior at 0%, 1% and 100% churn. Measure list time, fetch makespan, bytes, process starts, throttling, memory and rotation-to-availability latency. Reject stale results from superseded sweeps and distinguish a completed attempt from a successful fetch.

Recovery authority and rollout

LegLocal observationRecovery owner
TailnetDaemon state and intended peer reachabilityHost service manager restores a failed local daemon. A peer outage stays attributed to that route.
RelayListener and authenticated upstream round tripRelay reconnects with bounded backoff after transport recovery.
Session brokerFramed challenge via the normal relay pathBroker supervisor repairs its listener or diagnoses negotiation failure.
Secrets brokerRefresh stage, age of last success, scoped synthetic readThe refresh worker owns bounded upstream timeout and retry. A reachable, refreshing process stays running.
GitHubAuthorized read of the intended repoCredential owner handles denial. Rate-limited requests back off using provider evidence.

Size cold readiness gates from measured list time, fetch batches, installation, allowed retries and probe delay. A user-facing rollout timeout should preserve the previous usable generation. It must not repeatedly kill a cold refresh before the inventory becomes usable. Preflight an isolated listener, serialize heal and deployment per service, and journal activation intent before changing the registry pointer. Verify the running executable, generation directory, listener and authenticated client. On interrupted activation, reconcile the pointer with the durable journal and restore the previous working closure when the candidate fails. Use the registry deployment path for the real cutover.

For the deliberately deferred secrets-broker cutover, first read the active generation and build revision at the registry. Retain the known-working generation throughout an isolated cold rehearsal. Set the deployment window from that rehearsal and its measured retry allowance. Require an authorized synthetic read and complete inventory before promotion. Observe at least a second successful refresh across a heal tick after the flip, with a recorded operator and rollback target. Until those receipts exist, the proposed cutover remains open. Health-gate tracker

Qualify recovery on a disposable instance with independent control. Pause listing and then a second fetch across two heal ticks. Require a stable process, eventual completed refresh and readable synthetic entry. Restore a broken executable candidate with its executable bit set and a missing interpreter. Require the resolver to select the next candidate that actually passes its version probe, then recycle the full restored prelude. Bring up all five legs from cold and rerun the drill against the healthy stack. The second run should cause zero restarts. A warm health check leaves cold recovery open. Resolver regression · Restore acceptance

November 23, 2026 readback

An AMD operator can reconcile three separate facts: the executable accepting requests, the deploying registry’s record and the state returned by a normal client. During this readback the local Fleet CLI reported 22ec90b9c29d. The queue service still served the earlier release. This was a read-only observation.

Reconciliation of the 37 repairs

The 15:25 UTC operator receipt names 37 distinct tasks. Use the configured client credential without printing it. The CLI’s show and timeline implementations at the inspected source enumerate particular event kinds and omit repaired. A missing line in either display is therefore insufficient evidence of a missing stored event. Compare release capabilities and error responses before extrapolating to other deployments.
